scenarios.math: Dynamic takes the amount from each EVENT rather than from the charge, summing precise_total_amount_cents: 1_000 + 2_000 + 3_000 = 6_000¢. Units still come from the metric (sum_agg → 60), so units and amount are decoupled here in a way no other charge model does — that decoupling is the point of the row. The charge carries no properties at all.

Three events read on 20 March. Units come from the metric: sum_agg 10 + 30 + 20 = 60. The amount comes from the EVENTS: precise_total_amount_cents is summed on the events table (sum_service.rb:82-84 → postgres_store.rb:264-266) and divided by subunit_to_unit (charge_models/dynamic_service.rb:7-14) → (700 + 1_100 + 1_300) / 100 = 31.00 → 3_100¢. The three amounts are deliberately NOT proportional to their units — 70.0¢, 36.67¢ and 65.0¢ per unit — so no single per-unit price reproduces the total: an implementation that read one fixed price off the charge (which has no properties) or extrapolated the first event's rate over 60 units would report 4_200¢, not 3_100¢. This is the cell that proves dynamic reads per-event pricing rather than a cumulative delta at one rate. Contrast the green b01/dynamic/sum_agg/arrears/invoice, whose 1_000/2_000/3_000 ARE proportional to 10/20/30 and so cannot make that distinction.

NO events, read on 20 March. sum_agg gives 0 units and DynamicService#compute_amount returns 0 before touching precise_total_amount_cents (charge_models/dynamic_service.rb:7-9), so 0¢. charge_model dynamic is asserted on the usage entry itself (customers/charge_usage_serializer.rb:67) rather than only declared in axes, so the row proves which model produced the zero. The two surfaces disagree on PRESENCE, not on value. Fees::ChargeService returns before the reject! that drops zero fees (fees/charge_service.rb:63-68 — `return result if current_usage` precedes it), and the empty default bucket makes init_charge_fees hydrate a zero-units fee in memory instead (charge_service.rb:112-123 with 185-197). So current usage REPORTS the charge at units 0.0 / 0¢ while the paired invoice cell omits the fee entirely (fees_count 1). Both surfaces agree the amount is 0¢; only the fee's existence differs. usage.amount_cents is fees_amount_cents — charges only, never the subscription fee (invoices/customer_usage_service.rb:257-266).

One event, read on 20 March: units 40 from sum_agg, amount 1_234¢ read off the event's precise_total_amount_cents (charge_models/dynamic_service.rb:7-14). Same number as b01/dynamic/sum_agg/invoice/one — the usage path calls the identical charge model through Fees::ChargeService, so a divergence would mean the two surfaces disagree about where the price comes from. 1_234¢ over 40 units is 30.85¢/unit, which no charge property could supply (the dynamic charge has none), so a fallback to charge-based pricing cannot pass this row.

NO events. sum_agg gives 0 units, and DynamicService#compute_amount returns 0 the moment total_units is zero (charge_models/dynamic_service.rb:7-9) — it never reaches precise_total_amount_cents at all, so there is nothing for the event-priced model to read. Zero units, zero amount, zero events. `should_persist_fee?` (fees/charge_service.rb:353-360) then DROPS that fee: perform_billing runs with context :finalize (invoices/subscription_service.rb:41-45), never :recurring, and there is no adjusted fee and no true-up, so the units == 0 && amount_cents == 0 && events_count == 0 fee fails every clause. Only the subscription fee lands: fees_count 1, 1_000¢. The plan amount is deliberately NON-zero here, against this file's amount_cents-0 convention: with a 0 plan the invoice would be 0¢ everywhere and the row could not tell 'charge fee dropped' from 'charge fee present at 0¢'. An implementation that persisted the zero fee reports the same 1_000¢ total with fees_count 2 — which is why fees_count carries this row. Contrast b01/graduated/sum_agg/arrears/invoice/no-events, where tier 1's flat_amount makes the zero-usage fee non-zero and it DOES persist.

Dynamic takes its amount from the EVENT, not from the charge: amount = aggregation_result.precise_total_amount_cents / subunit_to_unit (charge_models/dynamic_service.rb:7-14), and precise_total_amount_cents is summed straight off the events table (sum_service.rb:82-84 → postgres_store.rb:264-266). One event, units 40 from sum_agg, precise_total_amount_cents 1_234 → 12.34 → 1_234¢. 1_234 is deliberately not a whole multiple of 40 units: 30.85¢ per unit cannot be produced by any per-unit price the charge could carry, and the charge carries no properties at all, so an implementation that priced from charge properties instead of the event cannot land here. Units and amount are decoupled — units 40.0 with 1_234¢. Same number expected from b01/dynamic/sum_agg/current_usage/one.

Three events carrying 10, 30, 20. count_agg counts events and never reads a field, so the period aggregates to 3 units. Banded pricing then walks the tiers and ADDS them (charge_models/graduated_service.rb:28-34 walking amount_details (:11-18) with per-range widths from range_graduated_service.rb:54-65): t1 (0–2) prices 2 units → flat 100.00 + 2 × 2.00 = 104.00; t2 (3–25) prices 1 units → flat 50.00 + 1 × 1.00 = 51.00. Total 155.00 → 15_500¢. Tier set B puts the first boundary at 2 units on purpose: with the file's 10/30/20 event set, count_agg yields 3 and unique_count_agg 4, and against the 0–10 tier of set A those would never leave tier 1 — a graduated row whose units all sit in one tier tests nothing graduated. Wrong implementations this row catches: pricing ALL 3 units at the reached tier's rate — volume rather than graduated — gives 5_300¢; summing the flat_amounts of the 1 tier never reached gives 17_500¢. usage.amount_cents is fees_amount_cents — charges only, never the subscription fee (invoices/customer_usage_service.rb:255-266), which is why the plan amount does not appear here. The paired invoice cell for the same aggregation and event set must report the same 15_500¢ charge fee: two different computations of one number, not two numbers. The 10/30/20 values are chosen so every candidate answer is distinct: sum_agg would report 60 units (21_450¢), max_agg would report 30 units (19_950¢), latest_agg would report 20 units (17_200¢).

Graduated percentage applies a rate per tier, like graduated but proportional. 60 units: tier 1 covers 25 units → flat 1.00 + 10% of 25 = 1.00 + 2.50 = 3.50; tier 2 covers the remaining 35 → flat 2.00 + 20% of 35 = 2.00 + 7.00 = 9.00. Total 12.50 → 1_250¢. Requires `premium: true` — the charge model is licence-gated.

(fees/charge_service.rb:353-360) then DROPS the charge fee: perform_billing runs with context :finalize, never :recurring, there is no adjusted fee and no true-up, and units == 0 && amount_cents == 0 && events_count == 0 fails every clause. Its current-usage twin REPORTS the charge at units 0.0 / 0¢, so that pair legitimately DISAGREES on the fee's existence while agreeing on 0¢. (fees/charge_service.rb:353-360) keeps it on the first clause and the invoice carries fees_count 2. Plan amount 0¢ → total 350¢, no tax configured. weighted_sum_agg time-weights each value by how long it was held: units = value × held_duration / period_duration. A value of 62 arriving on 16 March is held for the remaining 16 days of a 31-day March → 62 × 16/31 = 32 units → 3_200¢. The value and date are chosen so the fraction lands on a whole number AND so the row is DISCRIMINATING: sum_agg, max_agg and latest_agg would all report 62 units here. An earlier version of this row put its single event at the exact period start, making the weighting 1 and the answer 60 — identical to what three other aggregations would produce, so it asserted a number without testing the time-weighting it claimed to cover. calendar_sensitive because the weighting divides by the length of this specific month.

The same three deltas as b01/standard/weighted_sum_agg/invoice/many — 10 on 03-06, 30 on 03-10, 20 on 03-16 — read as usage on 20 March. The upper bound is the same on both surfaces: for current usage charges_to_datetime is still the end of the period in progress (subscriptions/dates/monthly_service.rb:26-28), raised to 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z by to_datetime.ceil (postgres_store.rb:358), so the last delta is weighted over 16 days of which 11 have not happened yet at the moment of the read. The invoice cell and this one must therefore report the SAME 4_000¢ — they are two computations of one number, not two numbers. sum would give 60 units (6_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢), latest 20 (2_000¢). calendar_sensitive because the divisor is the length of this March.

The zero fee is then dropped by filter_non_persistable_fees_for_caching (charge_service.rb:251-256, which DOES apply on the usage path) and immediately re-hydrated by init_charge_fees (charge_service.rb:121-123, 185-197) — so it is reported, at 0.0 units and 0¢, exactly as for the non-recurring aggregations. So current usage REPORTS the charge at units 0.0 / 0¢ while the paired invoice cell omits the fee entirely (fees_count 1). Both surfaces agree the amount is 0¢; only the fee's existence differs. usage.amount_cents is fees_amount_cents — charges only, never the subscription fee (invoices/customer_usage_service.rb:257-266).

One event of 62 on 16 March, usage read on 20 March → 32.0 units → 3_200¢, the SAME number the already-green b01/standard/weighted_sum_agg/arrears/invoice asserts on the invoice surface for the same event. Deriving it once explains why: current usage does NOT stop the weighting at 'now'. The aggregation window is the charge boundaries of the period in progress — charges_to_datetime is compute_charges_from_date.end_of_month (subscriptions/dates/monthly_service.rb:26-28) even when billing_at is the 20th — and WeightedSumQuery projects the last held value out to that upper bound, so 62 is weighted over 03-16→04-01 = 16 of 31 days: 62 × 16 / 31 = 32. Eleven of those sixteen days are in the FUTURE relative to the read. That is not a rounding artefact of this row; it is the behaviour spec/scenarios/current_usage/by_aggregation_type/weighted_sum_agg_spec.rb already pins (2500 read on the day of ingestion reports 2500 × 27/31 = 2177.42, and the invoice a month later reports the identical 217_742¢). Three events, and the FIRST weighted_sum cell in the suite with more than one. weighted_sum treats each event value as a DELTA and time-weights the running total: units = Σ(cumulative_value × seconds_until_next_event) / charges_duration_in_seconds (events/stores/postgres/weighted_sum_query.rb:99-116; the denominator is charges_duration.days.to_i = 31 days). Boundaries for the March period are charges_from 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z and charges_to 2024-03-31T23:59:59.999999Z, and the query raises the upper bound with to_datetime.ceil (postgres_store.rb:358), i.e. 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z. Segments: 03-01→03-06 at cumulative 0 contributes nothing; 03-06→03-10 is 4 days at 10 → 40 day-units; 03-10→03-16 is 6 days at 40 → 240; 03-16→04-01 is 16 days at 60 → 960. Total 1_240 / 31 = 40.0 units exactly → 40 × 1.00 = 4_000¢. The dates and values are picked so all four candidate answers are DISTINCT: sum_agg would give 60 units (6_000¢), max_agg 30 (3_000¢), latest_agg 20 (2_000¢), weighted_sum 40 (4_000¢). No other B1 row pins the deltas-and-duration shape — b01/standard/weighted_sum_agg/arrears/invoice has one event, where the cumulative sum cannot be told from the value. calendar_sensitive because the divisor is the length of THIS month; runners is [rspec] only for the same reason (a live shift changes 31). The paired b01/standard/weighted_sum_agg/current_usage/many must produce this same 4_000¢.

NO events, and unlike the other zero-usage cells the aggregation is not short-circuited: the metric is recurring, and charge_service.rb:141-147 exempts recurring metrics from the unused-bucket skip because usage carries over between periods. WeightedSumQuery therefore runs, and its events_data CTE holds only the two synthetic rows — (from_datetime, 0) and (to_datetime, 0) (events/stores/postgres/weighted_sum_query.rb:82-97). The cumulative sum is 0 on the first and the LEAD duration is 0 on the second, so both period_ratios are 0 (same file, 99-116) and the aggregation is 0 units → 0 × 1.00 = 0¢. `should_persist_fee?` (fees/charge_service.rb:353-360) then DROPS that fee: perform_billing runs with context :finalize (invoices/subscription_service.rb:41-45), never :recurring, and there is no adjusted fee and no true-up, so the units == 0 && amount_cents == 0 && events_count == 0 fee fails every clause. Only the subscription fee lands: fees_count 1, 1_000¢. The plan amount is deliberately NON-zero here, against this file's amount_cents-0 convention: with a 0 plan the invoice would be 0¢ everywhere and the row could not tell 'charge fee dropped' from 'charge fee present at 0¢'. An implementation that persisted the zero fee reports the same 1_000¢ total with fees_count 2 — which is why fees_count carries this row. Volume set B is byte-for-byte the tier set the sibling `graduated` rows of this file use, on purpose: every counterfactual above is then a number an existing green row already asserts rather than a fresh derivation. The fee is non-zero, so should_persist_fee? (fees/charge_service.rb:353-360) keeps it on the first clause and the invoice carries fees_count 2. Plan amount 0¢ → total 3_600¢, no tax configured. With ONE event sum_agg, max_agg and latest_agg all report the same units, so this cell cannot tell them apart — that IS the cell, and its value is as the degenerate partner of the `many` row for the same aggregation, where they diverge.

Anniversary monthly starting Jan 31: February has no 31st, so Subscriptions::DatesService#build_date clamps and the period runs Jan 31 00:00:00 → Feb 28 23:59:59, with the next period starting Feb 29 (boundaries cross-checked against spec/scenarios/subscriptions/billing_boundaries_spec.rb:57-58, which asserts exactly these two datetimes on invoice_subscription). The subscription fee period starts at midnight even though the subscription was created at 01:00 — only charges_from_datetime carries the creation time. A whole period bills the full plan amount, unprorated → 2_900¢.

An anniversary monthly subscription bills on its own day of the month (organization_billing_service.rb:274-285), so one created 2024-03-15 bills 2024-04-15. The period is whole by construction: base_date = billing_date - 1.month = 2024-03-15 (monthly_service.rb:48-60), previous_anniversary_day returns 2024-03-15 (:109-130), and compute_to_date takes the day BEFORE the next anniversary — month + 1, day subscription_at.day - 1 = 2024-04-14 (:62-81). So from_datetime .. to_datetime is 2024-03-15T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-14T23:59:59Z and compute_duration is 2024-04-15 - 2024-03-15 = 31 days (:35-39) — a period that crosses a month boundary and is priced on its OWN length, not on either calendar month. A 10-day trial ends 2024-03-25. first_subscription_amount:162-170 moves its local from_datetime to initial_started_at + 10.days = 2024-03-25T00:00:00Z and bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-25T00:00, 2024-04-14T23:59:59) = 21 days x 100_000/31 = 67_741.935…¢ → 67_742¢. The fee still records the full period as its from_date/to_date, because the fee is built from the invoice_subscription's boundaries (calculate_fees_service.rb:30-38), not from the trial-shifted local variable. What a wrong boundary gives. Dividing by MARCH's 31 days happens to coincide here, which is why the row's discriminating denominators are the wrong ones: April's 30 days gives 70_000¢, and the 30 days from 2024-03-15 to 2024-04-13 (a compute_to_date that used subscription_at.day rather than day - 1, closing the period on the next anniversary itself and overlapping it) gives 21 x 100_000/30 = 70_000¢ over a window one day too long. A trial appended rather than subtracted bills 100_000¢; a trial counted from the following midnight bills 20 days = 64_516¢.

Continues b02/monthly/anniversary/first-full-period/jan31-into-leap-february into its SECOND period, which is where the clamping gets interesting: does a month too short for the 31st drag the following periods with it? Period 1 is 2024-01-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-02-28T23:59:59Z (29 days, billed 29 x 100_000/29 = 100_000¢). Period 2 is billed on 2024-03-31 — reached because monthly_anniversary treats the last day of a short month as standing in for every later day of the month (organization_billing_service.rb:274-285). base_date is 2024-03-31 - 1.month = 2024-02-29, since the last-day-of-month branch at monthly_service.rb:51-57 does not fire (2024-03-31's day is not less than the anniversary day 31). previous_anniversary_day(2024-02-29) then returns 2024-02-29 itself: 2024-02-29 IS the last day of its month and its day (29) is below the anniversary day (31), so the special case at :115-116 uses the date's own day rather than 31. compute_to_date (:62-81) takes month + 1 and day 30, build_date gives 2024-03-30, and 2024-03-30 is not its month's last day, so no further subtraction: period 2 is 2024-02-29T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-30T23:59:59Z, 31 days, and the anniversary re-anchors to the 31st for the period that opens on 2024-03-31. The amount is plan.amount_cents outright — should_use_full_amount? line 147 sees period 1's fee (fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156, :247-273) — so both invoices read 100_000¢ and this row's entire content is the two windows. What a wrong boundary gives. If the February clamp dragged forward, previous_anniversary_day would return 2024-01-31 and period 2 would be 2024-01-31 .. 2024-02-28 — the window period 1 already used, which CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 refuses as duplicated_invoices, so the run would show ONE invoice instead of two. A compute_to_date that returned 2024-03-31 instead of 2024-03-30 would overlap the next period by a day and leave 2024-03-31 billed twice.

The sharpest arithmetic in the monthly family, because the DENOMINATOR is neither 30 nor 31. Terminating on 2024-02-15 sends compute_from_date down the terminated_pay_in_arrears? branch (dates_service.rb:273-277, monthly_service.rb:7-9): previous_anniversary_day(2024-02-15) is not a last-day-of-month case, so it uses the anniversary day 31, sees 15 < 31 and walks back to build_date(2024, 1, 31) = 2024-01-31 (:109-130). to_datetime would be 2024-02-28T23:59:59Z — compute_to_date builds 2024-02-30, build_date clamps it to 2024-02-29, and :78 subtracts a further day because 2024-02-29 is the month's last day and the anniversary day 31 is above it — and dates_service.rb:87-89 then clamps down to terminated_at, giving 2024-01-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-02-15T10:00:00Z. terminated_amount bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-01-31T00:00, 2024-02-15T10:00) = 16 days against compute_duration for the period that HOLDS 2024-01-31, which is 2024-01-31 .. 2024-02-28 = 29 days (monthly_service.rb:35-39). 16 x 100_000/29 = 55_172.413…¢ → 55_172¢. What a wrong boundary gives, and this is the whole point of the row: the naive denominators are all wrong and all plausible. 31 days (January's length) gives 51_613¢; 30 gives 53_333¢; 28 (forgetting the leap day) gives 57_143¢. Dropping the -1.day at monthly_service.rb:78 makes the period 2024-01-31 .. 2024-02-29 and the duration 30, giving 53_333¢. Excluding the termination day bills 15 days = 51_724¢. Only 16/29 reaches 55_172¢.

The control for the row above: same plan, same billing day, subscription created ON the calendar boundary. compute_from_date already returns 2024-03-01 (monthly_service.rb:6-12) and the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 only pulls the time of day back to midnight, so the period is 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z. This still goes through the prorating branch — should_use_full_amount? is false on all four of its conditions (fees/subscription_service.rb :141-156) because the plan is in arrears, no earlier subscription fee exists and the subscription did not start in the past — so the 100_000¢ is 31 x 100_000/31 rather than a short-circuit to plan.amount_cents. What a wrong boundary gives. A period read as 2024-03-01 .. 2024-03-30 bills 30/31 = 96_774¢; one read as 2024-02-29 .. 2024-03-31 bills 32/31 = 103_226¢. Both are only visible because the row asserts the two dates beside the amount: 100_000¢ alone is also what any implementation that gave up and returned plan.amount_cents would print.

A calendar monthly subscription bills on the 1st (organization_billing_service.rb:157-164), so one created on 2024-03-16 first bills on 2024-04-01. base_date = billing_date - 1.month = 2024-03-01 (monthly_service.rb:48-60) and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_month = 2024-03-01 (:6-12); dates_service.rb:73-75 clamps it up to the subscription's start, giving from_datetime 2024-03-16T00:00:00Z at MIDNIGHT rather than the 10:00 creation instant. compute_to_date runs on the UNCLAMPED from_date (monthly_service.rb:62-63: calendar, so end_of_month), so the period closes on 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z. compute_duration is measured from the beginning of the period holding from_date, not from from_date itself (monthly_service.rb:35-39), which is why the denominator is March's 31 days and not the 16 billed: first_subscription_amount bills 16 x 100_000/31 = 51_612.903…¢ → 51_613¢. March is deliberate. What a wrong boundary gives, and each wrong answer is a different number: dividing by the 16 days billed gives 100_000¢; dividing by APRIL's 30 days (the month being billed IN rather than the month billed FOR) gives 16 x 3_333.33 = 53_333¢; taking the duration from base_date - 1.month (February's 29) gives 55_172¢; and skipping the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 bills all 31 days = 100_000¢. Only the pairing of a 31-day denominator with a 16-day numerator lands on 51_613¢.

A partial March followed by a whole April, on one subscription, so the row pins the transition rather than either end of it. March bills 16/31 = 51_613¢ as in the partial row. On 2024-05-01, base_date = 2024-04-01, compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_month = 2024-04-01 (monthly_service.rb:6-12, :48-60), the clamp at dates_service.rb:73 does not fire because 2024-04-01T00:00 is after started_at (2024-03-16T10:00), and the period is 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z. should_use_full_amount? line 147 finds the March fee created before this invoice, so full_period_amount returns plan.amount_cents = 100_000¢ (fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273) with no division — the 30-day April is billed the same 100_000¢ as a 31-day March, which is the behaviour: a full period is a full period regardless of its length. What a wrong boundary gives. April prorated as if it were still a first period would bill 30 x 100_000/30 = 100_000¢ too, so the amount cannot separate the two; the from_date is what does. A second period still clamped to started_at would report 2024-03-16T00:00:00Z as its from_date over an April window. And a base_date that walked back only to 2024-04-30 rather than a month would resolve the period to April as well, but a base_date left on 2024-03-01 would reproduce the March window, which InvoiceSubscription.matching? already holds and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse — one invoice, not two.

The exact mirror of b02/monthly/calendar/first-partial-period: 16 days of the same 31-day March for the same 51_613¢, counted from the other end. That symmetry is the assertion — proration on the way in and proration on the way out are computed by different methods, and if either were off by a day the two rows would disagree. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) makes compute_from_date take billing_date.beginning_of_month = 2024-03-01 (monthly_service.rb:7-9); to_datetime would be 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it down to terminated_at, giving 2024-03-16T10:00:00Z — again a to_datetime that is not an end of day. CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:113-127 keeps these boundaries rather than rebuilding the period, because the termination instant precedes the period's charges_to_datetime (:125). terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-01T00:00, 2024-03-16T10:00) = 16 days — the termination DAY is billed — and divides by compute_duration measured over the whole of March, 31 days (monthly_service.rb:35-39, reached through single_day_price's optional_from_date at subscription_service.rb:209-213). 16 x 100_000/31 = 51_612.903…¢ → 51_613¢. What a wrong boundary gives. The ADVANCE convention — treat the termination day as unused and credit FROM it — bills 15 days = 48_387¢, which is the off-by-one this block exists to catch. Leaving to_datetime at end of month bills 100_000¢. Dividing by the 16 days billed gives 100_000¢. Dividing by April's 30 days gives 53_333¢.

The trial row's control: the same three months with nothing subtracted from them. The period is 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-14T23:59:59Z — previous_anniversary_day(2024-02-15) returns the date itself (quarterly_service.rb:96-122) and compute_to_date is the day before 2024-02-15 >> 3 = 2024-05-15 (:62-80) — and compute_duration is 90 days (:37-41), so 90 x 100_000/90 = 100_000¢ through the prorating branch, not through a short-circuit (should_use_full_amount? is false on all four conditions, fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156). What a wrong boundary gives. This anniversary quarter is 90 days while every 2024 calendar quarter is 91 or 92, so a period closing on 2024-05-15 instead of 2024-05-14 bills 91/90 = 101_111¢, and one closing on 2024-05-13 bills 89/90 = 98_889¢. A CALENDAR reading puts the period on 2024-04-01 .. 2024-06-30 and also bills 100_000¢, over a window that has not finished — invisible in the total, caught by the dates.

An anniversary quarterly subscription bills on its own day, in its own month and every third month after it (organization_billing_service.rb:295-331), so 2024-02-15 bills on 2024-05-15, 2024-08-15 and 2024-11-15. The period is whole by construction, which is why the trial is here: base_date = billing_date - 3.months = 2024-02-15, previous_anniversary_day resolves it to 2024-02-15 (quarterly_service.rb:96-122 — February IS one of the four billing months and the date's day is not below the anniversary day), and compute_to_date takes the day before the next anniversary: from_date >> 3 = 2024-05-15, minus a day = 2024-05-14 (:62-80). So the period is 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-14T23:59:59Z and compute_duration is 2024-05-15 - 2024-02-15 = 90 days (:37-41). A 20-day trial ends 2024-03-06. first_subscription_amount:162-170 moves its local from_datetime to 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z and bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-06T00:00, 2024-05-14T23:59:59) = 70 days x 100_000/90 = 77_777.777…¢ → 77_778¢, while the fee still carries the whole period as its from_date/to_date (calculate_fees_service.rb:30-38). What a wrong boundary gives. 90 is the length of THIS quarter, not of a calendar quarter: using Q1's 91 days gives 76_923¢, using 92 gives 76_087¢. A compute_to_date that closed the period on the next anniversary itself (2024-05-15, without the -1.day at :67) makes the duration 91 and the days 71, giving 78_022¢ over a window that overlaps the next period. A trial appended rather than subtracted bills 100_000¢.

A 31st-of-the-month anniversary on a quarterly plan, followed across the month that has no 31st. The question the row answers is whether the clamp is remembered — whether April dragging the anniversary to the 30th keeps it there. Period 1: billing on 2024-04-30 (organization_billing_service.rb:295-331 treats the last day of a short month as standing in for the 31st). base_date takes the last-day branch at quarterly_service.rb:51-57 — 2024-04-30 is its month's last day and its day 30 is below the anniversary day 31 — and returns (2024-04-30 - 3.months).end_of_month.change(day: 31) = 2024-01-31. previous_anniversary_day(2024-01-31) = 2024-01-31 (:96-122), and compute_to_date is next_anniversary - 1.day where next_anniversary clamps through anniversary_day_in: 2024-01-31 >> 3 = 2024-04-30, day min(31, 30) = 30, so 2024-04-30 - 1 = 2024-04-29 (:62-80, dates_service.rb:307-309). Period 1 = 2024-01-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-29T23:59:59Z, 90 days, billed 90 x 100_000/90 = 100_000¢. Period 2: billing on 2024-07-31. base_date is 2024-07-31 - 3.months = 2024-04-30 (the last-day branch does not fire — 2024-07-31's day is not below 31). previous_anniversary_day(2024-04-30) resolves to 2024-04-30 via anniversary_day_in(2024, 4) = min(31, 30) = 30, and compute_to_date(2024-04-30) takes 2024-04-30 >> 3 = 2024-07-30, clamps the day to min(31, 31) = 31 giving 2024-07-31, minus a day = 2024-07-30. Period 2 = 2024-04-30T00:00:00Z .. 2024-07-30T23:59:59Z — 92 days — and the anniversary RECOVERS to the 31st for the period opening 2024-07-31. The amount is plan.amount_cents outright (should_use_full_amount? line 147, fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273): 100_000¢ for 92 days just as for 90, so this row is entirely about the four dates. What a wrong boundary gives. An anniversary resolved from the PREVIOUS period's clamped day rather than from subscription_at would keep the 30th and close period 2 on 2024-07-29, shifting every later period by a day — and if it instead walked back to 2024-01-31, period 2 would repeat period 1's window and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse it, leaving one invoice. Dropping the -1.day at quarterly_service.rb:67 would make the periods end on the anniversaries themselves and bill 2024-04-30 and 2024-07-31 twice each.

Terminated on 2024-03-15, in a month that is NOT one of this subscription's four billing months (January, April, July, October), which is the branch this row exists for. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) sends compute_from_date to previous_anniversary_day(2024-03-15) (quarterly_service.rb:9-11). There, should_find_previous_billing_date? returns true on its FIRST check — March is not in billing_months — rather than falling through to the same-month comparison, so the month is rfind { m < 3 } = 1 and build_date(2024, 1, anniversary_day_in(2024, 1) = 31) = 2024-01-31 (:96-139). to_datetime would be 2024-04-29T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it down to terminated_at: 2024-01-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-15T10:00:00Z. terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts date_diff_with_timezone(2024-01-31T00:00, 2024-03-15T10:00) = 45 days against compute_duration for the period holding 2024-01-31, which is 2024-01-31 .. 2024-04-29 = 90 days (quarterly_service.rb:37-41). 45 x 100_000/90 = exactly 50_000¢ — half the plan, half the quarter, chosen so any off-by-one is a round-number miss. What a wrong boundary gives. Falling through to the same-month branch resolves the anniversary FORWARD to 2024-03-31 (the comment at quarterly_service.rb:131-134 is about exactly this), dates_service.rb:91 then collapses to_datetime onto started_at and the fee lands on a zero-length period. Excluding the termination day bills 44 days = 48_889¢; including one day too many bills 46 = 51_111¢. A 91-day denominator gives 49_451¢ and a 92-day one 48_913¢. Only 45/90 is 50_000¢.

The control for the row above, and the row that pins where a calendar quarter starts and ends. Created on 2024-01-01, compute_from_date already returns beginning_of_quarter (quarterly_service.rb:8-14) and the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 only lowers the time of day, so the period is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z. It is still the prorating branch — should_use_full_amount? is false on all four conditions (fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156) — so the 100_000¢ is 91 x 100_000/91. What a wrong boundary gives. A quarter closing on 2024-03-30 bills 90/91 = 98_901¢; one opening on 2023-12-31 bills 92/91 = 101_099¢. A period resolved with the MONTHLY rule (2024-01-01 .. 2024-01-31) bills 31 x 100_000/31 = 100_000¢ — the same total over a third of the time — which is why the two dates are asserted beside the amount rather than trusted to it.

A calendar quarterly subscription bills on the 1st of January, April, July and October (organization_billing_service.rb:166-181), so one created 2024-02-15 first bills 2024-04-01. base_date = billing_date - 3.months = 2024-01-01 (quarterly_service.rb:48-60) and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_quarter = 2024-01-01 (:8-14); dates_service.rb:73-75 clamps up to the subscription's start for from_datetime 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z, at midnight rather than the 10:00 creation instant. compute_to_date is taken from the unclamped from_date and, for a calendar subscription, is end_of_quarter (:62-68) — 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z. compute_duration (:37-41) measures the period holding from_date, Q1 2024 = 31 + 29 + 31 = 91 days, and first_subscription_amount bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-02-15T00:00, 2024-03-31T23:59:59) = 46 days: 46 x 100_000/91 = 50_549.450…¢ → 50_549¢. Q1 of a LEAP year is deliberate — 91 days, not 90. What a wrong boundary gives. Using 90 days (Q1 of a common year, i.e. losing the leap day) gives 51_111¢; using Q2's 91 days coincides, but using the 92 days of Q3 gives 50_000¢; dividing by the 46 days billed gives 100_000¢; taking a MONTHLY period instead (2024-02-15 .. 2024-02-29, 15 of 29 days) gives 51_724¢; and skipping the clamp bills the whole quarter, 100_000¢. Only 46/91 reaches 50_549¢.

A partial Q1 followed by a whole Q2. Q1 bills 46/91 = 50_549¢ as in the partial row. On 2024-07-01, base_date = 2024-04-01, compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_quarter = 2024-04-01 (quarterly_service.rb:8-14, :48-60), the clamp at dates_service.rb:73 does not fire because 2024-04-01T00:00 is after started_at, and the period is 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-06-30T23:59:59Z. should_use_full_amount? line 147 finds the Q1 fee and full_period_amount returns plan.amount_cents = 100_000¢ (fees/subscription_service.rb :247-273) without dividing — Q2's 91 days and Q1's 91 days both cost the plan amount, as would Q3's 92. What a wrong boundary gives. Q2 prorated as a first period is also 91/91 = 100_000¢, so the amount alone cannot tell a full period from a re-clamped one; the from_date is the assertion. A base_date that walked back one MONTH rather than three (2024-06-01.beginning_of_quarter is still 2024-04-01) is indistinguishable here, but a base_date left in Q1 would reproduce 2024-01-01 .. 2024-03-31, a window InvoiceSubscription.matching? already holds, and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse the second invoice altogether.

The mirror of b02/quarterly/calendar/first-partial-period: the same 46 days of the same 91-day Q1 for the same 50_549¢, counted from the other end of the quarter. If proration in and proration out disagreed by a day the two rows would print different numbers. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) makes compute_from_date take billing_date.beginning_of_quarter = 2024-01-01 (quarterly_service.rb:9-11); to_datetime would be 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it to terminated_at, so the period is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-02-15T10:00:00Z. CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:113-127 keeps these boundaries because the termination instant precedes the period's own charges_to_datetime (:125). terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts 46 days — the termination day included — over compute_duration 91 (quarterly_service.rb:37-41), giving 46 x 100_000/91 = 50_549.450…¢ → 50_549¢. What a wrong boundary gives. Excluding the termination day bills 45 days = 49_451¢. Not clamping to_datetime bills the whole quarter, 100_000¢. A 90-day denominator (Q1 without the leap day) gives 51_111¢, a 92-day one gives 50_000¢.

The trial row's control: the same six months with nothing subtracted. The period is 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z .. 2024-08-14T23:59:59Z — previous_anniversary_day(2024-02-15) returns the date itself (semiannual_service.rb:174-198), compute_to_date is the day before 2024-02-15 >> 6 (:140-158) — and compute_duration is 182 days (:108-112), so 182 x 100_000/182 = 100_000¢ through the prorating branch rather than a short-circuit (should_use_full_amount? false on all four conditions, fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156). What a wrong boundary gives. A period closing 2024-08-15 bills 183/182 = 100_549¢ and one closing 2024-08-13 bills 181/182 = 99_451¢. Reading the plan as calendar semiannual gives 2024-01-01 .. 2024-06-30 and the same 100_000¢ over a window that ended six weeks before the invoice — undetectable in the total, which is what the two dates are for.

An anniversary semiannual subscription bills on its own day, in its own month and six months later (organization_billing_service.rb:417-450), so 2024-02-15 bills 2024-08-15 and 2025-02-15. The period is whole by construction — which is why the trial is here: base_date = billing_date - 6.months = 2024-02-15, previous_anniversary_day resolves it to 2024-02-15 (semiannual_service.rb:174-198 — February is one of the two billing months and the date's day is not below the anniversary day), and compute_to_date is the day before 2024-02-15 >> 6 = 2024-08-15, i.e. 2024-08-14 (:140-158). Period 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z .. 2024-08-14T23:59:59Z, compute_duration 2024-08-15 - 2024-02-15 = 182 days (:108-112). A 20-day trial ends 2024-03-06; first_subscription_amount:162-170 moves its local from_datetime there and bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-06T00:00, 2024-08-14T23:59:59) = 162 days x 100_000/182 = 89_010.989…¢ → 89_011¢, while the fee still records the whole period (calculate_fees_service.rb:30-38). What a wrong boundary gives. This anniversary half happens to be 182 days like calendar H1, so the discriminating errors are elsewhere: a compute_to_date that closed on the anniversary itself (2024-08-15, dropping the -1.day at :145) makes the duration 183 and the days 163, giving 89_071¢ over an overlapping window; a trial appended rather than subtracted bills 100_000¢; a trial measured from the following midnight bills 161 days = 88_462¢. And reading this plan with the CALENDAR rule puts the period on 2024-01-01 .. 2024-06-30 and bills 2024-03-06 .. 2024-06-30 = 117 days = 64_286¢.

A 31st-of-the-month anniversary on a semiannual plan, followed across September, which has no 31st, and back again. Period 1: billed 2024-09-30 (organization_billing_service.rb:417-450 lets the last day of a short month stand in for the 31st). base_date takes the last-day branch at semiannual_service.rb :129-135 — 2024-09-30 is its month's last day and its day 30 is below the anniversary day 31 — giving (2024-09-30 - 6.months).end_of_month.change(day: 31) = 2024-03-31. previous_anniversary_day(2024-03-31) = 2024-03-31 (:174-198), and compute_to_date is next_anniversary - 1.day, where next_anniversary clamps through anniversary_day_in: 2024-03-31 >> 6 = 2024-09-30, day min(31, 30) = 30, so 2024-09-30 - 1 = 2024-09-29 (:140-158, dates_service.rb:307-309). Period 1 = 2024-03-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-09-29T23:59:59Z, 183 days, billed 183 x 100_000/183 = 100_000¢. Period 2: billed 2025-03-31. base_date is 2025-03-31 - 6.months = 2024-09-30 (the last-day branch does not fire). previous_anniversary_day(2024-09-30) resolves to 2024-09-30 via anniversary_day_in(2024, 9) = min(31, 30) = 30, and compute_to_date takes 2024-09-30 >> 6 = 2025-03-30, clamps the day to min(31, 31) = 31 giving 2025-03-31, minus a day = 2025-03-30. Period 2 = 2024-09-30T00:00:00Z .. 2025-03-30T23:59:59Z, 182 days, and the anniversary RECOVERS to the 31st for the period opening 2025-03-31. The amount is plan.amount_cents outright (should_use_full_amount? line 147, fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273), so 183 days and 182 days both cost 100_000¢ and this row is entirely about the four dates. What a wrong boundary gives. An anniversary resolved from the previous period's CLAMPED day rather than from subscription_at would keep the 30th and close period 2 on 2025-03-29, shifting every later period; one that walked back to 2024-03-31 would repeat period 1's window and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse the invoice, leaving one instead of two. Dropping the -1.day at semiannual_service.rb:145 would bill 2024-09-30 and 2025-03-31 twice each.

Terminated on 2024-06-15, in a month that is not one of this subscription's two billing months (March and September). terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) sends compute_from_date to previous_anniversary_day(2024-06-15) (semiannual_service.rb:57-59), where should_find_previous_billing_date? returns true on its first check — June is not in billing_months — so the month is rfind { m < 6 } = 3 and build_date(2024, 3, anniversary_day_in(2024, 3) = 31) = 2024-03-31 (:174-215). to_datetime would be 2024-09-29T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it to terminated_at: 2024-03-31T00:00:00Z .. 2024-06-15T10:00:00Z. terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-31T00:00, 2024-06-15T10:00) = 77 days against compute_duration for the period holding 2024-03-31, which is 2024-03-31 .. 2024-09-29 = 183 days (semiannual_service.rb:108-112). 77 x 100_000/183 = 42_076.502…¢ → 42_077¢. What a wrong boundary gives. Falling through to the same-month branch would resolve the anniversary forward to 2024-06-30, dates_service.rb:91 would collapse to_datetime onto started_at, and the fee would land on a zero-length period. Excluding the termination day bills 76 = 41_530¢. A 182-day denominator (the length of the NEXT half, and of a calendar H1) gives 42_308¢; 184 gives 41_848¢. Only 77/183 is 42_077¢.

The control for the row above, pinning where a calendar half-year begins and ends. Created 2024-01-01, compute_from_date already returns beginning_of_half_year (semiannual_service.rb:56-62) and the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 only lowers the time of day, so the period is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-06-30T23:59:59Z. Still the prorating branch (should_use_full_amount? false on all four conditions, fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156), so the 100_000¢ is 182 x 100_000/182. What a wrong boundary gives. A half closing 2024-06-29 bills 181/182 = 99_451¢; one opening 2023-12-31 bills 183/182 = 100_549¢. A period resolved with the QUARTERLY rule (2024-01-01 .. 2024-03-31) also bills 100_000¢, for half the time — which is why the dates are asserted next to the amount.

A calendar semiannual subscription bills on 1 January and 1 July (organization_billing_service.rb:221-246), so one created 2024-02-15 first bills 2024-07-01. base_date = billing_date - 6.months = 2024-01-01 (semiannual_service.rb:126-138) and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_half_year = 2024-01-01 (:56-62); dates_service.rb :73-75 clamps up to the subscription's start for from_datetime 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z at midnight. compute_to_date works on the unclamped from_date and, for a calendar subscription, is end_of_half_year (:140-146) = 2024-06-30T23:59:59Z. compute_duration measures the whole half (:108-112): 31 + 29 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 = 182 days, the LEAP first half. first_subscription_amount bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-02-15T00:00, 2024-06-30T23:59:59) = 137 days: 137 x 100_000/182 = 75_274.725…¢ → 75_275¢. What a wrong boundary gives. A 181-day first half (the common-year length, i.e. losing the leap day) gives 75_691¢; the SECOND half's 184 days give 74_457¢; a 180-day "six times thirty" approximation gives 76_111¢; dividing by the 137 days billed gives 100_000¢; and skipping the clamp bills the whole half, 100_000¢. Only 137/182 reaches 75_275¢.

A partial first half of 2024 followed by a whole second half. H1 bills 137/182 = 75_275¢ as in the partial row. On 2025-01-01, base_date = 2024-07-01 and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_half_year = 2024-07-01 (semiannual_service.rb:56-62, :126-138); the clamp at dates_service.rb:73 does not fire, and the period is 2024-07-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-12-31T23:59:59Z. should_use_full_amount? line 147 finds the H1 fee and full_period_amount returns plan.amount_cents = 100_000¢ (fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273) with no division — so a 184-day half costs the same as the 182-day one before it, which is the behaviour. What a wrong boundary gives. H2 prorated as a first period would be 184/184 = 100_000¢ too, so only the from_date separates a full period from a re-clamped one. A second period still clamped to started_at would report 2024-02-15T00:00:00Z over an H2 window; a base_date that stayed in H1 would reproduce 2024-01-01 .. 2024-06-30, which InvoiceSubscription.matching? already holds and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 refuses — one invoice instead of two.

Terminated 46 days into a 182-day half. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) makes compute_from_date take billing_date.beginning_of_half_year = 2024-01-01 (semiannual_service.rb:57-59); to_datetime would be 2024-06-30T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it down to terminated_at, so the period is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-02-15T10:00:00Z, and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:113-127 keeps those boundaries because the termination instant precedes the period's charges_to_datetime (:125). terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts date_diff_with_timezone(2024-01-01T00:00, 2024-02-15T10:00) = 46 days — the termination day included — against compute_duration 182 (semiannual_service.rb:108-112): 46 x 100_000/182 = 25_274.725…¢ → 25_275¢. Note the pair with b02/quarterly/calendar/terminated-mid-period: the same 46 days of the same calendar, priced against a half instead of a quarter, is 25_275¢ rather than 50_549¢. The interval is doing the work, and if the semiannual service fell back on the quarterly denominator this row would print 50_549¢. What a wrong boundary gives. Excluding the termination day bills 45 = 24_725¢; not clamping to_datetime bills the whole half, 100_000¢; a 181-day denominator gives 25_414¢ and the second half's 184 gives 25_000¢.

The trial row's control, and the row that pins where an anniversary week actually falls. Created Wednesday 2024-03-06 at 10:00 and billed Wednesday 2024-03-13, base_date = billing_date - 1.week = 2024-03-06 and previous_anniversary_day returns it unchanged because its weekday already matches subscription_at's (weekly_service.rb:60-64). compute_to_date adds six days (:25), so the period is 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-12T23:59:59Z; the from_datetime is midnight even though the subscription was created at 10:00, via the beginning_of_day clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75. 7 days x 100_000/7 = 100_000¢. What a wrong boundary gives. The calendar rule would put this week on 2024-03-04 .. 2024-03-10: the same seven days and the same 100_000¢, two days early — undetectable in the amount and caught only by from_date/to_date. Using next_occurring instead of prev_occurring in previous_anniversary_day would open the period on 2024-03-13, after the clamp collapses it onto started_at, and bill 2024-03-06 .. 2024-03-12 anyway; the case that moves money is a compute_to_date of `from_date + 7.days` instead of 6, which bills 8 days = 114_286¢ and overlaps the next period.

An anniversary weekly subscription bills on the weekday it started (organization_billing_service .rb:263-272, matching ISODOW), so a Wednesday subscription bills on Wednesday 2024-03-13. The period is whole by construction: base_date is 2024-03-06, previous_anniversary_day returns the date itself when the weekday already matches (weekly_service.rb:60-64), and compute_to_date adds six days (:22-26), so from_datetime .. to_datetime is 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-12T23:59:59Z. That is why the trial is here: an anniversary subscription starts ON its own boundary, so nothing for dates_service.rb:73-75 to clamp and no date alone can make its first period partial. A 3-day trial ends 2024-03-09. first_subscription_amount:162-170 sees trial_end_date inside the period and moves its LOCAL from_datetime to initial_started_at + 3.days = 2024-03-09T00:00:00Z, then bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-09T00:00, 2024-03-12T23:59:59) = 4 days x 100_000/7 = 57_142.857…¢ → 57_143¢. The fee's from_date is NOT moved with it: the fee records boundaries.from_datetime, which came from the invoice_subscription (calculate_fees_service.rb:30-38), so the labelled window stays the whole period while the money covers four sevenths of it. Both facts are asserted, because a fee period narrowed to the post-trial days would leave the amount right and the invoice wrong. What a wrong boundary gives. A trial counted as calendar days from midnight of the day AFTER creation ends 2024-03-10 and bills 3 days = 42_857¢. A trial appended to the period rather than subtracted from it (bill the full week, credit later) shows 100_000¢. And reading this weekly plan with the CALENDAR rule puts the period on 2024-03-04 .. 2024-03-10, with the trial ending inside it, and bills 2024-03-09 .. 2024-03-10 = 2 days = 28_571¢.

Two anniversary Wednesdays. Both invoices are 100_000¢ — an anniversary period is always whole — so the entire content of this row is that the two windows are adjacent and neither repeats: 2024-03-06 .. 2024-03-12, then 2024-03-13 .. 2024-03-19. On the second, base_date is 2024-03-13, previous_anniversary_day returns it (weekday matches, weekly_service.rb:60-64), the clamp at dates_service.rb:73 does not fire because 2024-03-13T00:00 is after started_at, and should_use_full_amount?:147 short-circuits to plan.amount_cents because a subscription fee already exists (fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273). What a wrong boundary gives. A second period re-clamped to started_at would report from_date 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z with the same 100_000¢, so the amount cannot detect it and only the dates can. A previous_anniversary_day that walked back a full week from 2024-03-20 would give 2024-03-06 .. 2024-03-12, which InvoiceSubscription.matching? already holds, and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse the invoice entirely — one invoice, not two.

Terminated on Saturday 2024-03-09, three days into a week that started Wednesday 2024-03-06. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) sends compute_from_date down the billing_date branch, and previous_anniversary_day walks BACK to the subscription's own weekday: 2024-03-09 is a Saturday, so prev_occurring(:wednesday) = 2024-03-06 (weekly_service.rb:15-17 and :60-64). to_datetime would be 2024-03-12T23:59:59Z and is clamped down to terminated_at by dates_service.rb:87-89, so the period is 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-09T10:00:00Z. terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) bills 4 days — the period start and the termination day are both charged — against WEEK_DURATION 7, so 4 x 100_000/7 = 57_142.857…¢ → 57_143¢. Identical to the anniversary trial row's 57_143¢ from the opposite end of the same seven days, which is the point: proration in and proration out are computed by different methods and must agree on the day count. What a wrong boundary gives. Using next_occurring rather than prev_occurring resolves the anniversary forward to 2024-03-13, dates_service.rb:91 then collapses to_datetime onto started_at and the fee lands on a zero-length period. Not clamping to_datetime bills the full week, 100_000¢. Excluding the termination day (the ADVANCE convention) bills 3 days = 42_857¢.

The control for the row above: the same plan and the same billing Monday, with the subscription created ON the boundary instead of two days into it. Monday 2024-03-04 is beginning_of_week, so compute_from_date (weekly_service.rb:14-20) already returns 2024-03-04 and the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 only moves the time of day down to midnight. The period is 2024-03-04T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-10T23:59:59Z, date_diff_with_timezone returns 7 days and single_day_price is 100_000/7, so the first period bills 7 x 14_285.714…¢ = 100_000¢ exactly — the whole plan amount, unprorated, reached through the SAME prorating expression as the partial row (fees/subscription_service.rb:158-179); should_use_full_amount? is false here on every one of its four branches (:141-156), because the plan is in arrears, no subscription fee exists yet and the subscription did not start in the past. What a wrong boundary gives. A period read one day short (2024-03-04 .. 2024-03-09) bills 6/7 = 85_714¢; one day long (.. 2024-03-11) bills 8/7 = 114_286¢. Both are visible only because the row pins from_date and to_date next to the amount: 100_000¢ on its own is also what a boundary computation that gave up and returned plan.amount_cents would produce.

A calendar weekly subscription is billed on Mondays and only on Mondays (organization_billing_service.rb:148-155, ISODOW = 1), so a subscription created on Wednesday 2024-03-06 first bills on Monday 2024-03-11. base_date is billing_date - 1.week = 2024-03-04 (dates/weekly_service.rb:10-12) and compute_from_date is base_date.beginning_of_week = 2024-03-04 (:14-20); dates_service.rb:73-75 then clamps that up to the subscription's own start, giving from_datetime 2024-03-06T00:00:00Z. It is MIDNIGHT and not the 10:00 creation instant: only charges_from_datetime carries the creation time (dates_service.rb:112). compute_to_date is computed from the UNCLAMPED from_date (:22-26), so the period still closes on the calendar week's Sunday, 2024-03-10T23:59:59Z. Fees::SubscriptionService #first_subscription_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:158-179) bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-06T00:00, 2024-03-10T23:59:59) = 5 days at a single_day_price of 100_000 / compute_duration, and compute_duration for weekly is the constant WEEK_DURATION = 7 (weekly_service.rb:70-72), so 5 x 14_285.714…¢ = 71_428.571…¢, rounded to 71_429¢ at subscription_service.rb:19-20. What a wrong boundary gives. Skipping the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 leaves from_datetime on 2024-03-04 and bills 7 days = 100_000¢ — two days the customer did not have. Reading the period with the ANNIVERSARY rule instead (previous_anniversary_day, weekly_service.rb:60-64) gives 2024-03-06 .. 2024-03-12, also 7 days and 100_000¢, over a window that has not finished yet. Dividing by the 5 days actually billed rather than by WEEK_DURATION gives 100_000¢ again. Every plausible mistake here lands on the full plan amount, which is why the row asserts 71_429¢ together with both period ends.

Two Mondays, so two invoices, and the pair is the assertion. The first is the partial row's 5/7 = 71_429¢ over 2024-03-06 .. 2024-03-10. The second is billed on 2024-03-18, where base_date is 2024-03-11 and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_week = 2024-03-11 (weekly_service.rb:10-20); dates_service.rb:73 finds 2024-03-11T00:00 is NOT before started_at (2024-03-06T10:00), so nothing is clamped and the period is 2024-03-11T00:00:00Z .. 2024-03-17T23:59:59Z. The amount no longer goes through the prorating branch at all: should_use_full_amount? line 147 sees a subscription fee created before this invoice and full_period_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273) returns plan.amount_cents = 100_000¢ with no division. What a wrong boundary gives. A second period still clamped to started_at would repeat 2024-03-06 as its from_datetime; the amount would stay 100_000¢ because full_period_amount does not look at the dates, and the error would be invisible in the totals — which is precisely why both from_date values are asserted. A base_date that walked back a day instead of a week (2024-03-17.beginning_of_week is still 2024-03-11, but 2024-03-18 - 1.day = 2024-03-17 gives 2024-03-11 too) is indistinguishable here; the case that IS caught is an off-by-one week, 2024-03-04 .. 2024-03-10, which would collide with the first invoice's window and be refused as a duplicate by CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77, leaving one invoice instead of two.

Terminating does not wait for Monday: the termination itself invoices the part of the week that was used. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) is true — terminated, in arrears, not downgraded — so compute_from_date takes billing_date.beginning_of_week rather than base_date's (weekly_service.rb:15-17), giving 2024-03-04T00:00:00Z. compute_to_date would close the week on 2024-03-10, but dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps to_datetime down to terminated_at, so the period ends at 2024-03-07T10:00:00Z — a to_datetime that is NOT an end-of-day, which is the signature of a termination boundary. CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:113-127 keeps these boundaries rather than rebuilding the whole period, because the termination instant is before the period's own charges_to_datetime (:125). Proration on the way out is a different expression from proration on the way in: Fees::SubscriptionService#terminated_amount (:188-214) is selected by should_compute_terminated_amount? (:125-130) and counts subscription.date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-04T00:00, 2024-03-07T10:00) = 4 days — the termination day is billed — against single_day_price computed with an explicit optional_from_date of 2024-03-04 (:209-213). WEEK_DURATION is 7 either way, so 4 x 14_285.714…¢ = 57_142.857…¢ → 57_143¢. What a wrong boundary gives. Treating termination the way an ADVANCE subscription is treated — crediting FROM the termination day rather than billing THROUGH it — bills 2024-03-04 .. 2024-03-06, 3 days = 42_857¢. Leaving to_datetime at 2024-03-10T23:59:59Z bills the whole week, 100_000¢, for three days the customer will not have. And a from_datetime taken from base_date (2024-02-26, the PREVIOUS week, because compute_from_date without the terminated_pay_in_arrears? branch walks back one week) bills 11 days = 157_143¢.

The trial row's control, and the row that pins the length of an anniversary year that skips a leap day. The period is 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z .. 2025-02-28T23:59:59Z — previous_anniversary_day returns 2024-03-01 (yearly_service.rb:143-149) and compute_to_date resolves day 0 of March 2025 through build_date into 2025-02-28 (:73-87, dates_service.rb:284-299) — and compute_duration is 365 days (:155-161). 365 x 100_000/365 = 100_000¢ through the prorating branch, not a short-circuit (should_use_full_amount? false on all four conditions, fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156). What a wrong boundary gives. Using days_in_year(2024) = 366 as the denominator against 365 billed days gives 99_727¢ — a full period that silently bills less than the plan, and the reason this row asserts a round 100_000¢ rather than trusting the total. A period closing 2025-03-01 (compute_to_date without the day - 1) bills 366/365 = 100_274¢ and overlaps the next period. The CALENDAR reading, 2024-01-01 .. 2024-12-31, also bills 100_000¢ over the wrong twelve months.

An anniversary yearly subscription bills on its own month and day (organization_billing_service.rb:333-361), so 2024-03-01 bills 2025-03-01. The period is whole by construction, hence the trial: base_date = billing_date - 1.year = 2024-03-01 (yearly_service.rb:47-59), previous_anniversary_day returns 2024-03-01 (:143-149, since period_started_in_last_year? is false for a date sitting exactly on its anniversary, :175-182), and compute_to_date takes year + 1, the same month, and day subscription_at.day - 1 = 0 — build_date then walks that zero back into the previous month (dates_service.rb:284-299) giving 2025-02-28 (:73-87). Period 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z .. 2025-02-28T23:59:59Z, and compute_duration is 2025-03-01 - 2024-03-01 = 365 days (:155-161) — NOT days_in_year, which is the calendar-only branch. A 30-day trial ends 2024-03-31. first_subscription_amount:162-170 moves its local from_datetime to initial_started_at + 30.days = 2024-03-31T00:00:00Z and bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-31T00:00, 2025-02-28T23:59:59) = 335 days x 100_000/365 = 91_780.821…¢ → 91_781¢, while the fee records the whole period (calculate_fees_service.rb:30-38). What a wrong boundary gives. A denominator of 366 (days_in_year(2024), which is what the CALENDAR branch would return for this from_date) gives 91_530¢ — the single most likely mistake here, and a 251¢ difference. 365 is right because the period spans March 2024 to February 2025 and misses the leap day entirely. A trial appended rather than subtracted bills 100_000¢; a trial measured from the following midnight bills 334 days = 91_507¢.

A subscription whose anniversary is 29 February, followed through the two common years after it. Period 1: billed 2025-02-28, because yearly_anniversary explicitly folds day 29 into 28 February of a common year (organization_billing_service.rb:333-361, the ARRAY[28, 29] branch). base_date takes the last-day branch at yearly_service.rb:50-55 — 2025-02-28 is its month's last day and its day 28 is below the anniversary day 29, and (2025-02-28 - 1.year).end_of_month is 2024-02-29 whose day 29 is not below 29 — giving 2024-02-29. previous_anniversary_day(2024-02-29) returns 2024-02-29 (:143-149, with anniversary_day_in guarding the comparison at :181). compute_to_date then takes year + 1, month 2, day 28, and subtracts a FURTHER day at :84 because 2025-02-28 is its month's last day and the anniversary day 29 is above it: 2025-02-27. Period 1 = 2024-02-29T00:00:00Z .. 2025-02-27T23:59:59Z. compute_duration is (2025-02-28 - 2024-02-29) = 365 (:155-161), and the period is 365 days inclusive, so 365 x 100_000/365 = 100_000¢ — the -1.day at :84 does not shorten the period relative to its own denominator, which is the fact this row nails down. Period 2: billed 2026-02-28. base_date takes the last-day branch again, but this time (2026-02-28 - 1.year).end_of_month is 2025-02-28 whose day 28 is BELOW 29, so the fallback at yearly_service.rb:55 returns that end of month, 2025-02-28. previous_anniversary_day(2025-02-28) resolves through build_date(2025, 2, 29) → 2025-02-28, and compute_to_date gives 2026-02-28 minus a day = 2026-02-27. Period 2 = 2025-02-28T00:00:00Z .. 2026-02-27T23:59:59Z, 365 days, billed plan.amount_cents outright (should_use_full_amount? line 147, fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273). What a wrong boundary gives. Dropping the -1.day at yearly_service.rb:84 makes period 1 end 2025-02-28 — 366 days against a 365 denominator, 100_274¢ — and makes period 2 start on a day period 1 already billed. Using days_in_year(2024) = 366 as the denominator gives 99_727¢. And an anniversary_day_in that compared against the raw day 29 rather than the clamped 28 (dates_service.rb:307-309) would leave 2025-02-28 trailing the PREVIOUS period, so period 2 would open on 2025-03-01 and lose a day of revenue outright.

Terminated 107 days into an anniversary year that runs March to February. terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) sends compute_from_date to previous_anniversary_day(2024-06-15) (yearly_service.rb:66-68): period_started_in_last_year? is false because June is after the March anniversary month (:175-182), so the year stays 2024 and build_date(2024, 3, 1) = 2024-03-01. to_datetime would be 2025-02-28T23:59:59Z and dates_service.rb:87-89 clamps it to terminated_at, giving 2024-03-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-06-15T10:00:00Z. CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:113-127 keeps those boundaries because the termination precedes the period's charges_to_datetime (:125). terminated_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:188-214) counts date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-01T00:00, 2024-06-15T10:00) = 107 days — 31 + 30 + 31 + 15, the termination day billed — against compute_duration for the period holding 2024-03-01, which is 365 (yearly_service.rb:155-161). 107 x 100_000/365 = 29_315.068…¢ → 29_315¢. What a wrong boundary gives. A 366-day denominator, which is what the calendar branch of compute_duration returns for a 2024 from_date, gives 29_235¢. period_started_in_last_year? answering true would put from_date on 2023-03-01 and bill 473 days instead of 107 — more than the whole plan amount. The control for the row above. Created 2024-01-01, compute_from_date already returns beginning_of_year (yearly_service.rb:65-71) and the clamp at dates_service.rb:73-75 only lowers the time of day, so the period is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-12-31T23:59:59Z. Still the prorating branch (should_use_full_amount? false on all four conditions, fees/subscription_service.rb:141-156): 366 days over a days_in_year(2024) of 366 (yearly_service.rb:155-157) = 100_000¢, and the two 366s must be the same 366 for that to hold. What a wrong boundary gives. A period closing 2024-12-30 bills 365/366 = 99_727¢; a denominator of 365 against 366 billed days gives 100_274¢ — the leap-year mismatch, and the number this row exists to exclude. A QUARTERLY reading (2024-10-01 .. 2024-12-31) also bills 100_000¢ for a quarter of the time, which is why the dates are asserted.

A calendar yearly subscription with bill_charges_monthly off is billed once, on 1 January (organization_billing_service.rb:209-220), so one created 2024-03-16 first bills 2025-01-01. base_date = billing_date - 1.year = 2024-01-01 (yearly_service.rb:47-59) and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_year = 2024-01-01 (:65-71); dates_service.rb:73-75 clamps up to the subscription's start, giving 2024-03-16T00:00:00Z at midnight rather than the 10:00 creation instant. compute_to_date runs on the unclamped from_date and, for a calendar subscription, is end_of_year (:73-74) = 2024-12-31T23:59:59Z. The denominator is where yearly differs from every other interval: compute_duration does NOT measure the period, it returns Time.days_in_year(from_date.year) for a calendar subscription (yearly_service.rb:155-157) — 366 for 2024. first_subscription_amount bills date_diff_with_timezone(2024-03-16T00:00, 2024-12-31T23:59:59) = 291 days: 291 x 100_000/366 = 79_508.196…¢ → 79_508¢. 2024 is chosen deliberately: a leap year makes the 366 visible. What a wrong boundary gives. A 365-day denominator (the leap day forgotten, or days_in_year(2025) taken from the BILLING year rather than the period's) gives 79_726¢ — a 218¢ difference that a row asserting only round numbers would never see. Dividing by the 291 days billed gives 100_000¢; skipping the clamp bills the whole year, 100_000¢; and a MONTHLY reading of the period (2024-12-01 .. 2024-12-31) bills 100_000¢ for one month.

A partial leap year followed by a whole common year, which is the pairing worth having: 2024 is 366 days and 2025 is 365, and the plan costs 100_000¢ either way. 2024 bills 291/366 = 79_508¢ as in the partial row. On 2026-01-01, base_date = 2025-01-01 and compute_from_date = base_date.beginning_of_year = 2025-01-01 (yearly_service.rb:47-71); the clamp at dates_service.rb:73 does not fire because 2025-01-01T00:00 is after started_at, and the period is 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z .. 2025-12-31T23:59:59Z. should_use_full_amount? line 147 finds the 2024 fee and full_period_amount returns plan.amount_cents = 100_000¢ (fees/subscription_service.rb:247-273) with no division, so the different year length never enters the arithmetic. What a wrong boundary gives. 2025 prorated as a first period is 365/365 = 100_000¢ too, so the amount cannot distinguish it; the from_date is the assertion. A second period still clamped to started_at would report 2024-03-16T00:00:00Z over a 2025 window. A base_date left in 2024 would reproduce 2024-01-01 .. 2024-12-31, which InvoiceSubscription.matching? already holds, and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService:69-77 would refuse — one invoice instead of two.

Dynamic in advance is the most direct combination in the suite: the event carries its own price, so the fee is exactly precise_total_amount_cents = 2_500¢, billed the moment the event lands. Units still come from the metric (sum_agg → 10), so units and amount stay decoupled.

Units and price are decoupled on purpose: the events carry amounts 10 / 30 / 20 but prices 2_500 / 500 / 1_250 cents, so no fee can be reconstructed from its units and the three fees are three different numbers. dynamic_service.rb:7-12 divides the SUMMED precise_total_amount_cents by the currency subunit, and the delta subtracts the event's own contribution (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:64-77 subtracts pay_in_advance_precise_total_amount_cents, set from the event at sum_service.rb:83-86): event 1 = 25.00 − 0 (units 0 short-circuits compute_amount to 0), event 2 = 30.00 − 25.00 = 5.00, event 3 = 42.50 − 30.00 = 12.50 → 2_500¢, 500¢, 1_250¢, total 4_250¢ = the summed event prices, which is also the arrears answer. Dynamic is the one model where delta pricing and per-event pricing provably agree, so the counterfactual worth ruling out is the other one: a service pricing the cumulative precise_total_amount_cents without the subtraction would bill 2_500 + 3_000 + 4_250 = 9_750¢. Units still come from sum_agg's per-event delta (10, 30, 20), never from the price.

DROPPED. invoiceable: false with regroup_paid_fees nil creates the fee and then attaches it to nothing: events/pay_in_advance_service.rb:26 routes the event to Fees::CreatePayInAdvanceJob, which persists 3 fee(s) worth 2_500 / 500 / 1_250¢ with invoice_id nil (create_pay_in_advance_service.rb:151), and nothing ever picks them up - advance_charges_service.rb:83 requires regroup_paid_fees: :invoice, and calculate_fees_service.rb:130 scopes arrears charge fees to `invoiceable: true`. So the only invoice that exists is the period one, carrying the 0¢ subscription fee, and 4_250¢ of real usage is billed nowhere. An absence assertion on its own would pass for three WRONG reasons, so this row pairs it with positive evidence. (a) The events never landed: usage would read 0 units and 0¢ instead of 60.0 units and 4_250¢. (b) The charge was never matched at all (wrong metric code or field_name): assert_golden_usage raises "no charge usage for metric" rather than comparing anything. (c) The licence gate silently dropped invoiceable, so the row was really exercising the invoiceable path: expect.resource would read invoiceable true, and the per-event invoices would push the count past 1 (compare b14/invoiceable/silently-ignored-*). The usage number is independent evidence rather than a restatement of the fee: Fees::ChargeService runs in :current_usage context against the ARREARS charge model over the whole aggregation (customer_usage_service.rb:129-159), so it reaches 4_250¢ by a different route - and that it equals the sum of the per-event deltas above is the invariant that makes the dropped amount unambiguous (the summed precise_total_amount_cents, 4_250¢). This is NOT the zero-fee discard of fees/charge_service.rb:353-360, which drops a fee whose units, amount and events_count are ALL zero under context :finalize; here a fee worth 4_250¢ is built, taxed and saved, and simply never invoiced.

Tier 1 is deliberately narrow (0..2) so the THIRD count event crosses into tier 2 and the three fees come out unequal — a constant sequence is what per-event pricing would also produce and proves nothing. Cumulative costs (range_graduated_service.rb:54-65, non-adjacent ranges so tier 2 bills to_value−from_value+1 units): f(1) = 100 + 1×2 = 102.00, f(2) = 100 + 2×2 = 104.00, f(3) = (100 + 2×2) + (50 + 1×1) = 155.00; f(0) = 0 via the exclude_event guard (graduated_service.rb:31). Deltas: 102.00 → 10_200¢, 2.00 → 200¢, 51.00 → 5_100¢, total 15_500¢ = f(3), the arrears answer. Counterfactual: per-event pricing prices each event as a lone unit in tier 1, 102.00 × 3 = 30_600¢ — and the naive cumulative reading without subtraction gives 10_200 + 10_400 + 15_500 = 36_100¢. Both tier flat fees are charged once per PERIOD, not once per event, and only a multi-event row can see that.

ONE count event, so the cumulative aggregation is 1: tier 1 (0..10) bills its flat_amount 100.00 plus 1 × 2.00 = 102.00 → 10_200¢ (range_graduated_service.rb:54-65 — from_value 0 means the range's units are min(total, to_value), here 1). The excluding side is f(0) with exclude_event, and graduated_service.rb:31 returns 0 there rather than the bare tier-1 flat: that guard is exactly what this row pins. Without it, f(0) would be the 100.00 flat (range_graduated_service.rb:47 keeps flat_unit_amount even at units 0) and the first event would be billed 2.00 → 200¢, with the tier-1 flat fee never charged at all. Contrast the sum_agg sibling on the same ranges, where the single event carries 10 units and pays 120.00.

REGROUPED, not recomputed. invoiceable: false routes the event to Fees::CreatePayInAdvanceJob rather than to an invoice (events/pay_in_advance_service.rb:26), and that service persists the fee with invoice_id nil and payment_status PENDING (create_pay_in_advance_service.rb:120,151), applying taxes there and then because nothing downstream will (:147-148). regroup_paid_fees means literally PAID fees: advance_charges_service.rb:69-70 collects only fees whose payment_status is succeeded and whose succeeded_at precedes billing_at, which is why this row has a pay_fees step - without it no advance_charges invoice is produced at all and the usage is silently uninvoiced. At 1 April the fee above is moved onto an advance_charges invoice (:110-115, update_all invoice_id) totalling 10_200¢, its taxes SUMMED from the fees rather than recomputed (AggregateAmountsAndTaxesFromFees at :126, deliberately not ComputeAmountsFromFees) and its payment_status stamped succeeded at :130. The row pins the two facts separately, because they are two facts: HOW MUCH (the regrouped fee is 10_200¢) and WHICH invoice carries it (the expectation is selected by invoice_type: advance_charges, not by index). With a single event the advance reading and the arrears reading are numerically identical (f(1) = flat 100.00 + 1 × 2.00 = 102.00 → 10_200¢), so what distinguishes REGROUPED from RECOMPUTED-AT-INVOICE-TIME here is purely WHERE the money sits: a recomputation in arrears would hang a 10_200¢ charge fee off the period (subscription) invoice, and the second expectation asserts that invoice has exactly one fee and it is the 0¢ subscription fee. The count discrimination is the many-event sibling's job. The second expectation also pins that the usage is not billed TWICE: the period invoice carries only the 0¢ subscription fee because calculate_fees_service.rb:130 scopes arrears charge fees to `invoiceable: true`. `premium: true` is load-bearing - Charges::CreateService assigns invoiceable and regroup_paid_fees only under a licence, and advance_charges_service.rb:83 requires regroup_paid_fees: :invoice, so without the licence there would be no advance_charges invoice to select at all.

A pay-in-advance charge is priced as a CUMULATIVE DELTA, not per event in isolation: Charges::ApplyPayInAdvanceChargeModelService computes amount_from_aggregation − amount_excluding_persisted_event. Event 1 (10 units): cost(10) − cost(0) = (flat 100 + 10 × 2) − 0 = 120.00 → 12_000¢. Event 2 (10 more): cost(20) − cost(10) = (120 + flat 50 + 10 × 1) − 120 = 60.00 → 6_000¢. The row asserts the SECOND advance invoice precisely because that is where the two readings diverge: the tier-1 flat fee is charged ONCE for the period, not again on each event. A single-event row cannot tell the two apart, which is why this one ingests two.

The FIRST event of a graduated pay-in-advance charge, isolated: 10 units fill tier 1 exactly, so f(10) = flat 100.00 + 10 × 2.00 = 120.00 → 12_000¢, and the excluding side is f(0) which graduated_service.rb:31 forces to 0 under exclude_event. The single event therefore pays the tier-1 flat fee in full. This is the same charge shape as the existing many-event b03/graduated/sum_agg/invoiceable row and asserts its FIRST leg standalone, so a regression that moved the flat fee off the opening event (delta 20.00 → 2_000¢, the number an unguarded f(0) = 100.00 would give) fails here even if the second-event delta stayed right. Note that one event cannot distinguish delta pricing from per-event pricing at all — 12_000¢ is what both produce; that discrimination is the many-event sibling's job, and this row exists only to pin the opening flat fee.

Two equal-sized events with UNEQUAL fees, which is the whole point: the second crosses out of tier 1 (0..10) and so pays a different price for the same 10 units. f(10) = 100 + 10×2 = 120.00; f(20) = (100 + 10×2) + (50 + 10×1) = 180.00 (range_graduated_service.rb:54-65 - tier 2 is non-adjacent, so at total 20 it bills 20 − 11 + 1 = 10 units); f(0) = 0 by the exclude_event guard (graduated_service.rb:31). Deltas: 120.00 → 12_000¢, 60.00 → 6_000¢. The tier-1 flat is charged ONCE for the period, not again on the second event. Counterfactual: per-event pricing prices each event alone in tier 1, 12_000 × 2 = 24_000¢; the unsubtracted cumulative reading gives 12_000 + 18_000 = 30_000¢. DROPPED. invoiceable: false with regroup_paid_fees nil creates the fee and then attaches it to nothing: events/pay_in_advance_service.rb:26 routes the event to Fees::CreatePayInAdvanceJob, which persists 2 fee(s) worth 12_000 / 6_000¢ with invoice_id nil (create_pay_in_advance_service.rb:151), and nothing ever picks them up - advance_charges_service.rb:83 requires regroup_paid_fees: :invoice, and calculate_fees_service.rb:130 scopes arrears charge fees to `invoiceable: true`. So the only invoice that exists is the period one, carrying the 0¢ subscription fee, and 18_000¢ of real usage is billed nowhere. An absence assertion on its own would pass for three WRONG reasons, so this row pairs it with positive evidence. (a) The events never landed: usage would read 0 units and 0¢ instead of 20.0 units and 18_000¢. (b) The charge was never matched at all (wrong metric code or field_name): assert_golden_usage raises "no charge usage for metric" rather than comparing anything. (c) The licence gate silently dropped invoiceable, so the row was really exercising the invoiceable path: expect.resource would read invoiceable true, and the per-event invoices would push the count past 1 (compare b14/invoiceable/silently-ignored-*). The usage number is independent evidence rather than a restatement of the fee: Fees::ChargeService runs in :current_usage context against the ARREARS charge model over the whole aggregation (customer_usage_service.rb:129-159), so it reaches 18_000¢ by a different route - and that it equals the sum of the per-event deltas above is the invariant that makes the dropped amount unambiguous (f(20) = (100 + 10×2) + (50 + 10×1) = 180.00 → 18_000¢). This is NOT the zero-fee discard of fees/charge_service.rb:353-360, which drops a fee whose units, amount and events_count are ALL zero under context :finalize; here a fee worth 18_000¢ is built, taxed and saved, and simply never invoiced.

Tier 1 is 0..2 so the THIRD count event crosses into tier 2, and the three fees are three different numbers. range_graduated_percentage_service.rb:53-60 counts a full range as to_value − 1 + 1 = to_value units when from_value is 0, and a non-zero from_value range as total − from_value + 1: f(1) = 1 + 1×0.10 = 1.10, f(2) = 1 + 2×0.10 = 1.20, f(3) = (1 + 2×0.10) + (2 + 1×0.20) = 3.40. f(0) = 0 by the exclude_event zeroing at graduated_percentage_service.rb:17. Deltas: 1.10 → 110¢, 0.10 → 10¢, 2.20 → 220¢, total 340¢ = f(3), the arrears answer. The 10¢ middle fee is the discriminating observation — it is the tier-1 rate on ONE unit with no flat fee attached, and only delta pricing produces it. Counterfactual: per-event pricing bills each event as a lone tier-1 unit, 110¢ × 3 = 330¢, which is close enough to 340¢ that a row asserting only the total would miss it; the unsubtracted cumulative reading gives 110 + 120 + 340 = 570¢. `premium: true` for the licence gate.

One count event, cumulative 1 unit, entirely inside tier 1 (0..2): range_graduated_percentage_service.rb:53-60 bills total_units = 1 for a range whose from_value is 0, so 1 × 10 / 100 = 0.10 plus flat_amount 1.00 = 1.10 → 110¢.
