Package rounds up: 10 units at package_size 25 → ceil(10 / 25) = 1 package × 10.00 = 1_000¢. Because the amount is a cumulative delta rather than a per-event price, ten one-unit events would together buy ONE package, not ten — each event is charged the difference its arrival makes to the running total, which is zero once the package is already paid for.

Event sizes 10 / 20 / 5 push the cumulative sum to 10, 30, 35 so the second event straddles the 25-unit package boundary — it is billed the SECOND package, not a package of its own, and the third buys nothing. f = ceil(n / 25) × 10.00 (package_service.rb:12-13) gives f(10) = 10.00, f(30) = 20.00, f(35) = 20.00; deltas 1_000¢, 1_000¢, 0¢, total 2_000¢ = f(35), the arrears answer. The equal first two amounts are not a constant sequence in disguise — the third fee is 0¢, and only cumulative delta pricing produces a 0¢ fee for 5 real units. Counterfactual: per-event pricing rounds each event up on its own, ceil(10/25) + ceil(20/25) + ceil(5/25) = 3 packages = 3_000¢ for 35 units that only ever needed two packages.

Package rounds up: 10 units at package_size 25 give ceil(10 / 25) = 1 package × 10.00 = 1_000¢ (package_service.rb:12-13), against f(0) = 0 packages = 0. An invoiceable pay-in-advance charge bills the moment the event arrives: the first invoice holds only that charge fee, 10 units × 1.00 = 10.00 → 1_000¢. The period invoice at 1 April is the second, and carries only the 0¢ subscription fee — the charge is not billed twice. Two invoices from one event is the shape this row exists to pin.

Values 10 / 30 / 20 are deliberately unequal so no two fees coincide and so sum (60), max (30) and latest (20) all disagree — a row whose events are all the same size cannot tell which aggregation ran. sum_agg's pay_in_advance_aggregation is the delta the event makes to the running total (sum_service.rb:139-171: cached current_aggregation + value, minus the cached max), so the deltas are 10, 30, 20 units and the amounts f(10)−f(0) = 10.00 → 1_000¢, f(40)−f(10) = 30.00 → 3_000¢, f(60)−f(40) = 20.00 → 2_000¢. Total advance-billed 6_000¢ equals the 60 × 1.00 an arrears charge would have produced, which is the invariant standard must obey. Counterfactual: pricing the cumulative aggregation without the subtraction (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:21) gives 1_000 + 4_000 + 6_000 = 11_000¢ and units 10.0 / 40.0 / 60.0.

Same setup, finalized instead of refreshed. Finalizing closes the draft at 3_000¢ without changing the arithmetic — the amounts are identical to what the draft held, and only `status` moves. payment_status is asserted as pending because finalizing makes an invoice owed, not paid; the pair status=finalized / payment_status=pending is the state a dunning run acts on.

Without a grace period there is no draft to finalize, so the finalize operation is a no-op on both of its surfaces — and this row pins the one that can be exercised. `PUT /invoices/:id/finalize` is not reachable at all here: the controller looks the invoice up in `current_organization.invoices.draft` (`invoices_controller.rb:111`) and answers 404 for an already-issued invoice. The clock is, so the row runs `Clock::FinalizeInvoicesJob`, whose scope is `Invoice.ready_to_be_finalized` = `draft.where(COALESCE(expected_finalization_date, issuing_date) <= today)` (`invoice.rb:197`). With the April invoice finalized on creation the scope is empty and nothing is enqueued. The 20 units timestamped 20 March and ingested on 2 April therefore stay unbilled: 1_000¢, not 3_000¢. That is the same number, for the same reason, as b04/refresh/no-grace-period — neither surface re-reads an issued invoice — and the contrast is b04/finalize/grace-period, where the finalize call does recompute because there is still a draft to recompute. `invoices: 1` is load-bearing: a finalize pass that re-billed the period would leave two invoices for March.

The other half of b04/refresh/with-coupon: same setup, same late event, `finalize_invoice` instead of `refresh_invoice`. Fees are identical, 3_000¢, and for a reason worth pinning: finalization recomputes unconditionally. `RefreshDraftAndFinalizeService` calls `RefreshDraftService` with `context: :finalize` (`refresh_draft_and_finalize_service.rb:23`) without consulting `ready_to_be_refreshed`, so the 20 late units are picked up whether or not anything flagged the draft. Now the coupon lands. `finalizing_invoice?` is true (`calculate_fees_service.rb:420-422`), so `should_create_coupon_credit?` passes and `Credits::AppliedCouponsService` allocates the fixed 2_000¢ against the 3_000¢ base: `coupons_amount_cents` 2_000¢, base 1_000¢, no tax, 1_000¢ due. The applied coupon is spent here and only here — `credit_amount (2_000) >= remaining_amount (2_000)` terminates it (`applied_coupon_service.rb:78-86`). `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` is asserted separately from the total because with no tax the two coincide; it is the field that would betray a coupon applied AFTER tax, which on a 20%-taxed version of this invoice would cost the customer 400¢ more.

b04/refresh/with-credit-note finalized instead of refreshed, so the two rows differ in exactly one verb and every number that moves is attributable to it. March invoice 3_000¢, credited 1_000¢ of its charge fee. The note is `finalized` because `credit_note_status` copies the invoice's status (`credit_notes/create_service.rb:168-173`) and `Credits::CreditNoteService` only looks at finalized, available notes (`credit_note_service.rb:74-82`) — a note raised against a draft would be a draft note and silently ineligible. April invoice: 10 units on time plus 20 timestamped 20 April and ingested on 2 May, recomputed by the finalize path to 3_000¢. Now `should_create_credit_note_credit?` is true, so the note is applied post-tax at `calculate_fees_service.rb:61`: `compute_credit_amount` takes `min(balance 1_000, remaining 3_000)` = 1_000¢, the invoice owes 2_000¢, and the note is consumed to a 0 balance (`credit_note_service.rb:96-102`). Two ways to get this wrong are excluded: the note is not applied twice (the refresh row proves the draft left it alone, so 1_000¢ and not 2_000¢ is available), and it is not spread by gross fee amount — with a single non-zero fee there is nothing to spread, which is why the weighting cases live in B17 rather than here.

b04/refresh/with-prepaid-credit finalized, and the point where the wallet actually moves. Fees 3_000¢ (10 units on time, 20 timestamped 20 March and ingested on 2 April — finalization recomputes unconditionally). Prepaid credit is the LAST reducer, spent on the post-tax total: `should_create_applied_prepaid_credit?` now passes, `AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService` caps each fee at `sub_total_excluding_taxes + taxes − precise_credit_notes` = 3_000¢ and takes `min(fee cap 3_000, wallet balance 2_000, remaining invoice 3_000)` (`allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:53`) = 2_000¢. So 2_000¢ of credit, 1_000¢ due in cash, and the wallet drained to 0 by the outbound transaction and `Wallets::Balance::DecreaseService` (`applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:28-36`). The wallet is asserted on both rows of the pair because that is the only field that distinguishes "the draft did not spend it" from "the draft spent it and the invoice reports it late": here 0, there 2_000¢. Note what is NOT here — the granted credit is spent in full and the invoice keeps a positive balance, so `payment_status` stays pending. A wallet large enough to cover the invoice would issue it `succeeded` instead.

The exception that proves the gate. For coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit the draft and the issued invoice DISAGREE — compare b04/refresh/with-coupon with b04/finalize/with-coupon. For progressive billing they must AGREE, and this row is b04/refresh/with-progressive-billing run to the same numbers through the other verb: 10_000¢ of fees, 6_000¢ credited, 4_000¢ due. They agree because `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService` is called at `calculate_fees_service.rb:53`, before the `not_in_finalizing_process?` gate that holds the other three back at lines 54, 61 and 62. Nothing about the credit depends on `context`, so a draft and a finalization of the same period compute the same 6_000¢: `to_credit_amount` is the threshold invoice's collected amount (`progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63`), capped by the 10_000¢ of creditable charge fees. That is also why it is safe to expose on a draft while a coupon is not — the threshold invoice was already finalized and paid for by the customer, so crediting it back cannot consume anything a refresh would have to return. `payment_status: pending` is asserted because 4_000¢ remains owed (`calculate_fees_service.rb:64`); had the credit covered the fees entirely the invoice would be issued `succeeded` with nothing to collect.

A preview is worth something only if it equals the invoice it predicts, so the same numbers are asserted twice — and with no reducer in play, a preview and a DRAFT are the two computations that should agree. The preview is a projection, not a proposal: the step sends `subscriptions.external_ids` for the persisted subscription (`golden_runner.rb:496-508`), so `PreviewService#add_charge_fees` does not return early and real usage is aggregated. A proposal — no external_ids, a top-level `plan_code` — would report 0 fees here and look like a broken preview. Taken on 25 March, `billing_time` is `end_of_periods.first + 1.day` = 1 April (`preview_service.rb:139-149`), so the previewed period is March and the 30 units already ingested price at 3_000¢. The 1 April invoice bills the same March period to the same 3_000¢. The grace period is what makes this cell distinct from b04/preview/no-grace-period, and it changes exactly one thing: `status` is `draft` rather than `finalized`. It does NOT change either arithmetic — the grace period only shifts `issuing_date` (`preview_service.rb:154-163`, `issuing_date_service.rb:17-18`), a field no golden row may pin. The three zeroes are asserted rather than omitted because a draft is fees plus tax and nothing else, and preview only mirrors that while there is nothing to mirror; b04/preview/with-coupon is the same setup with a coupon, and there the two surfaces legitimately disagree.

The sibling of b04/preview/grace-period, and the one that puts a non-zero subscription fee in the preview so both producers are exercised rather than only the charge. Plan 50.00 monthly in arrears plus 30 units × 1.00: the 1 April invoice carries two fees, 5_000¢ for 1–31 March and 3_000¢ of usage, 8_000¢ in total, and it is `finalized` on creation because this customer has no grace period. The preview taken on 25 March predicts that same invoice — `billing_time` = 1 April, so the subscription fee spans the whole March period rather than being prorated to the preview date, and `should_create_subscription_fee?` is unconditionally true in the `:default` preview context (`preview_service.rb:422-426`). 8_000¢ both ways. That agreement is not free: preview does not share the invoice pipeline at all, it reimplements the totals in `#compute_tax_and_totals` (`preview_service.rb:289-320`). This row and b04/preview/grace-period together pin the useful invariant — preview matches the issued invoice AND the draft, so the grace period is not something a caller has to reason about when reading a preview. `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` is asserted on the preview because that field is where preview's own arithmetic is visible: it is recomputed as `fees − coupons − progressive_billing_credit` (`preview_service.rb:298-300`) rather than carried over, so with nothing to subtract it must equal the 8_000¢ of fees.

The row where a preview and a draft MUST disagree, and both sides are pinned so neither can be "fixed" into the other. Same 3_000¢ of fees on both surfaces: 30 units × 1.00 for March, previewed on 25 March with `billing_time` = 1 April and billed on 1 April. Preview applies the coupon. `Invoices::PreviewContextService#find_or_build_applied_coupons` reads the customer's own ACTIVE applied coupons first and only falls back to the request's `coupons` array when there are none (`preview_context_service.rb:98-105`), and `Coupons::PreviewService` then allocates the fixed 2_000¢ against the 3_000¢ base and writes `coupons_amount_cents` (`coupons/preview_service.rb:62-63`). Base 1_000¢, no tax, 1_000¢ quoted. The draft does not. `should_create_coupon_credit?` is gated on finalization (`calculate_fees_service.rb:368-373`), so the 1 April draft shows `coupons_amount_cents: 0` and 3_000¢ owing. Both are correct. The preview answers "what will this invoice cost me", and the invoice WILL cost 1_000¢ once issued — b04/finalize/with-coupon shows exactly that. The draft answers "what has been computed so far", and allocating the discount early would spend a `once` coupon that every subsequent refresh would have to give back. Reading the draft as the preview's ground truth is how a working preview gets reported as a 2_000¢ bug; reading the preview as the draft's would hide the gate. Preview also leaves the coupon alone: `Coupons::PreviewService` never calls `mark_as_terminated!`, so the applied coupon is still active for the real invoice — if it did not, the mere act of previewing would consume the customer's discount.

Preview against a FINALIZED invoice this time, because the interesting question for a credit note is whether the quote spends it and whether previewing consumes it. The 1 April invoice bills March at 3_000¢ (30 units); 1_000¢ of its charge fee is then credited → note `available`, balance 1_000¢. 30 more units are ingested on 10 April, inside the April period. Preview on 25 April: `billing_time` = `end_of_periods.first + 1.day` = 1 May, so the previewed period is April with its 30 units = 3_000¢, and `Invoices::Preview::CreditsService` calls `Credits::CreditNoteService` with `context: :preview` (`preview/credits_service.rb:23-27`). The credit is `min(balance 1_000, remaining 3_000)` = 1_000¢ → 2_000¢ quoted. 1 May invoice: the same 3_000¢, the same 1_000¢ of note, 2_000¢ due. They agree, which is the assertion — and the reason they can is that the preview wrote nothing: every persistence step in `Credits::CreditNoteService` is skipped under `context == :preview` (`credit_note_service.rb:44-63`), so no `Credit` row is saved, no fee is re-weighted and `update_remaining_credit` is not called. The note is consumed exactly once, by the real invoice, and ends at 0. That last point is what the `credit_note` assertion is for. Had preview consumed it, the note would be at 0 before 1 May, the real invoice would apply nothing and bill 3_000¢, and the two surfaces would disagree by the entire credit — a preview that costs the customer their credit note merely by being requested.

Preview quotes prepaid credit, and the wallet proves it quoted rather than spent. Both surfaces price March at 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ and both apply 2_000¢ of wallet: `min(fee cap 3_000, wallet balance 2_000, remaining invoice 3_000)` = 2_000¢, leaving 1_000¢. Preview reaches that number through `Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService` (`preview_service.rb:369-378`), the real invoice through `Credits::AppliedPrepaidCreditsService`, which calls the SAME allocator (`applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:26`) and then creates the outbound transaction the allocator itself never creates. That shared allocator is why the two agree; a preview that reimplemented the per-fee cap would be free to drift from it. `balance_cents: 0` is the load-bearing assertion. It is 0 because the 1 April invoice spent the credits, not because the 25 March preview did — the allocator only returns a `{wallet => amount}` hash and writes nothing (`allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:29-67`). If previewing did burn credits, the wallet would be empty before 1 April, the real invoice would apply 0 and bill 3_000¢, and the row would fail on the invoice rather than on the wallet. Contrast the draft surface: b04/refresh/with-prepaid-credit leaves the wallet at 2_000¢ because a draft is gated out of prepaid credit entirely, so preview agrees with the ISSUED invoice here and would disagree with a draft of the same period by the full 2_000¢.

A preview is only worth anything if it equals the invoice it predicts, so this row asserts the same three numbers twice: once on the real period invoice and once on the preview taken while usage is already final. 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ crosses the 5_000¢ threshold, so a threshold invoice bills the whole 10_000¢ on 5 March. The period invoice on 1 April re-bills the same 10_000¢ and credits the 10_000¢ already invoiced, settling at 0 — nothing more is owed. The preview, taken on 25 March with no further usage, predicts the 1 April invoice: Preview's `billing_time` for a persisted subscription is `end_of_periods.first + 1.day`, so it is the same invoice, and it must therefore also read 0.

The customer's three-day grace period holds April's invoice open as a draft, worth 1_000¢ from the single March event. A second event then arrives LATE — ingested on 2 April but timestamped 20 March, so it belongs to the period already drafted. Refreshing recomputes the draft from its period and picks it up: 10 + 20 = 30 units → 3_000¢. Late-arriving usage is the whole reason grace periods exist, and a refresh that failed to see it would under-bill silently.

The control for b04/refresh/grace-period, and the reason the grace period is the context axis: the same late event, the same refresh call, and a completely different outcome. With no grace period the April invoice is finalized the moment it is created (`subscription_service.rb:193` sets draft only when `grace_period?`), so `PUT /invoices/:id/refresh` bails at `refresh_draft_service.rb:34` — `return result unless invoice.draft?` — before it recomputes anything. It answers HTTP 200 with the invoice untouched, which is why this row asserts a *successful* no-op rather than an error. So the 20 units timestamped 20 March, ingested on 2 April, are never billed: the invoice stays at the 10 units it saw on time, 1_000¢. b04/refresh/grace-period runs the identical timeline against a draft and reaches 3_000¢. A refresh that ignored the draft guard would show 3_000¢ here too, re-opening an issued invoice; one that returned an error instead would fail on the HTTP status.

Two things must both be true, so both are asserted: the refresh DID recompute the period, and it did NOT spend the coupon. Recompute: 10 units billed on time plus 20 units timestamped 20 March but ingested on 2 April = 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ of charge, exactly as in b04/refresh/grace-period. No coupon: `Invoices::CalculateFeesService#should_create_coupon_credit?` (`calculate_fees_service.rb:368-373`) returns false unless the invoice is being finalized, and a plain refresh passes `context: :refresh` (`refresh_draft_service.rb:7`). So `coupons_amount_cents` is 0 and the taxable base is the full 3_000¢. That gating is deliberate, not an oversight: this coupon is `frequency: once`, and `Credits::AppliedCouponService#should_terminate_applied_coupon?` would terminate the applied coupon the moment it were spent (`applied_coupon_service.rb:78-86`). A draft that consumed it would have to give it back on every subsequent refresh. b04/finalize/with-coupon runs this identical timeline and finalizes instead — 3_000¢ of fees, 2_000¢ of coupon, 1_000¢ due. A draft showing 1_000¢ here would mean the discount had been allocated before the invoice was issued.

A credit note needs a finalized invoice to be raised against, so March is issued explicitly (`finalize_invoice`) before the note is created; the note is then still unspent when April's invoice is drafted, which is the state this cell is about. March invoice: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢. `credit_notes_amount_cents` on it is 0 — that field counts notes CONSUMED by an invoice, not notes issued against it. Crediting 1_000¢ of its charge fee with no tax gives an item of 1_000¢ and a credit of 1_000¢ (`credit_notes/create_service.rb:68-72` sets `balance_amount_cents` from `credit_amount_cents`). April invoice: 10 units on time plus 20 units timestamped 20 April and ingested on 2 May, so the refresh recomputes it to 3_000¢. It applies nothing: `should_create_credit_note_credit?` is `!not_in_finalizing_process?` (`calculate_fees_service.rb:364-366`), false for `context: :refresh`, so `Credits::CreditNoteService` never runs and the note keeps its full 1_000¢ balance and `available` status. The credit note is asserted through `select` on purpose — without a selector the harness compares against the payload captured at creation time, which cannot show whether the refresh consumed it. b04/finalize/with-credit-note is the same timeline finalized instead: 1_000¢ consumed, 2_000¢ due, note `consumed` with balance 0. A draft that spent the note would show 2_000¢ here and would owe the customer their credit back on the next refresh.

The refresh recomputes the period — 10 units on time plus 20 timestamped 20 March and ingested on 2 April = 3_000¢ — and spends none of the wallet. `should_create_applied_prepaid_credit?` (`calculate_fees_service.rb:375-379`) returns false unless the invoice is being finalized, so `Credits::AppliedPrepaidCreditsService` never runs, the invoice reports `prepaid_credit_amount_cents` 0 and the wallet still holds its 20 granted credits at rate 1.00 = 2_000¢. The wallet is asserted as well as the invoice because the invoice alone cannot distinguish "not spent" from "spent and returned": prepaid credit is consumed by creating an OUTBOUND wallet transaction and decreasing the balance (`applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:95-108`), so a draft that had spent it would leave the balance at 0 even if a later refresh reset the invoice field. b04/finalize/with-prepaid-credit finalizes the identical timeline: 2_000¢ applied, 1_000¢ due, wallet emptied. Spending prepaid credit on a draft is the case that gating exists to prevent — every refresh would have to unwind a real money movement.

Progressive billing is the ONE reducer a draft carries, so this is the cell where a refresh has to re-run a credit rather than skip one. Threshold invoice: 60 units × 1.00 = 6_000¢ crosses the 5_000¢ threshold on 5 March, and a threshold is a trigger not a cap, so it bills the whole 6_000¢. It is finalized regardless of the grace period — `Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService` calls `FinalizeService.call!` unconditionally (`progressive_billing_service.rb:47`) — which matters because `Subscriptions::ProgressiveBilledAmount` only counts finalized or failed invoices (`progressive_billed_amount.rb:29-33`). The threshold fires once: afterwards `invoiced_usage` (6_000¢) is above the only fixed threshold and there is no recurring one, so `LifetimeUsages::UsageThresholds::CheckService:36-46` selects nothing more. Period draft, after the 40 late units timestamped 20 March arrive on 2 April and the refresh recomputes: 100 units = 10_000¢ of charge. The credit is re-derived from scratch — `reset_invoice_values` destroys the old progressive-billing credits and zeroes `progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents` (`refresh_draft_service.rb:130-138`), then `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService` runs at `calculate_fees_service.rb:53`, AHEAD of the `not_in_finalizing_process?` gate that blocks coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit. `to_credit_amount` is the threshold invoice's own figure, 6_000¢ less nothing (`progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63`), and 6_000¢ is under the 10_000¢ of creditable charge fees, so no excess credit note is raised and the credit is 6_000¢. Base 10_000 − 6_000 = 4_000¢, no tax, 4_000¢ due. Crediting the 10_000¢ now billed instead of the 6_000¢ actually collected would settle at 0 and lose 4_000¢ of revenue. This row is deliberately tax-free: with tax it would also trip the fee-level clamp recorded by b17/full-stack/invoice, which is a different finding.

A draft cannot be voided, and this is the row that says so in numbers rather than in prose. The grace period holds April's 3_000¢ invoice open as a draft. `POST /invoices/:id/void` reaches `invoice.void!`, and the state machine only permits that transition `from: :finalized` (`invoice.rb:184-186`), so AASM raises `InvalidTransition`, `Invoices::VoidService` rescues it at line 62-63 into `not_allowed_failure!(code: "not_voidable")`, and the surrounding `with_lock` transaction rolls back. The invoice is left exactly as it was: still `draft`, still 3_000¢. Everything the service does after the transition is therefore skipped as well — no lifetime-usage reflag, no coupon recredit, no wallet recredit — which is the reason the other four void rows all have to reach a finalized invoice first. The correct way to discard a draft is `mark_as_deleted` (`invoice.rb:180-182`), a different transition to a different terminal state; voiding is reserved for invoices that were actually issued, because a voided invoice keeps its number and its amounts as a record of what was billed. A row that read `voided` here would mean an invoice could be voided before it ever existed as a document.

With no grace period the invoice is finalized on creation, so voiding it is the only way back. Voiding changes `status` and nothing else: fees_amount_cents and total_amount_cents still read 3_000¢. That is deliberate — a voided invoice remains a record of what was billed rather than being zeroed — and it is why a voided invoice must be excluded by status when summing revenue, not by trusting its total to be 0.

Voiding gives a spent coupon back, and the only way to observe that is to spend it again. April invoice: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢, the fixed 2_000¢ coupon applied before tax → 1_000¢ due. The coupon is `frequency: once` and `credit_amount (2_000) >= remaining_amount (2_000)`, so `Credits::AppliedCouponService` terminates the applied coupon (`applied_coupon_service.rb:78-86`). On its own, that ends it: May would be billed the full 3_000¢. Voiding April changes that. `Invoices::VoidService` walks `invoice.credits` and calls `AppliedCoupons::RecreditService` for every credit carrying an `applied_coupon_id` (`void_service.rb:37-39`); `should_reactivate_coupon?` is satisfied (not `forever`, coupon itself not terminated), so the applied coupon goes back to `active` with `terminated_at` cleared (`recredit_service.rb:21-25`). May invoice: 30 more units = 3_000¢, and the resurrected coupon takes 2_000¢ again → 1_000¢ due. Without the recredit May would read `coupons_amount_cents: 0` and `total_amount_cents: 3_000`, so the second invoice is what makes this row discriminating; asserting only the voided invoice would pass whether or not the coupon came back. The voided invoice keeps its own 3_000¢/2_000¢/1_000¢ — voiding never rewrites amounts (`handle_void_transition!` touches only `voided_at` and the payment flags, `invoice.rb:644-650`), which is why revenue must be summed by excluding voided STATUS rather than by trusting the total.

The asymmetry in what voiding gives back, and the reason this row asserts the credit note rather than only the invoice. April invoice 3_000¢, credited 1_000¢ of its charge fee, note `available` with a 1_000¢ balance. May invoice: 30 more units = 3_000¢, the note applied post-tax for `min(balance 1_000, remaining 3_000)` = 1_000¢ → 2_000¢ due, note consumed to a 0 balance (`credit_note_service.rb:96-102`). May is then voided, and `Invoices::VoidService` recredits exactly two things: applied coupons (`void_service.rb:37-39`) and outbound wallet transactions (`void_service.rb:46-49`). Credit-note credits are in neither list, and nothing else in the service touches `credit_note.balance_amount_cents`, so the derivation says the note stays `consumed` at 0 even though the invoice that consumed it no longer bills anything. The customer's 1_000¢ of credit is spent against a voided document. Compare b04/void/with-coupon, where the identical structure — a reducer spent on an invoice that is then voided — does give the value back, and b04/void/with-prepaid-credit, where the wallet is refilled. Same pipeline, same void, three different answers, and only one of the three loses the customer money. The note is read through `select` deliberately: without a selector the harness would compare against the payload captured at creation time, which still shows `available` / 1_000¢ and would make this row pass while asserting nothing about the void at all.

Voiding refills the wallet, and the wallet is the only place that shows it. April invoice: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢, finalized on creation because the customer has no grace period, so prepaid credit is applied straight away: `min(fee cap 3_000, wallet balance 2_000, remaining invoice 3_000)` = 2_000¢ (`allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:53`), leaving 1_000¢ due and the wallet at 0. Voiding takes the `generate_credit_note` = false branch, so `WalletTransactions::RecreditService` runs for each outbound transaction on the invoice (`void_service.rb:46-49`) and creates a fresh inbound grant of the same 20.0 credits with `reset_consumed_credits: true` (`recredit_service.rb:25-34`). The balance returns to 2_000¢. The invoice keeps `prepaid_credit_amount_cents: 2_000` and a 1_000¢ total: a voided invoice is a record of what was billed and what was applied to it, not a reversal of those figures. So the invoice fields alone cannot tell a refilled wallet from a drained one — reading only the invoice, this row and b04/finalize/with-prepaid-credit are indistinguishable, and only `balance_cents` (2_000¢ here, 0 there) separates them. Note the branch that is NOT taken: with `generate_credit_note` the wallet is deliberately not recredited because its value is counted into the creditable amount instead (`void_service.rb:41-49`). The harness's void step sends no parameters, so this row is the recredit branch.

Voiding a threshold invoice must un-credit the period invoice, or the customer pays nothing at all. 5 March: 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ crosses the 5_000¢ threshold, and a threshold invoice is finalized on creation (`progressive_billing_service.rb:47`), so it is voidable immediately. It is voided on 6 March and keeps its 10_000¢ — voiding never rewrites amounts. 1 April: the period invoice bills the same 100 units = 10_000¢ and credits NOTHING. `Subscriptions::ProgressiveBilledAmount` restricts its search to `Invoice.finalized.or(Invoice.failed)` (`progressive_billed_amount.rb:29-33`), and a voided invoice is in neither, so `progressive_billing_invoice` comes back nil and `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService` returns at `progressive_billing_service.rb:24` without creating a credit. Base 10_000¢, no tax, 10_000¢ due — the whole period, collected once. Had the voided invoice still counted, `to_credit_amount` would be 10_000¢, the credit would cover the fees exactly and the invoice would settle at 0 with `payment_status: succeeded`: the customer would be credited for an invoice that was cancelled and pay for March twice over — that is, never. `invoices: 2` also matters. The threshold does not re-fire after the void even though the billed amount has vanished, because `LifetimeUsages::UsageThresholds::CheckService` measures `invoiced_usage` from finalized invoices, and by the time thresholds are re-checked the 1 April invoice has itself invoiced the 10_000¢ (`check_service.rb:28-46`). A third invoice here would mean the void re-armed a threshold that had already been served.

Usage lands EXACTLY on the threshold: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ against a 3_000¢ threshold. The boundary is inclusive — reaching the threshold triggers billing, it does not have to be exceeded — so the same two invoices appear as in the previous row. An off-by-one that required strictly greater-than would produce a single invoice here and nothing would look wrong until the customer was billed a period late.

An exact hit that later has to be given back — the two behaviours the block treats separately, on one invoice pair. 5 March, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents against a 3_000 threshold. check_service.rb:40 is `threshold.amount_cents <= total_usage`, inclusive, so exactly-on fires and the invoice bills 3_000. At 2_999 (`amount: 29.99`) nothing fires, there is one invoice, no credit note, and the customer is billed 2_999 in April instead — so this row fails on the invoice count AND on the absence of the credit note if that comparison ever loses its equality. 15 March the latest event drops to 5 units = 500, so the period is worth 500 and no further threshold can arm (actual_current_usage 500 - 3_000 is negative, :25-27). 1 April: `to_credit_amount` 3_000 against `total_charges_amount` 500 (credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:26-34), so :36-42 refunds 3_000 - 500 = 2_500 as a credit note on the threshold invoice and credits 500 to the period invoice, which settles at 0. 2_500 is grossed up by nothing (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:69-79, no tax, no coupon), so credit_amount_cents, balance and total all read 2_500. Cash: 3_000 in, 2_500 back, 500 kept.

An exact hit whose period then ends early. 5 April, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents against a 3_000 threshold: check_service.rb:40 is inclusive, so it fires and bills 3_000. At 2_999 nothing fires and the termination invoice on 16 April is the only invoice, carrying 2_999 due — so the row fails on the invoice count as well as on the amounts. Terminating on 16 April bills the usage consumed in the shortened period, which is the same 30 units = 3_000, and credits the 3_000 already taken: total 0. The credit survives the shortened period because the lookup is by the invoice's `charges_from_datetime` (1 April) against the threshold invoice's own window, which still runs to 30 April (credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:20-21, progressive_billed_amount.rb:34-41). Keying it on the period END would find nothing here and bill the customer 6_000 for 3_000 of usage.

Two non-recurring thresholds on one plan, crossed at two different moments: three invoices describe one period and all three are asserted. Which thresholds arm is decided by check_service.rb:39-41 — `threshold.amount_cents > invoiced_usage && threshold.amount_cents <= total_usage` — where `invoiced_usage` is the last threshold invoice's own fees (check_service.rb:28 feeding on progressive_billed_amount.rb:58) and `total_usage` is everything accrued. 5 March, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents accrued: invoiced_usage 0, total_usage 3_000, so the 2_000 threshold arms and the 5_000 one does not. progressive_billing_service.rb:94-107 then bills the FULL accrued usage over the whole period boundaries (:118-136), so the demand is 3_000 cents, not the 2_000 of the threshold. 12 March, +50 units = 8_000 cents accrued: invoiced_usage is now 3_000, total_usage 8_000, so the 5_000 threshold arms while the 2_000 one is excluded by `> invoiced_usage` — it cannot fire twice. The second threshold invoice re-bills the whole 8_000 and credits the first invoice's 3_000 back (credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:20-58), demanding 5_000 of new cash. 3_000 + 5_000 = 8_000 collected, exactly the usage. 1 April the period invoice re-computes the same 8_000 of fees and credits `to_credit_amount`, which reads ONLY the last threshold invoice (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63): 8_000 cents. That is right because threshold invoices are cumulative and each already credited its predecessor. Summing every threshold invoice instead would credit 11_000 and hand the customer 3_000 they never paid; taking the FIRST invoice instead would credit 3_000 and charge the 5_000 a second time. Both are visible here and neither can be seen in a single-crossing row.

Two threshold invoices, then a collapse — the case that decides WHICH invoice the refund comes off. 5 March, latest event 30 units = 3_000: the 2_000 threshold arms, invoice 1 bills 3_000. 12 March, latest event 80 units = 8_000: invoiced_usage is 3_000, so check_service.rb:39-41 arms 5_000 only; invoice 2 re-bills 8_000, credits invoice 1's 3_000 and demands 5_000. Cash so far 3_000 + 5_000 = 8_000. 20 March, latest event 10 units = 1_000. `actual_current_usage` = 1_000 - 8_000 is negative (check_service.rb:25-27), so nothing further arms. 1 April the period's charges are 1_000. `to_credit_amount` reads only the LAST threshold invoice (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63) = 8_000, which is the whole cash position precisely because invoice 2 already absorbed invoice 1. 8_000 > 1_000, so the credit note is raised on invoice 2 for 7_000 and the credit clamps to 1_000. Invoice 1 gets NO credit note, and that is the assertion: refunding both invoices, or refunding the first, would return 10_000 or 3_000 against 8_000 of cash. 8_000 - 7_000 = 1_000 kept, exactly what the period is worth. The note has one item: create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:46-58 walks invoice 2's fees largest-first and its single 8_000 fee covers the 7_000 in one go.

TWO threshold invoices and then a termination — the case where the "last threshold invoice" lookup and the shortened-period lookup have to be right at the same time. 5 April, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents arms the 2_000 threshold (check_service.rb:39-41, invoiced_usage 0) and is billed in full. 10 April, +50 units = 8_000 accrued: invoiced_usage is now 3_000 so the 2_000 rung is excluded by `> invoiced_usage` and the 5_000 one arms. Invoice 2 re-bills 8_000 and credits invoice 1's 3_000, demanding 5_000. Cash 3_000 + 5_000 = 8_000. Terminating on 16 April closes the period there and bills the consumed usage in arrears — the same 100 units accrued before termination, so 8_000 of charge. The credit is `to_credit_amount` of the LAST threshold invoice (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63) = 8_000, so nothing more is owed and no credit note is issued (8_000 is not GREATER than the 8_000 of charges, so credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36 is false). Two wrong answers are excluded: crediting invoice 1 only would leave 5_000 due for usage already paid, and crediting the sum 11_000 would exceed the 8_000 of charges, trip the :36 branch and refund 3_000 the customer never overpaid.

30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ of accrued usage crosses the 2_000¢ threshold, and the mid-period progressive_billing invoice then bills ALL accrued usage — 3_000¢, not the 2_000¢ of the threshold. The threshold is a TRIGGER, not a cap; billing only up to it would leave the remaining 1_000¢ uncollected until period end. At period end the subscription invoice re-computes the same 3_000¢ of fees and credits back everything already collected, so progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents is 3_000¢ and nothing further is owed. fees_amount_cents stays 3_000: the credit reduces what is due, not what was charged — the same shape as a wallet in B6, and the reason double-billing here is invisible in the fees total.

Money already taken for a period that then shrinks. 5 March a single event of 100 units x 1.00 = 10_000 cents crosses the 5_000 threshold and is billed in full — one crossing, one threshold invoice of 10_000. 15 March a second event of 20 units arrives. With `latest_agg` the period is now worth the LAST event only (latest_service.rb:17-19), so accrued usage falls to 2_000. No further threshold can arm: check_service.rb:25-27 computes `actual_current_usage = current - progressive_billed` = 2_000 - 10_000 = -8_000 and returns immediately on the negative. 1 April the period invoice's charges are 2_000 while `to_credit_amount` is still the threshold invoice's 10_000 (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63: fees, less its own coupons, less credits pointing AT it, less credit notes on it — all zero here). credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:26-31 measures what the period can absorb — `total_charges_amount` = 2_000, the charge fees sharing the threshold invoice's charge_id — and :36-42 finds 10_000 > 2_000, so it issues a credit note on the THRESHOLD invoice for 10_000 - 2_000 = 8_000 and clamps the credit to 2_000. The credit note is 8_000 exactly: create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:41-58 takes items off the threshold invoice's fees largest-first (one 10_000 fee, creditable 10_000, so a single 8_000 item) and :69-79 grosses it up by taxes less coupon adjustment — both zero — giving credit_amount_cents 8_000, balance 8_000, total 8_000 (create_service.rb:68-73). The period invoice therefore reads 2_000 of fees fully credited, total 0, and credit_notes_amount_cents 0 — the 8_000 is NOT spent on it, because credit_note_service.rb:41-47 starts from `invoice.total_amount_cents`, which the progressive credit already took to 0. Net cash: 10_000 collected, 8_000 returned as credit, 2_000 kept — the period's real value. Had the clamp at :41 been omitted the period invoice would carry a 10_000 credit against 2_000 of fees and a negative total; had the credit-note branch been omitted the customer would simply keep paying 10_000 for 2_000 of usage.

A threshold invoice is money taken for a period that then ends early, so the credit has to survive a boundary the customer never reached. 100 units on 5 April cross the 5_000¢ threshold and are billed immediately — 10_000¢. Terminating on 16 April closes the period there and bills the consumed usage, which is the same 100 units, so the final invoice is 10_000¢ of charges credited by the 10_000¢ already collected: nothing more is owed. The credit survives because ProgressiveBillingService looks the threshold invoice up by the charges_from_datetime of the invoice being built (1 April), not by the period's end, and the threshold invoice's own window still contains it. Had it matched on the period end instead, the shortened period would find nothing and the customer would pay 20_000¢ for 10_000¢ of usage. The plan bills in arrears and carries no subscription fee, so the only thing on either invoice is the charge — which is what makes the double-charge visible rather than buried in a proration.

The LOWEST rung of a three-threshold ladder, hit exactly, with two higher thresholds present to prove they do not interfere. 20 units x 1.00 = 2_000 cents against fixed 2_000 / fixed 5_000 / recurring 4_000. invoiced 0 < largest 5_000, so the fixed branch runs and check_service.rb:40 asks `2_000 > 0 && 2_000 <= 2_000` — true on the inclusive upper bound, so exactly one threshold arms. The recurring guard at :43 sees 2_000 - 5_000, negative, and stays out. One cent below (`amount: 19.99`, 1_999 cents) nothing arms and the whole period is a single invoice of 1_999 a month later; one cent above, 2_001, the same single threshold arms and bills 2_001. So `<=` becoming `<` at :40 collapses this row from two invoices to one, and the failure names the invoice count. Settlement: fees 2_000, `to_credit_amount` 2_000, credited in full, nothing owed. The higher fixed threshold and the recurring one contribute nothing — which is the assertion, since a ladder that armed everything at or below the largest threshold would demand 2_000 and then re-demand it.

The lowest rung of a three-threshold ladder, hit exactly, and then refunded almost entirely. 5 March, 20 units x 1.00 = 2_000 cents. invoiced 0 < largest fixed 5_000, so the fixed branch runs and check_service.rb:40 asks `2_000 > 0 && 2_000 <= 2_000` — the inclusive bound is what arms it. 5_000 is above total usage and the recurring guard at :43 sees 2_000 - 5_000, negative, so exactly one threshold arms and the invoice bills 2_000. At 1_999 nothing arms: no threshold invoice, no credit note, one invoice of 1_999 in April. 15 March the latest event falls to 4 units = 400. 1 April: charges 400 against `to_credit_amount` 2_000, so 1_600 comes back as a credit note on the threshold invoice and 400 is credited. Period invoice 0, cash kept 400. The two idle thresholds are the point of the `multiple` shape here: neither the higher fixed rung nor the recurring one may change the exact hit or the size of the refund.

The lowest rung of a three-threshold ladder, hit exactly, on a period cut short. 5 April, 20 units x 1.00 = 2_000 cents. invoiced 0 < largest fixed 5_000, so the fixed branch runs and check_service.rb:40 asks `2_000 > 0 && 2_000 <= 2_000` — the inclusive upper bound is what arms it. 5_000 is above total usage and the recurring guard at :43 sees 2_000 - 5_000, negative. One threshold arms, one invoice, 2_000 billed. At 1_999 nothing arms and the 16 April termination invoice is the only invoice, carrying 1_999 due. Terminating on 16 April bills the consumed 2_000 and credits the 2_000 collected: total 0. The two idle thresholds must change neither the exact hit nor the credit — which is what makes this distinct from b05/fixed/exact-hit/terminated-mid-period rather than a copy of it.

The hand-off from the fixed ladder to the recurring threshold, which no other cell in this block reaches: check_service.rb:36 chooses between two entirely different branches on `invoiced_usage < largest_threshold_amount`, and this row crosses that line mid-period. Thresholds: fixed 2_000 and 5_000, recurring 4_000, so `largest_threshold_amount` is 5_000. 5 March, 30 units = 3_000: invoiced 0 < 5_000, fixed branch, armed = [2_000] (5_000 > 3_000). Recurring guard 3_000 - 5_000 is negative, disarmed. Invoice 1 bills 3_000. 12 March, +40 units = 7_000 accrued: invoiced = 3_000, still < 5_000, fixed branch, armed = [5_000] (`> 3_000` drops 2_000, `<= 7_000` admits 5_000). Recurring guard 7_000 - 5_000 = 2_000 < 4_000, still disarmed. Invoice 2 bills 7_000 and credits 3_000, demanding 4_000. 20 March, +50 units = 12_000 accrued: invoiced = 7_000, and 7_000 < 5_000 is now FALSE, so the elsif at :47 takes over: remainder = 7_000 % 4_000 = 3_000, actual = 12_000 - 7_000 = 5_000, 5_000 + 3_000 = 8_000 >= 4_000, so the recurring threshold arms for the first time. Invoice 3 bills 12_000 and credits 7_000, demanding 5_000. Cash 3_000 + 4_000 + 5_000 = 12_000, exactly the usage. 1 April: fees 12_000, `to_credit_amount` = the LAST threshold invoice's fees = 12_000 (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63), so nothing is owed. If the two branches were merged — recurring armed while the ladder was unfinished — a fourth threshold invoice would appear on 12 March; if the modulo at :48 used the recurring amount against total usage instead of invoiced usage, 20 March would arm nothing and 5_000 would go uncollected until April.

The deepest chain this block reaches: the fixed ladder, then the recurring re-arm, then a collapse — four invoices and a refund, all asserted. Thresholds fixed 2_000 / 5_000 and recurring 4_000, so largest_threshold_amount is 5_000. 5 March, latest 30 units = 3_000: fixed branch (0 < 5_000), armed [2_000]; invoice 1 bills 3_000. 12 March, latest 70 units = 7_000: invoiced 3_000, still < 5_000, armed [5_000]; recurring guard 7_000 - 5_000 = 2_000 < 4_000. Invoice 2 bills 7_000, credits 3_000, demands 4_000. 18 March, latest 120 units = 12_000: invoiced 7_000, so `7_000 < 5_000` is false and check_service.rb:47-52 takes over — remainder 7_000 % 4_000 = 3_000, actual 12_000 - 7_000 = 5_000, 5_000 + 3_000 >= 4_000, so the recurring threshold arms. Invoice 3 bills 12_000, credits 7_000, demands 5_000. Cash 3_000 + 4_000 + 5_000 = 12_000. 25 March, latest 20 units = 2_000: `actual_current_usage` 2_000 - 12_000 is negative, nothing arms (:25-27). 1 April: charges 2_000 against `to_credit_amount` = invoice 3's 12_000 — the single latest threshold invoice, which is also exactly the cash collected because each invoice credited its predecessor (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63). 12_000 > 2_000, so credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42 refunds 10_000 on invoice 3 and clamps the credit to 2_000. Cash kept 2_000. Two failure modes are pinned here that a shallower chain cannot see: refunding against the SUM of the three threshold invoices would return 20_000 for 12_000 collected, and refunding against the FIRST would return 1_000 and leave 9_000 of the customer's money with Lago.

Three threshold invoices spanning the fixed-to-recurring hand-off, and then a termination eleven days before the period would have ended. Thresholds fixed 2_000 / 5_000 and recurring 4_000, largest fixed 5_000. 5 April, 30 units = 3_000: fixed branch, armed [2_000], invoice 1 bills 3_000. 9 April, +40 units = 7_000: invoiced 3_000 < 5_000, armed [5_000] (2_000 excluded by `> invoiced_usage`); recurring guard 7_000 - 5_000 = 2_000 < 4_000. Invoice 2 bills 7_000, credits 3_000, demands 4_000. 13 April, +50 units = 12_000: invoiced 7_000, so `7_000 < 5_000` is false and the recurring branch at check_service.rb:47-52 applies — remainder 7_000 % 4_000 = 3_000, actual 12_000 - 7_000 = 5_000, 5_000 + 3_000 >= 4_000. Invoice 3 bills 12_000, credits 7_000, demands 5_000. Cash 3_000 + 4_000 + 5_000 = 12_000. Terminating on 16 April bills the consumed 12_000 and credits `to_credit_amount` of the LAST threshold invoice = 12_000 (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63), so nothing is owed and the excess branch at credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36 is not entered — hence no credit note. Both wrong readings are excluded by the numbers on the page: summing the three invoices gives 20_000 against 12_000 of charges, which would clamp the credit and refund 8_000; taking the first gives 3_000 and leaves 9_000 due for usage already paid.

Three thresholds on one plan — two fixed and the one recurring one a plan is allowed (UsageThreshold:20-21) — and a single jump that passes TWO of them at once. The point of the row is that two armed thresholds still produce exactly ONE invoice. 60 units x 1.00 = 6_000 cents on 5 March. invoiced_usage 0, total_usage 6_000, so check_service.rb:39-41 arms both 2_000 and 5_000. The recurring one is guarded separately at :42-46 by `total_usage - largest_threshold_amount >= recurring_threshold.amount_cents`: 6_000 - 5_000 = 1_000, which is under 4_000, so it stays disarmed — the recurring threshold only starts counting once the whole fixed ladder is behind it. Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService is handed the armed set as one list and creates ONE invoice for it (progressive_billing_service.rb:15-19, with one AppliedUsageThreshold per threshold at :138-147), billing the accrued 6_000 once. An implementation that invoiced per armed threshold would produce three invoices here, and by billing accrued usage each time would demand 6_000 twice — 12_000 for 6_000 of usage. That is what `invoices: 2` pins, and it is unreachable from a plan with a single threshold. 1 April: fees 6_000, `to_credit_amount` 6_000, credited in full, nothing owed.

Two fixed thresholds armed at once on a plan that also holds a recurring one, then a collapse. 5 March, 60 units x 1.00 = 6_000 cents: invoiced 0 < largest fixed 5_000 so the fixed branch arms both 2_000 and 5_000 (check_service.rb:39-41), while the recurring guard at :43 sees 6_000 - 5_000 = 1_000 < 4_000 and stays out. Two armed thresholds, ONE invoice, billing the accrued 6_000 (progressive_billing_service.rb:15-19 takes the whole armed list). 15 March the latest event falls to 15 units = 1_500; nothing arms (1_500 - 6_000 negative). 1 April: charges 1_500, `to_credit_amount` 6_000, so 4_500 is refunded as a credit note on the single threshold invoice and 1_500 is credited — period invoice 0, cash kept 1_500. The refund is one note of 4_500, not one per armed threshold: credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42 is driven by the invoice, not by AppliedUsageThreshold, so the two thresholds that produced this invoice share its single refund. An implementation that refunded per threshold would return 9_000 against 6_000 collected.

Two fixed rungs armed in one jump on a plan that also holds a recurring threshold, then a termination. 5 April, 60 units x 1.00 = 6_000 cents: invoiced 0 < largest fixed 5_000, so the fixed branch arms both 2_000 and 5_000 (check_service.rb:39-41); the recurring guard at :43 sees 6_000 - 5_000 = 1_000 < 4_000 and stays out. Both armed thresholds go into ONE invoice (progressive_billing_service.rb:15-19), billing the accrued 6_000. Terminating on 16 April bills the consumed 6_000 and credits the 6_000 collected: total 0. An implementation invoicing per armed threshold would have produced two threshold invoices of 6_000 each, and the termination invoice would then credit only the later one — 6_000 credited against 12_000 collected, so the customer would be 6_000 out of pocket with a zero-total invoice to look at. `invoices: 2` is what stops that reading.

The recurring boundary, hit exactly. 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents against a 3_000 recurring threshold. The recurring branch is check_service.rb:48-52 and the comparison is `actual_current_usage + recurring_remainder >= recurring_threshold.amount_cents`: with invoiced_usage 0 the remainder is 0 and 3_000 >= 3_000 is true, so the threshold fires. The row sits on the boundary on purpose. One cent below — `amount: 29.99`, 2_999 cents — the comparison fails and there is ONE invoice, 2_999 cents charged a month later. One cent above, 3_001 cents, it fires and bills 3_001. So a `>` in place of `>=` at check_service.rb:50 turns `invoices: 3` worth of assertions here into a single invoice of 3_000, and the failure is the invoice count rather than a rounding argument. The settlement is the same shape as the fixed rows: 3_000 billed early, `to_credit_amount` = 3_000 (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63, nothing having reduced the threshold invoice), credited in full, nothing owed. That is deliberate — the recurring flag changes how often the trigger arms, never the settlement arithmetic.

The recurring boundary hit exactly, then refunded. 5 March, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents against a recurring 3_000 threshold: invoiced_usage 0 so the remainder is 0, and check_service.rb:50 asks `3_000 + 0 >= 3_000` — true only because the comparison is inclusive. At 2_999 (`amount: 29.99`) there is no threshold invoice and no credit note, so this row fails on both counts if the equality is ever lost. 15 March the latest event falls to 8 units = 800; nothing re-arms (actual 800 - 3_000 negative). 1 April: charges 800 against `to_credit_amount` 3_000, so credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42 refunds 2_200 on the threshold invoice and credits 800. Period invoice total 0; credit note available at 2_200; net cash kept 800.

The recurring boundary hit exactly, on a period that then ends early. 5 April, 30 units x 1.00 = 3_000 cents against a recurring 3_000 threshold: invoiced_usage 0 so the remainder is 0 and check_service.rb:50 asks `3_000 + 0 >= 3_000`, true on the equality. The invoice bills the accrued 3_000. At 2_999 nothing fires and the 16 April termination invoice is the only one, carrying 2_999 due. Terminating on 16 April bills the same 3_000 of consumed usage and credits the 3_000 already taken, so total 0 — the credit found through the threshold invoice's own still-open window (progressive_billed_amount.rb:34-41), not through the shortened period's end.

The recurring threshold is the only one that can fire twice for the same amount, and this is the row that makes it do so. With no fixed threshold `largest_threshold_amount` is 0 (check_service.rb:32), so `invoiced_usage < largest_threshold_amount` is false from the very first check and every crossing goes through the recurring branch at check_service.rb:47-52: `actual_current_usage + (invoiced_usage % R) >= R`. 5 March, 30 units = 3_000 cents: invoiced_usage 0, remainder 0, actual 3_000 >= 2_000, so it fires and bills all accrued usage — 3_000 cents. 12 March, +30 units = 6_000 accrued: invoiced_usage = the first invoice's fees = 3_000 (progressive_billed_amount.rb:58), remainder = 3_000 % 2_000 = 1_000, actual = 6_000 - 3_000 = 3_000, and 3_000 + 1_000 = 4_000 >= 2_000, so it re-arms. The second invoice re-bills 6_000 and credits the first's 3_000, demanding 3_000. Cash 3_000 + 3_000 = 6_000. Note this second invoice only exists because progressive_billing_service.rb:32-34 widens the idempotency key with `previous_progressive_billing_invoice_id` when the last armed threshold is recurring — without it the key (invoiced_usage 0, threshold_amount 2_000, :21-26) is identical to the first invoice's and the second demand is swallowed as a duplicate, leaving 3_000 of usage uncollected until period end. 1 April: fees 6_000, credit = the LAST threshold invoice's `to_credit_amount` = 6_000, nothing owed. Crediting the sum of both threshold invoices would give 9_000 and refund 3_000 that was never paid.

A recurring threshold firing twice and then having to hand most of it back. 5 March, 30 units = 3_000: remainder 0 % 2_000 = 0, 3_000 >= 2_000, invoice 1 bills 3_000. 12 March, latest event 60 units = 6_000: invoiced_usage = 3_000, remainder 3_000 % 2_000 = 1_000, actual 6_000 - 3_000 = 3_000, and 3_000 + 1_000 >= 2_000, so it re-arms (check_service.rb:48-52). Invoice 2 bills 6_000, credits 3_000, demands 3_000. Cash 6_000. 20 March the latest event falls to 10 units = 1_000 and nothing arms. 1 April: `to_credit_amount` is invoice 2's 6_000 — one figure, not the 9_000 the two invoices add up to, because invoice 2 already carries invoice 1's credit inside it (progressive_billed_amount.rb:55-63). Charges are 1_000, so 5_000 is refunded as a credit note on invoice 2 and 1_000 is credited. Cash 6_000 - 5_000 = 1_000, the period's value. A refund computed from the SUM of the threshold invoices would return 8_000 against 6_000 of cash — a 2_000 gift; one computed from invoice 1 would return 2_000 and keep 4_000 of the customer's money.

A recurring threshold that fires twice and then has its period cut short. 5 April, 30 units = 3_000: remainder 0 % 2_000 = 0, actual 3_000 >= 2_000, invoice 1 bills 3_000. 10 April, +30 units = 6_000 accrued: invoiced_usage 3_000, remainder 3_000 % 2_000 = 1_000, actual 3_000, and 3_000 + 1_000 >= 2_000, so it re-arms (check_service.rb:48-52). Invoice 2 re-bills 6_000, credits 3_000, demands 3_000. This second invoice exists only because progressive_billing_service.rb:32-34 adds `previous_progressive_billing_invoice_id` to the idempotency key for a recurring threshold — the rest of the key (:21-26) is identical between the two demands. Terminating on 16 April bills the consumed 6_000 and credits `to_credit_amount` of the LAST threshold invoice = 6_000, so nothing is owed. Cash 3_000 + 3_000 = 6_000 = the period's value. Crediting the sum of both threshold invoices would give 9_000, exceed the 6_000 of charges, trip the excess branch at credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36 and refund 3_000 that was never overpaid — which is why the credit-note count matters here even though this row expects none.

A RECURRING threshold re-arms after each crossing rather than firing once per period, so it bills every further 2_000¢ of usage. Over a single crossing the outcome is identical to the fixed row — 3_000¢ billed early, 3_000¢ credited back, nothing owed — which is deliberate: this row pins that the recurring flag does not change the settlement arithmetic, only how often the trigger arms. A plan may hold at most one recurring threshold (UsageThreshold validates uniqueness on [plan_id, recurring]), so this is the only shape it can take.

The same refund, reached through the recurring branch rather than the fixed one — the pair with b05/fixed/single/excess-to-credit-note, which is what makes it worth a row: it pins that the refund path does not depend on which branch armed the threshold. With no fixed threshold `largest_threshold_amount` is 0, so check_service.rb:36 is false from the start and the recurring test at :48-52 applies: remainder 0 % 5_000 = 0 and 10_000 >= 5_000, so 100 units x 1.00 = 10_000 cents is billed on 5 March. 15 March the latest event falls to 20 units = 2_000 and nothing re-arms — a recurring threshold re-arms on `actual_current_usage`, which is 2_000 - 10_000, negative, and :27 returns. 1 April: to_credit 10_000 versus charges of 2_000, so credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42 refunds 8_000 as a credit note on the threshold invoice and credits 2_000. Period invoice total 0, credit note available at 8_000. A recurring threshold that re-armed on TOTAL usage rather than on usage net of what was already billed would fire again here on 15 March, producing a third invoice and a second refund.

A recurring threshold whose period is cut short before it can re-arm — the control for b05/recurring/multiple-in-period/terminated-mid-period. With no fixed threshold `largest_threshold_amount` is 0, so check_service.rb:36 is false and the recurring test at :48-52 runs: remainder 0, actual 10_000 >= 5_000. 100 units x 1.00 = 10_000 cents is billed on 5 April. Terminating on 16 April bills the consumed usage — the same 10_000 — and credits the 10_000 already collected, so nothing more is due. `to_credit_amount` is the threshold invoice's fees with nothing subtracted (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63: no coupons, no credits pointing at it, no credit notes on it). Compare with the fixed row of the same shape: the recurring flag changes only how often the trigger arms, and termination gives it no second chance to.

Two charges on the same subscription: metric a sums 10+30+20 = 60 units → 6_000¢, metric b sums 5+10+5 = 20 units → 2_000¢, fees 8_000¢. Three events per metric so sum is distinguishable from max and latest. The wallet is limited to metric a and holds 8_000¢ (20 granted + 60 purchased): "full cover" of its allowed slice, with a surplus left over. Buckets are keyed `[fee_type, billable_metric_id]` and sorted by descending amount (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:82-89), so metric a's 6_000 is offered first. `applicable_fee?` (:108-122) matches it via `targets` — the wallet_targets array is `[["charge", bm_a_id]]` (:37-41) — and metric b's key matches neither targets nor types, so it is skipped. Draw: min(6000, 8000, 8000) = 6_000. Total 8_000 − 6_000 = 2_000, exactly metric b's fee, owed in cash; wallet keeps 2_000. This is a DIFFERENT lookup from the fee-types rows (wallet_targets versus allowed_fee_types, ORed at :121), which is why both limitations get their own rows. Name the wrong answers: a wallet ignoring wallet_targets takes 8_000 and leaves 0 owed; one that matched on fee_type alone would also take 8_000 because both fees are `charge`. Asserting the per-fee amounts alongside prepaid_credit_amount_cents 6_000 excludes both. Pools: 2_000 granted then 4_000 purchased (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88); created_at FIFO would give 0 granted / 6_000 purchased.

Granted-heavy versus paid-heavy again, this time discriminating on billable metric rather than fee type. b06_grt_bmp_granted holds 30 granted credits (3_000¢) at priority 1; b06_grt_bmp_paid holds 40 purchased (4_000¢) at priority 20; both are limited to metric a and the purchased one is declared first so declaration order cannot be mistaken for `Wallet.in_application_order` (wallet.rb:69-71, priority ASC then created_at). Fees 8_000¢ = metric a 6_000 + metric b 2_000. Only metric a's bucket is reachable by either wallet. Wallet at priority 1: min(6000, 3000, 8000) = 3_000, bucket down to 3_000, invoice remaining 5_000. Wallet at priority 20: min(3000, 4000, 5000) = 3_000. Prepaid 6_000, total 2_000 (metric b's fee, cash), balances 0 and 1_000. The amounts are chosen so the wrong order gives different numbers on BOTH sides: creation order first would draw min(6000, 4000, 8000) = 4_000 from the purchased wallet then min(2000, 3000, 4000) = 2_000 from the granted one → prepaid_granted 2_000 / prepaid_purchased 4_000, and wallet[b06_grt_bmp_granted].balance_cents 1_000 rather than 0. Both wallets are pinned with a single `expect.wallet`: the granted one directly, the purchased one as prepaid_credit − prepaid_granted = 3_000, valid because one wallet holds only granted and the other only purchased inbounds, so the breakdown (applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:83-92) maps one-to-one onto wallets.

10_000¢ of credits (40 granted + 60 purchased) against an 8_000¢ invoice — enough to push the total negative twice over. It does not go negative and it does not zero out either. The metric limitation caps the reachable amount at metric a's 6_000¢ bucket (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:108-122, matching on wallet_targets), and the draw is min(6000, 10000, 8000) = 6_000. Total 8_000 − 6_000 = 2_000 — metric b's fee, which the wallet may not pay for, owed in CASH while 4_000¢ of credit sits unused. The alternatives, with their numbers: (a) limitation ignored → the invoice clamp `remaining_invoice_amount` (:53, :57) takes over and prepaid is 8_000, total 0, wallet 2_000; (b) no clamp at all → total −2_000; (c) the unusable 4_000 refunded or expired — neither happens, no credit note and no wallet transaction beyond the 6_000 outbound. Asserting the total alone cannot separate (a) from the truth once the total is small, so balance_cents 4_000 and consumed_amount_cents 6_000 carry the row. Pools: 4_000 granted exhausts the grant, then 2_000 purchased (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88); a created_at FIFO would report 0 granted / 6_000 purchased.

Mid-period, the ongoing allocator path (allocate_ongoing_usage_by_wallets_service.rb:33-65 via Clock::RefreshWalletsOngoingBalanceJob → Customers::RefreshWalletsService), with a wallet limited to metric a. Both charges are unbilled usage: metric a 6_000¢, metric b 2_000¢. Fee keys here are `[fee_type, billable_metric_id, target_wallet_code, currency]` (:118-124) — one element wider than the billing allocator's key, a second implementation of the same idea. The pool is sorted descending (:98-104) so metric a is offered first and `budgets["EUR"]` starts at 6_000 + 2_000 = 8_000. Metric a: remaining = min(6000, 8000) = 6_000; `applicable` is just this wallet, so `index == applicable.length - 1` and it takes all 6_000 (:48-51). Metric b: `applicable` is EMPTY because the wallet's targets do not include it (:126-137), so its 2_000 is dropped from the allocation entirely — the budget still fell to 2_000 but no wallet can claim it. ongoing_usage_balance_cents 6_000, and ongoing_balance_cents = 8_000 − 6_000 = 2_000 (refresh_ongoing_usage_service.rb:63). Wrong answers: ignoring the metric limitation gives 8_000 / 0 and would additionally flip `depleted_ongoing_balance` (:41-46); charging the limitation against `credits_ongoing_usage_balance` instead of cents would leave ongoing_usage_balance_cents at 0. balance_cents stays 8_000 (20 granted + 60 purchased): ongoing figures are a projection and never debit the wallet, and no WalletTransactionConsumption is written, so the granted-before-purchased order is simply not observable on this path. invoices is 1 — the `credit` top-up invoice; no billing ran.

Two charges, 30 units and 20 units at 1.00 → 3_000¢ + 2_000¢ = 5_000¢ of fees. The wallet is limited to the metric b06_bm_covered, so it pays that charge's 3_000¢ and leaves the other charge's 2_000¢ owing. Same shape as the fee-types row but discriminating on metric rather than fee kind — worth separate rows because they are separate lookups in Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService.

Rate 2.2225 — above 1, so a credit is worth more than a euro and the rounding runs the other way. Each 10-credit top-up converts as `(10 × 2.2225).round(2) × 100` = 22.225 → 22.23 → 2_223¢ (wallet_credit.rb:26-27), so the settled balance is 4_446¢. Truncating gives 22.22 → 2_222¢ twice = 4_444¢: name both, 4_446 vs 4_444, with the invoice total 3_554 vs 3_556. A third candidate, rounding the 20-credit total once (20 × 2.2225 = 44.45 → 4_445¢), is also wrong and is excluded because prepaid_granted and prepaid_purchased are asserted separately at 2_223 each. Fees 8_000¢ (metric a 6_000, metric b 2_000). The wallet is limited to metric a, so the reachable bucket is 6_000 and the draw is min(6000, 4446, 8000) = 4_446 — the whole balance. Total 8_000 − 4_446 = 3_554, which includes metric b's untouchable 2_000¢ in full. Granted is consumed before purchased (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88) even though the purchased inbound was created first (create_from_params_service.rb:36-53); with equal pools the discriminator is that both breakdown fields are non-nil, which no single-pool-first order produces.

Two fees: a 5_000¢ subscription fee and a 6_000¢ charge fee (60 units × 1.00), 11_000¢ total. Under a limitation, "full cover" means the wallet fully covers the slice it is ALLOWED to pay and keeps a surplus — as opposed to partial cover, where it runs dry before finishing that slice. Balance is 20 granted + 60 purchased = 8_000¢; the allowed slice is the charge bucket only, 6_000¢. `applicable_fee?` (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:108-122) sees types=["charge"], so the subscription bucket matches neither `types` nor `targets` and `unrestricted_wallet` is false — it is skipped entirely, never merely reduced. The draw is min(6000, 8000, 11000) = 6_000, leaving balance 8_000 − 6_000 = 2_000 and total 11_000 − 6_000 = 5_000, i.e. the subscription fee still owed in CASH. Name the wrong answers: a wallet that ignored allowed_fee_types would take 8_000 and leave 3_000 owed; one that read the limitation as a discount on the whole invoice rather than a per-bucket filter would leave the same 5_000 total but a 0 balance. Both are excluded by asserting balance_cents 2_000 alongside the total. Draw order: the 2_000 granted pool goes first and 4_000 comes from purchased (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88 sorts granted ahead of purchased at equal priority 50). The purchased inbound was created FIRST (create_from_params_service.rb:36-53), so a created_at FIFO would report 0 granted / 6_000 purchased.

Granted-heavy versus paid-heavy, the sharpest form of this cell: wallet b06_grt_ftp_granted holds 20 GRANTED credits (2_000¢) at priority 1, wallet b06_grt_ftp_paid holds 60 PURCHASED credits (6_000¢) at priority 20, and they are declared in the wrong order on purpose because consumption follows `Wallet.in_application_order` — priority ASC then created_at (wallet.rb:69-71) — not declaration order. Fees 11_000¢ (5_000 subscription + 6_000 charge); both wallets are limited to fee_type `charge`, so only the 6_000¢ bucket is reachable. Wallet 1 (priority 1): min(6000, 2000, 11000) = 2_000, leaving the bucket at 4_000 and the invoice at 9_000. Wallet 2: min(4000, 6000, 9000) = 4_000. Total prepaid 6_000, total owed 5_000, and the subscription fee is still cash. Balances end 0 and 2_000. Wrong order gives DIFFERENT numbers, which is why the amounts are 2_000/6_000 against a 6_000 bucket: creation order first would draw 6_000 from the purchased wallet and 0 from the granted one, so prepaid_granted would be nil and prepaid_purchased 6_000, with wallet[b06_grt_ftp_granted].balance_cents still 2_000. Both wallets' contributions are pinned without an `expect.wallets` list: the granted wallet directly (balance 0, consumed 2_000) and the purchased wallet as prepaid_credit − prepaid_granted = 4_000. Because one wallet is granted-only and the other purchased-only, the breakdown (applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:83-92) maps one-to-one onto the wallets.

The wallet holds 14_000¢ (30 granted + 110 purchased) against an 11_000¢ invoice, so it could over-pay the whole invoice, let alone its allowed slice. Two clamps could fire and only one does. The limitation clamp: `applicable_fee?` (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:108-122) with types=["subscription"] admits only the 5_000¢ subscription bucket, so the 6_000¢ charge bucket is never touched. The draw is min(5000, 14000, 11000) = 5_000. The invoice clamp never has to fire here, which is the finding: the ALLOWED SLICE bounds the draw before `remaining_invoice_amount` does. Result: prepaid 5_000, total 6_000 — exactly the charge fee, owed in cash — and the wallet keeps 9_000. Name the alternatives: (a) limitation ignored → prepaid 11_000, total 0, wallet 3_000; (b) neither clamp → total −3_000 with a 14_000 draw; (c) the surplus refunded as a credit note — no credit note is created. Asserting the total alone cannot separate these from the truth, so balance_cents 9_000 and the per-fee split are asserted too. Pools: 3_000 granted then 2_000 purchased (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88); a created_at FIFO would report 0 granted / 5_000 purchased.

The mid-period path (Wallets::Balance::AllocateOngoingUsageByWalletsService, reached via Clock::RefreshWalletsOngoingBalanceJob → Customers::RefreshWalletsService), and the row where the fee-type limitation bites hardest. The pool of unbilled amounts is built from `current_usage_fees` (refresh_wallets_service.rb:52-54), which is Invoices::CustomerUsageService output — CHARGE fees only; a subscription fee is not usage and never appears. This wallet may pay only `subscription` fees, so `applicable_fee?` (allocate_ongoing_usage_by_wallets_service.rb:126-137) finds types=["subscription"] against a fee_key whose fee_type is "charge": no type match, targets empty but non-empty types means `unrestricted_wallet` is false. `applicable` is therefore EMPTY for the only key in the pool, and the loop at :45-61 allocates nothing (:40-62 simply moves on — an unallocatable key is dropped, not forced onto some wallet). So with 6_000¢ of unbilled usage sitting there, ongoing_usage_balance_cents is 0 and ongoing_balance_cents = 5_000 − 0 = 5_000 (refresh_ongoing_usage_service.rb:63). The wrong answer, and the one a reader expects: 6_000 and −1_000, which is what an implementation that ignored allowed_fee_types on the ongoing path would print. The 6_000¢ of charge usage is the fee this wallet may not pay for, and it will be owed in cash at period end — the wallet reserves nothing against it, which is exactly what the mid-period number should say and the reason `depleted_ongoing_balance` never fires here. Balance is 20 granted + 30 purchased = 5_000¢; invoices is 1, the `credit` top-up invoice.

The invoice holds two kinds of fee: a 5_000¢ subscription fee and a 3_000¢ charge fee, 8_000¢ total. The wallet is limited to fee_type `charge`, so despite holding 10_000¢ of cover it may only pay the 3_000¢ charge fee — the subscription fee is left owing. That the limitation caps what credits may touch rather than how much they are worth is the whole point of the row.

Rate 0.4445 with two 30-credit top-ups. Each converts as `(30 × 0.4445).round(2) × 100` = 13.335 → 13.34 → 1_334¢ (wallet_credit.rb:26-27, HALF-UP), so the settled balance is 2_668¢. Truncating the third decimal instead gives 13.33 → 1_333¢ twice = 2_666¢: name both, 2_668 vs 2_666, and the invoice total 8_332 vs 8_334. The error doubles because each top-up rounds independently — a per-wallet rounding of the 60-credit total (60 × 0.4445 = 26.67 → 2_667¢) is a third candidate and also wrong. The wallet may only pay `subscription` fees, so the reachable bucket is the 5_000¢ subscription fee; the 6_000¢ charge fee is skipped by `applicable_fee?` (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:108-122) and stays owed in cash. The draw is min(5000, 2668, 11000) = 2_668, the whole balance, so total = 11_000 − 2_668 = 8_332 and the wallet ends empty. Granted goes first (wallet_transaction.rb:81-88) and here both pools are equal at 1_334, but the split is still load-bearing: the purchased inbound is created first (create_from_params_service.rb:36-53), so a created_at FIFO would report prepaid_purchased 1_334 and prepaid_granted 1_334 only by coincidence of equal pools — the assertion that matters is that BOTH are non-nil, which fails under any order that drains one pool first.

100 granted credits = 10_000¢ of cover against 3_000¢ of fees, so the wallet absorbs the invoice entirely: prepaid_credit_amount_cents equals fees_amount_cents and nothing is owed. The wallet is debited only 3_000¢, not its whole balance. payment_status is asserted because a zero total is marked succeeded rather than pending (CalculateFeesService sets it from total_amount_cents), which is the difference between "paid by credits" and "awaiting payment".

Two wallets holding 10 and 100 credits. Together they cover the 3_000¢ invoice completely, so the total is 0 and prepaid_credit_amount_cents is the full 3_000¢. The wallets are declared in the wrong order on purpose — the low-priority one first — because consumption follows `priority` ascending, not creation order (Wallet.in_application_order). The 10-credit wallet at priority 1 is drained first and the remaining 2_000¢ comes from the other; a regression that ignored priority would still total 0 here, so the paired balance check belongs in a follow-up row rather than this one.

A wallet holding 10_000¢ (20 granted + 80 purchased at rate 1) against an invoice whose total is only 4_000¢ — the case where the total could go negative. It does not. Lago CLAMPS at zero and leaves the surplus in the wallet: every draw is bounded by `remaining_invoice_amount` (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:53, decremented at :57), so exactly 4_000¢ leaves the wallet and 6_000¢ stays. The three alternatives, named: (a) total −6_000 if the applicable balance were drained, (b) a `credit` invoice or credit note for the 6_000 surplus — none is issued, (c) the wallet drained to 0. None happens. The 4_000 ceiling is itself the row's second half. Prepaid credit is the LAST reducer (calculate_fees_service.rb:57-62: coupon → tax → credit note → prepaid), and the per-fee cap is `sub_total_excluding_taxes + taxes_precise − precise_credit_notes` (:77-79) where `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents = amount_cents − precise_coupons_amount_cents` (fee.rb:238-240): 6_000 − 2_000 = 4_000, matching invoice.total exactly so `reconcile_remaining_amounts` (:93-106) adds nothing. Credits applied BEFORE the coupon would have taken 6_000 and left the wallet at 4_000 — name both: wallet 6_000 vs 4_000, prepaid 4_000 vs 6_000. The coupon is `frequency: once` and the `credit` top-up invoice is issued first, but credit invoices never run the coupon or prepaid stages (invoices/paid_credit_service.rb:80-91 computes their totals directly), so the coupon is still unspent when the period invoice is built. Draw order: granted 2_000 is exhausted first, then 2_000 of purchased — a created_at FIFO would report 0 granted / 4_000 purchased.

A mid-period read, and a DIFFERENT code path from every other row in this slice: no invoice is built. `perform_wallet_refresh` runs Clock::RefreshWalletsOngoingBalanceJob (premium-gated at refresh_wallets_ongoing_balance_job.rb:8, hence `premium: true`) → Customers::RefreshWalletsService → Wallets::Balance::AllocateOngoingUsageByWalletsService, a reimplementation of the billing allocator, not the same code (allocate_ongoing_usage_by_wallets_service.rb:33-65). Balance is 20 granted + 30 purchased = 5_000¢ once the top-up invoice is settled. Unbilled usage is 60 units × 1.00 = 6_000¢, pooled as `fee.amount_cents + fee.taxes_amount_cents` (:90) — note this bucket does NOT subtract credit notes the way the billing cap does. With one wallet, `applicable` has length 1 so `index == applicable.length - 1` and it takes the whole remaining amount with no room check (:48-51): the wallet is allowed to go NEGATIVE. `ongoing_balance_cents = balance_cents − ongoing_usage_balance_cents` (refresh_ongoing_usage_service.rb:63) = 5_000 − 6_000 = −1_000. An implementation that clamped at zero — the plausible wrong answer — would report ongoing_usage 5_000 and ongoing_balance 0. invoices is 1: the purchased top-up's `credit` invoice, and nothing else, because no billing ran. `balance_cents` stays 5_000: the ongoing figures are a projection and never debit the wallet. There is no granted/purchased breakdown on this path at all — ongoing usage is allocated against `balance_cents`, a single pool, and no WalletTransactionConsumption rows are written, so the draw order this block exists to pin is invisible mid-period.

30 units × 1.00 = 30.00 → 3_000¢ of fees.
