Wallet b is asserted rather than a because a ends at 0 in every variant and because its rule re-arms after billing (applied_prepaid_credits_service.rb:39 sees a drained wallet at 0 credits, which is not > 0), which changes a's balance after the invoice is final.

Does the counter reset? Derived, not assumed. Reading on 2 May makes base_date the 2nd (dates_service.rb:233), so the window is 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-31T23:59:59.999999Z (monthly_service.rb:20,26). April's four events all have timestamps below that lower bound and Event.from_datetime is `timestamp >= ?` (event.rb:18), so none of them is in scope: count_agg is not recurring-capable at all (billable_metric.rb:113-118 forbids `recurring` on count_agg), so there is no carry-forward path and the aggregation is 0. The charge is still REPORTED at zero rather than omitted: with no in-period event Events::BillingPeriodFilterService leaves the default bucket empty, charge_service.rb:132-146 skips the aggregation and charge_service.rb:112-123 hydrates a zero-units fee instead, which the serializer maps like any other (charge_usage_serializer.rb:31-47). Hence units "0.0" and 0¢ in charges_usage, not a missing entry. The 400¢ does not vanish — it is on the April invoice (4 units x 1.00), which the row asserts on the same breath so a usage figure that leaked into May would show up as 400¢ charged twice.

The refusal PRECEDES the aggregation, and that is the honest content of this cell: CustomerUsageService.with_external_ids resolves the subscription through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer_usage_service.rb:36 → customer.rb:216) before any charge is priced, so `subscription.blank?` at :52 answers not_allowed_failure!(code: "no_active_subscription") → HTTP 405 with the metric never consulted. All five current-usage after-termination rows therefore carry the SAME expectation and differ only in what a wrong 200 would say — which is exactly why each is written rather than one standing in for all: the four events ingested before the DELETE are what make this row's counterfactual 4 units / 400¢ (count_agg counts events, count_service.rb:9-11, not the 90 their amounts sum to), so a regression that resolved through `subscriptions` instead of `active_subscriptions` fails here with a number attributable to count_agg. The events also prove the 405 is about the subscription's STATE and not about there being nothing to report. The last obtainable 200 read for count_agg is pinned by b7/usage-equals-invoice/count_agg/after-termination above.

count_agg on the usage surface counts EVENTS, not property values: CountService#compute_aggregation is `event_store.count` with no aggregation_property at all (count_service.rb:9-11, postgres_store.rb:100-102), so the four events ingested by 5 April give 4 units, priced 4 x 1.00 = 400¢ by StandardService#compute_amount (standard_service.rb:7-9). The four amounts are 10/30/20/30 deliberately: an implementation that summed the only numeric property would report 90 units (9_000¢), one that took the max 30 (3_000¢), one that took the latest 30 (3_000¢), and one that counted DISTINCT amounts 3 (300¢). All four are visible against 400¢. The three extra events on the 20th land AFTER the fetch_current_usage snapshot — live usage would read 7 events and 700¢ — so the row also proves the snapshot is what is being asserted (golden_runner.rb:380-383).

THE BOUNDARY ROW. Usage read at the last whole second of the period, with six events placed so that both ends of the aggregation window are pinned. Current usage takes its window from DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180), so base_date is the READ date rather than a period behind it (dates_service.rb:233): reading on 30 April, compute_charges_from_date is 2024-04-01 (monthly_service.rb:20, calendar) and compute_charges_to_date is that month's end_of_month taken to end_of_day (monthly_service.rb:26 + dates_service.rb:242-246) = 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z. The window is INCLUSIVE at both ends: Event.from_datetime is `timestamp >= ?` and the to-boundary is `timestamp <= ?` (event.rb:18-19, postgres_store.rb:11-13). So the two events stamped exactly 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z are IN, the 15 April one is IN, the one at 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z is IN (23:59:59 <= 23:59:59.999999), the one a second before the period at 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z is OUT and the one at exactly the next period's first instant 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z is OUT. 4 events -> 4 units -> 400¢. Every single off-by-one moves the number, and the counts are deliberately asymmetric (two events sit on the lower boundary, one on the upper) so that two simultaneous off-by-ones cannot cancel: an exclusive `>` at from_datetime gives 2 (200¢), including the pre-period event gives 5 (500¢), including the next-period event gives 5 (500¢), an exclusive `<` at to_datetime gives 3 (300¢), and dropping both boundary events gives 2 (200¢). Reading at 23:59:59 also proves the period has not rolled early: if it had, the answer would be 1 (the 05-01 event, 100¢) or 0.

"Latest" reads like a gauge, and a gauge that resets to zero on the 1st of the month is a surprising behaviour to leave unasserted — so this row derives it. LatestService has no state beyond the event store and `recurring` is forbidden on latest_agg outright (billable_metric.rb:113-118), so there is nothing to carry: reading on 2 May the window is 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-31T23:59:59.999999Z (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26), `event_store.last` finds no event in it (latest_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:233-237), and the charge is hydrated as a zero-units fee rather than omitted (charge_service.rb:112-146) -> units "0.0", 0¢. April's last event carried 20 -> 20 units -> 2_000¢ on the April invoice, asserted here so a latest value surviving into May reads as 2_000¢ billed twice. If the row instead reports 20 units in May, the gauge is persisting across periods and every customer watching it is being shown last month's reading.

405 at customer_usage_service.rb:52; :36 resolves through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216) and a terminated subscription is not in it. The aggregation never runs, so this row's job is to make the counterfactual latest-attributable: 10, 30, 20 at strictly increasing timestamps in three SEPARATE steps (events sharing one step share its instant and the ordering would rest on created_at alone) means a wrong 200 would report LatestService's `event_store.last` = 20 units → 2_000¢ (latest_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:233-237) — distinguishable at a glance from a sum's 60, a max's 30, a first-seen 10 and a count's 3. The 20 is neither the largest nor the smallest so "latest" cannot be satisfied by accident. Note that termination is what makes latest_agg's read unobtainable forever rather than merely stale: unlike the invoiced path there is no terminal snapshot on this surface.

LatestService takes `event_store.last`, which is the in-window event ordered `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC` (latest_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:233-237), and clamps a negative value to zero (latest_service.rb:59-64). The three values are 10, 30, 20 with strictly increasing timestamps, which is the arrangement that separates every candidate aggregation at once: latest = 20 units -> 2_000¢, sum would be 60 (6_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢), first-seen 10 (1_000¢), count 3 (300¢). The 20 is deliberately neither the largest nor the smallest, so "latest" cannot be satisfied by accident. The three events are ingested in three SEPARATE steps rather than one: events in a single step share that step's instant, which would leave the ordering resting on created_at alone and make the row a test of ingestion order rather than of timestamp order. The 99 on the 19th is ingested AFTER the snapshot — live usage would read 9_900¢ — so the row proves the assertion reads the snapshot (golden_runner.rb:380-383).

latest_agg is the aggregation the UPPER boundary can break on its own, because the answer IS the last in-window event. `event_store.last` orders by `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC` within the window (latest_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:233-237), and for a read on 30 April the window is 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z, inclusive at both ends (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26, event.rb:18-19). The last in-window event is the one stamped exactly 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, carrying 20 -> 20 units -> 2_000¢ (standard_service.rb:7-9). An exclusive `<` at to_datetime would drop it and answer 30 (3_000¢); admitting the event at the next period's first instant 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z would answer 777 (77_700¢); admitting the one a second before the period cannot change `latest` but would change sum, which is why units is asserted rather than only the total. Sum over the window is 60 (6_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢), count 3 (300¢) — all distinct from 2_000¢.

A period high-water mark is the aggregation most likely to be implemented as remembered state, so this row derives whether it survives billing. It does not. MaxService reads only the event store over the current window (max_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:209-213) and keeps nothing else; `recurring` is forbidden on max_agg outright (billable_metric.rb:113-118), so there is no carry-forward path. Reading on 2 May the window is 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-31T23:59:59.999999Z (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26), April's events are all below `timestamp >= from_datetime` (event.rb:18), and the charge is hydrated as a zero-units fee rather than dropped (charge_service.rb:112-146) -> units "0.0", 0¢. April's max(10, 40, 25) = 40 units -> 4_000¢ stays on the April invoice, asserted here so that a max leaking into the next period reads as 4_000¢ billed twice rather than as a plausible-looking usage figure.

Same 405 as its four siblings, reached at customer_usage_service.rb:52 because :36 resolves through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216) and the DELETE has already moved the subscription out of that scope. The aggregation axis is inert at this cell by construction — the lookup fails before MaxService is instantiated — so what this row contributes is the max-attributable counterfactual: 10/40/25 with the largest in the middle would have priced max(10, 40, 25) = 40 units → 4_000¢ (max_service.rb:16-18), not the 75 a sum gives nor the 25 a latest gives. A 200 here fails with a number that names which aggregation ran. Deliberately NOT written as an upgrade, which would leave an ACTIVE subscription under the same external_id and make the read succeed against the new one.

max_agg on the usage surface: max(10, 40, 25) = 40 units → 4_000¢, not the 75 a sum would give and not the 25 a latest would. The largest value arrives in the middle of the three so that a regression to either neighbour changes the answer.

MaxService is `events.maximum((properties->>'amount')::numeric)` over the period window (max_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:209-213), and the window is 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z inclusive at both ends (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26, event.rb:18-19). The largest in-window value is placed ON the lower boundary on purpose: max(40, 25, 10) = 40 units -> 4_000¢ (standard_service.rb:7-9). That makes the boundary comparison the thing the number depends on, which no mid-period row can do. An exclusive `>` at from_datetime drops the 40 and the answer collapses to 25 (2_500¢); the two out-of-window values are larger than everything in the period, so pulling in the event one second early answers 999 (99_900¢) and pulling in the next period's first instant answers 500 (50_000¢). Sum would give 75 (7_500¢), latest 10 (1_000¢), count 3 (300¢).

Once March is billed the subscription is in a fresh April period, so current usage resets to 0 while the 3_000¢ stays on the March invoice. Usage is per-period, not cumulative — the row that would catch usage leaking across a period boundary and double-billing the customer. A metered (non-recurring) metric is used deliberately: a recurring one legitimately carries units forward.

Usage read on 10 March sees only the events that have happened by then: 10 units → 1_000¢. The 99-unit event on the 20th is ingested AFTER the snapshot on purpose — if the assertion were reading live usage rather than the snapshot it would see 109 units and 10_900¢, so this row also proves the snapshot mechanism itself works.

The window for a usage read on 30 April is 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180, dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26), inclusive at both ends (event.rb:18-19). SumService therefore sums only the three in-window amounts: 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 units -> 6_000¢ at 1.00 the unit (standard_service.rb:7-9). The two out-of-window amounts are deliberately large and unequal so each off-by-one is separately identifiable: an exclusive lower bound drops the 10 and gives 50 (5_000¢); pulling in the event a second BEFORE the period gives 560 (56_000¢); pulling in the event at exactly the next period's first instant gives 760 (76_000¢); an exclusive upper bound drops the 20 and gives 40 (4_000¢). The three in-window values 10/30/20 also separate the aggregations: max would answer 30 (3_000¢), latest 20 (2_000¢), count 3 (300¢).

unique_count is the one aggregation where "does the counter reset" has two legitimate answers, and the metric attribute decides which: UniqueCountService sets `event_store.use_from_boundary = !billable_metric.recurring` (unique_count_service.rb:10). This metric declares `recurring: false`, so the lower bound IS applied and the ledger restarts every period. Reading on 2 May the window is 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-31T23:59:59.999999Z (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26); no event falls in it, so the aggregation is 0 and the charge is hydrated as a zero-units fee rather than omitted (charge_service.rb:112-146) -> units "0.0", 0¢. A recurring unique_count would legitimately still report 2 here, which is exactly why the row pins the flag instead of relying on the default. April's ledger is s1 = +1 then 0, s2 = +1 (unique_count_query.rb:276-287) = 2 units -> 200¢ on the April invoice; 3 events, 2 units, so a count_agg regression on the invoice side would read 300¢.

405 at customer_usage_service.rb:52, the subscription having left Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216) on termination — the read never reaches UniqueCountService, so the aggregation axis cannot change the outcome and this row's value is the counterfactual it makes attributable. The five events form the signed add/remove ledger (unique_count_query.rb:276-287): s1 = +1 then 0 for the repeat, s2 = +1 then -1 on the 7th, s3 = +1, so a wrong 200 would report 2 units / 200¢ and not the 5 a count gives nor the 3 a COUNT(DISTINCT) that ignored the removal gives. `recurring: false` is explicit so the ledger is confined to this period (unique_count_service.rb:10) and the counterfactual is a period number rather than a lifetime one.

unique_count is not "distinct values": it is a signed add/remove ledger per property, summed. UniqueCountQuery#operation_value_sql (unique_count_query.rb:276-287) gives +1 for the first `add` on a property, 0 for a repeated `add`, -1 for a `remove` that follows an `add`, and 0 for a `remove` with nothing to remove; operation_type defaults to `add` when the property is absent (postgres_store.rb:598-599). Per property: s1 = +1 then 0 (already added) = 1; s2 = +1 then -1 (removed on the 7th) = 0; s3 = +1 = 1. Total 2 units -> 200¢ (standard_service.rb:7-9). Five events for two units is the whole point of the row: count_agg would answer 5 (500¢), a naive COUNT(DISTINCT sub_id) that ignored the removal would answer 3 (300¢), and an implementation that double-counted the repeated s1 add would answer 3 or 4. The metric is declared `recurring: false` explicitly, which sets use_from_boundary = true (unique_count_service.rb:10) and confines the ledger to this period.

Non-recurring unique_count sets use_from_boundary = true (unique_count_service.rb:10), so the ledger is confined to 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z, inclusive at both ends (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26, event.rb:18-19). In window: s1 (+1, at exactly the lower boundary instant), s2 (+1), s2 again (0, repeated add suppressed by unique_count_query.rb:276-287), s3 (+1, at exactly 23:59:59 of the last day) = 3 units -> 300¢. Out of window: `before` at 2024-03-31T23:59:59Z and `after` at 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z. Each boundary property is distinct from every other, so no off-by-one is masked by a duplicate: an exclusive `>` at from_datetime loses s1 and answers 2 (200¢); an exclusive `<` at to_datetime loses s3 and answers 2 (200¢); including `before` answers 4 (400¢); including `after` answers 4 (400¢). count_agg over the same window would answer 4 (400¢), so the dedup is exercised too.

weighted_sum is the aggregation with a real carry-forward mechanism — initial_value from the previous period's cached aggregation (weighted_sum_service.rb:91-109) — so whether it resets after billing is a genuine question, and the answer is decided by `recurring`. This metric is non-recurring, so `initial_value` returns 0 unconditionally (weighted_sum_service.rb:91-95) and nothing is carried. Reading on 2 May the window is 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-31T23:59:59.999999Z (dates_service.rb:233, monthly_service.rb:20,26) and holds no event, so the charge is hydrated as a zero-units fee (charge_service.rb:112-146) -> units "0.0", 0¢. A recurring weighted_sum would legitimately report the 60 units still "active" at 60 x 31/31 = 60 units (6_000¢) in May, which is the number to look for if this row goes red. April is unchanged from the mid-period row: 0 for 3 days, 10 for 3 days (=1), 40 for 6 days (=8), 60 for 18 days (=36) over a 30-day denominator (weighted_sum_query.rb:102-119) = 45 units -> 4_500¢ on the April invoice, and the row asserts that side too so a weighted sum leaking into May reads as double billing rather than as usage.

405 at customer_usage_service.rb:52 via the active_subscriptions lookup at :36 (customer.rb:216). weighted_sum is the aggregation this cell loses most: it is the only one whose value depends on WHEN the read happens rather than only on the events, because WeightedSumQuery integrates the running total against a synthetic end-of-period row (weighted_sum_query.rb:68-100) and current usage keeps that bound at the month end even mid-period (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180). No number is stated here, and that is deliberate rather than lazy: the read is unobtainable after termination, so any figure would be unverifiable — the arithmetic itself is carried by b07/current-usage/weighted_sum_agg/mid-period and /period-boundary above, and the terminated-period integral by b7/usage-equals-invoice/weighted_sum_agg/after-termination. What this row pins is that the surface refuses rather than answering with a truncated or a full-month integral, either of which would be a defensible-looking 200. The three events (running total 31 → 93 → 124) exist so the refusal cannot be confused with an empty period. `runners` includes `live` because nothing here is a date-dependent amount — there is no amount at all — so the live runner's timeline shift cannot invalidate it, which is why this row is not calendar_sensitive while its mid-period sibling is.

weighted_sum is a time-weighted average of the RUNNING TOTAL, and it exists on no invoice in the suite — this is the arithmetic that only current usage reaches. WeightedSumQuery builds one row per event plus a synthetic row at from_datetime carrying `initial_value` and one at to_datetime carrying 0 (weighted_sum_query.rb:68-100), then sums cumulative_sum x seconds_to_next_row / charges_duration_in_seconds (weighted_sum_query.rb:102-119). initial_value is 0 because the metric is not recurring (weighted_sum_service.rb:91-95). April is a 30-day calendar period so the denominator is 30.days = 2_592_000s, and the upper bound is ceil'd to 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z (postgres_store.rb:350-372), making the window exactly 30 days. The three events are placed so every term divides exactly, leaving no rounding to argue about: 2024-04-01 -> 04-04 the running total is 0 (3 days, contributes 0); 04-04 -> 04-07 it is 10 for 3 days = 10 x 259_200 / 2_592_000 = 1; 04-07 -> 04-13 it is 40 for 6 days = 40 x 518_400 / 2_592_000 = 8; 04-13 -> 05-01 it is 60 for 18 days = 60 x 1_555_200 / 2_592_000 = 36. Total 45 units -> 4_500¢ (standard_service.rb:7-9). Note the tail runs to the PERIOD END, not to the read instant: current usage keeps charges_to_datetime at the end of the month even mid-period (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180, monthly_service.rb:26), so an implementation that weighted only up to "now" (20 April) would answer (30 + 240 + 420)/30 = 23 units (2_300¢). A plain sum answers 60 (6_000¢), latest 20 (2_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢), and an implementation that dropped the zero-valued lead-in and rescaled would answer 45 x 30/27 = 50 (5_000¢).

The same time-weighted sum as the mid-period row, but with the first event sitting exactly ON from_datetime and decoys one second either side of the period. Window: 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-30T23:59:59.999999Z, ceil'd to 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z for the weighting (postgres_store.rb:350-372), 30 days = 2_592_000s in the denominator (weighted_sum_query.rb:102-119). The event at 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z shares its timestamp with the synthetic initial_value row (weighted_sum_query.rb:84-91); that tie is harmless because the zero-difference row contributes nothing whichever side of it it lands on — LEAD gives a 0-second gap and the CASE zeroes that term (weighted_sum_query.rb:105-107). Terms: 04-01 -> 04-07 running total 10 for 6 days = 10 x 518_400 / 2_592_000 = 2; 04-07 -> 04-13 it is 40 for 6 days = 8; 04-13 -> 05-01 it is 60 for 18 days = 36. Total 46 units -> 4_600¢. This is the only place the inclusive `>=` at from_datetime (event.rb:18) changes a weighted answer: excluding the boundary event makes the running total 30 from 04-07 and 50 from 04-13, i.e. 30 x 6/30 + 50 x 18/30 = 6 + 30 = 36 units (3_600¢). Admitting the 999 stamped one second before the period lifts every later running total by 999, giving 999 x 1/2_592_000 + 1_009 x 6/30 + 1_039 x 6/30 + 1_059 x 18/30 = 1_045.0004 units (104_500¢). Admitting the 777 at the next period's first instant makes it the last row before the synthetic end-of-period row, which sits at the same ceil'd instant, so its own term is zero but the 46 above becomes 46 + 777 x 0 = 46 with a raw difference sum of 837 instead of 60 — the reason both units and amount_cents are asserted rather than the total alone. A plain sum answers 60 (6_000¢), latest 20 (2_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢).

The `after-termination` cell of the current-usage surface is a REFUSAL, and that refusal is the only thing there is to assert — so the row states it as one rather than pretending a number exists. Invoices::CustomerUsageService resolves the subscription through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216 via customer_usage_service.rb:36), which scopes to status active; once the DELETE has terminated it the lookup finds nothing and :52 answers not_allowed_failure!(code: "no_active_subscription") → HTTP 405 (api_errors.rb:49-58). The 30 units ingested before termination are deliberately present: they prove the refusal is about the subscription's STATE and not about there being no usage to report. The alternative outcomes are both nameable and both wrong — a 200 with the pre-termination usage (which the six usage-equals-invoice/*/after-termination rows show is what the LAST legal read returns), or a 404 on the customer. Asserted through expect.error at the `usage` stage, which is the read this row exists to name.

CHARACTERIZATION, and the number is the finding. Two invoices exist and the row pins both: March's 30 units → 3_000¢ from the 1 April billing run, and April's 20 units → 2_000¢ on the termination invoice. The lineage total is therefore 5_000¢, which is what CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents would return — it sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the external_id/subscription_at lineage (calculate_service.rb:41-52) and the termination invoice is one of them. It is never asked. :17-20 returns EARLY for any subscription that is not active, clearing recalculate_invoiced_usage and recalculate_current_usage without recomputing either, so the column keeps the 3_000¢ it was last given on 1 April and the 2_000¢ of terminal usage never reaches it. The explicit perform_usage_update on 11 April is there to prove the point rather than to fix it: even a deliberate refresh after termination cannot move the number. So 3_000¢ records what Lago does and 5_000¢ is what the field claims to mean — a subscription's lifetime invoiced usage permanently understates it by whatever the termination invoice carried. Read with `select: {status: terminated}` because subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20 defaults the lookup to status active and answers 404 otherwise.

CHARACTERIZATION with count_agg's numbers. count_agg counts EVENTS (count_service.rb:9-11), so March's 3 events are 3 units → 300¢ on the 1 April run and April's 4 events are 4 units → 400¢ on the termination invoice; both are asserted so the addends are checkable apart from the sum. What the row records is that invoiced_usage_amount_cents stays at 300¢. The field's own definition says 700¢: CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents sums `invoice.fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over EVERY finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the external_id/subscription_at lineage (calculate_service.rb:41-52) and the termination invoice is one of them. It is never asked — :17-20 returns early for a subscription that is not active, clearing recalculate_invoiced_usage and recalculate_current_usage without recomputing either, so the column keeps the 300¢ it was last given on 1 April. The explicit perform_usage_update on 11 April proves the point rather than fixing it. The alternatives are all nameable and all different from 300: 700¢ if the lineage were re-summed, 400¢ if only the last invoice counted, 0¢ if the row were reset on termination. The amounts are deliberately unequal across the two periods (3 events then 4) so "kept the first period" and "took the last period" cannot both be satisfied by one number. current_usage_amount_cents is 0 and is asserted rather than omitted: April's usage was billed out by the termination invoice and a stale current component would double-count it. Read with `select: {status: terminated}` because subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20 defaults the lookup to status active and 404s otherwise.

CHARACTERIZATION with latest_agg's numbers. LatestService takes `event_store.last`, the in-window event ordered `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC` (latest_service.rb:16-18, postgres_store.rb:233-237), so March's 10/30/20 give 20 units → 2_000¢ and April's 40/5 give 5 units → 500¢ on the termination invoice. Each event is its own step because events sharing a step share its instant and the ordering would then rest on created_at alone. Within March the 20 is neither largest nor smallest, so a sum (60 → 6_000¢), a max (30 → 3_000¢) or a first-seen (10 → 1_000¢) is visible against it; April's last value 5 is the SMALLEST of the whole life, which is what keeps the four candidate lifetime readings apart. The defect: invoiced_usage_amount_cents holds 2_000¢, written on 1 April, because calculate_service.rb:17-20 returns early for an inactive subscription and clears both refresh flags without recomputing. calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (:41-52) would sum the lineage to 2_500¢; only-the-last-invoice would give 500¢, "latest across the whole life" also 500¢, a reset 0¢. current_usage_amount_cents is 0 — April's usage left on the termination invoice and no recalculation can run afterwards, as the explicit perform_usage_update on 11 April demonstrates rather than repairs. Read with `select: {status: terminated}` (subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20).

CHARACTERIZATION with max_agg's numbers, and this row is the one where the four candidate readings are furthest apart. max is per PERIOD, never across the lifetime: MaxService takes `event_store.max` inside the period window (max_service.rb:16-18), so March gives max(10, 40, 25) = 40 units → 4_000¢ and April gives max(15, 55, 5) = 55 units → 5_500¢ on the termination invoice. April's maximum is deliberately LARGER than March's, which is what makes the row discriminate: invoiced_usage_amount_cents stays at 4_000¢ (what it was given on 1 April, calculate_service.rb:17-20 returning early once the subscription is inactive and clearing both refresh flags without recomputing), whereas 9_500¢ is what calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents would return over the lineage (calculate_service.rb:41-52), 5_500¢ is what both "only the last invoice" AND "max over the whole life" would give, and 0¢ is what a reset on termination would give. Had April's max been the smaller of the two, 4_000¢ would have been indistinguishable from a lifetime max and the row would have proved nothing about the defect. current_usage_amount_cents is 0 — April's 5_500¢ was invoiced out and no recalculation can run after termination. `select: {status: terminated}` is required by subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20.

CHARACTERIZATION with unique_count_agg's numbers. March is the signed add/remove ledger (unique_count_query.rb:276-287, operation_type defaulting to `add`, postgres_store.rb:598-599): s1 = +1 then 0 for the repeat, s2 = +1 then -1 on the 7th, s3 = +1 → 2 units → 200¢, from five events, so a count_agg regression would show 500¢ and a naive COUNT(DISTINCT) that ignored the removal 300¢. April uses three FRESH ids s4/s5/s6 → 3 units → 300¢ on the termination invoice; the ids are fresh rather than reused so the number cannot depend on whether the ledger carried over, and `recurring: false` sets use_from_boundary = true (unique_count_service.rb:10) confining each period's ledger to itself. The defect: invoiced_usage_amount_cents holds 200¢ — the value written on 1 April — because calculate_service.rb:17-20 returns early for an inactive subscription and clears both refresh flags without recomputing, so the 300¢ the termination invoice carried never reaches the column even though calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents would include it (:41-52 → 500¢). 300¢ would mean only-the-last-invoice, 0¢ a reset. current_usage_amount_cents is 0. Read with `select: {status: terminated}` (subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20).

CHARACTERIZATION with weighted_sum_agg's numbers, and the two periods use DIFFERENT denominators on purpose. WeightedSumQuery inserts a synthetic row at from_datetime carrying initial_value and one at to_datetime carrying 0 (weighted_sum_query.rb:68-100, :93-99), then sums cumulative_sum x seconds_to_next_row / charges_duration.days (:102-119); the trailing row's own span is zero and the CASE at :105-107 zeroes it. initial_value is 0 in both periods because the metric is not recurring (weighted_sum_service.rb:91-95). Every event value is chosen so its term divides exactly and no rounding is in question. MARCH, denominator 31 days: 03-01→03-05 running total 0 (4 days, 0); 03-05→03-11 total 31 for 6 days = 31x6/31 = 6; 03-11→03-19 total 93 for 8 days = 93x8/31 = 24; 03-19→04-01 total 124 for 13 days = 124x13/31 = 52. Total 82 units → 8_200¢ (standard_service.rb:7-9). A plain sum would give 124 (12_400¢), max 62 (6_200¢), latest 31 (3_100¢). APRIL, the TERMINATION invoice: charges_to_datetime is clamped to terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117-122) so the window is 04-01→04-11, but charges_duration_in_days is the WHOLE period (dates_service.rb:202 → monthly_service.rb:35-41 measures from the period start), so the denominator is 30 days and not the 10 the window spans. 04-01→04-03 total 0 (2 days, 0); 04-03→04-07 total 15 for 4 days = 15x4/30 = 2; 04-07→04-11 total 45 for 4 days = 45x4/30 = 6. Total 8 units → 800¢. An implementation that used the truncated window as its denominator would give 8 x 30/10 = 24 units (2_400¢) — that mismatch between window and denominator is the whole reason this cell is worth an assertion. THE DEFECT: invoiced_usage_amount_cents holds 8_200¢, the value written by the 1 April run, because calculate_service.rb:17-20 returns early once the subscription is inactive and clears both refresh flags without recomputing; calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (:41-52) would sum the lineage to 9_000¢. 800¢ would mean only-the-last-invoice, 0¢ a reset. current_usage_amount_cents is 0. calendar_sensitive because March's 31 days and April's 30 ARE the arithmetic, hence rspec only. Read with `select: {status: terminated}` (subscriptions/base_controller.rb:20).

THE INVARIANT. 10 + 20 = 30 units at 1.00 → 3_000¢, and that same 3_000¢ must appear twice: once as current usage on the last hour of March, and again as the charge fee on the invoice April's billing run produces. The row states the number in both places rather than comparing them programmatically, so a divergence fails on whichever side moved and the diff names it. The plan amount is 0 deliberately: usage covers charges only, so a non-zero subscription fee would make the invoice legitimately larger and destroy the equality this row is built on.

The baseline for the origin, and the only row of the twelve where nothing else is in play. 5 March: 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ accrued crosses the 5_000¢ threshold and the threshold invoice bills the FULL accrued usage, not the threshold — 10_000¢. 15 March: a 20-unit event. With `latest_agg` the period is worth the LAST event only, so accrued usage falls to 2_000¢ and no further threshold can arm. 1 April: `to_credit_amount` is the threshold invoice's `fees_amount_cents` less its own coupons, credits and credit notes = 10_000¢ (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63), while the period's charge fees sharing that charge_id total 2_000¢. 10_000 > 2_000, so credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42 asks for a credit note of 10_000 − 2_000 = 8_000¢ and clamps the credit applied to the period invoice to 2_000¢. The note takes its items off the threshold invoice's fees largest-first — one fee, creditable 10_000¢, so a single item of 8_000¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:41-67) — and grosses it up by `amount − coupons_adjustment + taxes` = 8_000 − 0 + 0 (:69-80). credit_amount 8_000¢, balance 8_000¢. The 8_000¢ is NOT spent on the period invoice: `Credits::CreditNoteService` starts from `invoice.total_amount_cents` (credit_note_service.rb:40-47), which the progressive credit has already taken to 0, so `credit_notes_amount_cents` on that invoice is 0 and the balance survives for a later period. Both are asserted — a note of 8_000¢ that was also consumed here would credit the customer twice. Net cash: 10_000¢ demanded, 8_000¢ returned as credit, 2_000¢ kept — the period's real value. Had the clamp at :41 been missing, the period invoice would carry a 10_000¢ credit against 2_000¢ of fees; had the credit-note branch been missing, the customer would simply keep paying 10_000¢.

The coupon reaches this credit note TWICE, through two different services, and the two reductions do not cancel out. 5 March: 10_000¢ of accrued usage crosses the threshold. The `once` coupon is spent on the THRESHOLD invoice, not on the period invoice — it is finalized first (see judgment 3 of the skill) — so that invoice is 10_000 − 3_000 = 7_000¢ and the charge fee carries 3_000¢ of `precise_coupons_amount_cents`. 15 March: usage falls to 2_000¢ (`latest_agg`). 1 April, reduction one: `to_credit_amount` subtracts the threshold invoice's coupons — `fees_amount_cents − coupons_amount_cents` = 10_000 − 3_000 = 7_000¢ (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63). The excess is therefore 7_000 − 2_000 = 5_000¢ of FEE, not 8_000¢ as in the plain row: Lago only gives back what it actually collected. Reduction two: the note's own value re-applies the coupon at ITEM level. `create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:41-67` takes one item of 5_000¢ off the 10_000¢ fee, and :69-80 computes `5_000 − coupons_adjustment + taxes` where the adjustment is `fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents × item/fee` = 3_000 × 5_000/10_000 = 1_500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). Credit 3_500¢. So the same 3_000¢ coupon shrinks the excess by 3_000 and then shrinks the note by another 1_500. That is correct — the customer paid 7_000¢, kept 2_000¢ of value and gets 3_500¢ back, leaving 1_500¢ which is the discounted price of the 2_000¢ of usage they kept (2_000 × 7_000/10_000 = 1_400 … and the 100¢ gap is the second reduction being taken pro rata of the ITEM rather than of the retained usage) — but it is emphatically not `excess × (1 − coupon/fees)`, and either reduction on its own gives a different number: skipping the first gives 8_000 − 2_400 = 5_600¢, skipping the second gives 5_000¢. The period invoice carries no coupon (the `once` one is exhausted) and its 2_000¢ of fees is fully credited, so its total is 0 and the 3_500¢ stays available.

A wallet drained by a threshold invoice for usage that then evaporated — and the value comes back as credit-note balance rather than as credits. 5 March: 10_000¢ of usage crosses the threshold; the wallet's 50 credits settle 5_000¢ of the threshold invoice, leaving 5_000¢ of cash due and the wallet at 0. 15 March: `latest_agg` drops the period's worth to 2_000¢. 1 April: `to_credit_amount` is `fees_amount_cents` less coupons, progressive credits and credit notes (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63) — PREPAID CREDIT IS NOT IN THAT LIST — so it is the full 10_000¢ and the excess is 8_000¢. Had prepaid credit been netted off, the note would be 3_000¢ and the customer would lose the 5_000¢ of credits they had already spent. The 8_000¢ therefore exceeds the 5_000¢ of cash the invoice ever asked for, which is correct: the customer parted with 5_000¢ of cash AND 5_000¢ of credits for 2_000¢ of usage, so 8_000¢ of value is owed back. It arrives entirely as credit-note balance — the wallet is not refilled, because `void_prepaid_credit?` fires only for a wallet top-up invoice (create_service.rb:315-317) — so both the 8_000¢ and the 0¢ wallet are asserted; a refill on top of the note would return 13_000¢ of value against 10_000¢ collected. The period invoice is fully credited to 0 and the wallet contributes nothing further, since `should_create_applied_prepaid_credit?` needs a positive total (calculate_fees_service.rb:375-379).

`to_credit_amount` is measured PRE-tax while the credit note is issued POST-tax, and this row pins both halves. Threshold invoice (5 March): 10_000¢ of charge, 20% = 2_000¢, total 12_000¢. Usage falls to 2_000¢ on 15 March. 1 April: `to_credit_amount` reads `invoice.fees_amount_cents` — 10_000¢, the pre-tax figure, with no tax term anywhere in progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63 — against the period's 2_000¢ of charges, so the excess is 8_000¢ of FEE. The note then grosses that up by the credited fee's own tax: 8_000 × taxes_base_rate 1 × 20% = 1_600¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:69-80 → apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,112-116), giving credit_amount_cents 9_600¢ against an item of 8_000¢. Mixing the two conventions gives 8_000¢ (keeping the customer's VAT on usage that evaporated) or 10_000¢ pre-tax grossed to 12_000¢ (returning the VAT on the 2_000¢ they kept). THE PERIOD INVOICE'S CHARGE FEE IS TAXED AT 0 AND THAT IS THE ZERO-WEIGHT RULE IN ACTION. `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService#apply_credit_to_fees` (:68-83) writes the threshold invoice's BILLED amount into the period fee's `precise_coupons_amount_cents`, clamped to the fee amount, so the 2_000¢ fee's taxable base becomes 2_000 − 2_000 = 0 and it carries no tax. Here the clamp and the credit coincide at 2_000¢, so the invoice's own base is also 0 and the two agree — which is exactly why this row is green while b17/full-stack/invoice, where they diverge, is a characterization row. The per-fee `taxes_amount_cents: 0` is asserted because the invoice-level figure is 0 under both readings.

THE INVOICE THE CREDIT NOTE IS RAISED ON STAYS FULLY DUE. That is the assertion, and it is the sharpest of the three type rows for this origin because the alternative is materially better for everyone. The threshold invoice demanded 10_000¢ on 5 March and was never paid. Usage falls to 2_000¢ and on 1 April Lago raises an 8_000¢ credit note ON THAT INVOICE (credits/progressive_billing_service.rb:36-39). An offset would be the obvious settlement: the ceiling is `min(total_due 10_000, creditable 10_000)` = 10_000¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138), so all 8_000¢ could have been applied, leaving 2_000¢ due — exactly the period's real value — with no money changing hands in either direction. Instead `offset_amount_cents` is 0 and no InvoiceSettlement is created (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31 supplies only `credit_amount_cents`, so create_service.rb:82-89 is skipped), leaving the customer owing the full 10_000¢ on one invoice while holding 8_000¢ of spendable balance on their account. `total_due_amount_cents: 10000` with `payment_status: pending` is what pins it, and neither can be seen from the credit note alone. Whether that is a defect or a deliberate separation of concerns is not this row's call; the row exists so a change to either answer is visible.

The coupon shrinks the note twice over (see b08/from-progressive-billing-excess/credit/with-coupon for the two reductions: `to_credit_amount` drops to 7_000¢ so the excess is 5_000¢ of fee, and the item's own coupon share of 1_500¢ takes the note to 3_500¢) and STILL none of it settles the invoice it was raised on. The threshold invoice asks for 7_000¢ and is unpaid, so the offset ceiling is `min(total_due 7_000, creditable 10_000)` = 7_000¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138) — twice the note's value, so the whole 3_500¢ would have fitted. `offset_amount_cents` is 0 regardless (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31), `total_due_amount_cents` stays at 7_000¢ and the 3_500¢ becomes balance instead. Pairing this with the plain sibling is what shows the zero is structural rather than a consequence of the amounts: the coupon changes every figure in the note and does not change the column it lands in.

The one PB-excess cell where an offset could not have absorbed the whole note, so the zero has a second reading — and the row separates the two. Threshold invoice: 10_000¢ of usage, 5_000¢ settled from the wallet, 5_000¢ still due and unpaid. Usage falls to 2_000¢ and the excess is the full 8_000¢, since prepaid credit is absent from `to_credit_amount` (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63). The offset ceiling is `min(total_due 5_000, creditable 10_000)` = 5_000¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138), so an offset could have cancelled the remaining 5_000¢ of cash and the other 3_000¢ would have had to become credit — a MIXED note, exactly the shape b08/from-termination/refund/with-prepaid-credit produces on the same kind of asymmetry. Lago produces neither part: `offset_amount_cents` 0, `credit_amount_cents` 8_000, invoice still 5_000¢ due, wallet still empty (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31, create_service.rb:315-317). That is the whole point of asserting this cell rather than dismissing it as "offset is not supported here": the ceiling is genuinely below the note, so a future implementation has a real decision to make, and the numbers it would have to produce (5_000 offset + 3_000 credit) are written down here.

The widest gap between what is owed and what is held: a 12_000¢ unpaid invoice and a 9_600¢ credit-note balance that does not touch it. Threshold invoice 10_000¢ + 2_000¢ VAT = 12_000¢, unpaid. Usage falls to 2_000¢, the excess is 8_000¢ pre-tax, and the note is grossed up to 9_600¢ by the credited fee's own tax (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:69-80, apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40). The offset ceiling is `min(total_due 12_000, creditable 12_000)` = 12_000¢ — creditable includes the fees' taxes (invoice.rb:297-301) — so the full 9_600¢ would have fitted and would have left 2_400¢ due, the tax-inclusive value of the 2_000¢ of usage actually kept. Instead `offset_amount_cents` is 0, the invoice stays at 12_000¢ due, and 9_600¢ sits as balance. The tax makes this the row where the consequence is largest, and asserting the note's `taxes_amount_cents` alongside the zero offset keeps the two questions separate: the note grosses up correctly, and it still does not settle anything.

THE CASH IS ON THE TABLE AND LAGO STILL RETURNS CREDIT. That is the cell. Same shape as b08/from-progressive-billing-excess/credit/plain — 10_000¢ billed on 5 March, usage falling to 2_000¢ on 15 March, an 8_000¢ excess on 1 April — with one addition: the threshold invoice is PAID in full on 6 March, so `total_paid_amount_cents` is 10_000 and `refundable_amount_cents` is `min(paid − refunded, creditable)` = 8_000¢ (invoice.rb:460-476). A refund of the whole excess is therefore legally available: validate_service.rb:97-109 would accept it, and `cannot_refund_unpaid_invoice` — the reason a refund is impossible on the unpaid variant — does not apply. Lago issues a pure credit anyway. `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService` calls `CreditNotes::CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice` (progressive_billing_service.rb:36-39), which passes `credit_amount_cents:` and no refund or offset amount at all (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31), so create_service.rb:70-75 computes total 8_000 = credit 8_000 + refund 0 + offset 0 and balance 8_000. The payment does not reach the decision: it is not an input to `to_credit_amount` (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63) either. refund_amount_cents 0 WITH total_amount_cents 8_000 is the pair that proves it — the total alone is identical to the credit variant, and refund_amount_cents 0 on an UNPAID invoice would prove only that a refund was impossible. Whether that is right is a policy question this row deliberately does not answer: the customer handed over 10_000¢ of cash for 2_000¢ of usage and gets store credit for the difference. It is recorded here so that a future decision to refund instead turns this row red rather than shipping silently.

The coupon variant of the same question, and the reason it is worth a row of its own: the amount that COULD have been refunded is not the excess. Threshold invoice: 10_000¢ of usage less the `once` coupon's 3_000¢ = 7_000¢, paid in full on 6 March, so `total_paid_amount_cents` is 7_000. Usage falls to 2_000¢; on 1 April `to_credit_amount` = 10_000 − 3_000 = 7_000¢ (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63), the excess over the period's 2_000¢ of charges is 5_000¢ of fee, and the note is worth 5_000 − 3_000 × 5_000/10_000 = 3_500¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:41-80, apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). `refundable_amount_cents` = min(7_000 paid − 0 refunded, creditable) = 3_500¢ (invoice.rb:460-476), so the whole note could have been cash. It is credit: create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31 sets only `credit_amount_cents`, so refund_amount_cents is 0 and balance_amount_cents is the full 3_500¢. Asserting refund_amount_cents 0 next to credit_amount_cents 3_500 is what makes this a statement about the TYPE rather than about the amount; and the amount itself is the coupon-weighted 3_500¢ rather than the raw 5_000¢ excess, so a fix that started refunding the excess in cash would have to get the coupon weighting right too.

The case where a refund could only ever have been PARTIAL, so returning credit is the least surprising of the three outcomes — and the row records where the boundary would have been. Threshold invoice: 10_000¢ of usage, 5_000¢ settled from the wallet, 5_000¢ paid in cash on 6 March, so `total_paid_amount_cents` is 5_000 and the wallet is empty. Usage falls to 2_000¢, and on 1 April the excess is the full 10_000 − 2_000 = 8_000¢, because neither prepaid credit nor payments enter `to_credit_amount` (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63). `refundable_amount_cents` = min(5_000 paid, creditable 10_000) = 5_000¢ (invoice.rb:460-476), so at most 5_000¢ of the 8_000¢ could ever have come back as cash: the other 3_000¢ was paid for with granted credits and there is no cash to return. Lago sidesteps that split entirely and credits all 8_000¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31) — contrast b08/from-termination/refund/with-prepaid-credit, which faces the same asymmetry and DOES split the note 500¢ credit / 1_000¢ refund. Two automatic paths, the same problem, opposite answers. Asserted together: refund_amount_cents 0, credit 8_000, and a wallet still at 0 — the credits are not restored either, so the entire 8_000¢ of value exists as one credit-note balance.

A paid, taxed threshold invoice: the largest sum in the block that could have gone back as cash and does not. Threshold invoice 10_000¢ + 2_000¢ VAT = 12_000¢, paid in full on 6 March. Usage falls to 2_000¢. On 1 April the excess is 10_000 − 2_000 = 8_000¢ of pre-tax fee, grossed up by the credited fee's own tax to 9_600¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:69-80, apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40). `refundable_amount_cents` = min(12_000 paid, creditable 12_000) = 12_000¢ (invoice.rb:460-476) — comfortably above 9_600 — so the entire tax-inclusive excess was refundable. Lago credits it: refund_amount_cents 0, balance 9_600¢ (create_from_progressive_billing_invoice.rb:22-31, create_service.rb:70-75). The VAT matters here beyond the arithmetic: 1_600¢ of the balance is tax the customer paid to the business, which paid it on. Returning it as store credit rather than cash is a different accounting outcome from a refund, and this row is where a change of policy would surface — as a red row with 9_600 in refund_amount_cents instead of a silent behaviour change.

The baseline for the whole family. A 3_000¢ pay-in-advance plan bills the whole of April up front on 1 April, and terminating on 15 April returns the days from the 15th onward: `day_price × remaining_duration` where day_price is 3_000/30 = 100¢ (dates_service.rb:197-200, calendar monthly duration = 30) and remaining_duration is 30 April − 15 April = 15 (create_from_termination.rb:114-129). Base creditable 1_500¢, capped at the subscription fee (:66-81) which is 3_000¢, so no clamp applies. With no coupon and no tax, `adjust_for_coupon_and_taxes` returns the 1_500¢ unchanged (:149-159), and `on_termination: credit` puts all of it in the credit column — `[total_creditable, 0, 0]` (:131-147) — so balance_amount_cents starts at 1_500¢ and nothing is refunded or offset. THE INVOICE IS UNTOUCHED: still 3_000¢ due and payment_status pending. That is the difference from the offset sibling on the identical setup, which settles 1_500¢ of this very invoice instead. A credit note that reduced the invoice AND created a balance would return the money twice, and total_amount_cents 1_500 is the same in both cases — only the pair of assertions separates them. Off-by-one is the failure mode this row is shaped to catch: counting from the 16th gives 14 days and 1_400¢, and the arrears convention (billing THROUGH the termination day, b09/terminate) would give 16 days used and 1_400¢ unused.

An automatic credit note has to give back the coupon too, and it computes that through exactly the same weighting a manual one does. The advance invoice is 3_000¢ of subscription fee less a 1_000¢ coupon = 2_000¢, and the fee carries the whole 1_000¢ of coupon (it is the only fee, so `compute_precise_credit_amount_cents(1_000, 3_000) = 1_000 × 3_000/3_000`, fee.rb:232-236). Termination credits 15 of 30 days = 1_500¢ of FEE, then grosses it down and up: `precise_amount − coupons_adjustment + taxes` (create_from_termination.rb:149-159), where coupons_adjustment is `fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents × item/fee` = 1_000 × 1_500/3_000 = 500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). So the credit is 1_500 − 500 = 1_000¢ — half of what the customer actually paid, which is the right answer for half a period. Crediting the raw 1_500¢ would hand back 500¢ of a discount as spendable money; that error is invisible in `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` alone (1_000 either way once the adjustment is applied), so `coupons_adjustment_amount_cents` is asserted directly. Note the near miss: a coupon of 3_000¢ instead of 1_000¢ would make the fee's `precise_coupons_amount_cents` equal its amount, the adjustment would consume the whole creditable figure, and create_from_termination.rb:33 would return WITHOUT CREATING A CREDIT NOTE AT ALL. That is the zero-weight case, and it is the reason this row uses a coupon smaller than the fee.

Termination prices the unused days off the FEE, so a wallet that part-paid the invoice does not reduce the credit. The wallet holds 5 credits at 1.00; the advance invoice is 3_000¢ of fee with 500¢ settled from the wallet, leaving 2_500¢ of cash due and the wallet at 0. Terminating on 15 April credits 15/30 × 3_000 = 1_500¢, and every input to that figure — day price, remaining duration, the fee's coupons and taxes (create_from_termination.rb:66-81,149-159) — is drawn from the fee and its invoice's tax rows. Prepaid credit appears in none of them, so the credit is 1_500¢ and not 1_250¢ (half of the 2_500¢ actually charged). That is defensible — the customer bought half a month they will not use, whether they paid for it in cash or in credits — but it means the 500¢ of granted credit comes back as credit-note balance rather than as wallet credits: the wallet stays at 0 (`void_prepaid_credit?` is gated on `invoice.credit?`, create_service.rb:315-317). Asserting the wallet is what stops a future refill from double-counting it.

Termination has to gross the prorated fee back up by tax, and it does it through the fee's own applied taxes rather than by re-applying the rate to the credit. Advance invoice: 3_000¢ of fee, 20% = 600¢, total 3_600¢. Terminating on 15 April credits 15/30 days = 1_500¢ of fee; `adjust_for_coupon_and_taxes` builds a throwaway CreditNoteItem for that amount and asks CreditNotes::ApplyTaxesService for its tax (create_from_termination.rb:149-159), giving 1_500 × taxes_base_rate 1 × 20% = 300¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,84-94,112-116 — taxes_base_rate is 1 because Invoices::ApplyTaxesService leaves `taxable_base_amount_cents` unset and invoice/applied_tax.rb:29-34 falls back to fees_amount_cents). Credit 1_500 + 300 = 1_800¢, which is exactly half of the 3_600¢ the customer paid up front. Two wrong answers: 1_500¢ (the pre-tax half, keeping the customer's VAT on days they never used) and 2_160¢ (20% applied to a 1_800¢ base — taxing the already-inclusive figure). The credit note's own `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` and `taxes_amount_cents` are asserted separately so the two components cannot compensate for each other.

The termination setting that is only useful on an UNPAID invoice: instead of granting credit or paying cash out, it reduces what the customer still owes for the period they are leaving. The 3_000¢ advance invoice is not paid, so `paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription` is 0 and potential refund = 0 − 1_500 is negative → refund 0 (create_from_termination.rb:161-169). With `on_termination: offset`, :145 then puts the whole creditable amount in the offset column: `[0, 0, 1_500]`. create_service.rb:82-89 raises an InvoiceSettlement of 1_500¢ against that same invoice, so `total_due = 3_000 − 0 − 1_500` = 1_500¢ (invoice.rb:407-410) — the customer now owes exactly the half-month they used. payment_status stays pending because the due amount is still positive (invoice_settlements/create_service.rb:58-60). Every one of the three settings produces total_amount_cents 1_500 on this timeline; only the column and the invoice's due amount tell them apart. `offset` here is materially better for the business than `credit` — the same 1_500¢ cancels a receivable instead of becoming a liability — and a row asserting the total alone would not notice which one it got.

A discounted period abandoned half way, settled against itself — and the coupon has to be honoured in the offset or the customer is let off part of the discount as well as part of the fee. Advance invoice: 3_000¢ of fee − 1_000¢ coupon = 2_000¢, unpaid. Unused half = 1_500¢ of fee, less its share of the coupon 1_000 × 1_500/3_000 = 500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82) → 1_000¢ creditable (create_from_termination.rb:149-159). Nothing was paid, so refund is 0 and the whole 1_000¢ becomes offset (:145). `total_due = 2_000 − 1_000` = 1_000¢ (invoice.rb:407-410), which is exactly what the used half cost after the discount — the invoice ends up charging half of 2_000¢ rather than half of 3_000¢. Offsetting the un-adjusted 1_500¢ would leave 500¢ due and the customer would pay 500¢ for a half-month that cost 1_000¢, quietly spending the coupon twice. The offset ceiling is `min(total_due 2_000, creditable 3_000)` (validate_service.rb:125-138), so nothing else constrains the figure and the coupon weighting is the only thing that can be wrong.

Prepaid credit and an offset reduce two different quantities on the same invoice, and here they both do it before anyone pays anything. The wallet's 500¢ is applied when the advance invoice is issued, taking `total_amount_cents` to 2_500¢. The offset is applied at termination, taking `total_due_amount_cents` to 2_500 − 0 − 1_500 = 1_000¢ (invoice.rb:407-410) — the total itself does not move. The offset is the full 1_500¢ of unused days because termination prices off the FEE (create_from_termination.rb:66-81) and nothing paid means no refund (:161-169). It is legal because the ceiling is `min(total_due 2_500, creditable 3_000)` = 2_500¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138), which 1_500 clears comfortably — unlike b08/manual-full/offset/with-prepaid-credit, where the request is pushed up to that ceiling and a full-fee offset becomes impossible. Net effect: the customer used half a month, was charged 2_500¢ of cash for the whole of it, and now owes 1_000¢. Their 500¢ of granted credit is not returned in any form — the wallet stays at 0 and the offset is the only relief — which is the arithmetic worth pinning, because "offset the unused part" and "put the customer back where they started" are not the same thing here.

The offset has to be the tax-INCLUSIVE half, because the receivable it cancels is tax-inclusive. Advance invoice: 3_000¢ + 600¢ VAT = 3_600¢, unpaid. Terminating on the 15th credits 15/30 days: 1_500¢ of fee grossed up by its own tax, 1_500 × 1 × 20% = 300¢, giving 1_800¢ (create_from_termination.rb:149-159, apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,112-116). Nothing was paid so refund is 0 and all 1_800¢ goes to the offset column (:145). `total_due = 3_600 − 1_800` = 1_800¢, exactly the used half including its VAT. Offsetting only the net 1_500 would leave 2_100¢ due — the customer paying VAT on 15 days they never had. The credit note's `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` (1_500) and `taxes_amount_cents` (300) are asserted alongside the 1_800¢ offset so a note that reached the right total with the wrong split — e.g. treating the whole 1_800 as untaxed — still fails.

`on_termination_credit_note: refund` does not mean "refund everything" — it means "refund whatever the customer has ALREADY OVERPAID, and credit the rest", and this row is the case where the overpayment happens to be the whole creditable amount. The 3_000¢ advance invoice is paid in full on 1 April. Terminating on the 15th: total_creditable = 1_500¢ (15 unused days at 100¢); `paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription` = fee share of the invoice (3_000/3_000 = 1) × 3_000¢ paid = 3_000¢ (create_from_termination.rb:179-189); `creditable_used_amount` = the same gross-up applied to the 15 USED days = 1_500¢ (:175-177); potential refund = 3_000 − 1_500 = 1_500¢, capped at total_creditable → 1_500¢ (:161-169). `[creditable − refund, refund, 0]` = [0, 1_500, 0] (:131-147), so it is a PURE refund: cash goes back, balance_amount_cents is 0, refund_status pending. Compare b08/from-termination/credit/plain on the identical timeline minus the payment: same 1_500¢ total, all of it in the credit column with a 1_500¢ balance. The type axis here is a subscription attribute, so a row that asserted only total_amount_cents would pass with the setting ignored entirely.

The coupon has to be netted out of BOTH sides of the refund calculation, and this row is where a one-sided fix would show. Advance invoice: 3_000¢ of fee − 1_000¢ coupon = 2_000¢, paid in full. total_creditable = adjust(1_500) = 1_500 − 1_000 × 1_500/3_000 = 1_000¢ (create_from_termination.rb:149-159, apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). The refund side uses the SAME gross-up on the used half: `creditable_used_amount` = adjust(1_500) = 1_000¢ (:175-177), while `paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription` is the fee's share of the cash — `(fee.sub_total_excluding_taxes_precise + fee.taxes_precise) / invoice.sub_total_including_taxes × total_paid` = (3_000 − 1_000)/2_000 × 2_000 = 2_000¢ (:179-189, fee.rb:242-244). Note the fee share is computed NET of the coupon on both numerator and denominator, so it is 1 rather than 1.5. potential refund = 2_000 − 1_000 = 1_000¢, capped at total_creditable 1_000 → 1_000¢, leaving credit 0. Had the used amount been taken gross (1_500) the refund would be 500¢ and 500¢ would be left as credit; had the paid amount been taken gross the refund would be capped at 1_000 anyway — so the row is sharpest on the used side, and `credit_amount_cents: 0` is the assertion that catches it.

THE ONLY MIXED NOTE IN THE BLOCK: the wallet's contribution decides how much of the unused period comes back as cash and how much as credit. The wallet's 5 credits settle 500¢ of the 3_000¢ advance invoice, so the customer pays 2_500¢ in cash and `total_paid_amount_cents` is 2_500 — a wallet application never lands there (payments/manual_create_service.rb:38-41). total_creditable = 1_500¢ (15 unused days at 100¢, no coupon, no tax). `paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription` = fee share × cash paid = (3_000/3_000) × 2_500 = 2_500¢ (create_from_termination.rb:179-189) — note the denominator is `sub_total_including_taxes_amount_cents` = 3_000, which is BEFORE prepaid credit, so the share is 1 and the whole 2_500¢ is attributed to this fee. `creditable_used_amount` = 1_500¢. potential refund = 2_500 − 1_500 = 1_000¢, which is BELOW total_creditable, so `calculate_refund` returns 1_000 and :143 splits the note as `[1_500 − 1_000, 1_000, 0]` = 500¢ credit + 1_000¢ refund, total 1_500¢, balance 500¢. That split is the behaviour: the customer only ever handed over 2_500¢ of money, of which 1_500¢ bought the days they used, so only 1_000¢ can come back as cash and the remaining 500¢ — the part the wallet paid for — comes back as credit. Refunding all 1_500¢ would pay out 500¢ of cash for credits that were granted for free.

A refund of tax-inclusive cash, where the prorated PAID amount is also tax-inclusive — the two have to be measured in the same units or the split between credit and refund goes wrong. Advance invoice: 3_000¢ + 600¢ VAT = 3_600¢, paid in full. total_creditable = 1_500 + 300 = 1_800¢ (create_from_termination.rb:149-159). `paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription` = (fee net 3_000 + fee tax 600) / invoice sub_total_including_taxes 3_600 × 3_600¢ paid = 3_600¢ (:179-189) — inclusive on both sides. `creditable_used_amount` = adjust(1_500) = 1_800¢. potential = 3_600 − 1_800 = 1_800¢, capped at 1_800 → the whole creditable amount is refunded and credit_amount_cents is 0 (:131-147,161-169). If the paid side were compared EXCLUSIVE of tax (3_000) against an inclusive used amount (1_800), potential would be 1_200¢ and the note would split 600¢ credit / 1_200¢ refund — same 1_800¢ total, different money. That is why both columns are asserted rather than the total.

The invoice holds a single 3_000¢ charge fee and no tax, so crediting it whole means one item of 3_000¢ pre-tax and a credit of 3_000¢ inclusive — the two coincide only because the tax rate is zero, which is why the with-tax row below exists. A `credit` credit note is spendable on future invoices, so its balance starts at the full 3_000¢ and its credit_status is `available`.

A credited fee gives back its share of the coupon, and the share is per FEE, not per invoice. The invoice is 5_000¢ of subscription + 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ of charge = 15_000¢ of fees. The 3_000¢ fixed coupon is spread over the fees pro rata of their gross amounts — `credit_amount × (fee.amount_cents − fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents) / base` (fee.rb:232-236, applied_coupon_service.rb:34-41) — so the subscription fee carries 3_000 × 5_000/15_000 = 1_000¢ and the charge fee 3_000 × 10_000/15_000 = 2_000¢. Invoice base 15_000 − 3_000 = 12_000¢, no tax, total 12_000¢. Crediting BOTH fees whole returns the whole coupon: `coupons_adjustment` sums, per item, `fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents × item/fee` (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82) = 1_000 × 5_000/5_000 + 2_000 × 10_000/10_000 = 3_000¢. So the note is items 15_000 − coupon 3_000 + tax 0 = 12_000¢ (credit_note.rb:171-173, create_service.rb:62-75) and the balance starts at the full 12_000¢ because a `credit` note is spendable rather than paid out. Passing 15_000 as credit_amount_cents — the gross fee total — is rejected as `does_not_match_item_amounts` (validate_service.rb:90-94), and had the coupon been ignored the customer would hold 15_000¢ of credit for an invoice that only ever cost them 12_000¢. The per-fee amounts are asserted because a coupon spread equally over the two fees (1_500 each) gives the same 12_000¢ note and only the fee split tells the two weightings apart.

Prepaid credit is the LAST reducer on the invoice and the FIRST thing a credit note ignores. The wallet holds 50 credits at 1.00, so 5_000¢ of the 15_000¢ of fees is settled from it and the invoice asks for 10_000¢ of cash. The creditable ceiling, however, is `invoice.fee_total_amount_cents − credited − offsets` (validate_service.rb:36-40,112-123 and invoice.rb:297-301), which is built from the FEES and their taxes and knows nothing about prepaid credit: 15_000¢. So all 15_000¢ is creditable even though only 10_000¢ was ever payable, and both fees can be credited whole in one note — items 15_000 − coupon 0 + tax 0 = 15_000¢ of balance. Had prepaid credit been netted off the base first, the note would be 10_000¢ and the customer would silently lose the 5_000¢ of wallet money they had already spent on this invoice. The wallet is NOT refilled: `void_prepaid_credit?` fires only for a `credit`-type invoice, i.e. a wallet top-up invoice (create_service.rb:315-317), and this is a subscription invoice — so its balance stays at 0 and the returned value arrives as credit-note balance instead. Both are asserted, because a note of 15_000¢ AND a refilled wallet would be the customer paid twice over. Contrast b08/manual-full/refund/with-prepaid-credit, where the same invoice can only be refunded for 10_000¢: the credit ceiling and the refund ceiling are different code and they disagree here by exactly the wallet's contribution.

This is the row that pins the pre-tax / inclusive asymmetry. A 20% organization tax makes the invoice 3_000¢ of fees plus 600¢ of tax. Crediting it whole means an item of 3_000¢ — the PRE-tax fee amount — while credit_amount_cents must be 3_600¢, the INCLUSIVE total. Passing 3_000 as the credit amount would under-credit the customer by exactly the tax; passing 3_600 as the item amount would over-credit by 20% of it.

The third type, and the only one that acts on the invoice it is raised against. 15_000¢ of fees (5_000 subscription + 10_000 charge), no tax, no coupon, nothing paid. `offset_amount_cents` makes create_service.rb:82-89 raise an InvoiceSettlement for the offset amount against this very invoice, and invoice_settlements/create_service.rb:34,58-68 marks the invoice paid as soon as `total_due_amount_cents` — `total − paid − offsets`, invoice.rb:407-410 — reaches 0. So the invoice is settled with no cash and no balance: total_due 0 and payment_status succeeded, while balance_amount_cents is 0 because balance tracks the CREDIT part only (create_service.rb:70-75). That is the entire distinction from the two siblings on the same 15_000¢: `credit` leaves 15_000¢ spendable on the NEXT invoice and this one still due; `refund` needs the invoice paid first and sends cash back. All three report total_amount_cents 15_000, so the type field and the invoice's own due amount are what the row asserts. The ceiling is `min(total_due, creditable)` (validate_service.rb:125-138) = min(15_000, 15_000), so this is the largest legal offset here; a 15_001 request would be `offset_amount_cents/higher_than_remaining_invoice_amount`.

An offset that has to agree with a coupon in TWO places at once, and the two are computed by different code. Fees 15_000¢ (5_000 + 10_000), coupon 3_000¢ spread 1_000/2_000 pro rata of the gross fee amounts (fee.rb:232-236), invoice total 12_000¢. The note's own value comes from the items less the coupon they carry: 15_000 − (1_000 + 2_000) = 12_000¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82, credit_note.rb:171-173). The offset CEILING comes from somewhere else entirely — `min(total_due, creditable)` where creditable is `fee_total_amount_cents − credited − offsets` = 15_000 and total_due is 12_000 (validate_service.rb:125-138, invoice.rb:297-301,407-410) — so the binding constraint is the DUE amount, 12_000. The coupon reaches both numbers by different routes and they meet exactly, which is why the invoice settles to total_due 0 and payment_status succeeded. Had the coupon been left out of the item arithmetic the request would be 15_000 and fail on the due-amount ceiling; had it been left out of the invoice total, 12_000 would have left 3_000¢ still due. Both failure modes are visible only because the note and the invoice are asserted together.

THE ONLY CELL IN THIS FAMILY WHERE A FULL-INVOICE OFFSET IS ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE, and the row records where the limit lands. 15_000¢ of fees, 5_000¢ settled from the wallet, 10_000¢ due. The offset ceiling is `min(total_due, creditable)` = min(10_000, 15_000) = 10_000¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138), so offsetting all 15_000¢ of fees is refused with `offset_amount_cents/higher_than_remaining_invoice_amount`: prepaid credit lowers what is DUE without lowering what is CREDITABLE, and an offset can never exceed the smaller of the two. "Full" here therefore means the full remaining due, 10_000¢ — one item of 10_000 against the charge fee, leaving the 5_000¢ subscription fee uncredited and still creditable. That the invoice reaches total_due 0 and payment_status succeeded on 10_000¢ is the point: the wallet had already settled the other third, and an offset of 15_000 would have handed back 5_000¢ of value the business never received in either cash or credits. The wallet is not refilled (`void_prepaid_credit?` is gated on `invoice.credit?`, create_service.rb:315-317), so balance_cents stays 0. The rejection case is a real cell of its own and is NOT expressible today: the interpreter's `expect.error` supports only the setup stages metric/plan/charge/subscription (golden_runner.rb:65), so a credit-note-level rejection cannot be asserted.

An offset settles a TAX-INCLUSIVE invoice, so the offset amount must be the gross figure while the items stay pre-tax — the same asymmetry as b08/manual-full/credit/with-tax, but now checked against a second, independent number: the invoice's own due amount. Fees 15_000¢, 20% on each fee → 1_000 + 2_000 = 3_000¢ of tax, invoice 18_000¢, unpaid. The note's tax is derived from the credited fees: base 15_000 × taxes_base_rate 1 × 20% = 3_000¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,84-94,112-116), so the offset is 18_000¢ and the ceiling `min(total_due 18_000, creditable 18_000)` — creditable includes fee taxes (invoice.rb:297-301) — is met exactly, taking total_due to 0 and the invoice to succeeded. Offsetting only the pre-tax 15_000 would leave 3_000¢ of VAT outstanding on an invoice everybody considered closed, which is precisely the failure this row is here to catch; the balance stays 0 because an offset creates no spendable credit.

The same 3_000¢ credited as a REFUND rather than a credit: money leaves rather than becoming spendable, so balance_amount_cents is 0 where the credit row has 3_000. total_amount_cents is 3_000 in both. That balance difference is the whole distinction between the two types, and it is what makes a mis-typed credit note either a giveaway or a double charge. The invoice must be PAID before it can be refunded — an unpaid one is rejected with refund_amount_cents/cannot_refund_unpaid_invoice — hence the pay_invoice step, and with it the premium licence plus the manual_payments integration that recording a payment requires.

The same 12_000¢ as b08/manual-full/credit/with-coupon, taken out of the business instead of left on the customer's account — so the arithmetic of the coupon is identical and only the destination differs. Fees 15_000¢ (5_000 subscription + 10_000 charge), coupon 3_000¢ split 1_000/2_000 over the two fees pro rata (fee.rb:232-236), base and total 12_000¢. Crediting both fees whole returns the whole coupon (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82), so the note is items 15_000 − 3_000 = 12_000¢ — and here that figure is doubly forced, because the refund is also capped at the cash received: `total_paid_amount_cents − already refunded` (validate_service.rb:97-109), and the customer paid exactly 12_000¢. Asking for the gross 15_000 fails twice over, as `refund_amount_cents/higher_than_remaining_invoice_amount` and as `does_not_match_item_amounts`. refund_amount_cents 12_000 with balance_amount_cents 0 is the whole distinction from the credit sibling, which has the same total_amount_cents and a balance of 12_000. A mis-typed note is therefore either a giveaway or a double charge, and `total_amount_cents` alone cannot see it. refund_status is `pending` because create_service.rb:68 marks the refund pending and the actual payout is a provider job (:254-263); with a manual payment there is no provider, so it stays pending rather than succeeding.

THE REFUND CEILING IS CASH, THE CREDIT CEILING IS FEES, and this is the invoice where they differ. 15_000¢ of fees, 5_000¢ settled from the wallet, so the customer paid 10_000¢ and `total_paid_amount_cents` is 10_000 — a wallet application is not a payment and never lands there (payments/manual_create_service.rb:38-41 sums succeeded payments only). validate_service.rb:100-108 caps the refund at `total_paid_amount_cents − already refunded` = 10_000¢, so the largest legal refund on this invoice is 10_000 even though `fee_total_amount_cents` is 15_000 and the credit sibling (b08/manual-full/credit/with-prepaid-credit) may take all 15_000. Asking for 15_000 here is refused with `refund_amount_cents/higher_than_remaining_invoice_amount`. 10_000¢ happens to be exactly the charge fee, so ONE item of 10_000 satisfies `valid_items_amount?` (validate_service.rb:90-94) and the 5_000¢ subscription fee is left uncredited and still creditable — which is why items_count is asserted as 1 and the fee split is spelled out: crediting 5_000 of each fee would give the same 10_000¢ refund but leave a different invoice behind. The wallet stays at 0. Refunding cash does not put credits back — `void_prepaid_credit?` is gated on `invoice.credit?` (create_service.rb:315-317) and this is a subscription invoice — so the 5_000¢ of granted credit is simply spent, and the row asserts that rather than letting a silent refill pass.

The pre-tax / tax-inclusive asymmetry on the REFUND side, where getting it wrong short-changes the customer in cash rather than in balance. Invoice: 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ charge, 20% organization tax on each fee → 1_000¢ and 2_000¢ of tax, 3_000¢ in total, invoice 18_000¢, paid in full. The credit note's tax is DERIVED FROM THE CREDITED FEES' TAXES, not recomputed from the refund: per tax code the base is `item − prorated coupon` = 15_000¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:84-94), multiplied by `taxes_base_rate` and the fee's tax rate (:36-40). `taxes_base_rate` is `taxable_amount_cents / fees_amount_cents` (:112-116) and equals 1 here because Invoices::ApplyTaxesService never writes `taxable_base_amount_cents`, so invoice/applied_tax.rb:29-34 falls back to `fees_amount_cents` — the ratio is only ever below 1 with a tax provider. Tax on the note is therefore 3_000¢ and the refund is 15_000 + 3_000 = 18_000¢, while the ITEMS stay at the pre-tax 5_000/10_000. Passing 15_000 as refund_amount_cents would return the fees and keep the VAT, under-refunding by exactly 3_000¢; passing 18_000 as the item amounts would over-credit the fees by 20% and be refused by `higher_than_remaining_fee_amount` (validate_item_service.rb:68-77). The per-fee taxes are asserted, not just the 3_000¢ total: a tax computed on the invoice's sub_total instead of fee by fee gives the same 3_000¢ here, and only the fee-level split distinguishes them — which is what localised the tax defect in b17/full-stack/invoice.

A third of the 3_000¢ fee credited: one item of 1_000¢ → 1_000¢ credited, 2_000¢ of the fee still standing. The `reason` is asserted too, since it is caller-supplied metadata that ends up on the customer-facing document.

THE ROW THE PER-FEE WEIGHTING RULE DECIDES. Fees are 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ charge, and the 3_000¢ coupon is limited to the charge's billable metric, so `base_amount_cents` is the charge fee alone (applied_coupon_service.rb:92-101 → :123-128) and the whole 3_000¢ lands on the charge fee: `compute_precise_credit_amount_cents(3_000, 10_000) = 3_000 × 10_000/10_000` (fee.rb:232-236). The subscription fee carries NOTHING. Invoice base 15_000 − 3_000 = 12_000¢. Crediting 5_000¢ — half the charge fee — returns half of the coupon that fee carries: `fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents × item/fee` = 3_000 × 5_000/10_000 = 1_500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). So the note is 5_000 − 1_500 + 0 = 3_500¢ (credit_note.rb:171-173), and 3_500¢ becomes spendable balance. A NAIVE WEIGHTING GIVES 4_000¢ HERE. Prorating the coupon over the invoice's fees instead of the credited fee — 3_000 × 5_000/15_000 = 1_000 — gives 5_000 − 1_000 = 4_000¢, and that weighting is indistinguishable from the correct one for an UNLIMITED coupon (both reduce to `C × item/total`), which is why the coupon here is limited. Over-crediting by 500¢ is the customer being handed back a discount they never paid for. The remaining 5_000¢ of the charge fee and the whole subscription fee stay creditable (validate_item_service.rb:68-77 caps each item at `fee.creditable_amount_cents`), which is what makes this partial rather than full.

A partial credit on an invoice a wallet part-paid. 15_000¢ of fees, 5_000¢ taken from the wallet, 10_000¢ of cash due. Crediting 5_000¢ of the charge fee is priced off the FEE, not off what the customer paid: no coupon, no tax, so the note is exactly 5_000¢ and the wallet's involvement changes nothing — `creditable_amount_cents` is `fee_total_amount_cents − credited − offsets` (validate_service.rb:36-40, invoice.rb:297-301) and is blind to prepaid credit. Had prepaid credit been prorated into the item's value (5_000 × 10_000/15_000 = 3_333¢) the customer would be short 1_667¢ on a fee they were fully charged for. The wallet balance stays 0 rather than regaining 5_000¢ of credits: a subscription invoice's credit note never touches a wallet (`void_prepaid_credit?`, create_service.rb:315-317). Both halves are asserted because a note of 5_000¢ *and* a refilled wallet would hand back the same money twice.
