Half of one fee on a taxed two-fee invoice: 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ charge, 20% on each → 1_000¢ and 2_000¢ of tax, invoice 18_000¢. The note credits 5_000¢ of the CHARGE fee only. Tax follows the credited fee's own tax code and base: `(item − prorated coupon) × taxes_base_rate × rate` = 5_000 × 1 × 20% = 1_000¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,84-94), so credit_amount_cents is 6_000¢ and the item stays at the pre-tax 5_000. `taxes_rate` is 20 because the pro-rata is over the items of the note, not the invoice (:99-106) — the untouched subscription fee does not dilute it. Two wrong answers this excludes: 5_000¢ (the pre-tax item passed as the credit — under-credits by the VAT the customer paid on that half) and 3_600¢ (20% of the invoice's tax prorated by 5_000/15_000 = 1_000 applied to a 3_000¢ base, i.e. tax taken from the invoice rather than the fee). The remaining 5_000¢ of the charge fee and the entire subscription fee are still creditable.

A PARTIAL offset, which is the only arrangement where the invoice survives the credit note in a third state — neither fully due nor settled. 15_000¢ of fees, unpaid, 5_000¢ of the charge fee offset. create_service.rb:82-89 raises an InvoiceSettlement for 5_000¢, and invoice.rb:407-410 recomputes `total_due = total − paid − offsets` = 15_000 − 0 − 5_000 = 10_000¢. Because that is still positive, invoice_settlements/create_service.rb:58-60 does NOT mark the invoice paid, so payment_status stays `pending` — the assertion that distinguishes a partial offset from the full one in b08/manual-full/offset/plain. The offset ceiling here is `min(total_due 15_000, creditable 15_000)` (validate_service.rb:125-138) and is nowhere near binding, so the 5_000¢ comes purely from the item. balance_amount_cents is 0: an offset never creates spendable credit, so the customer's 5_000¢ of relief exists only as a lower bill on THIS invoice — the sibling `credit` note would instead leave this invoice at 15_000¢ due and 5_000¢ available for the next one.

The per-fee coupon weighting decides how much of an unpaid invoice a credit note can settle — this row is where the weighting rule shows up as a DUE AMOUNT rather than as a balance. The 3_000¢ coupon is limited to the charge's metric, so all of it sits on the 10_000¢ charge fee (applied_coupon_service.rb:92-101,123-128). Invoice 15_000 − 3_000 = 12_000¢, unpaid. Offsetting 5_000¢ of that fee is worth 5_000 − 3_000 × 5_000/10_000 = 3_500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82), so the settlement is 3_500¢ and `total_due = 12_000 − 0 − 3_500` = 8_500¢, still positive, so payment_status stays pending (invoice.rb:407-410, invoice_settlements/create_service.rb:58-60). Under the naive invoice-level weighting the note would be worth 4_000¢ and the invoice would show 8_000¢ due — 500¢ of the customer's bill written off against a discount they had already been given. The due amount is asserted precisely because it is the field a reviewer would sanity-check, and it is wrong by exactly the weighting error.

Two settlement mechanisms on one invoice, each reducing a different quantity, and the row asserts both so neither can absorb the other. 15_000¢ of fees; the wallet's 5_000¢ is applied BEFORE the invoice is issued and lowers `total_amount_cents` to 10_000¢ (prepaid credit is the last reducer of calculate_fees_service.rb:62). The offset is applied AFTER, as an InvoiceSettlement, and lowers `total_due_amount_cents` without touching the total: 10_000 − 0 − 5_000 = 5_000¢ (invoice.rb:407-410). So the same 5_000¢ of relief appears in two different fields depending on which mechanism delivered it, and payment_status stays pending because 5_000¢ is still owed. The offset is legal because the ceiling is `min(total_due 10_000, creditable 15_000)` = 10_000¢ (validate_service.rb:125-138) and 5_000 is well inside it — the contrast with b08/manual-full/offset/with-prepaid-credit, where the request is pushed up to that ceiling and a full-fee offset becomes impossible. The wallet ends at 0 and is not refilled (create_service.rb:315-317).

A partial offset must settle the TAX-INCLUSIVE share of what it credits, or the invoice keeps VAT on units nobody is being charged for. Invoice 15_000¢ of fees + 3_000¢ tax = 18_000¢, unpaid. Offsetting 5_000¢ of the charge fee carries its own 1_000¢ of VAT (apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,84-94), so the settlement is 6_000¢ and `total_due = 18_000 − 6_000` = 12_000¢, leaving payment_status pending (invoice.rb:407-410, invoice_settlements/create_service.rb:58-60). Offsetting the pre-tax 5_000 instead would leave 13_000¢ due — 1_000¢ of it VAT on a fee half written off. The remaining 12_000¢ is exactly the untouched half of the charge fee (5_000 + 1_000) plus the whole subscription fee (5_000 + 1_000), which is the cross-check that the tax followed the FEE and not the invoice.

The simplest refund arithmetic in the block, kept simple on purpose so the type is the only variable: 15_000¢ of fees paid in full, half the charge fee refunded. No coupon and no tax, so the item and the refund coincide at 5_000¢ (credit_note.rb:171-173), and the ceilings are both slack: `total_paid − already refunded` = 15_000 (validate_service.rb:100-108) and `fee_total_amount_cents − credited − offsets` = 15_000 (:36-40). What the row pins is where the 5_000¢ went. refund_amount_cents 5_000 with balance_amount_cents 0 and refund_status `pending` (create_service.rb:68) means cash leaves; the credit sibling would show credit_amount_cents 5_000 and balance 5_000 for the identical total_amount_cents. The invoice keeps total_due 0 and payment_status succeeded — a refund does NOT reopen it, unlike an offset, which would have reduced the due amount instead. The remaining 5_000¢ of the charge fee and the whole subscription fee stay creditable, so a later note can still take them.

A partial REFUND of a discounted fee: the customer gets back cash, and the cash is net of the discount they never paid. The 3_000¢ coupon is limited to the charge's billable metric, so the whole 3_000¢ sits on the 10_000¢ charge fee and none on the 5_000¢ subscription fee (applied_coupon_service.rb:92-101,123-128, fee.rb:232-236). Invoice: 15_000 − 3_000 = 12_000¢, paid in full. Refunding 5_000¢ of that fee returns 5_000 − 3_000 × 5_000/10_000 = 3_500¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:75-82). The customer paid 7_000¢ for that fee in total, so half of it is 3_500¢ — the refund is the cash they actually parted with for the units being credited. Prorating the coupon across the invoice instead (3_000 × 5_000/15_000 = 1_000) would refund 4_000¢, i.e. 500¢ of a discount handed back as money; ignoring the coupon entirely would refund 5_000¢ and turn a discount into a profit. The refund ceiling (`total_paid` = 12_000, validate_service.rb:100-108) is slack, so nothing else forces the figure — the coupon weighting is the only thing deciding it.

A partial refund small enough that the cash ceiling does not bind — the control for b08/manual-full/refund/with-prepaid-credit, where it does. 15_000¢ of fees, 5_000¢ from the wallet, 10_000¢ paid in cash. Refunding 5_000¢ of the charge fee is allowed because 5_000 ≤ `total_paid_amount_cents − already refunded` = 10_000 (validate_service.rb:100-108); the note itself is 5_000¢ because there is no coupon and no tax to adjust. Pairing the two rows is what separates the rule from the symptom: at 5_000¢ prepaid credit is invisible, at 15_000¢ it is the binding constraint. A single row at either amount would read as "prepaid credit does not affect refunds" or "prepaid credit caps refunds", and only one of those is true. The wallet is not refilled by refunding cash (create_service.rb:315-317 gates that on `invoice.credit?`), so balance_cents stays 0 while 5_000¢ leaves as money.

Refunding half a taxed fee: the VAT on that half has to travel with it. Invoice 15_000¢ of fees + 3_000¢ of tax (1_000 on the subscription fee, 2_000 on the charge fee) = 18_000¢, paid in full. The note credits 5_000¢ of the charge fee, and the tax it carries is computed on the item's own base: 5_000 × taxes_base_rate 1 × 20% = 1_000¢ (apply_taxes_service.rb:36-40,84-94,112-116), so the refund is 6_000¢ tax-inclusive against a 5_000¢ pre-tax item. The mirror of b08/manual-partial/credit/with-tax on identical numbers: same 6_000¢ total_amount_cents, but refund_amount_cents 6_000/balance 0 instead of credit 6_000/balance 6_000. Refunding only 5_000 would keep 1_000¢ of the customer's VAT, which for a partial refund is the error most likely to survive review — the total still looks like "half the fee".

The explicit sibling of b09/create-mid-period/advance/none, and it must produce identical numbers: 1_500¢ billed up front for 16–30 April, 5 unused days credited at the plan's 100¢/day = 500¢, spendable (balance 500) rather than refunded. Writing `credit` where the record was already going to be coerced to `credit` (terminate_service.rb:11) has to be a no-op, and the pair is the only way to prove the coercion rather than assume it — if these two rows ever disagree, the default moved. Were the same dates handled as an ARREARS plan instead, nothing would be collected on 16 April and the termination on the 25th would BILL 10 days (16–25 inclusive, 1_000¢) rather than credit 5 — the two modes are not mirror images, because the arrears path bills THROUGH the boundary day (b09/terminate/arrears/none charges the 16th) while the advance path treats the termination day as still consumed and credits only from the following day.

A pay-in-advance subscription created on 16 April collects the REST OF THE PERIOD up front, not a full month: Fees::SubscriptionService#first_subscription_amount (:157-177) bills date_diff(16 Apr, 30 Apr) = 15 days at single_day_price = 3_000¢ / 30 = 100¢, so 1_500¢. The fee window is asserted as 16–30 April because DatesService#from_datetime clamps the computed 1 April to started_at (dates_service.rb:73-75); an implementation that charged 1_500¢ for 1–30 April would otherwise pass. Terminating on 25 April then credits the unused tail. remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:114-129) is next_end_of_period (30 April) minus terminated_at.end_of_day.to_date (25 April) = 5 days. THE DAY PRICE IS THE PLAN'S, NOT THE PRORATED FEE'S: plan_amount_cents reads last_subscription_fee.amount_details["plan_amount_cents"], which Fees::SubscriptionService#initialize_fee (:60) always sets to plan.amount_cents = 3_000¢, so day_price stays 100¢ and the credit is 5 × 100 = 500¢. Deriving it from the fee instead (1_500¢ / 30 = 50¢/day) would give 250¢ — half — which is why the mid-period cell is worth a row of its own rather than being read off the full-period terminate row. `none` and `credit` are the SAME behaviour here, and that is the point of this row. on_termination_credit_note is nullable with no column default (db/structure.sql:3703) but TerminateService coerces blank to `:credit` (terminate_service.rb:11), so an advance subscription that never mentions the field still issues a spendable credit note — and update_on_termination_actions! (:190) writes `credit` onto the record afterwards. The alternative reading of `none` — "no credit note at all" — would give no credit note; that is what b09/create-mid-period/advance/skip asserts instead. credit_amount_cents 500 with refund_amount_cents 0 and total_due_amount_cents still 1_500 on the first invoice is what separates this from the refund and offset siblings: a credit note issued AGAINST an invoice does not reduce that invoice's due (invoice.rb:407), it only becomes balance the customer can spend later. The second invoice is the termination invoice (`on_termination_invoice: generate`, bill_in_arrears_fees?, terminate_service.rb:184-186) and it is empty because the plan has no charges and no subscription fee is due — see b09/terminate/advance/credit for the charge-bearing version.

The mirror of the refund row: the invoice is deliberately LEFT UNPAID, so there is nothing to refund and the whole 500¢ of unused days is written off against the open invoice instead. calculate_amounts (create_from_termination.rb:145) gives offset `total_creditable − refund`, and refund is 0 here because paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0 on an unpaid invoice — so offset_amount_cents is the full 500. THE OBSERVABLE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM EVERY OTHER VALUE IS ON THE INVOICE, NOT THE NOTE. CreditNotes::CreateService (:82-89) raises an InvoiceSettlement for a positive offset, and Invoice#total_due_amount_cents (invoice.rb:407) is total − paid − offset, so the first invoice now owes 1_500 − 0 − 500 = 1_000¢ where the credit, none and skip siblings all still owe 1_500. total_amount_cents stays 1_500 in every case, which is exactly why the row asserts the due. Note the asymmetry this creates with the refund cell: PAY the invoice and `offset` collapses onto `refund` (creditable − refund = 0, so offset_amount_cents would be 0 and refund_amount_cents 500); leave it unpaid and `refund` collapses onto `credit`. Neither payment state distinguishes all five values, so the five rows of this family are split across both.

Same 1_500¢ collected on 16 April and same 500¢ of unused days on the 25th, but this time the money LEAVES instead of becoming spendable, and only because the invoice was paid first. calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169) takes paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription − creditable_used_amount. paid_amount_prorated is fee_amount / invoice.sub_total_including_taxes × total_paid = 1_500/1_500 × 1_500 = 1_500¢. creditable_used_amount is day_price × used_duration, and used_duration (:195-211) runs from date_service.from_datetime.to_date — 16 April, because from_datetime is clamped to started_at — through 25 April inclusive = 10 days, so 1_000¢. potential_refund = 1_500 − 1_000 = 500, capped at the total creditable 500 → refund 500, credit 500 − 500 = 0 (calculate_amounts :143). WITHOUT THE pay_invoice STEP THIS ROW WOULD BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ITS `credit` SIBLING: total_paid_amount_cents would be 0, potential_refund would be −1_000, calculate_refund would return 0 and the whole 500¢ would come back as credit_amount_cents. That is why the distinguishing assertions here are credit_amount_cents 0 / refund_amount_cents 500 / balance_amount_cents 0 rather than total_amount_cents, which is 500 under both. refund_status stays `pending`: should_handle_refund? (create_service.rb:243-248) needs a payment with a provider, and a manual payment has none, so no provider refund job is enqueued. credit_status reads `available` even though nothing is spendable — CreateService sets it at build time (:45) and only the consumption path (credit_note_service.rb:101) ever moves it — so balance_amount_cents, not credit_status, is what says the money is gone.

`skip` is the only value that produces NO credit note: generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) requires on_termination_credit_note to be one of credit/refund/offset, so CreateFromTermination is never reached. The customer keeps having paid 1_500¢ for 16–30 April and walks away on the 25th with the 5 unused days (500¢ at the plan's 100¢/day) forfeited — exactly the amount the `none`, `credit`, `refund` and `offset` siblings each return by a different route. There is no `credit_notes: 0` expectation to write, so the guard is the pair of amounts: total_due_amount_cents 1_500 on the first invoice (unchanged, so nothing was offset) together with an empty termination invoice (so nothing was spent). A credit note appearing here would not move either number by itself, which is why the sibling rows assert the note directly and this one asserts that the invoices stayed exactly as billed.

A calendar subscription starting mid-period is billed only for the part of the period it existed: 16 March through 31 March inclusive is 16 days, and at 3_100¢ / 31 days = 100¢ per day that is 1_600¢. The from_date is asserted as the 16th rather than the 1st, because a proration bug that charged the right amount for the wrong window would otherwise pass.

`credit` set explicitly, and asserted to change nothing. This is the control row for b09/downgrade/advance/none: the field is honoured on the terminate and upgrade paths, so if it were read here too the May invoice would be settled by a 2_903¢ credit note (day_price 3_000/31 = 96.77¢ over the 30 remaining days of May, capped at the 3_000¢ April fee) and read total_amount_cents 0 with credit_notes_amount_cents 900. It reads 900 and 0 because ActivateService#activate_for_downgrade terminates the old subscription with `mark_as_terminated!` (activate_service.rb:98) instead of going through TerminateService, so CreateFromTermination is unreachable on this path. Nothing about that is wrong for the money: the switch lands exactly on the period boundary, so there are no unused days to return. What the row pins is that the mechanism is ABSENT rather than merely computing zero — the two give the same total but a different number of credit notes, and only asserting both invoices' credit_notes_amount_cents tells them apart.

THE on_termination_credit_note AXIS IS INERT ON THE DOWNGRADE PATH, AND THAT IS THIS ROW'S FINDING. A downgrade does not terminate anything now: PlanDowngradeService creates a PENDING next_subscription (plan_downgrade_service.rb:33-47) and April is billed in full. At the boundary Subscriptions::OrganizationBillingService (:20) enqueues TerminateJob, which calls TerminateService#terminate_and_start_next → ActivateService#activate_for_downgrade — and that method calls `previous_subscription.mark_as_terminated!` DIRECTLY (activate_service.rb:98). TerminateService#call, the only place generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? and CreateFromTermination are reached, never runs. So no credit note is issued whatever the field says, and the field is not even copied onto the new subscription (:33-47 omits it). The numbers that guard this are not the 3_000¢ and 900¢ — they are credit_notes_amount_cents 0 on both invoices together with the May invoice reading its full 900¢. HAD TerminateService BEEN USED, the credit would have been large: terminated_at is 1 May, so day_price would be 3_000 / 31 = 96.77¢, next_end_of_period 31 May and remaining_duration 31 − 1 = 30 days → 2_903¢, capped at the 3_000¢ April fee, and the 900¢ May invoice would have settled at 0. A row asserting only "two invoices" would not see the difference. Two invoices rather than three is itself the upgrade/downgrade asymmetry: the same endpoint on the same day with a DEARER plan produces a rotation invoice on 16 April (b09/upgrade/advance/none), and April is prorated. Here 16 April produces nothing at all, and the May invoice is a full period — first_subscription_amount over 1–31 May at 900/31 per day — not a prorated one.

`offset` is the value with the loudest invoice-level side effect — an InvoiceSettlement that reduces Invoice#total_due_amount_cents (create_service.rb:82-89, invoice.rb:407) — which makes it the sharpest probe for whether the downgrade path reads the field at all. It does not: total_due_amount_cents on the unpaid April invoice is still the full 3_000¢, so no settlement was raised, because ActivateService#activate_for_downgrade never calls TerminateService#call (activate_service.rb:98). Had it been read, the April invoice would now owe 3_000 − 2_903 = 97¢: unpaid means paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0, refund clamps to 0, and calculate_amounts (:145) routes the entire 2_903¢ of unused May to offset. 97¢ versus 3_000¢ is not a number any other defect produces, which is what makes this the best of the five downgrade rows at localising the behaviour. Compare b09/create-mid-period/advance/offset and b09/terminate/advance/offset, where the same field on the same kind of plan does drop the due — one endpoint, two paths, opposite outcomes, decided only by whether the target plan is cheaper.

The row is built so that a refund WOULD have been possible and still does not happen. April's 3_000¢ advance invoice is paid in full on 2 April, so total_paid_amount_cents is 3_000 and calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169) would have had real cash to hand back — on the terminate path that is exactly what b09/terminate/advance/refund shows. Here the downgrade reaches ActivateService#activate_for_downgrade, which terminates the previous subscription with `mark_as_terminated!` (activate_service.rb:98) and never enters TerminateService#call, so CreateFromTermination is not invoked and no cash moves. Assertions: total_due_amount_cents 0 on the April invoice proves the payment really landed (so the row is not passing because there was nothing to refund), and credit_notes_amount_cents 0 on both invoices plus a full 900¢ May invoice prove nothing was returned. Had TerminateService run with `refund`, the note would have been 2_903¢ of unused May (3_000/31 per day × 30 days, capped at the April fee), and with 3_000¢ paid against 96.77¢ of used May the entire amount would have gone out as refund_amount_cents rather than credit.

`skip` is the one value whose intended behaviour — issue nothing — coincides with what the downgrade path does anyway, which is exactly why it is worth writing down: it is the cell where a reader would wrongly conclude the axis is honoured. April 3_000¢ in advance, May 900¢ in advance, no credit note, no proration. Identical to b09/downgrade/advance/none and /credit, and reached by a completely different route: those two are coerced-to-credit and explicit-credit that never get read, while this one would have produced nothing even on the terminate path (generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription?, terminate_service.rb:170-174). The five downgrade rows are therefore a single assertion made five times: on this transition on_termination_credit_note never reaches CreditNotes::CreateFromTermination, because ActivateService#activate_for_downgrade bypasses TerminateService#call (activate_service.rb:98). Any of the five turning red while the others stay green would mean the field started being read on this path.

A downgrade is the opposite of an upgrade in the one way that matters: it does not happen now. Asking for the cheaper plan on 16 April leaves the customer on plan A for the rest of the period — PlanDowngradeService creates a PENDING subscription instead of terminating anything, and the switch happens at the period boundary. So April bills the full 9_000¢ with no proration and no credit note, and May is the first period billed at plan B's 3_000¢. Contrast b09/upgrade/advance/credit, where the same API call on the same day terminates immediately, credits the unused 15 days and bills the new plan from the 16th. Same endpoint, same customer, opposite behaviour — decided only by whether the target plan costs more. Two invoices and nothing else is the assertion: a proration on the April invoice would mean the downgrade took effect early and the customer was refunded for a plan they still had, and a third invoice around 16 April would mean it was treated as an upgrade.

The explicit sibling of b09/ending-at/advance/none, and it must produce identical numbers: 2_000c collected on 11 April for 11-30 April, 9 unused days credited at the plan's 100c/day = 900c, spendable (balance 900) rather than refunded or written off. Writing `credit` where the record was going to be coerced to `credit` anyway (terminate_service.rb:11) has to be a no-op, and the pair is the only way to PROVE the coercion instead of assuming it — if these two rows ever disagree, the default moved. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY FROM THE OTHER FOUR VALUES, with numbers: `skip` produces no credit note at all and forfeits the 900c; `refund` on the same dates with the invoice paid would report credit_amount_cents 0 / refund_amount_cents 900 / balance 0; `offset` with the invoice unpaid would report offset_amount_cents 900 and drop invoice 0's total_due from 2_000c to 1_100c. Only `credit` (and `none`) leaves total_due at 2_000c while handing the customer a 900c spendable balance, so the trio credit_amount_cents / balance_amount_cents / total_due_amount_cents is what pins this cell rather than total_amount_cents, which is 900 under three of the five. The credited invoice carries a single fee, so apply_credit_to_fees has nothing to distribute. Note that the transition axis is doing real work here even though the arithmetic equals b09/create-mid-period/advance/credit's shape: nothing but Clock::TerminateEndedSubscriptionsJob reaches this state, and an ending_at termination that billed a different window from a manual one would be a second, unspecified convention.

Creation on 11 April on a pay-in-advance calendar plan collects the rest of the period up front: Fees::SubscriptionService#first_subscription_amount (:158-179) bills date_diff(11 Apr 00:00, 30 Apr 23:59) = 20 days at single_day_price = 3_000c / 30 = 100c, so 2_000c. from_date is asserted as the 11th, not the 1st, because DatesService#from_datetime clamps the computed 1 April up to started_at.beginning_of_day (dates_service.rb:73-75) — an implementation that charged 2_000c for 1-30 April would otherwise pass. `ending_at` then schedules a termination it does not perform. Only Clock::TerminateEndedSubscriptionsJob flips the subscription (terminate_ended_subscriptions_job.rb:19-29, whose DATE(ending_at) = DATE(now) filter is why the verb runs on the 21st and not the 22nd), it hands the subscription to Subscriptions::TerminateEndedSubscriptionJob -> the same Subscriptions::TerminateService as an explicit DELETE, and TerminateService gets its policy from the record (terminate_service.rb:7-14). perform_billing cannot substitute: organization_billing_service.rb:117-120 EXCLUDES subscriptions whose ending_at is today, so a row built on it would find the subscription still active and neither invoice would exist. pay_in_advance_invoice_issued? (terminate_service.rb:133-155) returns true on the short path — previous_beginning_of_period (1 April) is before started_at (11 April), so this is the first period and the advance invoice was issued with the subscription — which is what lets the credit note be raised at all; a termination in a LATER period would have to match an InvoiceSubscription instead. remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:114-128) is next_end_of_period (30 April) minus terminated_at.end_of_day.to_date (21 April) = 9 days. THE DAY PRICE IS THE PLAN'S, NOT THE PRORATED FEE'S: plan_amount_cents reads last_subscription_fee.amount_details["plan_amount_cents"], which Fees::SubscriptionService#initialize_fee (:60) always sets to plan.amount_cents = 3_000c, so day_price stays 100c and the credit is 9 x 100 = 900c. Deriving it from the fee instead (2_000c / 30 = 66.66c/day) would give 600c. WHAT `none` ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY: nothing, and that is the point — it must equal its `credit` sibling to the cent. on_termination_credit_note is nullable with no column default, and terminate_service.rb:11 coerces blank to `:credit`, so an ending_at subscription that never mentions the field still issues a spendable 900c note; update_on_termination_actions! (:188-192) then writes `credit` onto the record. The alternative reading of `none` — "no credit note at all" — is what b09/ending-at/advance/skip asserts, and it produces no note and no 900c anywhere. Only ONE fee exists on invoice 0, so the note's by-weight spreading across fees (credit_note_service.rb#apply_credit_to_fees) is a single fee at weight 1 and cannot be wrong here. credit_amount_cents 900 with total_due_amount_cents still 2_000 on invoice 0 is what separates this from the refund and offset siblings: a credit note issued against an invoice does not reduce that invoice's due (invoice.rb:407), it only becomes spendable balance. Invoice 1 is the termination invoice (on_termination_invoice defaults to generate, bill_in_arrears_fees?, terminate_service.rb:105-127) and it is empty because the plan has no charges and the subscription fee was already collected in advance.

The mirror of the refund row on the same dates: invoice 0 is deliberately LEFT UNPAID, so there is nothing to refund and the whole 900c of unused days is written off against the open invoice instead. calculate_amounts (create_from_termination.rb:145) gives offset `total_creditable - refund`, and refund is 0 here because paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0 on an unpaid invoice (:182) — so offset_amount_cents is the full 900. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY, and it is ON THE INVOICE, NOT THE NOTE: CreditNotes::CreateService (:83-89) raises an InvoiceSettlement for a positive offset, and Invoice#total_due_amount_cents (invoice.rb:407) is total - paid - offset, so invoice 0 now owes 2_000 - 0 - 900 = 1_100c where the `none`, `credit` and `skip` siblings all still owe 2_000c and the `refund` sibling owes 0 because it was PAID. total_amount_cents stays 2_000 in every case, which is exactly why the row asserts the due. On the note side, offset_amount_cents 900 with credit_amount_cents 0 and refund_amount_cents 0 is unique to this value: `credit` would report 900/0/0 and `refund` 0/900/0. The asymmetry this creates with the refund cell is why the five rows of this family are split across two payment states: PAY the invoice and `offset` collapses onto `refund` (creditable - refund = 0, so offset would be 0 and refund 900); leave it unpaid and `refund` collapses onto `credit`. No single payment state distinguishes all five values. The single subscription fee on invoice 0 also means the offset lands entirely on it — apply_credit_to_fees has one fee at weight 1 — so no per-fee split is asserted here.

Same 2_000c collected on 11 April and same 900c of unused days when the clock job terminates on the 21st, but this time the money LEAVES instead of becoming spendable — and only because the invoice was paid first. calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169) takes paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription - creditable_used_amount. paid_amount_prorated (:179-190) is fee_amount / invoice.sub_total_including_taxes x total_paid = 2_000/2_000 x 2_000 = 2_000c. creditable_used_amount is day_price x used_duration, and used_duration (:195-211) runs from date_service.from_datetime.to_date — 11 April, because from_datetime is clamped to started_at.beginning_of_day — through terminated_at 21 April inclusive = 11 days, so 1_100c. potential_refund = 2_000 - 1_100 = 900, capped at the total creditable 900 -> refund 900, and credit = 900 - 900 = 0 (calculate_amounts :143). WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY, and why the pay_invoice step is load-bearing: WITHOUT IT THIS ROW WOULD BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ITS `credit` SIBLING. total_paid_amount_cents would be 0, paid_amount_prorated 0, potential_refund -1_100, calculate_refund would return 0 and the whole 900c would come back as credit_amount_cents 900 / balance 900 — the exact numbers of b09/ending-at/advance/credit. So the distinguishing assertions are credit_amount_cents 0 / refund_amount_cents 900 / balance_amount_cents 0, not total_amount_cents, which is 900 here and on the credit, none and offset siblings alike. `skip` would produce no note at all and leave the customer 900c out of pocket; `offset` on a PAID invoice collapses onto exactly these numbers (calculate_amounts :145 gives offset creditable - refund = 0), which is why the offset cell is written on an unpaid invoice instead. refund_status stays `pending`: should_handle_refund? (create_service.rb:243-248) needs a payment with a provider, and a manual payment has none, so no provider refund job is enqueued. credit_status reads `available` even though nothing is spendable — CreateService sets it at build time and only the consumption path (credit_note_service.rb:96-102) ever moves it — so balance_amount_cents, not credit_status, is what says the money is gone. total_due_amount_cents 0 on invoice 0 is the payment, not the note: a credit note never reduces an invoice's due (invoice.rb:407).

`skip` is the only value that produces NO credit note: generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) requires on_termination_credit_note to be one of credit/refund/offset, so CreditNotes::CreateFromTermination is never reached — and it is reached on this path, because the clock job routes through the same TerminateService as a manual DELETE. The customer keeps having paid 2_000c for 11-30 April and the subscription ends on the 21st with the 9 unused days (900c at the plan's 100c/day) forfeited — exactly the amount the `none`, `credit`, `refund` and `offset` siblings each return by a different route. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY: there is no `credit_notes: 0` expectation to write, so the guard is the pair of invoice amounts. total_due_amount_cents 2_000 on invoice 0 says nothing was offset (`offset` would show 1_100) and the empty termination invoice says nothing was spent or re-billed; together with the absent credit_note block, a note appearing here would have to be a 900c note that moved neither number, which is precisely the shape the sibling rows assert directly. The fee window 11-30 April is re-asserted here rather than only on the `none` row because this is the row with no credit note to cross-check the day price against.

Created on 1 April with subscription_at 11 April, so handle_future_subscription (create_service.rb:198-201) calls `pending!` and stops — no invoice on the 1st. The clock verb on the 11th runs ActivateAllPendingService -> ActivateService -> activate_standalone (activate_service.rb:125-140), which calls mark_as_active!(timestamp) — started_at is nil until then and is set to 11 April 01:00 (subscription.rb:124-126) — and then bill_subscription(skip_charges: true). On a pay_in_advance calendar plan that bills only the remainder of the period being entered: date_diff(11 Apr, 30 Apr) = 20 days at single_day_price = 9_000c / 30 = 300c, so 6_000c. from_date is 11 April 00:00 and not 01:00 because DatesService#from_datetime clamps to started_at.beginning_of_day (dates_service.rb:73-75); an implementation billing 1-30 April would show 9_000c instead. Terminating on the 21st then credits the unused tail through the same arithmetic as the ending-at family. remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:114-128) = next_end_of_period (30 April) - terminated_at.end_of_day.to_date (21 April) = 9 days; day_price is the PLAN's, read off last_subscription_fee.amount_details["plan_amount_cents"] = 9_000c, so 9 x 300 = 2_700c. Deriving the day price from the prorated fee instead (6_000 / 30 = 200c) would give 1_800c. pay_in_advance_invoice_issued? (terminate_service.rb:133-155) is true on the short path because previous_beginning_of_period (1 April) precedes started_at (11 April). WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY FROM THE OTHER AXIS VALUES, with numbers: `skip` produces no credit note and forfeits the 2_700c; `refund` (invoice paid first) reports credit 0 / refund 2_700 / balance 0; `offset` (invoice unpaid) reports offset 2_700 and drops invoice 0's total_due from 6_000c to 3_300c. `credit` is the only value that leaves total_due at 6_000c while handing over a 2_700c spendable balance. b09/hns/gated-activation/advance/none is the `none` cell of this axis and asserts no termination at all, so the coercion of nil to `:credit` (terminate_service.rb:11) is cross-checked by the ending-at none/credit pair above rather than here. The credit note also PROVES ACTIVATION rather than mere billing: had the gate raised the invoice without flipping the status, terminate_subscription would take TerminateService's `pending?` branch (:26-34), mark_as_canceled!, and never reach generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? — no note, no 2_700c. Invoice 0 carries one fee, so the note's by-weight spreading over fees (credit_note_service.rb#apply_credit_to_fees) is a single fee at weight 1. Invoice 1 is the termination invoice and is empty: no charges, and the subscription fee was collected in advance.

The mirror of the refund row on the same gate and the same dates: the activation invoice is deliberately LEFT UNPAID, so there is nothing to refund and the whole 2_700c of unused days is written off against the open invoice instead. calculate_amounts (create_from_termination.rb:145) gives offset `total_creditable - refund`, and refund is 0 here because paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0 on an unpaid invoice (:182) — so offset_amount_cents is the full 2_700. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY, and it is ON THE INVOICE, NOT THE NOTE: CreditNotes::CreateService (:83-89) raises an InvoiceSettlement for a positive offset, and Invoice#total_due_amount_cents (invoice.rb:407) is total - paid - offset, so invoice 0 now owes 6_000 - 0 - 2_700 = 3_300c — which is exactly the 11 used days at 300c/day — where the `credit` and `skip` siblings still owe 6_000c and the `refund` sibling owes 0 because it was PAID. total_amount_cents stays 6_000 in every case, which is why the row asserts the due. On the note side, offset 2_700 with credit 0 and refund 0 is unique to this value: `credit` reports 2_700/0/0 and `refund` 0/2_700/0. Neither payment state distinguishes all five values — pay and `offset` collapses onto `refund`, leave it unpaid and `refund` collapses onto `credit` — so this family is split across both, and this row is the unpaid half. The single subscription fee on invoice 0 means the offset lands entirely on it, apply_credit_to_fees having one fee at weight 1, so no per-fee split is asserted.

Same gate and same 6_000c raised by the activation on 11 April (20 days at 9_000c / 30 = 300c), same 2_700c of unused days on the 21st, but the money LEAVES instead of becoming spendable — and only because the activation invoice was paid first. The pay_invoice step has to sit AFTER the activation verb: before it the subscription is pending and no invoice exists to pay. calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169) takes paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription - creditable_used_amount. paid_amount_prorated (:179-190) is fee_amount / invoice.sub_total_including_taxes x total_paid = 6_000/6_000 x 6_000 = 6_000c. creditable_used_amount is day_price x used_duration, and used_duration (:195-211) runs from date_service.from_datetime.to_date — 11 April, clamped to started_at.beginning_of_day — through terminated_at 21 April inclusive = 11 days, so 3_300c. potential_refund = 6_000 - 3_300 = 2_700, capped at the total creditable 2_700 -> refund 2_700, credit = 2_700 - 2_700 = 0 (calculate_amounts :143). 20 days billed = 11 used + 9 credited, which is the arithmetic cross-check. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY, and why pay_invoice is load-bearing: WITHOUT IT THIS ROW WOULD BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ITS `credit` SIBLING. total_paid_amount_cents would be 0, paid_amount_prorated 0, potential_refund -3_300, calculate_refund would return 0 and the whole 2_700c would come back as credit_amount_cents 2_700 / balance 2_700 — the exact numbers of b09/gated-activation/advance/credit. So the distinguishing assertions are credit_amount_cents 0 / refund_amount_cents 2_700 / balance_amount_cents 0, not total_amount_cents, which is 2_700 under credit, refund and offset alike. `skip` would produce no note; `offset` on a PAID invoice collapses onto exactly these numbers (calculate_amounts :145 gives offset creditable - refund = 0), which is why the offset cell is written unpaid instead. refund_status stays `pending`: should_handle_refund? (create_service.rb:243-248) needs a payment with a provider and a manual payment has none. credit_status reads `available` even though nothing is spendable, so balance_amount_cents is what says the money is gone. total_due_amount_cents 0 on invoice 0 is the payment, not the note — a credit note never reduces an invoice's due (invoice.rb:407).

The gate opens exactly as in b09/gated-activation/advance/credit — nothing on 1 April, 6_000c for 11-30 April when the clock job activates on the 11th (20 days at 9_000c / 30 = 300c) — and then `skip` is the only axis value that produces NO credit note: generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) requires on_termination_credit_note to be one of credit/refund/offset, so CreditNotes::CreateFromTermination is never reached. The customer has paid 6_000c for 11-30 April and leaves on the 21st with the 9 unused days (2_700c at the plan's 300c/day) forfeited. WHAT THIS ROW ASSERTS DIFFERENTLY: with no note to read, the guard is the pair of invoice amounts. total_due_amount_cents 6_000 on invoice 0 says nothing was offset — `offset` on the same dates would show 3_300 — and the empty termination invoice says nothing was re-billed or spent. A 2_700c note appearing here would move neither number by itself, which is why the sibling rows assert the note directly and this one asserts that the invoices stayed exactly as billed. The fee window 11-30 April at 6_000c is re-asserted here because this is the row with no credit note to cross-check the 300c day price against. Note the one thing `skip` does NOT skip: the termination invoice. on_termination_invoice is a separate field defaulting to `generate` (bill_in_arrears_fees?, terminate_service.rb:184-186), so invoice 1 exists and is empty — asserting invoices: 2 rather than 1 is what keeps the two termination policies from being conflated.

The arrears half of the gate, and the only legal arrears cell of this axis: `on_termination_credit_note` is refused outright on an arrears plan (Subscription validates its absence, subscription.rb:80), which the block's `subscription_lifecycle` constraint encodes, so the field is left off the subscription entirely and the runner's termination-policy PUT (golden_runner.rb:364-373) sends nothing. Nothing happens on 1 April: handle_future_subscription (create_service.rb:198-201) calls `pending!` and returns. Activation on the 11th runs activate_standalone -> bill_subscription(skip_charges: true), which on an ARREARS plan with no pay-in-advance fixed charges enqueues NOTHING (activate_service.rb:181-196 bills only if plan.pay_in_advance? or fixed_charges.pay_in_advance.any?) — so unlike its advance sibling b09/hns/gated-activation/advance/none, which raises a 1_600c invoice at the moment of activation, this row's activation raises no invoice at all. The first and only invoice arrives when the period closes: 20 days from 11 April through 30 April inclusive at 3_000c / 30 = 100c per day = 2_000c, with from_date the 11th rather than the 1st because DatesService#from_datetime clamps the computed 1 April up to started_at.beginning_of_day (dates_service.rb:73-75) and started_at was set by mark_as_active! at activation, not at creation. WHAT THE AXIS VALUE ASSERTS HERE: `none` on the arrears side is the ABSENCE of the column, not a coerced default. TerminateService would still coerce blank to `:credit` (terminate_service.rb:11) but generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (:170-174) gates on pay_in_advance? first, so no arrears subscription can ever produce a termination credit note whatever the field said — which is why the other four values are illegal rather than merely untested here. `invoices: 1` is the load-bearing count. Without perform_subscriptions_activation it would be 0, not 1: the subscription stays pending for the whole timeline and OrganizationBillingService scopes to `.active`, so the 1 May run would find nothing to bill. And an implementation that activated but billed the full month would show 3_000c for 1-30 April.

`ending_at` schedules a termination it does not perform. Only Clock::TerminateEndedSubscriptionsJob flips the subscription (terminate_ended_subscriptions_job.rb:19-29, whose DATE(ending_at) = DATE(now) filter is why the verb runs on the 16th and not the 17th) and it hands the subscription to the same Subscriptions::TerminateService as an explicit DELETE, so the arithmetic must match b09/terminate/arrears/none exactly: 1 March through 16 March is 16 days at 3_100¢ / 31 = 100¢ per day = 1_600¢. That equality is the point of the row — an `ending_at` termination that billed a different window from a manual one would be a second, unspecified convention. perform_billing cannot substitute: organization_billing_service.rb:117-120 EXCLUDES subscriptions whose ending_at is today, so a row built on it would find the subscription still active and no invoice at all.

A subscription dated in the future is created PENDING and stays there: create_service.rb:198-201 (handle_future_subscription) only calls `pending!`, and the sole caller of ActivateService for such a row is Subscriptions::ActivateAllPendingService via Clock::ActivateSubscriptionsJob (activate_all_pending_service.rb:14-25). That is the gate — activation is withheld until the date arrives, and a pending subscription is invisible to billing because OrganizationBillingService scopes to `.active`. So the row asserts the two invoices from the two sides of the gate. Activation on the 16th runs activate_standalone -> bill_subscription(skip_charges: true) (activate_service.rb:124-140), which on a pay_in_advance calendar plan bills only the remainder of the period the subscription is entering: 16 through 31 March is 16 days at 3_100¢ / 31 = 100¢ per day = 1_600¢, from_date the 16th and not the 1st. April is then a full advance period, 3_100¢, which is what proves the subscription really became ACTIVE rather than merely being billed once — a gate that opened the invoice but not the status would show 1_600¢ and then nothing. Without the activation verb the count is 0, not 1: perform_billing raises no invoice for either month.

Explicit `credit` on the recreate shape, asserted to match b09/recreate-same-external-id/ advance/none: 3_000¢ for April, 1_400¢ credited for the 14 days after the 16th, 1_100¢ billed for 20–30 April on the new subscription and 1_100¢ of the credit spent against it, leaving 300¢ of balance. What makes `credit` distinguishable HERE and nowhere else in the block is the third invoice. On the terminate and create-mid-period families the credit either has nothing to land on or lands on a termination invoice, so the only witness is the note's own fields. Here the money visibly moves: credit_notes_amount_cents 1_100 and total_amount_cents 0 on the recreated subscription's first invoice. Its siblings all read 1_100 for that total — `skip` because no note exists, `refund` because the note's credit side is 0, `offset` because an offset settles the note's own invoice and never becomes spendable balance. The residual 300¢ also pins the DIRECTION of the clamp: min(balance, remaining), not min(balance, fee), and not the whole balance.

Reusing an external_id after a termination is the one transition where the credit note has a LATER invoice to land on, so it is where `credit` and `refund` finally diverge on the invoice rather than only on the note. 1 April: 3_000¢ billed in advance for the whole month. 16 April: terminated, credit note for 30 − 16 = 14 unused days at 3_000/30 = 100¢ → 1_400¢, plus an empty termination invoice (no charges on the plan, and no second subscription fee — should_create_subscription_fee?, calculate_fees_service.rb:270-293). 20 April, POST /subscriptions with the SAME external_id: CreateService finds no editable subscription (the old one is terminated, so it is neither active nor starting_in_the_future, create_service.rb:253-259) and no active conflict on the external_id (:66-70), so it builds a brand-new Subscription rather than upgrading — previous_subscription stays nil, which is what separates this transition from `upgrade`. Being pay-in-advance and starting today it bills at once: from_datetime is clamped to started_at (dates_service.rb:73-75) so first_subscription_amount covers 20–30 April = 11 days at 100¢ = 1_100¢. THEN THE 1_400¢ CREDIT IS SPENT ON IT. Credits::CreditNoteService takes the customer's available notes excluding those issued against the invoice being billed (credit_note_service.rb:73-81) and applies min(balance, remaining) = min(1_400, 1_100) = 1_100 (:88-94), so the third invoice settles at 0 and the note retains balance_amount_cents 300 with credit_status still `available` — consumed! only fires when the balance reaches zero (:101). That 300¢ is the row's sharpest number. A credit note that spread by GROSS fee amount, or one that was consumed in full, or one that was never applied, all give a different pair of (invoice total, remaining balance): 1_100/1_400 if unapplied, 0/0 if over-consumed. And `none` behaving as `credit` is again terminate_service.rb:11 coercing the nil column.

The third destination for the same 1_400¢: not spendable balance, not cash out, but a write-off against the invoice that collected it. With the April invoice unpaid, refund clamps to 0 (paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0) and calculate_amounts (create_from_termination.rb:145) routes everything to offset, raising an InvoiceSettlement (create_service.rb:82-89) that takes the first invoice's total_due_amount_cents from 3_000 to 1_600 (invoice.rb:407). An offset never becomes balance, so the recreated subscription on the 20th is billed its full 1_100¢ — credit_notes_amount_cents 0, total 1_100 — exactly like the `skip` and `refund` siblings, and unlike `credit`/`none` which settle it at 0. Between offset and skip the difference is the first invoice's due, 1_600 versus 3_000; between offset and refund it is which invoice was reduced and whether cash moved. Three assertions across two invoices and one note are the minimum that tells all five values apart, which is why none of these rows asserts a total on its own. Net position: the customer owes 1_600¢ for 1–16 April plus 1_100¢ for 20–30 April, and the three days between the termination and the new subscription are billed to nobody. That gap is real and intended — this transition is not an upgrade, so nothing bridges the two periods.

`refund` and `credit` produce the same 1_400¢ note and diverge entirely in where it goes, and this is the row where that has a cash consequence rather than only a field difference. The April invoice is paid in full on the 1st, so calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169) has 3_000¢ of paid_amount_prorated against 16 used days (1 April through 16 April inclusive, 1_600¢) and refunds potential 3_000 − 1_600 = 1_400, capped at the 1_400¢ creditable — the whole note. credit_amount_cents is therefore 0 and balance_amount_cents 0, so when the recreated subscription is billed on the 20th there is no available credit for Credits::CreditNoteService to find (its scope is `.available` with a positive balance, credit_note_service.rb:73-94) and the third invoice bills its 1_100¢ in full. So the same customer, the same dates and the same 1_400¢: with `credit` they pay 3_000 and owe nothing more (1_100 settled from balance, 300 left over); with `refund` they pay 3_000, get 1_400 back and then owe 1_100. Net identical, cash flow completely different — and total_amount_cents on the third invoice (0 versus 1_100) is the single field that says which happened. total_due_amount_cents 0 on the first invoice is asserted to prove the payment landed: without it, refund would clamp to 0 and this row would silently become the `credit` row.

The double-charge cell, and the reason this transition is worth five rows. April is collected twice over the overlap: 3_000¢ on the 1st for 1–30 April, then 1_100¢ on the 20th for 20–30 April, with the 1_400¢ covering 17–30 April of the first subscription forfeited because generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) excludes `skip`. The customer pays 4_100¢ for one calendar month of a 3_000¢ plan. credit_notes_amount_cents 0 with total_amount_cents 1_100 on the third invoice is what separates it from `none` and `credit`, which settle that invoice at 0 by spending the note. The gap is 1_100¢ of cash — larger than the 300¢ of residual balance those rows keep, because the forfeited amount exceeds what the new invoice could absorb. The recreated subscription's own arithmetic is asserted independently of the credit: 11 days (20–30 April) at the plan's 3_000/30 = 100¢, with from_date pinned to the 20th because DatesService#from_datetime clamps the computed 1 April to started_at (dates_service.rb:73-75). Note that the previous subscription having terminated on the 16th does NOT shift that window: started_at_for's clamp to last_invoiced_termination_time (create_service.rb:209-221) applies only to a BACKDATED subscription_at, and this one starts today.

The arrears half of the recreate transition, and the one place where reusing an external_id produces NO overlap at all: nothing was collected in advance, so the two subscriptions bill only the days they each existed and the gap between them is billed to nobody. March 2024 has 31 days and the plan is 3_100¢, so a day is exactly 100¢. Terminating on the 16th bills 1–16 March = 16 days = 1_600¢ immediately — terminated_pay_in_arrears? (dates_service.rb:273-277) takes from_date to the beginning of the period and to_datetime is clamped to terminated_at (:87-89) — which is the same 1_600¢ b09/terminate/arrears/none asserts. Recreating on 20 March produces no invoice at once: ActivateService#bill_subscription (activate_service.rb:188-200) enqueues nothing for an arrears plan with no pay-in-advance fixed charges, which is why the clock has to reach the period boundary. On 1 April the new subscription is billed first_subscription_amount over its own window — from_datetime clamped to started_at gives 20–31 March = 12 days at 100¢ = 1_200¢. Total for March: 1_600 + 1_200 = 2_800¢ for 28 of the month's 31 days, the missing 300¢ being 17, 18 and 19 March when the customer had no subscription. THAT is the arrears/advance contrast in one number: on the advance side the same three-day gap still leaves 3_000¢ collected for the whole month (b09/recreate-same-external-id/advance/skip pays 4_100¢ in total), which is why on_termination_credit_note only exists on that side — there is nothing unconsumed to return here, and Subscription validates the field's absence for an arrears plan (subscription.rb:80). credit_notes_amount_cents 0 on both invoices is asserted rather than assumed: a credit note on this path would mean the arrears termination had refunded days it never charged for.

Explicit `credit` on the calibration shape, and it must equal b09/terminate/advance/none to the cent: 3_000¢ up front for April, 14 unused days from the 16th at 100¢ = 1_400¢ credited, spent in full against the 2_000¢ of usage the termination invoice bills, leaving 600¢. `credit` means the money stays inside Lago as balance rather than going back to the customer, and here it is consumed the same instant it is created — the termination invoice exists precisely because on_termination_invoice is `generate` (terminate_service.rb:184-186), and Credits::CreditNoteService excludes only notes issued AGAINST the invoice being billed (credit_note_service.rb:73-81), which this one is not. With `on_termination_invoice: skip` there would be one invoice and a 1_400¢ balance left standing. The two candidates this row separates from `credit` are its siblings: `refund` on the same dates and a paid invoice sends the same 1_400¢ out as cash and leaves the termination invoice at its full 2_000¢, and `offset` on an unpaid invoice drops the FIRST invoice's due to 1_600¢ and also leaves the termination invoice at 2_000¢. All three notes total 1_400¢, so credit_notes_amount_cents on the second invoice plus credit_amount_cents on the note are what tell them apart.

The plainest shape in the block and the one the whole advance half is calibrated against: full month collected up front, terminated on the 16th, unused tail returned as spendable credit and immediately spent on the invoice the termination itself raises. 1 April, pay-in-advance: the whole period is billed, 3_000¢ for 1–30 April. The charge is arrears and skip_charges is set on the creation invoice (activate_service.rb:188-194), so it carries the subscription fee only. 16 April 10:00, DELETE /subscriptions: mark_as_terminated!, then a credit note, then bill_subscription (terminate_service.rb:32-61) — in that order, which is why the credit exists before the termination invoice is computed. THE CREDIT IS 14 DAYS, NOT 15. remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:114-129) is next_end_of_period (30 April) minus terminated_at.end_of_day.to_date (16 April) = 14, at 3_000/30 = 100¢ → 1_400¢. The `-= 1.day if upgrade` clause does not apply to a plain termination, so the 16th itself stays consumed. b09/upgrade/advance/none credits 15 days for the same calendar day precisely because that clause does apply there, and the difference is exactly this 100¢. The termination invoice bills 1–16 April of usage: charges_to_datetime is clamped to terminated_at (dates_service.rb:122), the two events of 10 units are inside it, and the standard charge at 1.00 gives 20 × 100¢ = 2_000¢. There is no second SUBSCRIPTION fee — should_create_subscription_fee? (calculate_fees_service.rb:270-293) ends at `terminated_at > invoice.created_at`, which is false when both land on the same frozen instant, while should_create_charge_fees? (:344-353) is unconditional. That `>` versus unconditional asymmetry is the whole reason the invoice has one fee and not two. The 1_400¢ credit then lands on that 2_000¢ invoice: Credits::CreditNoteService takes min(balance, remaining) (credit_note_service.rb:88-94), leaving total 600¢ and a consumed note with balance 0. Only one fee carries it, so the weighted split in apply_credit_to_fees (:104-115) is trivial here — with a second fee the credit would divide by (amount − precise_coupons + taxes) / invoice_total rather than by gross amount. `none` is the same behaviour as `credit`: the column is nullable with no default (db/structure.sql:3703) and terminate_service.rb:11 coerces blank to :credit. Read as "issue nothing", this cell would leave the termination invoice at 2_000¢ — which is what b09/terminate/advance/skip asserts.

The unpaid version: the April invoice was never settled, so there is no cash to refund and the 1_400¢ of unused days is written off against what is still owed. calculate_refund returns 0 because paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 0 on an unpaid invoice, and calculate_amounts (create_from_termination.rb:145) then hands the entire creditable amount to offset. total_due_amount_cents 1_600 on the first invoice is the number nothing else produces: an InvoiceSettlement of 1_400¢ (create_service.rb:82-89) enters Invoice#total_due_amount_cents as total − paid − offset = 3_000 − 0 − 1_400 (invoice.rb:407). `credit`, `none` and `skip` all leave that at 3_000, and `refund` on a paid invoice leaves it at 0 by a different mechanism (paid, not offset). The invoice's own total_amount_cents stays 3_000 throughout, so asserting the total would have proved nothing. The offset does NOT reach the termination invoice: offset settles the invoice the note was issued against, and only credit_amount_cents becomes spendable balance elsewhere, so the 2_000¢ of usage is billed in full where the `credit` sibling settles at 600¢. Two things worth pinning here. `credit_notes_amount_cents` on the first invoice is not asserted because it never reflects notes issued AGAINST that invoice — only CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice's sibling sets the invoice-side offset field — so the due is the honest observable. And with 3_000¢ owed and 1_400¢ offset the invoice is not fully settled, so InvoiceSettlements::CreateService#mark_invoice_as_paid! (:34) does not fire and payment_status stays pending; had the offset covered the whole invoice it would have been marked succeeded.

The paid version of the calibration shape, and the only one where money actually leaves. calculate_refund (create_from_termination.rb:161-169): paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is fee_amount / invoice.sub_total_including_taxes × total_paid = 3_000/3_000 × 3_000 = 3_000¢; creditable_used_amount is day_price × used_duration where used_duration (:195-211) runs from date_service.from_datetime (1 April) through terminated_at (16 April) inclusive = 16 days → 1_600¢. potential_refund = 3_000 − 1_600 = 1_400, and the cap is the 1_400¢ total creditable, so the refund takes the whole note: refund 1_400, credit 1_400 − 1_400 = 0 (calculate_amounts :143). Two things make this row hard to fake. First, WITHOUT the pay_invoice step it would be indistinguishable from b09/terminate/advance/credit — total_paid would be 0, potential_refund −1_600, refund 0, and the 1_400¢ would come back as credit. Second, because the credit side is 0 there is nothing left to spend, so the termination invoice bills its full 2_000¢ of usage where the `credit` sibling settles at 600¢. credit_amount_cents 0 / refund_amount_cents 1_400 on the note and credit_notes_amount_cents 0 on the second invoice are therefore two independent witnesses to the same split. That used and unused happen to sum to the paid amount is not a coincidence to lean on: 16 used days plus 14 unused is the whole 30-day period, so the refund is the full unused tail. Had the customer paid only part of the invoice, potential_refund would have been smaller than the creditable amount and the note would have carried BOTH a refund and a credit — the arrangement spec/scenarios/subscriptions/terminate_manually_spec.rb:144 exercises with a 75/90 payment. refund_status stays `pending` because should_handle_refund? (create_service.rb:243-248) requires a payment with a provider and a manual payment has none.

The forfeiting cell. Same 3_000¢ collected for April on the 1st and same 2_000¢ of usage billed on termination, but generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) refuses to reach CreateFromTermination for `skip`, so the 1_400¢ covering 17–30 April is simply kept. The customer pays 5_000¢ for half a month of plan plus its usage, where `credit` and `none` settle at 3_600¢. credit_notes_amount_cents 0 with total_amount_cents 2_000 on the termination invoice is the assertion, and it is exactly 1_400¢ away from the `credit` sibling's 600¢ — the gap is the entire behaviour of the axis. total_due_amount_cents 3_000 on the first invoice rules out the other way of not-crediting: an offset, which would have dropped it to 1_600¢. Note that the usage side is untouched: on_termination_credit_note controls only the credit note, while on_termination_invoice controls whether the usage invoice is raised at all (bill_in_arrears_fees?, :184-186). Setting `skip` on the wrong one of those two fields loses 2_000¢ of revenue instead of returning 1_400¢ to the customer, which is why both are asserted here rather than only the total.

Terminating mid-period bills immediately for the part consumed rather than waiting for the period to end: 1 March through 16 March is 16 days × 100¢ = 1_600¢. The mirror image of the row above — the same 1_600¢ from the opposite end of the month — which is what makes an off-by-one in either direction visible as an asymmetry between the two.

Explicit `credit` against the same trial-end shape, and it must match b09/trial-end/advance/none exactly: 2_000¢ billed at trial end for 11–30 April (20 days at 100¢), 1_000¢ credited for the 10 unused days after the 20th, balance spendable. Two candidate derivations this row rules out. The first: crediting from the TRIAL END rather than from the termination day would give 30 − 11 = 19 days = 1_900¢ — remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:114-129) measures from terminated_at, and its trial branch only intervenes when the trial has NOT yet ended by the termination day. The second: taking the day price from the invoiced fee (2_000¢ / 20 trial-free days = 100¢, coincidentally the same here) rather than from amount_details["plan_amount_cents"] / 30 — which is why the create-mid-period family, where those two differ by a factor of two, carries that assertion instead.

A trial on a PAY-IN-ADVANCE plan produces no invoice at all on creation: ActivateService#bill_subscription (activate_service.rb:188) enqueues BillSubscriptionJob only `if plan.pay_in_advance? && !subscription.in_trial_period?`, and the 10-day trial from 1 April is still running. The clock has to move for the invoice to exist — hence needs_forward_time and the perform_billing step on 11 April, which is Clock::FreeTrialSubscriptionsBillerJob → Subscriptions::FreeTrialBillingService (:18-25) billing the subscription with invoicing_reason :subscription_starting and skip_charges. The amount is 2_000¢: first_subscription_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:157-177) moves from_datetime to initial_started_at + 10 days = 11 April, leaving date_diff(11 Apr, 30 Apr) = 20 days at 3_000¢ / 30 = 100¢. THE FEE WINDOW IS STILL THE WHOLE PERIOD — 1–30 April — because the trial shift is local to the amount computation while properties come from the boundaries (:56); a row asserting a 11 April from_date would be asserting a window Lago does not record. Terminating on 20 April credits 30 − 20 = 10 days = 1_000¢. The trial branch of remaining_duration (create_from_termination.rb:118-124) does NOT fire: it needs trial_end_date >= billed_from, and 11 April is before 20 April. It matters that the credit base is capped at last_subscription_fee.amount_cents (:73) — 2_000¢ here, not the plan's 3_000¢ — so a longer trial plus an earlier termination is where that clamp becomes visible. `none` behaves as `credit` for the same reason as the create-mid-period family: terminate_service.rb:11 coerces the blank column to :credit. Read as "no credit note", this cell would show no note and the customer would forfeit 1_000¢.

The unpaid counterpart of b09/trial-end/advance/refund. Same 2_000¢ trial-end invoice, same 1_000¢ of unused days after the 20th, but with total_paid_amount_cents at 0 the refund clamps to 0 (create_from_termination.rb:164) and calculate_amounts (:145) routes the whole creditable amount to offset instead. The distinguishing number is again on the invoice: an InvoiceSettlement for 1_000¢ (create_service.rb:82-89) drops total_due_amount_cents from 2_000 to 1_000 (invoice.rb:407), where the credit, none and skip siblings all still owe the full 2_000. The customer never paid the trial-end invoice and now owes only the ten days actually used — which is the same settlement the refund row reaches by taking cash in and handing cash back. Note that a `credit` note of 1_000¢ would NOT settle this invoice: Credits::CreditNoteService excludes notes issued against the invoice being billed (credit_note_service.rb:73-81, `where.not(invoice_id: invoice.id)`), so credit is only spendable on a LATER invoice. That is what b09/recreate-same-external-id/advance/credit asserts.

The trial makes the refund split turn on a number that only exists after the trial ended. used_duration (create_from_termination.rb:195-211) starts at date_service.from_datetime — 1 April — but its trial branch (:199-202) pushes billed_from to trial_end_date = 11 April, so the used window is 11–20 April inclusive = 10 days = 1_000¢. paid_amount_prorated_to_subscription is 2_000/2_000 × 2_000 = 2_000¢, so potential_refund = 2_000 − 1_000 = 1_000, capped at the 1_000¢ total creditable → refund 1_000, credit 0. That the two halves come out equal is a property of terminating exactly one trial-length after the trial ended, and it is why the assertion is credit_amount_cents 0 versus refund_amount_cents 1_000 rather than the total: total_amount_cents is 1_000 for `credit`, `refund` and `offset` alike here. HAD THE TRIAL BRANCH OF used_duration NOT FIRED, billed_from would be 1 April, the used window would be 20 days = 2_000¢, potential_refund would be 0 and this row would silently degrade into the `credit` sibling — 1_000¢ of credit, no cash. So the pair (b09/trial-end/advance/credit, this row) is what proves the trial is excluded from "used". The pay_invoice step needs the premium licence plus the manual_payments integration; without a payment no refund is possible at all (a manual POST /credit_notes would be rejected with refund_amount_cents/cannot_refund_unpaid_invoice, validate_service.rb:100-103, while the automatic path silently returns credit instead).

The trial-end invoice is identical to its siblings — 2_000¢ for 11–30 April, 20 days at the 3_000¢/30 = 100¢ day price, billed by Subscriptions::FreeTrialBillingService when the clock reaches the trial end — and the termination on 20 April issues nothing, because generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) excludes `skip`. The 1_000¢ covering 21–30 April is forfeited. The guard is that both invoices stay exactly as billed: total_due_amount_cents 2_000 on the trial-end invoice (nothing offset) and an empty termination invoice (nothing spent). Note that `skip` still runs update_on_termination_actions! (:188-195) and persists `skip` on the record, so this is a deliberate choice recorded on the subscription rather than an absence.

A 10-day trial from 1 March covers 1–10 March free, so the first invoice charges only 11 March through 31 March: 21 days × 100¢ = 2_100¢. The trial is subtracted from the period, not appended to it — the subscription is not billed 3_100¢ and then credited, which would show the same total but a different fee.

The most entangled path in the product: one API call terminates a subscription, issues a credit note for money already taken, starts a different subscription and bills it — and the credit note has to land on the invoice the same call produces. April has 30 days, so plan A is 100¢/day and plan B is 300¢/day, chosen so nothing rounds. 1 April: plan A is pay-in-advance, so the whole month is billed up front — 3_000¢. 16 April, `POST /subscriptions` with the same external_id and plan B: PlanUpgradeService creates the new subscription and ActivateService#activate_for_upgrade terminates the old one, then bills BOTH in one rotation. Terminating a pay-in-advance subscription with `on_termination_credit_note: credit` returns the unused part as spendable credit: 16–30 April is 15 days × 100¢ = 1_500¢. The rotation invoice carries plan B's advance fee for the same 16–30 April, 15 days × 300¢ = 4_500¢. Plan A contributes nothing to it — no charges, and its subscription fee was taken up front — so the credit note is spent in full against it, leaving 3_000¢. Net for April: 3_000 paid up front − 1_500 credited + 4_500 for B = 6_000¢, i.e. 15 days of A at 100¢ plus 15 days of B at 300¢. Thirty days billed once each, no overlap and no gap. THE BOUNDARY DAY IS NOT TREATED THE SAME WAY BY BOTH TERMINATION PATHS, and this row is where that shows. Terminating an ARREARS subscription on the 16th bills through the 16th — b09/terminate/arrears/none charges 16 days of a 31-day March. Terminating an ADVANCE subscription on the 16th credits from the 16th, treating it as unused, which is what makes the upgrade add up: the new subscription also starts on the 16th, so crediting 14 days instead would have charged the customer for the 16th twice. Neither convention is wrong, but they are opposites, and a row that assumes the arrears rule applies here is off by exactly one day — as this one was when first written. Were the credit note NOT spent on this invoice it would sit as a balance while the customer paid 4_500¢. The total alone would look plausible, so credit_notes_amount_cents is what separates them.

The upgrade path with the field left unset, and it is NOT a no-credit-note path: TerminateService is called from ActivateService#activate_for_upgrade (:65-68) with on_termination_credit_note defaulting to the subscription's value, which is nil, which terminate_service.rb:11 coerces to :credit. So the numbers must equal b09/upgrade/advance/credit exactly — 3_000¢ collected on 1 April, a 1_500¢ credit note for 16–30 April, and a rotation invoice of 15 days of plan B at 9_000¢/30 = 300¢ = 4_500¢ against which the credit is spent in full, leaving 3_000¢. Note the extra day the upgrade path takes: remaining_duration subtracts one (create_from_termination.rb:116, `billed_from -= 1.day if upgrade`), so 16–30 April is credited as 15 days rather than the 14 a plain termination on the 16th credits (b09/terminate/advance/credit). Both are coherent — the new subscription also starts on the 16th, so crediting 14 would charge the customer for that day twice — but they are opposite conventions and assuming either one in the other row is off by exactly 100¢ here. This row adds two assertions the covered `credit` sibling does not make: balance_amount_cents 0 and credit_status `consumed`. Those are what prove the credit was actually SPENT on the rotation invoice rather than merely netted in a total — Credits::CreditNoteService#update_remaining_credit (credit_note_service.rb:96-102) is the only thing that moves either field, and it runs only when a positive credit is applied.

The most expensive cell in the block for a customer, and the one worth guarding hardest: upgrading a pay-in-advance subscription whose on_termination_credit_note is `skip` bills the new plan pro rata WITHOUT returning the unused part of the old one. April: 3_000¢ taken up front on the 1st, then 15 days of plan B at 300¢ = 4_500¢ on the 16th, with no credit note — generate_credit_note_for_unconsumed_subscription? (terminate_service.rb:170-174) excludes `skip` before CreateFromTermination is ever reached. The customer pays 7_500¢ for a month in which 1_500¢ of plan A (16–30 April) was never used. Against b09/upgrade/advance/none and /credit, which both settle at 3_000¢ on the second invoice, the whole 1_500¢ is the difference, and credit_notes_amount_cents 0 versus 1_500 is where it shows. total_amount_cents alone would not localise it: a rotation invoice that priced plan B wrongly could also read 4_500. Plan A contributes nothing to the rotation invoice — its subscription fee was collected in advance and should_create_subscription_fee? (calculate_fees_service.rb:270-293) refuses another one for a terminated advance subscription — so the 4_500¢ is plan B alone, computed by upgraded_amount (fees/subscription_service.rb:225-245) as date_diff(16 Apr, 30 Apr) × 9_000/30.

An upgrade with money already collected against a threshold — the same settlement as b05/fixed/single/terminated-mid-period, but reached through a plan change rather than a termination, which is the path a growing customer actually takes. 100 units on 5 April bill 10_000¢ at plan A's 1.00 per unit. Upgrading on 16 April terminates A and bills it in arrears for the usage consumed — the same 100 units, still priced at A's rate because they were metered while A was in force — and credits the 10_000¢ already taken. Total 0. Plan B prices the same metric at 2.00, and B bills in arrears with no advance fee, so it contributes nothing here and is not on either invoice: usage after the switch is B's to bill at the end of April. If the final invoice ever re-prices A's usage at B's 2.00 it would read 20_000¢ of fees against a 10_000¢ credit and charge the customer 10_000¢ for usage already paid. That is what the fees assertion pins, and why the two plans deliberately disagree on price.

The billing entity default is the LAST rung (apply_taxes_service.rb:77) — nothing can shadow it, so the only way to prove it is a rung rather than a global setting is to put a fee beside it that resolves higher. `b10_be_charge` carries 25% on the charge and takes rung 3 (:68); the subscription fee has no charge, no plan tax and no customer tax, so it falls all the way through :68-:74 and picks up the entity's 20%. Two different rates on one invoice is the assertion: a uniform 20% would mean rung 3 never fired, and a uniform 25% would mean the entity default is not a fallback at all. Which level won: billing-entity (rung 8, apply_taxes_service.rb:77). Overridden: rung 3 (the charge's own 25%) shadows the entity default for the charge fee; the entity default is itself the bottom of the ladder and shadows nothing. Had the shadowed rung won instead, the entity default's 20% applied to the charge fee as well would have made the discounted invoice total 7_200¢ rather than 7_440¢. Order of the reducers. calculate_fees_service.rb:54 applies the coupon and :56 computes the taxes, in that order, so the coupon lands on the raw fees and the tax lands on what is left. 10_000¢ of fees, a 4_000¢ fixed coupon, taxable base 6_000¢, taxes 1_440¢, total 7_440¢. Reverse the two lines and the tax is computed on the undiscounted 10_000¢ (2_400¢ instead of 1_440¢) and the invoice totals 8_400¢. A fixed coupon does not commute with a tax, so those two totals differ and the row can name which order produced its number. Per-fee arithmetic, and it is per-fee because the rates differ (or, where they do not, because the invoice total would hide a wrong rung behind a blend). applied_coupon_service.rb:37 with fee.rb:235 spreads the credit pro rata on amount_cents: 800¢ on the subscription fee + 3_200¢ on the charge fee. Each fee is then taxed at ITS own rate on what remains (apply_taxes_service.rb:37): 1_200 × 20% = 240¢; 4_800 × 25% = 1_200¢ — 1_440¢ in total. fees_amount_cents is 10_000¢ under either order and is therefore not load-bearing here. `forever` is asserted across THREE periods. applied_coupon_service.rb:79 returns false from should_terminate_applied_coupon? unconditionally for a forever coupon, and amount_service.rb:32-35 re-reads the full amount rather than a dwindling remainder, so every invoice carries the same credit. All three invoices are discounted identically — `once` would have discounted only the first and `recurring` with duration 2 only the first two, which is exactly the contrast the third period buys. The undiscounted invoice in this row is 10_000¢ of fees, 2_400¢ of tax, 12_400¢ total.

The charge rung (3, :68) against the plan rung (6, :71-73), with the entity default (8, :77) underneath as a witness that never fires. The metered charge carries its own 20% and takes rung 3; the subscription fee has no charge at all, so :68 cannot match and it drops to the plan's 10%. Two rates on one invoice, asserted per fee, because the invoice total cannot tell 10%-here-20%-there from a uniform blend. Which level won: charge (rung 3, apply_taxes_service.rb:68). Overridden: the plan (rung 6, 10%) for the charge fee, and the billing-entity default (rung 8, 5%) for everything. Had the shadowed rung won instead, the plan's 10% on every fee would have made the discounted invoice total 6_600¢ rather than 7_080¢. Order of the reducers. calculate_fees_service.rb:54 applies the coupon and :56 computes the taxes, in that order, so the coupon lands on the raw fees and the tax lands on what is left. 10_000¢ of fees, a 4_000¢ fixed coupon, taxable base 6_000¢, taxes 1_080¢, total 7_080¢. Reverse the two lines and the tax is computed on the undiscounted 10_000¢ (1_800¢ instead of 1_080¢) and the invoice totals 7_800¢.
