The undiscounted invoice in this row is 6_000¢ of fees, 1_000¢ of tax, 7_000¢ total.

Three rungs stacked so that the winner is unambiguous. The plan carries 20% (rung 6, :71-73), the customer 10% (rung 7, :74) and the billing entity 5% (rung 8, :77). Rung 6 is guarded by a fee-type check — it only fires for charge, subscription, commitment and fixed_charge fees — and both fees here qualify, so the plan's 20% is what lands. A 20% observed rate can come from nowhere else in this setup, which is precisely why the customer was given 10% rather than the same 20%. Which level won: plan (rung 6, apply_taxes_service.rb:71-73). Overridden: the customer (rung 7, 10%) and the billing-entity default (rung 8, 5%). Had the shadowed rung won instead, the customer's 10% would have made the discounted invoice total 8_250¢ rather than 9_000¢. Order of the reducers. calculate_fees_service.rb:54 applies the coupon and :56 computes the taxes. A percentage coupon COMMUTES with a percentage tax, so the total alone proves nothing: coupon-first gives 2_500¢ off a 10_000¢ base, taxes on 7_500¢ = 1_500¢, total 9_000¢ — and tax-first would give 2_000¢ of tax on the gross, then 25% of the tax-inclusive 12_000¢ = 3_000¢, for a total of 9_000¢. That is why this row asserts the INTERMEDIATE fields rather than only the total: coupons_amount_cents 2_500¢ (tax-first: 3_000¢), sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents 7_500¢ (tax-first: 12_000¢) and taxes_amount_cents 1_500¢ (tax-first: 2_000¢). Each of the three separates the orders even where the total does not. Per-fee arithmetic, and it is per-fee because the rates differ (or, where they do not, because the invoice total would hide a wrong rung behind a blend). applied_coupon_service.rb:37 with fee.rb:235 spreads the credit pro rata on amount_cents: 500¢ on the subscription fee + 2_000¢ on the charge fee. Each fee is then taxed at ITS own rate on what remains (apply_taxes_service.rb:37): 1_500 × 20% = 300¢; 6_000 × 20% = 1_200¢ — 1_500¢ in total. fees_amount_cents is 10_000¢ under either order and is therefore not load-bearing here. `recurring` with frequency_duration 2 is asserted across THREE periods, which is the only window that separates it from both neighbours. applied_coupon_service.rb:88-89 decrements frequency_duration_remaining on each application and :84 terminates when it reaches 0: 2 -> 1 after the first invoice (still active), 1 -> 0 after the second (terminated). So invoices 1 and 2 are discounted and invoice 3 is not. `once` would have discounted only the first; `forever` would have discounted all three. The undiscounted invoice in this row is 10_000¢ of fees, 2_000¢ of tax, 12_000¢ total.

Charges::OverrideService duplicates the parent charge's filters AND each filter's values onto the child charge (app/services/charges/override_service.rb:26-30), so the eu price of 3.00 follows the override even though the row never mentions the child: 30 units × 3.00 = 9_000¢, plus the overridden 5_000¢ subscription fee = 14_000¢. The un-filtered bucket receives no events, so its zero fee is rejected before saving and only two fees remain. Two distinct failure modes both land on 8_000¢ and are why fees_count is asserted with the amount: filters not duplicated at all, and filters duplicated without their values — in either case the 30 units fall through to the charge's own properties at 1.00 = 3_000¢.

The override raises the subscription price from the parent's 1_000¢ to 5_000¢ for this subscription only, while the charge is inherited untouched: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢. Total 5_000 + 3_000 = 8_000¢. Asserting BOTH fees is the point — an override that leaked into the charge, or failed to reach the subscription fee, changes exactly one of these two numbers.

Plans::OverrideService dups the plan and writes amount_cents onto the COPY, setting parent_id to the original (app/services/plans/override_service.rb:19-29); the original row is never touched. So this subscription bills 2_500¢ while GET /plans/golden_b11_sub_override — which the controller scopes to `.parents` (app/controllers/api/v1/plans_controller.rb:52) — still reports 1_000¢. The charge is inherited by Charges::OverrideService with empty params, so its properties survive verbatim: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢, total 5_500¢. Asserting the invoice AND the parent plan in one row is the point: an override implemented as a plan edit (Plans::UpdateService instead of OverrideService) would still bill 5_500¢ here while repricing every other subscription on the plan — the invoice alone cannot tell the two apart. An override that never reached the subscription fee would bill 1_000 + 3_000 = 4_000¢.

Deleting a charge takes its filters with it, on the child as well as the parent. Charges::DestroyService discards the charge and then stamps deleted_at on its filters and filter values with update_all, bypassing callbacks entirely (app/services/charges/destroy_service.rb:22-23); the cascade repeats the whole service on the child (app/services/charges/destroy_children_service.rb:19-21). The 30 units carrying region=eu, ingested five days before the deletion and priced at 3.00 by the inherited filter, therefore produce no fee at all: the April invoice is the overridden subscription fee alone, 5_000¢, one fee. fees_count is the load-bearing assertion here rather than the amount — a child filter that outlived its parent charge, or filter rows left un-stamped so Fees::ChargeService still iterated them, would add a 9_000¢ charge fee and a 14_000¢ total, and a filter surviving with its values stripped would add a 3_000¢ one. The amount alone cannot distinguish "no charge" from "a charge that aggregated nothing".

PUT /plans/:code is a full replacement, so an empty `charges` array IS the delete: sanitize_charges takes plan.charges minus the payload and discards what is left (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:241-248), and because cascade_updates was sent cascade_charge_removal enqueues Charges::DestroyChildrenJob (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:142-146), which discards the child's copy — the child plan carries an active subscription, which is exactly the scope DestroyChildrenService selects (app/services/charges/destroy_children_service.rb:19-21). Charge declares `default_scope -> { kept }` (app/models/charge.rb:62), so Invoices::CalculateFeesService iterating `subscription.plan.charges` sees nothing at all. The 30 units ingested on 5 March had already accrued when the charge was deleted on the 10th and are dropped anyway — the April invoice is the overridden subscription fee alone, 5_000¢, with a single fee. A deletion that failed to cascade leaves the child billing 30 × 1.00 and the total is 8_000¢, which is what the delete-charge/subscription-override row asserts; a deletion that also somehow spared the parent would leave two charge fees.

The surprising half of the pair, and the one worth pinning: the charge is deleted from the plan and the overridden customer keeps paying for it. Without cascade_updates, cascade_needed? is false (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:123-125) so cascade_charge_removal never enqueues Charges::DestroyChildrenJob and only the PARENT charge is discarded — Charges::DestroyService is called on it directly with cascade_updates defaulting to false (app/services/charges/destroy_service.rb:29-31). The child plan created for this subscription still owns its own Charge row with properties {amount: "1"}, so April bills 30 × 1.00 = 3_000¢ on top of the overridden 5_000¢ subscription fee = 8_000¢, for a charge that no longer appears on the plan an operator reads. An implementation that destroyed children unconditionally would bill 5_000¢ and stop invoicing this customer's usage without anyone asking it to; the cascade row above asserts exactly that 5_000¢, so the 3_000¢ between the two rows is the flag.

The parent charge had no filters when the override duplicated it, so the child has none either. Sending a one-element `filters` array creates the eu filter on the parent (ChargeFilters::CreateOrUpdateBatchService:74, accumulate_new_filter), and because cascade_updates was sent, cascade_filter_changes diffs before=[] against after=[eu] and CascadeDispatcher enqueues a "create" job (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:22-30), which ChargeFilters::CascadeService#create_child_filter runs against every child charge whose plan carries an active subscription (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:99-125). The child therefore gains an eu filter priced at 3.00 that it never had, and the 30 units carrying region=eu are priced by it: 30 x 3.00 = 9_000¢ on top of the overridden 5_000¢ subscription fee = 14_000¢. A create that never reached the child leaves it filterless and the 30 units fall to the child charge's own 1.00 = 3_000¢ for an 8_000¢ total. The parent charge's own properties are resent UNCHANGED at 1.00 so that this row moves only if the FILTER moved — a charge-level cascade cannot account for the difference, which is what separates this row from b11/filter-create/plan-override, where the same call reprices the charge as well.

One call creates a filter AND reprices the charge underneath it, and both halves of the cascade have to land on the same child. Charges::UpdateService captures the parent's old attributes before mutating it (app/services/charges/update_service.rb:22-24), so trigger_cascade enqueues Charges::UpdateChildrenJob with the NEW properties and the OLD parent for comparison; the child was still at 1.00, so `equal_properties: old_parent.equal_properties?(child_charge)` holds and Charges::UpdateChildrenService replaces its properties with 7.00 (app/services/charges/update_children_service.rb:37, app/models/charge.rb:90-92). Separately, cascade_filter_changes diffs before=[] against after=[eu] and CascadeDispatcher enqueues a "create" (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:22-30), which ChargeFilters::CascadeService#create_child_filter runs against the child (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:99-125). The 20 eu units are therefore priced by the brand-new filter at 3.00 = 6_000¢ and the 10 us units by the newly-cascaded charge default at 7.00 = 7_000¢ (the "events not matching any filters" bucket, app/services/fees/charge_service.rb:107-109), plus the overridden 5_000¢ subscription fee = 18_000¢ across three fees. Every partial outcome is a different number: the filter not created prices all 30 units at 7.00 for 21_000¢ and a 26_000¢ total over two fees; the charge properties not cascaded gives 6_000 + 10 x 1.00 = 7_000¢ and 16_000¢; the filter created but swallowing the us traffic gives 30 x 3.00 = 9_000¢ and 14_000¢ over two fees. fees_count is asserted rather than a `fees:` list because the two charge fees share every FEE_MATCH_KEYS identity field.

A cascading filter creation must not disturb the plan-level override, and must not be applied to the parent's own subscribers by accident. The filter cascade only ever touches ChargeFilter rows (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:83-125) — it never loads a Plan — so the child plan keeps the 2_500¢ Plans::OverrideService wrote onto the copy (app/services/plans/override_service.rb:19-29) and GET /plans/golden_b11_fcre_so, which the controller scopes to `.parents` (app/controllers/api/v1/plans_controller.rb:52), still reports 1_000¢. The eu filter reaches the child as in the charge-filter row, so usage is 30 x 3.00 = 9_000¢ and the total is 2_500 + 9_000 = 11_500¢. The resource assertion is the load-bearing half: an implementation that reached the child by repricing the PARENT plan's charge and letting every subscriber inherit it would still bill 11_500¢ here while moving every other customer on the plan. An override lost to the cascade would bill 1_000 + 9_000 = 10_000¢.

An EMPTY replacement array is the delete: CreateOrUpdateBatchService short-circuits to remove_all, which stamps deleted_at on every filter value and discards the filter (app/services/charge_filters/create_or_update_batch_service.rb:24-28, 227-237). CascadeDispatcher then finds an entry in `before` with no counterpart in `after` and enqueues "destroy" (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:33-43), which CascadeService#destroy_child_filter applies to the child's copy (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:139-144). The child charge is left with no kept filters, so Fees::ChargeService takes its `unless charge.filters.any?` branch (app/services/fees/charge_service.rb:97) and the 30 units of eu traffic, previously priced at 3.00 by the inherited filter, fall to the charge's own 1.00: 3_000¢ plus the overridden 5_000¢ = 8_000¢. This is the operationally dangerous direction of the three — deleting a filter makes usage CHEAPER rather than erroring — and it is why fees_count is asserted with the amount: a child filter that survived un-stamped would still price 9_000¢ for a 14_000¢ total, and a filter whose row survived with its values stripped would add a second, empty bucket.

Deleting the only filter COLLAPSES the two buckets into one, which is why this row asserts a fee list where its two siblings cannot. The empty replacement array sends CreateOrUpdateBatchService to remove_all on the parent (app/services/charge_filters/create_or_update_batch_service.rb:24-28, 227-237), CascadeDispatcher finds a `before` entry with no counterpart in `after` and enqueues "destroy" (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:33-43), and CascadeService#destroy_child_filter discards the child's copy and stamps its values (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:139-144). The child charge is left with no kept filters — Charge/ChargeFilter both carry a `kept` default scope — so Fees::ChargeService takes its `unless charge.filters.any?` branch (app/services/fees/charge_service.rb:97) and prices ALL 30 units, eu and us alike, from the properties the same call cascaded down: 30 x 7.00 = 21_000¢ plus the overridden 5_000¢ = 26_000¢ in two fees. The three failure modes are all distinguishable: a filter surviving on the child gives 20 x 3 + 10 x 7 = 13_000¢ and 18_000¢ over THREE fees; the charge properties not cascading gives 30 x 1.00 = 3_000¢ and 8_000¢; a filter whose row survived with its values stripped adds a third, empty bucket. Note the direction, which is the reason the cell is worth a row at all: deleting a filter here makes eu traffic MORE expensive, because the default it falls back on is dearer than the filter was.

The cascading delete reaches the child's filter, so its eu traffic falls to the charge's own 1.00 = 3_000¢, and the negotiated 2_500¢ subscription fee is untouched: 5_500¢. ChargeFilters:: CascadeService#destroy_child_filter discards a ChargeFilter and its values and nothing else (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:139-144), so neither the child plan's amount_cents nor the parent plan can move — GET /plans/golden_b11_fdel_so is asserted at 1_000¢ to show the whole operation stayed inside the child. The three numbers are separable on purpose: an override lost to the cascade bills 1_000 + 3_000 = 4_000¢, a filter that survived the cascade bills 2_500 + 9_000 = 11_500¢, and both leave GET /plans reading 1_000¢ — only asserting the subscription fee and the parent plan together tells the two apart.

Repricing an EXISTING filter, as opposed to the charge's own properties, which is what b11/update-parent-cascade/charge-filter already covers and which moved nothing. The replacement array names the same `values` as the filter already on the charge, so CreateOrUpdateBatchService resolves it through filters_by_values_key and UPDATES it rather than creating a second one (app/services/charge_filters/create_or_update_batch_service.rb:63-71). CascadeDispatcher sees the same values with different properties and enqueues "update" carrying both the old and the new properties (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:18-30). ChargeFilters::CascadeService#update_child_filter then checks whether the child had DIVERGED — `filter_customized?` compares old_properties against the child's (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:148-152) — and this child's filter is the verbatim duplicate Charges::OverrideService made of the parent's, still at 3.00, so it is overwritten to 5.00. 30 units of eu traffic x 5.00 = 15_000¢ plus the overridden 5_000¢ = 20_000¢. A cascade that wrongly judged the child customized would leave it at 3.00: 9_000¢ and a 14_000¢ total, and an "update" that created a SECOND filter instead of resolving the existing one by its values would double the eu bucket. The charge's own properties are resent unchanged at 1.00, so only the filter can account for this row's amount.

The filter is repriced 3.00 -> 5.00 and the charge under it 1.00 -> 7.00 in one call, and the two cascades write different rows on the same child: Charges::UpdateChildrenService the charge's properties, ChargeFilters::CascadeService the filter's. The "update" job carries the parent's OLD filter properties so the child can be checked for divergence (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:22-30); this child's filter is the verbatim duplicate Charges::OverrideService made (app/services/charges/override_service.rb:26-30), still at 3.00, so filter_customized? is false and it is overwritten to 5.00 (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:85-97, 148-152). 20 eu units x 5.00 = 10_000¢, 10 us units x 7.00 = 7_000¢, overridden subscription fee 5_000¢ = 22_000¢ over three fees. The row separates four outcomes that a single-bucket row cannot: neither cascade landing gives 20 x 3 + 10 x 1 = 7_000¢ and 12_000¢; only the charge cascade landing gives 6_000 + 7_000 = 13_000¢ and 18_000¢; only the filter cascade landing gives 10_000 + 1_000 = 11_000¢ and 16_000¢; and a filter wrongly judged customized would leave the eu units at 3.00 for 18_000¢ — the same total as "the filter edit never happened", which is why the charge half is repriced too rather than resent unchanged.

The filter reprice cascades to the child exactly as in the charge-filter row — 30 x 5.00 = 15_000¢ — while the negotiated 2_500¢ subscription fee is untouched, giving 17_500¢. The subscription fee lives on the child PLAN's amount_cents and the filter cascade only ever writes ChargeFilter rows (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_service.rb:83-125), so nothing in this path can reach it; GET /plans/golden_b11_fupd_so is asserted at 1_000¢ to show the edit also stayed off the parent, which the controller's `.parents` scope (app/controllers/api/v1/plans_controller.rb:52) is what makes observable. Two failures this pins that the invoice alone cannot: an override folded back into the parent plan reads 2_500¢ from GET /plans while billing the same 17_500¢, and a cascade that reset the child plan's amount to the parent's would bill 1_000 + 15_000 = 16_000¢.

A cascade that reaches the child and changes nothing the customer pays. The parent charge's own properties go 1.00 → 9.00 and the change is pushed down: trigger_cascade enqueues Charges::UpdateChildrenJob (app/services/charges/cascade_updatable.rb:9-20) and Charges::UpdateChildrenService replaces the child's properties because `equal_properties: old_parent.equal_properties?(child_charge)` holds — the child was still at 1.00 (app/services/charges/update_children_service.rb:37). The child's FILTER is untouched twice over: Charges::UpdateService only rewrites filters when the payload carries a `filters` key and never in cascade mode (`if filters && !cascade`, app/services/charges/update_service.rb:58-64), and ChargeFilters::CascadeDispatcher sees before == after and enqueues nothing (app/services/charge_filters/cascade_dispatcher.rb:18-20). All 30 units carry region=eu, so the filter prices them: 30 × 3.00 = 9_000¢, plus the overridden 5_000¢ = 14_000¢. Note what this means operationally — repricing the charge from 1.00 to 9.00 with cascade on moves nothing for this customer, because every one of their events is filtered. A cascade that overwrote the child's filter properties, or destroyed the filter and let the events fall to the new default, gives 30 × 9.00 = 27_000¢ and a 32_000¢ total either way.

The parent's charge is repriced from 1.00 to 2.00 WITH cascade_updates, so the child plan created by the override receives the change: 30 units × 2.00 = 6_000¢. The overridden subscription fee is untouched at 5_000¢ — cascading a charge must not undo an override of a different field — giving 5_000 + 6_000 = 11_000¢. Compare the no-cascade row below, which uses an identical setup and yields 8_000¢.

cascade_updates is TRUE and the child is still left alone. Plans::UpdateService only pushes a new amount_cents to children that had not diverged: the query is `plan.children.where(amount_cents: old_amount_cents)` (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:131), and Plans::UpdateAmountService guards it a second time with `return result if plan.amount_cents != expected_amount_cents` (app/services/plans/update_amount_service.rb:19). This child was created at 5_000¢ against an old parent amount of 1_000¢, so it matches neither guard and keeps 5_000¢ while the parent moves to 3_000¢. The charge is resent unchanged by the same call, so usage stays at 30 × 1.00 = 3_000¢ and the total is 8_000¢. An implementation that cascaded to every child would bill 3_000 + 3_000 = 6_000¢ — silently discarding a negotiated price, which is the failure this row exists to catch. Compare the create-child rows: the same 5_000¢ override, before anybody edits the parent.

Same repricing of the parent charge, 1.00 → 9.00, with cascade_updates false: trigger_cascade returns on its first line (`return unless cascade_updates`, app/services/charges/cascade_updatable.rb:10), so the child keeps both its 1.00 default AND the eu filter it inherited. The events carry region=us, which the charge's only filter does not cover, so Fees::ChargeService prices them from the child charge's own properties — the "events not matching any filters" bucket at app/services/fees/charge_service.rb:107-109 — giving 30 × 1.00 = 3_000¢ on top of the overridden 5_000¢ = 8_000¢. The eu bucket has no events, its zero fee is dropped, and fees_count is 2. The same setup with cascade_updates: true bills 30 × 9.00 = 27_000¢, so the 24_000¢ gap between this row and that is the whole flag. A charge filter that wrongly captured non-matching events would price these units at 3.00 = 9_000¢.

Identical to the cascade row except cascade_updates is false, so the child plan keeps the price it was created with: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢, total 8_000¢ rather than 11_000¢. The 3_000¢ difference between these two rows is the entire behaviour of the flag, and it is invisible on the parent plan — only a subscription billed against the child reveals which way it went.

The mirror image of the cascade row, and deliberately NOT its A/B twin. Here the override renames the plan and leaves amount_cents inherited, so the child sits at 1_000¢ — exactly the value `where(amount_cents: old_amount_cents)` (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:131) selects. It is spared anyway, because cascade_needed? is `cascade? && plan.children.present?` (app/services/plans/update_service.rb:123-125) and no cascade_updates was sent, so cascade_subscription_fee_update returns before enqueuing anything. The subscription therefore bills the old 1_000¢ against a parent now priced at 3_000¢, plus 30 × 1.00 = 3_000¢ of usage = 4_000¢. Sending cascade_updates: true on this same setup would give 3_000 + 3_000 = 6_000¢ — and that contrast is the reason the two subscription-override rows differ in their child rather than only in the flag: a child that inherited the price moves, a child that negotiated one does not, and only the pair shows both halves.

In advance the commitment reconciles the PREVIOUS period, so it is the SECOND invoice that carries the true-up and this row asserts both. Invoice 1 (2024-03-10, raised on subscription creation by activate_service.rb:181-196) is the period-1 subscription fee alone: 2_000¢, and no commitment fee at all — calculate_fees_service.rb:250 and commitments/minimum/in_advance/calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:9-19 both refuse a true-up while invoice_subscription.previous_invoice_subscription is nil — and no charge fee either, because a zero-units zero-amount fee is not persisted (fees/charge_service.rb:353-359). fees_count 1 is what pins that. Invoice 2 (2024-04-10) reconciles period 1 = 2024-03-10T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-09T23:59:59Z. That window is built from the PREVIOUS invoice_subscription with current_usage=true (in_advance/calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:122-127, in_advance/dates_service.rb:7-9), resolved for a anniversary monthly plan by subscriptions/dates/monthly_service.rb:62-81 and :103-107. fees_total = 2_000¢ + 3_000¢ = 5_000¢. The period-1 subscription fee is selected by properties->>'from_datetime' >= 2024-03-10T00:00:00Z AND properties->>'to_datetime' <= 2024-04-09T23:59:59Z (:21-37), which is exactly why the period-2 subscription fee sitting on this same invoice (2024-04-10T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-09T23:59:59Z) is NOT counted; the 30 units x 1.00 of usage arrives as the arrears charge fee for period 1 and is selected by invoice id rather than by date (:39-48). The floor is not prorated: calculate_amount_service.rb:36-44 hands the PREVIOUS invoice_subscription to CalculateProratedCoefficientService, whose 31 / 31 days come out even because the subscription started on the period's own boundary, so the commitment is the full 10_000¢ and calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:37-41 gives 10_000 - 5_000 = 5_000¢. Note what the invoice total does NOT say: invoice 2 sums to 10_000¢, but only 5_000¢ of that belongs to the reconciled period — the other 2_000¢ is period 2 charged in advance. An arrears invoice for the same money reads identically at invoice level, so the per-fee from_date / to_date are load-bearing: the commitment fee's period is copied off the reconciled invoice_subscription (fees/commitments/minimum/build_fee_base_service.rb:30-50) and names period 1, while the subscription fee beside it names period 2. What a wrong implementation gives. Both date comparisons are inclusive (>= and <=), so any window that does not fully span 2024-03-10T00:00:00Z .. 2024-04-09T23:59:59Z — one day short at either end is enough — no longer contains the period-1 subscription fee, fees_total drops to the invoice-selected 3_000¢ charge fee and the true-up becomes 10_000 - 3_000 = 7_000¢. A window whose end reaches 2024-05-09T23:59:59Z catches the period-2 subscription fee as well and gives 10_000 - (2_000 + 2_000 + 3_000) = 3_000¢. One failure mode the amount cannot catch, and the dates can: reconciling the CURRENT period instead of the previous one would still total 5_000¢, because the charge fee is chosen by invoice id and the two subscription fees cost the same — `fees_amount_cents` is blind to it, and the commitment fee's from_date / to_date is the only assertion that fails.

In advance the commitment reconciles the PREVIOUS period, so it is the SECOND invoice that carries the true-up and this row asserts both. Invoice 1 (2024-02-10, raised on subscription creation by activate_service.rb:181-196) is the period-1 subscription fee alone: 2_000¢, and no commitment fee at all — calculate_fees_service.rb:250 and commitments/minimum/in_advance/calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:9-19 both refuse a true-up while invoice_subscription.previous_invoice_subscription is nil — and no charge fee either, because a zero-units zero-amount fee is not persisted (fees/charge_service.rb:353-359). fees_count 1 is what pins that. Invoice 2 (2024-05-10) reconciles period 1 = 2024-02-10T00:00:00Z .. 2024-05-09T23:59:59Z. A minimum commitment tops the period up to a floor, and the true-up is the only fee whose amount is a function of the other fees on the same invoice. 2_000¢ subscription + 30 units × 1.00 = 5_000¢ of real usage against a 10_000¢ commitment, so Commitments::Minimum::CalculateTrueUpFeeService adds `commitment - fees_total` = 5_000¢ as a `commitment` fee and the invoice reaches exactly the floor: 10_000¢. The order is what this row pins. The true-up is a PRODUCER — it is created alongside the subscription and charge fees (calculate_fees_service.rb:46), before any reducer — and it reads raw `amount_cents`, so it neither knows nor cares that a coupon is coming. The 2_000¢ coupon then applies to the topped-up 10_000¢ and the customer pays 8_000¢ net against a floor they committed to at 10_000¢. That is the consequence worth knowing: a coupon discounts the commitment itself rather than being absorbed by the headroom beneath it. Had the true-up run after the coupon it would have seen 3_000¢ of discounted fees, topped up by 7_000¢ instead of 5_000¢, and the customer would have paid the full 10_000¢ with the coupon silently doing nothing. Both totals are 10_000¢ of fees, so `fees_amount_cents` cannot tell the two apart — the split across the three fees is what does, which is why each is asserted with its own tax: the coupon spreads pro rata (400¢, 600¢, 1_000¢) and each fee is taxed on the remainder at 20%.

The graduated mirror of the standard advance decrease, and the tiering makes the "no refund" rule cost visibly more: the units given back are the ones in the CHEAP tier, but nothing is credited at all. Invoice 0, activation: delta 40, coefficient 1 → GraduatedService tiers 40 → 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 400.00 and 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units × 5.00 + 50.00 = 100.00 → 500.00 → 50_000¢ at 12.50 per unit, for 2024-04-01..2024-04-30. Invoice 1, the change: `delta_units` = 20 - 40 = -20, so `build_zero_amount_fee` runs before the charge model is ever consulted (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:29-35) — a 0¢, 0-unit fee on April's boundaries, on an invoice that is finalized rather than closed (transition_to_final_status_service.rb:31-37). The charge model is irrelevant on a decrease, which is why this fee is byte-identical to the standard rows' middle invoice. Invoice 2, periodic: the last event before the readjusted MAY window carries 20 units → 20 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 300.00 → 30_000¢ at 15.00 per unit, dated 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, and tier 2 is never entered so its 50.00 flat disappears. So April was paid at 50_000¢ and May costs 30_000¢ for a position reduced on the 16th of April: 20_000¢ of tier-2-and-flat pricing the customer keeps paying for a fortnight after giving the units up. Excluded: a credit for the released units at their marginal price would be -(10 × 5.00 + 50.00 + 10 × 10.00) = -20_000¢ on invoice 1; a full credit of the difference 500.00 - 300.00 = -20_000¢ likewise; re-billing the reduced quantity for April 30_000¢; and suppressing the invoice would give `invoices: 2`.

The row where the advance delta and a tiered charge model meet, and the answer is the one a reviewer is least likely to guess: the DELTA is priced as if it were a fresh subscription, from tier 1 upward, INCLUDING tier 1's flat amount a second time. Invoice 0, activation: `already_paid_units` = 0, delta = 20, coefficient 1 (not prorated). The delta is handed to ChargeModels::Factory through a synthetic aggregation result whose `aggregation` and `full_units_number` are both 20 (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:148-164) → GraduatedService tiers 20: tier 1's `to_value` 30 exceeds 20 so `effective_total` is 20 → 20 × 10.00 = 200.00 plus 100.00 flat = 300.00, and the range loop breaks (graduated_service.rb:11-18). 300.00 → 30_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` = 300/20 = 15.00. Invoice 1, the change: `already_paid_units` = 20 read off invoice 0's fee by exact April-boundary match (:63-86) → delta = 20 again, and the SAME calculation runs on it → another 300.00 → 30_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` 15.00. So the customer pays 100.00 of tier-1 flat fee TWICE inside one April, and both 20-unit blocks are priced at tier 1's 10.00 even though the account is now at 40 units and its 31st..40th units are contractually worth 5.00. The incremental price a reader would expect is `cost(40) - cost(20)`, i.e. (30 × 10.00 + 100.00 + 10 × 5.00 + 50.00) - 300.00 = 500.00 - 300.00 = 200.00 → 20_000¢. Lago bills 30_000¢, 50% more, and the whole 100.00 excess is the re-charged flat amount. April therefore costs 60_000¢ in advance for a position that the ARREARS graduated rows bill at 50_000¢ for the same 40 closing units — the pay_in_advance axis is worth 10_000¢ here, all of it flat fee. Invoice 2, periodic: SimpleAggregationService over the readjusted MAY window (fixed_charge_service.rb:236-250) takes the last event's 40 units and tiers them ONCE: 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 400.00, then 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units × 5.00 + 50.00 = 100.00 → 500.00 → 50_000¢ at 12.50 per unit, dated 2024-05-01..2024-05-31 beside an APRIL subscription fee. So the same 40 units cost 60_000¢ in the month they were acquired and 50_000¢ in the next one, which is the clearest statement of the delta-pricing behaviour the block can make. Also excluded, on invoice 1: 20_000¢ (`cost(40) - cost(20)`, the incremental price), 50_000¢ (the full new quantity re-billed for April, which would double-charge the first twenty units), 10_000¢ (the delta priced entirely at the marginal tier the account now sits in, 20 × 5.00 with no flat), and `invoices: 2` — which is what `apply_units_immediately: false` gives, the event landing at 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z instead.

`graduated` + `pay_in_advance` + `prorated` is rejected outright (FixedCharge#validate_prorated, fixed_charge.rb:88-96), so this is the only advance cell graduated has, and it is un-prorated by construction. Both fees price 40 raw units through ChargeModels::GraduatedService. The ranges are NOT adjacent — 31 is 30 + 1, so `adjacent_ranges?` is false (graduated_service.rb:22-28) and RangeGraduatedService bills `to_value - from_value + 1` in every range after the first (range_graduated_service.rb:53-63). Tier 1: units capped at its `to_value` 30 → 30 × 10.00 = 300.00 plus 100.00 flat = 400.00. Tier 2: `to_value` is null so the effective total is 40 → 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units → 10 × 5.00 = 50.00 plus 50.00 flat = 100.00. Total 500.00 → 50_000¢, and `precise_unit_amount` = 500.00 / 40 = 12.50 (unit_amount divides by `full_units_number`, graduated_service.rb:76-81). The two flat amounts are what make the tiering visible: pricing all 40 units at tier 1 would give 40 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 500.00 too, but with only ONE flat fee, so the 150.00 of flats asserted here is what says the second range was entered. Invoice 1 comes from Fees::BuildPayInAdvanceFixedChargeService, which builds a synthetic aggregation result of `delta_units` and hands it to the same ChargeModels::Factory (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:146-165), so a full month is billed on the 16th: 50_000¢ for 15 days of service. Invoice 2 bills MAY, again through the readjusted advance window (fixed_charge_service.rb:238-252), so the invoice carries an April subscription fee beside a May fixed-charge fee and both dates are asserted. What this rules out: proration was not silently applied anywhere — half of 500.00 would be 25_000¢ on invoice 1, and the prorated-graduated split that b13/graduated/arrears/prorated/no-change measures would be 32_500¢. An implementation that dropped the two flat amounts would give 300.00 + 50.00 = 350.00 → 35_000¢, and one that used adjacent-range arithmetic (no `+ 1` on the second range) would give 300.00 + 9 × 5.00 + 150.00 = 495.00 → 49_500¢.

Graduated's only advance override cell, and it asserts the override against BOTH plan-level mechanisms at once: the event stream and the bulk invoice trigger. Invoice 0, activation: delta 20 at coefficient 1 → tier 1 only → 20 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 300.00 → 30_000¢ at 15.00 per unit. Invoice 1, the 2024-04-16 units-only override to 40. WriteService writes the Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride, emits ONE event for this subscription, and enqueues Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob itself (write_service.rb:27-38). `already_paid_units` = 20 → delta 20 → the delta is tiered from zero again → 300.00 → 30_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` 15.00, April boundaries. Identical to the plan-endpoint fee in b13/graduated/advance/not-prorated/increase-mid-period, including the re-charged 100.00 flat. The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 60 units changes the plan and does nothing here: no event (`.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for`, emit_events_service.rb:52) and no invoice (create_all_pay_in_advance_fixed_charges_job.rb:19-25 applies the same scope before enqueuing per subscription). Hence `invoices: 3`. Invoice 2, periodic: the last event before the readjusted MAY window is the 40-unit override → 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 + 10 × 5.00 + 50.00 = 500.00 → 50_000¢ at 12.50, dated 2024-05-01..2024-05-31 beside an April subscription fee. The counterfactuals are far apart here. If the plan-level update had reached this subscription there would be a FOURTH invoice for delta 60 - 40 = 20 → tier 1 from zero again → 30_000¢, and May would bill 60 units: 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 + (60 - 31 + 1) × 5.00 + 50.00 = 400.00 + 200.00 = 600.00 → 60_000¢. If the override had never applied, April would hold 20 then 60 and May would read 60_000¢ as well. Only 50_000¢ in May with three invoices says the override applied and held. `premium: true`: licence-gated (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

The mirror of the graduated increase, and the direction that proves the aggregation is last-event-wins rather than a high-water mark — a distinction that costs a whole TIER here, not just some units. The same two events are in range, the later one carries 10 units, and SimpleAggregationService takes it (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6). GraduatedService then tiers 10 from zero: tier 1's `to_value` 30 exceeds 10, so `effective_total` is 10 → 10 × 10.00 = 100.00 plus 100.00 flat = 200.00, and `amount_details` breaks out of the range loop because `range[:to_value] >= units` (graduated_service.rb:11-18) — tier 2 is never entered and its 50.00 flat is never charged. Total 200.00 → 20_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` = 200.00 / 10 = 20.00. That the SECOND flat amount disappears is the sharp part. A high-water-mark aggregation would keep 40 units, re-enter tier 2 and bill 50_000¢ — 30_000¢ more, of which 50.00 is pure flat fee that no unit justifies. Blending the period (which the prorated sibling does) gives 40 × 0.5 + 10 × 0.5 = 25 units, still inside tier 1, at 35_000¢. Crediting the released units would give a negative fee, which fixed_charge_service.rb:87-90 clamps to 0 in any case. Read with b13/graduated/arrears/not-prorated/increase-mid-period, the pair pins the aggregation exactly: 10 → 40 bills 50_000¢ and 40 → 10 bills 20_000¢, so neither the maximum nor the sum nor the opening value is what Lago uses. One row alone cannot say that. Boundaries are the un-readjusted arrears window shared with the subscription fee; both asserted.

A not-prorated graduated fixed charge does not blend and does not accumulate: the last event's units are re-tiered from zero for the whole period. SimpleAggregationService returns `events_in_range.last.units` (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6-9) over the two April events (10 at 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z, 40 at 2024-04-16T00:00:00Z, ordered by created_at, base_service.rb:39-47) → both `aggregation` and `full_units_number` are 40, and the ordinary ChargeModels::GraduatedService prices them. Tier 1 caps at its `to_value` 30 → 30 × 10.00 = 300.00 plus 100.00 flat = 400.00. Tier 2's `to_value` is null so the effective total is 40 → 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units → 10 × 5.00 = 50.00 plus 50.00 flat = 100.00. Total 500.00 → 50_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` = 500.00 / 40 = 12.50 (graduated_service.rb:63-68 divides by `full_units_number`). The units change is what makes the tier boundary do work here: the pre-change quantity, 10 units, sits entirely inside tier 1 and would bill 10 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 200.00 → 20_000¢, with ONE flat amount instead of two. So the number separates four behaviours. 50_000¢: last event wins, tiered from zero. 20_000¢: created units kept — and 20_000¢ is equally what `apply_units_immediately: false` yields, the event landing at 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z outside April's range. 70_000¢: both quantities tiered independently and summed (200.00 + 500.00). 30_000¢: only the INCREMENT tiered, 40 - 10 = 30 units → 300.00 + 100.00 flat, which is what an advance-style delta would compute — and is exactly what b13/graduated/advance/not-prorated/increase-mid-period does bill on its own middle invoice. Boundaries: arrears, so `readjust_boundaries` leaves the invoice's own window alone (fixed_charge_service.rb:242) and the fixed-charge fee shares 2024-04-01..2024-04-30 with the subscription fee. Both asserted.

The control for b13/graduated/arrears/prorated/no-change: identical ranges, identical 40 units, identical 15-of-30-day period, `prorated` off. SimpleAggregationService returns the last event's units unchanged (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6-9), so both `aggregation` and `full_units_number` are 40 and the ordinary ChargeModels::GraduatedService prices them: tier 1 caps at its `to_value` 30 → 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 flat = 400.00; tier 2 takes 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units (the ranges are not adjacent, range_graduated_service.rb:53-63) → 10 × 5.00 + 50.00 flat = 100.00. Total 500.00 → 50_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` 500.00 / 40 = 12.50. The pair is therefore 50_000¢ against 32_500¢ for the same units over the same half-period, and the 17_500¢ gap decomposes as exactly the per-unit half of the bill (350.00 → 175.00) with the 150.00 of flat amounts untouched on both sides. Reading either row alone cannot see that; the two together locate the proration precisely in the per-unit component. This row also pins that a mid-period start costs nothing when the charge is not prorated: 15 days of service are billed at a full month's 500.00, with a period boundary that openly says 2024-04-16..2024-04-30.

The override cell chosen so that the plan's later value lands in a DIFFERENT TIER from the override's — 25 units is inside tier 1, 40 crosses into tier 2 — so the assertion is not a units comparison but a price-structure one, and a leak would move the flat-fee count as well as the amount. The 2024-04-16 request is units-only, so Subscriptions::UpdateOrOverrideFixedChargeService writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride of 40 and emits one event for this subscription (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:41-58 → write_service.rb:19-32). The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 25 units succeeds, the plan really is at 25 afterwards, and this subscription is skipped: EmitEventsService's bulk scope is `.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for(fixed_charge)` (emit_events_service.rb:52). So the last April event is the 40-unit override, SimpleAggregationService returns 40, and GraduatedService bills both tiers: 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 400.00, then 40 - 31 + 1 = 10 units at 5.00 + 50.00 flat = 100.00. Total 500.00 → 50_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` 500.00 / 40 = 12.50, and 150.00 of that is flat fees — the second of which exists only because tier 2 was reached. Had the plan-level update reached this subscription, its 25 units would be the last event and the fee would be 25 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 350.00 → 35_000¢ with a SINGLE flat amount. Had the override never applied, the stream would be 10 then 25 and the answer would be 35_000¢ too — so 50_000¢ is reachable only if the override took effect AND survived the later plan change, and the 15_000¢ gap is not a rounding-sized difference that a wrong derivation could land on by accident. `premium: true`: the endpoint is licence-gated (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

The row that shows the prorated-graduated coefficient can exceed 1, and that the tier is chosen by the LAST event's units rather than by the period's unit-months or by the maximum held. The aggregation is 40 × 15/30 + 10 × 15/30 = 30.000000 unit-months, `full_units_number` = 10. So `per_event_aggregation` hands ProratedGraduatedService `event_aggregation = [10]` and `event_prorated_aggregation = [30]` (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:27-34) — a "prorated" figure THREE TIMES the full one, because half a month at 40 units outweighs the closing 10. In ProratedGraduatedService (:34-93), `full_sum` becomes 10 and `prorated_sum` 30. Tier selection runs off `full_sum`: 10 < tier 1's `to_value` of 30, so `skip_overflow_calculation?` is true (:163-167), no overflow is computed and the loop exits with everything in tier 1. The whole prorated sum is then priced at tier 1's rate: 30 × 10.00 = 300.00, and `result_with_flat_amount` adds only tier 1's flat amount because `max_full_units` (10) is inside it (:112-123). Total 350.00 → 35_000¢. `precise_unit_amount` = 350.00 / 10 = 35.00 — three and a half times the 10.00 tier rate — and `units` is 10, so the fee openly reports ten units at a price that thirty unit-months earned. Both fields are asserted; the amount alone cannot show it. That combination is the substantive claim, and it is a deliberate asymmetry with the increase sibling: 30 prorated unit-months are billed at TIER 1 here while 25 prorated unit-months are split across tiers there, purely because the closing quantity differs. Candidates. Ignoring proration is 10 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 200.00 → 20_000¢, the b13/graduated/arrears/not-prorated/decrease-mid-period sibling. A high-water aggregation — weighting both halves at the OPENING 40 units — gives prorated 40 and full 40, coefficient 1, and crosses into tier 2: 30 × 10.00 + 10 × 5.00 + 150.00 of flats = 500.00 → 50_000¢. Prorating first and then tiering gives 30 units, which lands exactly on tier 1's boundary and so reproduces 350.00 — indistinguishable here by construction, and separated by the increase sibling where the same alternative reads 35_000¢ against 36_875¢. Prorating the flat amount too would be 300.00 + 50.00 = 350.00, likewise indistinguishable here and separated by the increase sibling (150.00 of flats against a prorated 93.75). Boundaries: arrears, un-readjusted, shared with the subscription fee; both asserted.

The only cell in the block where a units change and a tier boundary and proration all bear on one number, and it is the one place the charge model itself is different: `graduated` + `prorated` is the sole combination for which ChargeModels::Factory swaps in ProratedGraduatedService (factory.rb:40-45). Step 1, the aggregation. ProratedAggregationService weights the two April events by days in force (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:119-154): 10 units for 2024-04-01..2024-04-16 → 10 × 15/30 = 5, then 40 units for 2024-04-16..2024-05-01 → 40 × 15/30 = 20. `aggregation` = 25.000000, while `full_units_number` is the LAST event's units, 40 (:22). Step 2, and this is the part worth pinning: the fixed-charge aggregator's `per_event_aggregation` does NOT return one entry per event. It returns two one-element arrays, `event_aggregation = [full_units_number]` = [40] and `event_prorated_aggregation = [aggregation]` = [25] (:27-34) — the whole period collapsed into a single synthetic "event". So ProratedGraduatedService sees one 40-unit event whose prorated value is 25, and the per-event structure the class was written for (charges, where each event is a separate row) is absent here. The consequence is that the tiering is driven by the period TOTAL, not by the order the units arrived in. Step 3, the pricing (prorated_graduated_service.rb:34-93). `full_sum` becomes 40, `prorated_sum` 25; tier 1's `to_value` is 30, so `overflow` = 40 - 30 = 10 full units spill upward and the prorated sum is split by `prorated_coefficient` = 25.fdiv(40) = 0.625: tier 1 keeps 30 × 0.625 = 18.75 prorated units at 10.00 = 187.50, tier 2 takes 10 × 0.625 = 6.25 at 5.00 = 31.25. `result_with_flat_amount` (:112-123) then adds every flat amount up to the highest range REACHED by the FULL units, in full and un-prorated: 100.00 + 50.00 = 150.00. Total 368.75 → 36_875¢, `precise_unit_amount` = 368.75 / 40 = 9.21875 (:103-108 divides by the full-units sum). Four candidates, all separated by these numbers. Prorating first and tiering the result would put 25 units wholly in tier 1 → 25 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 350.00 → 35_000¢ (and lose the second flat fee). Ignoring proration is the sibling b13/graduated/arrears/not-prorated/increase-mid-period's 500.00 → 50_000¢. Prorating the flat amounts too would give 187.50 + 31.25 + 93.75 = 312.50 → 31_250¢. And a high-water aggregation, weighting both halves of April at 40 units, would give a coefficient of 1 and reproduce the un-prorated 50_000¢ — so the 36_875¢ here also says the earlier ten units were not silently promoted. Boundaries: arrears, so nothing is readjusted and both fees report 2024-04-01..2024-04-30.

The one cell in the block where the charge model itself changes: `graduated` + `prorated` is the only combination for which ChargeModels::Factory swaps in a different class (ProratedGraduatedService, factory.rb:40-45). It is handed TWO parallel arrays by ProratedAggregationService#per_event_aggregation (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:27-37): `event_aggregation` = [40] (the full units) and `event_prorated_aggregation` = [20] (40 × 15/30, derived as in b13/standard/arrears/prorated/no-change). The tier is chosen by the FULL number and the price is paid on the PRORATED one (prorated_graduated_service.rb:31-92). With one event: `full_sum` becomes 40 and `prorated_sum` 20; tier 1's `to_value` is 30, so `overflow` = 40 - 30 = 10 full units spill into tier 2, and the prorated sum is split by `prorated_coefficient` = 20 / 40 = 0.5 → 10 × 0.5 = 5 prorated units moved out of tier 1. Tier 1 bills 15 × 10.00 = 150.00; tier 2 bills 5 × 5.00 = 25.00; and `result_with_flat_amount` (:110-122) then adds every flat amount up to the highest range REACHED by the full units, in full and un-prorated: 100.00 + 50.00 = 150.00. Total 325.00 → 32_500¢, with `precise_unit_amount` = 325.00 / 40 = 8.125 (:104-107 divides by the full-units sum). Three candidate behaviours, all excluded by that number. Prorating FIRST and then tiering would put all 20 units in tier 1 → 20 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 300.00 → 30_000¢. Ignoring proration is the sibling row's 500.00 → 50_000¢. Prorating the flat amounts too would give 150.00 + 25.00 + 75.00 = 250.00 → 25_000¢. That the flats are NOT prorated while the per-unit amounts are is the substantive finding in this row, and it is only visible because the ranges carry flat fees. Boundaries: in arrears nothing is readjusted, so the fixed-charge fee and the subscription fee both report 2024-04-16..2024-04-30, and both are asserted.

The strictest override assertion in the block, because both of the numbers that describe the period — the prorated total AND the tier-selecting full units — change if a single unwanted event reaches this subscription, and they change in different directions. The units-only PUT on 2024-04-16 writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride of 40 and emits one event for this subscription (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:41-58 → write_service.rb:19-32). The plan-level PUT on 2024-04-20 moves the plan to 25 units and skips this subscription (`.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for`, emit_events_service.rb:52). So April holds two events, 10 at 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z and 40 at 2024-04-16, giving `aggregation` = 10 × 15/30 + 40 × 15/30 = 25.000000 and `full_units_number` = 40 — identical to b13/graduated/arrears/prorated/increase-mid-period, so the fee is identical too: coefficient 25.fdiv(40) = 0.625, tier 1 30 × 0.625 × 10.00 = 187.50, tier 2 10 × 0.625 × 5.00 = 31.25, flats 100.00 + 50.00 un-prorated = 150.00 → 368.75 → 36_875¢ at `precise_unit_amount` 368.75 / 40 = 9.21875. Had the plan-level event reached this subscription, April would hold THREE events and both inputs would move: `aggregation` = 10 × 15/30 + 40 × 4/30 + 25 × 11/30 = 5 + 5.333333 + 9.166667 = 19.500000 and `full_units_number` = 25, which no longer reaches tier 2 at all — coefficient 19.5/25 = 0.78, 25 × 0.78 × 10.00 = 195.00 plus tier 1's flat 100.00 only = 295.00 → 29_500¢. Had the override never applied, the stream would be 10 then 25 → aggregation 10 × 19/30 + 25 × 11/30 = 6.333333 + 9.166667 = 15.500000, full 25, coefficient 0.62 → 25 × 0.62 × 10.00 = 155.00 + 100.00 = 255.00 → 25_500¢. Three distinct amounts and two distinct flat-fee counts, so 36_875¢ is reachable only if the override applied and then survived. `premium: true`: licence-gated endpoint (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

Deliberately identical, invoice for invoice, to b13/standard/advance/prorated/decrease-mid-period, and the equality is the finding rather than a duplicated row. A negative `delta_units` short-circuits at build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:29-35 — `build_zero_amount_fee` — BEFORE `build_delta_fee` ever computes `proration_coefficient` (:108-113). So the `prorated` flag is unreachable on a decrease: there is no code path on which it could change the answer. The pair of cells is written out because both are legal and a reader comparing them would otherwise assume the suite had simply not exercised one; the assertion is that the two agree at every field. Invoice 0: activation, 10 units, coefficient 1 → 100_000¢ for 2024-04-01..2024-04-30. Invoice 1: the change. delta = 4 - 10 = -6 → a 0¢, 0-unit fee documenting the change on the April boundaries, on a zero-total invoice that is FINALIZED (billing entity's `finalize_zero_amount_invoice` defaults to true and the customer inherits it, transition_to_final_status_service.rb:31-37). No credit note, no refund, no negative fee: Lago's comment at :29-30 says as much, and this is where the suite records it. Invoice 2: the periodic April invoice, whose fixed-charge fee covers the readjusted MAY window. SimpleAggregationService's last event before May is the 4-unit one → 4 × 100.00 = 400.00 → 40_000¢, dated 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, next to an April subscription fee. That the subscription fee and the fixed-charge fee on ONE invoice name different months is asserted here as everywhere in the advance half of the block. Excluded: a credit for the six released units would be -6 × 100.00 = -60_000¢ on invoice 1; a prorated credit -30_000¢; re-billing the remaining four for April 40_000¢; and suppressing the invoice entirely would give `invoices: 2`.

The control for b13/standard/advance/prorated/increase-mid-period: same units, same dates, same 100.00 per unit, `prorated` flipped off, and the pair differs on EXACTLY ONE of the three invoices — which is what makes the difference attributable to the flag. Invoice 0, activation: `proration_coefficient` is hard-coded to 1 when the charge is not prorated (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:108-113), so delta 10 → 10 × 100.00 = 1_000.00 → 100_000¢. The prorated sibling reads the same, because its own coefficient is 30/30 = 1 for a period-start subscription. Identical by construction. Invoice 1, the change: `already_paid_units` = 10 from the activation fee's stored April boundaries (:63-86) → `delta_units` = 15, coefficient 1 → 15 × 100.00 = 1_500.00 → 150_000¢ at a `precise_unit_amount` of 100.00. This is the axis: the customer is charged fifteen whole unit-months on the 16th for fifteen days of them. The prorated sibling charges 75_000¢ here, so the pair brackets the behaviour at 350_000¢ against 425_000¢ of April-and-May in total. Invoice 2, periodic: SimpleAggregationService returns `events_in_range.last.units` (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6-9) over the READJUSTED May window (fixed_charge_service.rb:236-250). No event falls inside May, so `events_in_range` is the last-before-range fallback (base_service.rb:39-47), the 25-unit event → 25 × 100.00 = 2_500.00 → 250_000¢ dated 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, beside an APRIL subscription fee on the same invoice. Also identical to the prorated sibling, since a full period prorates to 1. Excluded, with numbers: re-billing the whole new quantity for April would make invoice 1 read 250_000¢, not 150_000¢ — and would double-bill the original ten units. Billing nothing until the next period would make it 0¢ and is what `apply_units_immediately: false` does, with `invoices: 2` and a May fee of 250_000¢ instead. Treating the delta as prorated is the sibling's 75_000¢.

The control for b13/standard/advance/prorated/no-change: same 15-of-30 days, same 40 units, same 100.00 per unit, `prorated` flipped off. Fees::BuildPayInAdvanceFixedChargeService sets `proration_coefficient = 1` when the charge is not prorated (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:118-123), so the charge model is applied to the raw delta of 40 units: 40 × 100.00 = 4_000.00 → 400_000¢ for a period that is only half over. The customer pays the full month on the 16th, and `precise_unit_amount` stays at the properties' 100.00 rather than dropping to 50.00 as the prorated row's does. The two rows therefore differ by exactly 200_000¢ on invoice 1 while agreeing on invoice 2 — 440_000¢ of April-and-May under proration against 800_000¢ without it — which is what makes the pair worth having: the difference is the `prorated` flag and nothing else. The May fee is unchanged from the prorated row, because SimpleAggregationService returns the last event's units flat (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6-9) and the prorated aggregator happens to return a ratio of 1 for a full period. Its boundaries are still the readjusted MAY window (fixed_charge_service.rb:238-252) rather than the April period the subscription fee beside it reports, so both dates are asserted here too: with the amounts identical, the boundary is the only thing distinguishing "billed May in advance" from "billed April twice".

The un-prorated advance override, and the row that shows the override's protection is not a proration artefact: with the coefficient pinned at 1 the numbers are round, so the only thing left to explain them is WHICH events reached this subscription. Invoice 0: activation, delta 10, coefficient 1 (not prorated, build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:108-113) → 10 × 100.00 = 100_000¢, April. Invoice 1: the 2024-04-16 subscription-level override to 25 units. The body carries only `units` and `apply_units_immediately`, so Subscriptions::UpdateOrOverrideFixedChargeService takes the units-only path (fixed_charge_units_override_detection_concern.rb:26-31) and FixedChargeUnitsOverrides::WriteService emits one event for this subscription and enqueues the pay-in-advance invoice job itself (write_service.rb:27-38). `already_paid_units` = 10 → delta 15 → 15 × 100.00 = 150_000¢, `precise_unit_amount` 100.00, April boundaries. Same fee the PLAN endpoint produces in b13/standard/advance/not-prorated/increase-mid-period. The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 40 units then does nothing to this subscription — no event (emit_events_service.rb:52) and no invoice (create_all_pay_in_advance_fixed_charges_job.rb:19-25) — so the count stays at 3. Invoice 2: periodic. The last event before the readjusted MAY window is the 25-unit override → 25 × 100.00 = 250_000¢ for 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, beside an April subscription fee. The discriminating numbers. Had the plan-level update reached this subscription there would be a FOURTH invoice at delta 40 - 25 = 15 → 150_000¢, and May would read 40 × 100.00 = 400_000¢. Had the override been rejected or silently promoted to a plan-level write, invoice 1 would still be 150_000¢ (25 - 10 = 15 either way, which is why the plan-level event matters more than the override event here) but May would again be 400_000¢ — so the May figure, not the April delta, is what proves the override row exists and is still winning. `premium: true`: `forbidden_failure! unless License.premium?` (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

A pay-in-advance decrease is NOT refunded, and it still raises an invoice. That is the whole row, and the deliberately odd middle invoice is the assertion. Invoice 0 is the activation invoice, 10 units at a coefficient of 30/30 = 1 → 100_000¢ for April, as in the increase sibling. Invoice 1 is raised by the change, because the trigger in FixedCharges::UpdateService is `apply_units_immediately && pay_in_advance?` with no sign test (update_service.rb:51-53). Inside, `delta_units` = 4 - 10 = -6, so `build_zero_amount_fee` runs instead of `build_delta_fee` (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:29-35): a fee of 0¢ and 0 units carrying the April boundaries, whose stated purpose in the source is "we still generate an invoice to document the change". Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceFixedChargesService saves it unconditionally (create_pay_in_advance_fixed_charges_service.rb:30-33) and the zero-total invoice is FINALIZED rather than closed, because `finalize_zero_amount_invoice` defaults to true on the billing entity while the customer inherits it (transition_to_final_status_service.rb:31-37). All three of those — invoice exists, fee exists, status finalized — are asserted, because each is a place where a plausible implementation would produce nothing at all and the row would read `invoices: 2`. Invoice 2 is the periodic April invoice whose fixed-charge fee covers MAY (readjusted window, fixed_charge_service.rb:236-250). The last event before May is the 4-unit one, at a prorated ratio of 31/31 = 1 → 4 × 100.00 = 400.00 → 40_000¢. So the customer paid for 10 units all April, gave 6 back on the 16th, got nothing for them, and starts paying for 4 in May. Note what is NOT distinguishable here and why that is itself worth recording: this row's numbers are IDENTICAL to b13/standard/advance/not-prorated/decrease-mid-period. A decrease never reaches `build_delta_fee`, so the proration coefficient is never computed, and May is a full period either way — proration is structurally invisible on an advance decrease. The pair is kept because the axis cell is legal and the equality is the finding; b13/standard/advance/*/increase-mid-period is where the flag separates them (75_000¢ against 150_000¢). Candidates excluded: a pro-rata credit for the 6 released units would be -6 × 0.5 × 100.00 = -30_000¢, a full credit -60_000¢, and re-billing the reduced quantity for April would be 4 × 0.5 × 100.00 = 20_000¢. All three would show on invoice 1 instead of 0¢.

THREE invoices, from three different code paths, and the row exists to say that a mid-period increase on a pay-in-advance fixed charge is billed as an incremental DELTA rather than re-billed in full. Invoice 0 is the activation invoice: the plan pays in arrears but a fixed charge pays in advance, so Subscriptions::ActivateService enqueues Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob at `started_at + 1.second` (activate_service.rb:195-199). Its boundaries come from `fixed_charge_pay_in_advance_interval(2024-04-01T00:00:01)` = 2024-04-01..2024-04-30, duration 30, and because the subscription starts ON the period boundary the proration coefficient is `days / duration` = (2024-04-30 - 2024-04-01 + 1) / 30 = 30/30 = 1.0 (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:108-113). `already_paid_units` is 0, so delta = 10 and the fee is 10 × 100.00 = 1_000.00 → 100_000¢ at a `precise_unit_amount` of 100.00. Starting at the period start is what makes the prorated and not-prorated siblings AGREE on this invoice, which isolates the `prorated` axis onto the change itself. Invoice 1 is raised by the change. FixedCharges::UpdateService emits the new 25-unit event at Time.current and then enqueues Invoices::CreateAllPayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob because `apply_units_immediately && fixed_charge.pay_in_advance?` (update_service.rb:44-53). Fees::BuildPayInAdvanceFixedChargeService recomputes the SAME April window, finds the activation fee by exact string match on the stored `properties->>'fixed_charges_from_datetime'/'…to_datetime'` and sums its units (:63-86) → `already_paid_units` = 10, so `delta_units` = 25 - 10 = 15. The coefficient is now (2024-04-30 - 2024-04-16 + 1) / 30 = 15/30 = 0.5, and the charge model is applied to 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 units: 7.5 × 100.00 = 750.00 → 75_000¢. As with every advance fee, `units` stores the UN-prorated delta (:135) while `precise_unit_amount` is `amount / delta_units` = 750/15 = 50.00 — both asserted, since 75_000¢ alone cannot tell 7.5 units at 100.00 from 15 at 50.00. Its period is APRIL: the delta tops up the period already paid for, it does not open a new one. Invoice 2 is the ordinary periodic invoice for April, whose fixed-charge fee covers MAY because `readjust_boundaries` replaces the April window with `fixed_charge_pay_in_advance_interval(2024-05-01T01:00Z)` = 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, duration 31 (fixed_charge_service.rb:236-250). ProratedAggregationService finds no event inside May and falls back to the last event before it (base_service.rb:39-47), the 25-unit one, whose effective span is clamped to the period start and runs to `to_datetime + 1.day` → 31/31 = 1 → 25 × 100.00 = 2_500.00 → 250_000¢ at 100.00 per unit. April's `already_billed?` guard does not fire because it is evaluated against the readjusted MAY dates (:57-74). What this rules out, with numbers. Re-billing the full new quantity for April instead of the delta would make invoice 1 read 25 × 0.5 × 100.00 = 125_000¢. Ignoring proration on the delta is the sibling b13/standard/advance/not-prorated/increase-mid-period's 150_000¢. Prorating by days ELAPSED rather than remaining would be 16/30 → 15 × 0.5333 × 100.00 = 80_000¢. And with `apply_units_immediately: false` there would be only TWO invoices, the event landing at 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z instead — so `invoices: 3` is itself an assertion.

Two invoices, and they are produced by two DIFFERENT services — that is the first thing this row pins. Invoice 1 is raised at activation, because Subscriptions::ActivateService bills a plan that pays in arrears as soon as any fixed charge pays in advance (activate_service.rb:195-199 → Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob at `started_at + 1.second`). Its fee comes from Fees::BuildPayInAdvanceFixedChargeService, not from Fees::FixedChargeService, and it prorates by a formula of its own (build_pay_in_advance_fixed_charge_service.rb:118-126): `days = (fixed_charges_to_datetime.to_date - timestamp.to_date + 1)` = 30 - 16 + 1 = 15, over `fixed_charges_duration` = 30 → coefficient 0.5. `delta_units` is the event's 40 units minus the 0 already billed for this period (:64-84), so the charge model is applied to 40 × 0.5 = 20 units: StandardService#compute_amount = `units × amount` = 20 × 100.00 = 2_000.00 → 200_000¢. The `units` field is NOT the prorated number — :131-132 stores `units: delta_units` = 40 — while `precise_unit_amount` is `amount / delta_units` = 2_000/40 = 50.00, i.e. half the 100.00 in properties. Both are asserted, because the amount alone cannot tell 20 units at 100.00 from 40 units at 50.00, and the fields disagree about which happened. Invoice 2 is the ordinary periodic invoice for the April period, and its fixed-charge fee covers MAY. Fees::FixedChargeService#readjust_boundaries (fixed_charge_service.rb:238-252) throws away the invoice_subscription's April `fixed_charges_*` boundaries and replaces them with `fixed_charge_pay_in_advance_interval(boundaries.timestamp, subscription)`, evaluated with `current_usage: true` (dates_service.rb:40-52), so at a timestamp of 2024-05-01T01:00Z it returns 2024-05-01 → 2024-05-31, duration 31. ProratedAggregationService then finds no event inside May and falls back to the last event before it (base_service.rb:41-49), whose effective span runs from the period start to `to_datetime + 1.day` → ratio 31/31 = 1 → 40 units × 100.00 = 4_000.00 → 400_000¢, at a `precise_unit_amount` of 100.00. So one invoice carries a subscription fee for 2024-04-16..2024-04-30 and a fixed-charge fee for 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, which is exactly the separate-boundary computation this block exists to pin. Candidate behaviours that this row rules out. If the advance fee ignored proration it would be 400_000¢ on invoice 1 instead of 200_000¢. If it prorated by days ELAPSED rather than remaining it would use 16/30 → 40 × 0.5333 × 100 = 213_333¢. If the periodic invoice's fixed-charge fee took the invoice's own April boundaries instead of readjusting, it would either be suppressed by `already_billed?` (fixed_charge_service.rb:53-72 matches on the stored from/to pair, and April is already billed) or land on 200_000¢ with April dates — so the 400_000¢ May fee is the assertion that the readjustment happened.

The override cell where the override has to survive TWICE — once against the plan-level event stream and once against the plan-level INVOICE trigger, which are two separate filters in two separate files. Invoices 0 and 1 are the activation invoice (10 units, coefficient 30/30 = 1 → 100_000¢) and the override invoice. For the second, Subscriptions::FixedChargeUnitsOverrides::WriteService writes the 25-unit override row, emits one event for this subscription, and — because `apply_units_immediately && fixed_charge.pay_in_advance? && subscription.active?` — enqueues Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob itself (write_service.rb:27-38). The delta is 25 - 10 = 15 against the April fee already on the books, at a coefficient of 15/30, so 15 × 0.5 × 100.00 = 750.00 → 75_000¢ with `units` 15 and `precise_unit_amount` 50.00: byte for byte the same fee b13/standard/advance/prorated/increase-mid-period gets from the PLAN endpoint. That equality is deliberate — the override is a units change like any other for the subscription it names. The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 40 units is where the row earns its keep. It succeeds, and the plan is genuinely at 40 afterwards, but this subscription gets neither an event nor an invoice: EmitEventsService's bulk scope excludes it (`.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for`, emit_events_service.rb:52) and Invoices::CreateAllPayInAdvanceFixedChargesJob applies the same scope before enqueuing per subscription (create_all_pay_in_advance_fixed_charges_job.rb:19-25). So `invoices: 3`, not 4. Invoice 2 is the periodic invoice; the last event before the readjusted MAY window is still the 25-unit override → 25 × 100.00 = 250_000¢ for 2024-05-01..2024-05-31, beside an APRIL subscription fee. Two counterfactuals, both reachable by a one-line change. If only the event filter existed and not the job filter, there would be a FOURTH invoice for delta 40 - 25 = 15 at (2024-04-30 - 2024-04-20 + 1)/30 = 11/30 → 15 × 0.366667 × 100.00 = 55_000¢. If neither filter existed, that fourth invoice would appear AND May would bill 40 × 100.00 = 400_000¢ instead of 250_000¢. `premium: true`: the subscription endpoint is licence-gated (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

The mirror of the increase row, and it is the direction worth asserting: last-event-wins is not a high-water mark. The same two events are in range, the 2024-04-16 one carries 4 units, and it wins on created_at, so the customer is billed 4 × 100.00 = 400.00 → 40_000¢ for a period in which they held 10 units for the first fifteen days. Lago does not bill the maximum (100_000¢), does not blend to 10 × 15/30 + 4 × 15/30 = 7 units (70_000¢), and does not floor the decrease at the period boundary. Asserted deliberately as a pair with the increase: one row alone cannot distinguish "the last event wins" from "the largest event wins", and the two directions together can.

A NOT-prorated fixed charge does not blend the two halves of the period: SimpleAggregationService returns `events_in_range.last.try(:units)` (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6), and `events_in_range` orders by created_at (base_service.rb:44-46). Two events are in April — the activation event (10 units, 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z) and the update event (25 units, 2024-04-16T00:00:00Z, stamped at Time.current because apply_units_immediately is true, emit_events_service.rb:22). The later one wins outright, so the WHOLE period bills at 25 units: 25 × 100.00 = 2_500.00 → 250_000¢, with precise_unit_amount 100.00 and units "25.0" (Fee#units is amount_result.full_units_number, fixed_charge_service.rb:100). Three other answers are all plausible and all wrong, which is what this row is for. A per-day blend would give 10 × 15/30 + 25 × 15/30 = 17.5 units → 175_000¢ (that is what the PRORATED sibling will read). Keeping the units the charge was created with would give 100_000¢ — and 100_000¢ is also exactly what `apply_units_immediately: false` produces, because the event would then be stamped at fixed_charges_period_to_datetime + 1.second = 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z, outside April's range entirely. Charging both quantities in full would give 350_000¢. FixedCharges::UpdateService does not move `charge_model` here — `plan.attached_to_subscriptions?` is true by this point (update_service.rb:31) — so the charge_model axis is fixed at creation and only units move. `properties` is resent because the endpoint replaces them: omitted, they fall back to ChargeModels::BuildDefaultPropertiesService, i.e. amount "0" (update_service.rb:36-38), and the invoice would read 0¢.

5 units at 200.00 each = 1_000.00 → 100_000¢, billed for the whole period because the charge is neither prorated nor paid in advance and the units never changed. The fee carries fee_type `fixed_charge`, distinct from `charge` and `subscription`, which is what makes it visible as a third kind of line on the invoice. The add-on carries its own amount_cents (which must be positive — 0 is rejected with amount_cents/value_is_out_of_range), but the FIXED CHARGE prices it: properties.amount is what the fee uses, so the two numbers are independent and this row would still read 100_000¢ if the add-on were priced differently.

A subscription-level units change is NOT a plan-level one, and the plan-level update on the 20th is in this row to prove it rather than as scenery. The override request carries only `units` and `apply_units_immediately`, so Subscriptions::UpdateOrOverrideFixedChargeService takes the cheap path — `units_only_change?` is true (fixed_charge_units_override_detection_concern.rb:26-31) — and writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride row of 25 units instead of cloning the plan (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:47-58). It then emits ONE FixedChargeEvent for this subscription alone, at 25 units because `units_for` reads `fixed_charge.effective_units_for(subscription)` (emit_events_service.rb:62-66, fixed_charge.rb:54-58), stamped 2024-04-16T00:00:00Z. Four days later the plan-level fixed charge is moved to 40 units. That request succeeds and the plan really does now say 40 — but FixedCharges::EmitEventsService's bulk path scopes to `.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for(fixed_charge)` (emit_events_service.rb:52), so this subscription receives NO event from it. Its last event in April is still the 25-unit override, and the invoice is 25 × 100.00 = 2_500.00 → 250_000¢. That is the discriminating number. If the override were merely a plan-level write under another URL, the 40-unit event would be the last in range and the invoice would read 400_000¢; if the override row existed but the plan update still emitted over it, likewise 400_000¢. 250_000¢ is reachable only if the per-subscription override both took effect and then survived a later plan-level change. `premium: true` because the endpoint is licence-gated outright — `return result.forbidden_failure! unless License.premium?` (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:22).

The mirror of the prorated increase, and the reason the pair exists: proration is symmetric where last-event-wins is not. Same two events, same 15/30 weights, units going DOWN: `aggregation` = 10 × 0.5 + 4 × 0.5 = 7.000000, `full_units_number` = 4. StandardService prices the aggregation: 7 × 100.00 = 700.00 → 70_000¢. The reported fields invert in a way worth pinning: `units` is 4 and `precise_unit_amount` is 700/4 = 175.00, which is 1.75× the 100.00 in properties, because the fee divides a ten-unit fortnight by a four-unit headline. This is the same units-and-unit-amount disagreement the advance rows show at half rate, in the opposite direction, and it is asserted rather than left implicit. Candidates: last-event-wins un-prorated is the b13/standard/arrears/not-prorated sibling's 4 × 100.00 = 40_000¢. A high-water mark — weighting both halves at the OPENING 10 units — would be 10 × 100.00 = 100_000¢; that Lago does not floor a decrease at the period's opening value is the substantive claim here. Applying the decrease retroactively from the start of the period would be 4 × 100.00 = 40_000¢ again. Boundaries are the un-readjusted arrears window shared with the subscription fee, and both are asserted.

This is the row the not-prorated increase above names as its counterfactual, and it is the one cell where a fixed charge actually BLENDS two quantities inside one period. ProratedAggregationService weights each event by the days it was in force (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:119-154). Two events are in April: 10 units at 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z and 25 units at 2024-04-16T00:00:00Z (stamped at Time.current because apply_units_immediately is true). For the first, `period_start` is its own timestamp's DATE (2024-04-01) and `period_end` is the LEAD timestamp's DATE (2024-04-16) → 15/30. For the second, LEAD falls back to `to_datetime + 1.day` → DATE 2024-05-01 → (2024-05-01 - 2024-04-16)/30 = 15/30. So `aggregation` = 10 × 0.5 + 25 × 0.5 = 17.500000 in Postgres numeric, while `full_units_number` is the LAST event's units, 25 (:22). There is no ProratedStandardService (ChargeModels::Factory:38-39), so the plain StandardService prices the prorated aggregation: 17.5 × 100.00 = 1_750.00 → 175_000¢. The fee reports the other number — `units` is `full_units_number` = 25 (fixed_charge_service.rb:100) and `precise_unit_amount` is `compute_amount / full_units_number` = 1_750/25 = 70.00, which is NOT the 100.00 in properties. Both are asserted, because 175_000¢ alone cannot tell 17.5 units at 100.00 from 25 units at 70.00 and the two fields disagree about which happened. Three candidate behaviours, each with its own number. Last-event-wins without proration is the sibling row's 25 × 100.00 = 250_000¢. Keeping the created units is 10 × 100.00 = 100_000¢ — which is also what `apply_units_immediately: false` would produce, since the event would then be stamped 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z and fall outside April's range. Prorating only the INCREMENT and billing the base for the whole month would be 10 + 15 × 0.5 = 17.5 units too and is deliberately not separable here; b13/graduated/arrears/prorated/increase-mid-period separates them, because there the tier is chosen by the full units and the increment story would choose a different one. Boundaries: in arrears `readjust_boundaries` returns the invoice_subscription's own window untouched (fixed_charge_service.rb:242), so the fixed-charge fee and the subscription fee both report 2024-04-01..2024-04-30 and both are asserted — the arrears control for the advance rows' disagreement.

In arrears there is no activation invoice — Subscriptions::ActivateService only bills at the start when the plan pays in advance or a fixed charge does (activate_service.rb:190-199) — so the whole period is measured after the fact on one invoice, and `readjust_boundaries` leaves the invoice_subscription's own `fixed_charges_*` window alone (fixed_charge_service.rb:243). The fixed-charge fee and the subscription fee therefore share 2024-04-16..2024-04-30, and both are asserted: this is the row that says the two boundary computations AGREE when the charge is in arrears, which is what makes the advance rows' disagreement a finding rather than noise. The amount goes through FixedChargeEvents::Aggregations::ProratedAggregationService, whose SQL weights each event by `(period_end - period_start) / fixed_charges_duration` (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:130-160).
