The single event sits at 2024-04-16T00:00:01Z; `period_start` is its own timestamp (already inside the window, which itself was clamped up to `started_at` by dates_service.rb:124-143) and `period_end` is `to_datetime + 1.day` → 2024-05-01. (2024-05-01 - 2024-04-16) / 30 = 15/30 = 0.5 exactly, in Postgres numeric, so `aggregation` = 40 × 0.5 = 20.000000 while `full_units_number` stays at the event's 40 (:20-24). There is no ProratedStandardService — ChargeModels::Factory:38-39 returns the plain StandardService — and its `compute_amount` is `units × amount` where `units` is the PRORATED aggregation (base_service.rb:34): 20 × 100.00 = 2_000.00 → 200_000¢. The fee reports the other number: Fees::FixedChargeService:112 stores `units: amount_result.full_units_number` = 40, and StandardService#unit_amount divides by that same 40 → `precise_unit_amount` 50.00. So 40 units are shown and 20 unit-months are billed. Un-prorated would be 40 × 100.00 = 400_000¢ (the value the sibling b13/graduated/arrears/... rows show for their own flag flip); prorating by days elapsed instead of remaining would give 16/30 → 213_333¢; prorating the SUBSCRIPTION fee's way, off `from_datetime` rather than the event timestamp, would also give 15/30 here and is deliberately not distinguishable in this row — b13/graduated/arrears/prorated/no-change separates them, because there the event-level split into tiers has no subscription-level equivalent.

The prorated counterpart of b13/standard/arrears/not-prorated/subscription-override, and the proration is what makes the assertion sharp: a blended figure records not just WHICH units won but WHEN they started, so an event the row claims was never emitted cannot hide inside a last-event-wins answer. The 2024-04-16 request carries only `units` and `apply_units_immediately`, so Subscriptions::UpdateOrOverrideFixedChargeService takes the units-only path (fixed_charge_units_override_detection_concern.rb:26-31), writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride of 25 and emits ONE event for this subscription at 2024-04-16T00:00:00Z (write_service.rb:19-32, units from `fixed_charge.effective_units_for(subscription)`). The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 40 units really does change the plan, but EmitEventsService's bulk path scopes to `.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for(fixed_charge)` (emit_events_service.rb:52) and this subscription is excluded, so it receives NO third event. April therefore holds exactly two events, 10 at 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z and 25 at 2024-04-16, and the prorated aggregation is 10 × 15/30 + 25 × 15/30 = 17.500000 with `full_units_number` 25 → 17.5 × 100.00 = 1_750.00 → 175_000¢ at a `precise_unit_amount` of 1_750/25 = 70.00, identical to b13/standard/arrears/prorated/increase-mid-period. That the two agree is the point: the override behaves exactly like a plan-level increase FOR THIS SUBSCRIPTION and then stops tracking the plan. Had the plan-level update reached it, the blend would be three-termed and visibly different: 10 × 15/30 + 25 × 4/30 + 40 × 11/30 = 5 + 3.333333 + 14.666667 = 23.000000 → 2_300.00 → 230_000¢ at `full_units_number` 40. Had the override never taken effect at all, the plan's own stream would give 10 × 19/30 + 40 × 11/30 = 6.333333 + 14.666667 = 21.000000 → 210_000¢. Neither is 175_000¢, so this number is reachable only if the override both applied and then survived. `premium: true` because the endpoint is licence-gated outright (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

The mirror of the volume increase, and the row that shows a decrease can DROP a range: the account held 60 units for the first half of April and 10 for the second, and it is billed entirely in the first range. SimpleAggregationService takes the last event's 10 units, so `number_of_units` is 10 and `matching_range` is 0..30 (volume_service.rb:56-64): 10 × 10.00 = 100.00 plus that range's 100.00 flat = 200.00 → 20_000¢, `unit_amount` = 200.00 / 10 = 20.00. The upper range's 200.00 flat is not charged at all. That is the whole span of the volume decrease: 20_000¢, against 56_000¢ (60 × 6.00 + 200.00) had a high-water mark been used, and against 45_000¢ for the prorated sibling — a factor of nearly three between the cheapest and dearest defensible reading of the same April. Read with b13/volume/arrears/not-prorated/increase-mid-period, the pair pins last-event-wins: 10 → 50 bills 50_000¢ and 60 → 10 bills 20_000¢, so it is neither the maximum, nor the opening value, nor any blend. Boundaries: the un-readjusted arrears window, shared with the subscription fee; both asserted.

Volume is the charge model where a units change can move EVERY unit's price, not just the marginal ones, and this row measures that on an increase that crosses the range boundary. SimpleAggregationService returns the last April event's units (simple_aggregation_service.rb:6-9), so both `aggregation` and `full_units_number` are 50 and VolumeService's `number_of_units` is 50 either way (volume_service.rb:62-64, the `prorated?` branch being irrelevant here). `matching_range` is therefore the second range, 31..∞ (:56-60), and every unit is priced at ITS rate rather than tier by tier: 50 × 6.00 = 300.00, plus that range's 200.00 flat = 500.00 → 50_000¢, `unit_amount` = 500.00 / 50 = 10.00. The pre-change quantity would have billed in the FIRST range: 10 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 200.00 → 20_000¢, which is also what `apply_units_immediately: false` produces (the event landing at 2024-05-01T00:00:00Z, outside April's range). Graduated arithmetic on the same shape of ranges would keep the first thirty units at 10.00: 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 + 20 × 6.00 + 200.00 = 720.00 → 72_000¢, so the 50_000¢ here is the charge_model axis doing its job — volume RE-PRICES rather than stacks. A blend, which the prorated sibling performs, gives 10 × 0.5 + 50 × 0.5 = 30 unit-months and a different answer again (38_000¢ there, for reasons the sibling's math sets out). Note the direction of the effect: crossing into a range whose per-unit price is LOWER still raises the bill, because the flat amount doubles from 100.00 to 200.00. That is why these ranges were chosen with a cheaper upper rate. Boundaries: arrears, so `readjust_boundaries` leaves the invoice's own window alone (fixed_charge_service.rb:242) and the fixed-charge fee shares 2024-04-01..2024-04-30 with the subscription fee. Both asserted.

The control for b13/volume/arrears/prorated/no-change. SimpleAggregationService gives `aggregation` = `full_units_number` = 40, so VolumeService's `number_of_units` is 40 either way (volume_service.rb:63-65) and the second range applies: every unit is priced at that range's rate rather than tier by tier, which is what separates `volume` from `graduated` — 40 × 6.00 = 240.00, plus the 200.00 flat = 440.00 → 44_000¢, `unit_amount` = 440.00 / 40 = 11.00. Graduated arithmetic on the same shape of ranges would bill the first 30 units at the first range's rate, so the b13/graduated rows sit at 50_000¢ where volume sits at 44_000¢ despite both reaching the same tier with the same 40 units — that difference is the charge_model axis doing its job. Against the prorated sibling: 44_000¢ against 32_000¢, a gap of 12_000¢ that is exactly half the 240.00 of per-unit charge and none of the 200.00 flat. And as in every not-prorated row here, 15 days of service cost a full month, on a fee that reports 2024-04-16..2024-04-30 as its period.

The volume override, set up so the plan's later value (25 units) sits in the FIRST range while the override's (50) sits in the second — a leak would therefore change the flat amount and the per-unit rate together, not just the quantity. The 2024-04-16 request is units-only, so Subscriptions::UpdateOrOverrideFixedChargeService writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride of 50 and emits one event for this subscription (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:41-58 → write_service.rb:19-32). The 2024-04-20 plan-level move to 25 units succeeds against the plan and skips this subscription, because EmitEventsService's bulk scope is `.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for(fixed_charge)` (emit_events_service.rb:52). The last April event is therefore the 50-unit override. SimpleAggregationService returns 50, `number_of_units` is 50, `matching_range` is 31..∞ and every unit is priced at 6.00: 50 × 6.00 = 300.00 plus the 200.00 flat = 500.00 → 50_000¢, `unit_amount` 500.00 / 50 = 10.00. Had the plan-level update reached this subscription, 25 units would be the last event, the FIRST range would apply and the fee would be 25 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 350.00 → 35_000¢ — a lower amount at a HIGHER unit price of 14.00, which is the signature of dropping a range. Had the override never applied at all the answer would be 35_000¢ too. So 50_000¢ says the override applied and survived, and 10.00 per unit says which range it landed in. `premium: true`: licence-gated endpoint (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

The cell where volume's split of duties produces its most counter-intuitive bill: the range is chosen by the CLOSING 10 units, so the account is priced in the FIRST range, but the quantity priced is 35 unit-months — three and a half times the closing headcount, at the dearer rate. ProratedAggregationService gives 60 × 15/30 + 10 × 15/30 = 35.000000 (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:119-154) and `full_units_number` = 10 (:22). VolumeService's `number_of_units` is the FULL units when prorated (volume_service.rb:62-64), i.e. 10, so `matching_range` is 0..30 (:56-60) — the range the closing position sits in, not the one the period's volume would suggest. `per_unit_total_amount` then multiplies the prorated aggregation by THAT range's rate (:52-54): 35 × 10.00 = 350.00, and the 100.00 flat is added whole (:44-46) → 450.00 → 45_000¢. `unit_amount` divides by the full 10 → 45.00 (:30-33), four and a half times the range's own 10.00, and the fee reports `units` 10 beside it. Both are asserted: this pair of fields is the only place the discrepancy is visible. This is deliberately DEARER than the un-prorated sibling's 20_000¢ — proration here more than doubles the bill, because the units held for the first fortnight are re-priced at the closing range's higher per-unit rate instead of the 6.00 they were contracted at. Candidates, all distinct with these quantities. Actual: range by full 10, price 35 unit-months at 10.00, flat in full = 45_000¢. Choosing the range by the PRORATED 35 instead lands in the second range → 35 × 6.00 + 200.00 = 410.00 → 41_000¢. Ignoring proration is the sibling's 10 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 200.00 → 20_000¢. A high-water mark on 60 units would be 60 × 6.00 + 200.00 = 560.00 → 56_000¢. And prorating the flat amount by the period share the aggregation implies (35/10 is above 1, so the honest reading of that alternative is the un-scaled flat) is excluded by the total: 45_000¢ contains exactly 100.00 of flat and 350.00 of per-unit charge, and no other split of 450.00 matches both this row and its un-prorated sibling. Boundaries: arrears, un-readjusted, shared with the subscription fee; both asserted.

Volume prorated is the one charge model that uses the full units and the prorated units for two DIFFERENT jobs in the same computation, and a mid-period increase is what makes the two disagree. There is no ProratedVolumeService — ChargeModels::Factory:56-57 returns the ordinary VolumeService — but VolumeService is prorated-aware in exactly one place: `number_of_units`, which selects the RANGE, is `full_units_number` when the charge is prorated and the aggregation otherwise (volume_service.rb:62-64). ProratedAggregationService weights the two April events by days in force (prorated_aggregation_service.rb:119-154): 10 × 15/30 = 5 then 50 × 15/30 = 25, so `aggregation` = 30.000000, while `full_units_number` is the LAST event's units, 50 (:22). So the range is chosen by 50 → the second range, 31..∞ at 6.00/unit with a 200.00 flat — while `per_unit_total_amount` multiplies the PRORATED aggregation (:52-54): 30 × 6.00 = 180.00. `flat_unit_amount` is added whole (:44-46). Fee = 180.00 + 200.00 = 380.00 → 38_000¢, and `unit_amount` divides by the FULL 50 → 7.60 (:30-33). The reported `units` is `full_units_number` = 50 (fixed_charge_service.rb:100), so the fee says 50 units at 7.60 while 30 unit-months at 6.00 were actually priced — both asserted, because the amount alone cannot separate them. The quantities were chosen so all four candidate behaviours differ, which 40 units would not have achieved. Actual: range by 50, price 30, flat in full = 38_000¢. Prorate first and then choose the range: 30 unit-months lands in the FIRST range (30 ≤ 30) → 30 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 400.00 → 40_000¢ — dearer than the actual, despite pricing the same 30 unit-months, because the cheap upper rate is lost. Ignore proration entirely: the sibling's 50 × 6.00 + 200.00 = 500.00 → 50_000¢. Prorate the flat amount too: 180.00 + 200.00 × 0.6 = 300.00 → 30_000¢. That the flat is NOT prorated while the per-unit amount is is the substantive claim, and it is only visible because the ranges carry flat fees. Boundaries: arrears, un-readjusted, shared with the subscription fee; both asserted.

`volume` cannot pay in advance at all (FixedCharge#validate_pay_in_advance, fixed_charge.rb:79-85 rejects it), so volume has only the two arrears cells, and this is the prorated one. There is no ProratedVolumeService — ChargeModels::Factory:56-57 returns the ordinary VolumeService — but VolumeService is prorated-aware in one specific place: `number_of_units`, which selects the RANGE, is `full_units_number` when the charge is prorated and the aggregation otherwise (volume_service.rb:63-65). So the tier is chosen by 40 units → the second range (31..∞, 6.00/unit, 200.00 flat) — while `per_unit_total_amount` multiplies the PRORATED aggregation (:52-54): 20 × 6.00 = 120.00. `flat_unit_amount` is added whole (:44-46), so the fee is 120.00 + 200.00 = 320.00 → 32_000¢, and `unit_amount` divides by the full 40 → 8.00. The reported `units` is `full_units_number` = 40 (Fees::FixedChargeService:112). Four candidate behaviours, all distinct here, which is why these particular ranges were chosen. Actual: tier by 40, price 20, flat in full = 32_000¢. Prorate first and then tier: 20 units falls in the FIRST range → 20 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 300.00 → 30_000¢. Ignore proration entirely: 40 × 6.00 + 200.00 = 440.00 → 44_000¢ (the sibling row). Prorate the flat amount too: 120.00 + 100.00 = 220.00 → 22_000¢. The 32_000¢ asserted here is the only one of the four that both crosses into the dearer per-unit rate and pays the whole flat fee for half a month. Boundaries are the un-readjusted arrears window, shared with the subscription fee, and both are asserted.

The last of the 36 cells, and the one with the most inputs riding on a single filter: a stray plan-level event would move the prorated aggregation, the full units, the chosen RANGE and the flat amount, all at once. The 2024-04-16 units-only PUT writes a Subscription::FixedChargeUnitsOverride of 50 and emits one event for this subscription (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:41-58 → write_service.rb:19-32). The 2024-04-20 plan-level PUT moves the plan to 25 and skips this subscription (`.without_fixed_charge_units_override_for`, emit_events_service.rb:52). April therefore holds two events, 10 at 2024-04-01T00:00:01Z and 50 at 2024-04-16, so `aggregation` = 10 × 15/30 + 50 × 15/30 = 30.000000 and `full_units_number` = 50 — identical to b13/volume/arrears/prorated/increase-mid-period, and so is the fee: range chosen by 50 → 31..∞, 30 unit-months × 6.00 = 180.00, plus the 200.00 flat in full = 380.00 → 38_000¢, `unit_amount` 380.00 / 50 = 7.60 (volume_service.rb:30-33, 52-64). Had the plan-level event reached this subscription, all four inputs would change together: `aggregation` = 10 × 15/30 + 50 × 4/30 + 25 × 11/30 = 5 + 6.666667 + 9.166667 = 20.833334, `full_units_number` = 25, which selects the FIRST range → 20.833334 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 308.33334 → 30_833¢ at a unit amount of 12.33. Had the override never applied, the stream would be 10 then 25 → `aggregation` = 10 × 19/30 + 25 × 11/30 = 6.333333 + 9.166667 = 15.500000, full 25, first range → 15.5 × 10.00 + 100.00 = 255.00 → 25_500¢. Three distinct amounts, two distinct ranges and two distinct flat fees, so 38_000¢ with a 7.60 unit amount is reachable only if the override applied and then survived the plan change. `premium: true`: licence-gated endpoint (update_or_override_fixed_charge_service.rb:21).

Discovered while authoring B1, and the reason the whole custom_agg column of that grid has no rows: `custom_aggregator` is absent from BillableMetricsController#input_params, so a REST caller cannot create a custom_agg metric AT ALL. The row supplies a perfectly good aggregator and the API still answers custom_aggregator/value_is_mandatory, because the parameter is filtered out before it reaches the service — the request is refused for missing exactly what was sent. organization.custom_aggregation is enabled here on purpose, so the failure is the parameter gap and not the separate org feature gate (which answers 403 feature_unavailable instead).
The custom charge model requires a custom_agg metric. Note the reverse is NOT enforced — a custom_agg metric with a standard charge is legal, which is why B1 has that cell.
The dynamic charge model takes its amount from the event, which only sum_agg supports.

Not a rejection: a before_validation hook silently nils field_name for count_agg, so a POST that supplies one gets back null. Recorded as characterization — this is what Lago does today, not necessarily what it should do.
field_name is required for every aggregation except count_agg and custom_agg.
Runs under a premium licence deliberately, so the failure is the latest_agg rejection and not the licence gate — that gate has its own row below.
The only B1 cell that is legal but licence-gated. Deliberately has no `premium: true`, so the licence is absent.
Graduated ranges must be contiguous — the next from_value must be the previous to_value + 1. This row leaves a gap between 10 and 50.

The fourth site of the same pattern, and the one that changes invoice STATE rather than a flag: Customers::CreateService#assign_premium_attributes returns early without a licence, so invoice_grace_period (and timezone alongside it) are dropped with HTTP 200 and no warning. The consequence is not cosmetic — without the grace period every invoice is finalized on creation instead of staying a draft, so late-arriving usage can no longer be picked up by a refresh. Sits with the three charge-flag rows above; together they document a systemic behaviour rather than four separate quirks. The assertion reads the NESTED path deliberately: the field lives under billing_configuration in both request and response, so a row checking the top level would see nil either way and pass for the wrong reason — proving nothing about the premium gate.

A charge can only be non-invoiceable if it is paid in advance. Needs `premium: true`: Charges::CreateService only assigns invoiceable under a licence, so without one the param is dropped and the validation is never reached — see the characterization row below.

A legal request that is silently altered. Charges::CreateService only assigns invoiceable under a premium licence, so a non-premium caller asking for a non-invoiceable charge gets an invoiceable one back with HTTP 200 and no warning. Recorded as characterization, not endorsed: the caller cannot tell its intent was dropped.

The third flag behind the same licence gate, and the one whose silent loss costs money: a dropped min_amount_cents means the spending-minimum true-up fee is never created, so the customer is under-billed with no error anywhere. (accepts_target_wallet is gated in the same block; it additionally needs an organization feature flag, so it has no row here yet.)

A spending minimum produces a true-up at period end, which is incompatible with billing in advance. Needs `premium: true`: min_amount_cents sits in the same licence-gated block as invoiceable and regroup_paid_fees, so without one it is dropped to 0 and never validated.
package_size must be a positive integer — a zero-sized package would divide by zero.
Only AGGREGATION_TYPES_PAYABLE_IN_ADVANCE (count, sum, unique_count, custom) may be billed in advance; max_agg, latest_agg and weighted_sum_agg cannot.
Every volume charge is rejected in advance — there is no in-advance volume charge model.

Rejected by the charge-model properties validator rather than by Charge itself, so the error is reported on `properties` — not on `billable_metric`, which is where the validator's own add_error(field: :billable_metric) would suggest.
Needs `premium: true` — validate_per_transaction_min_max returns early without a licence, so without it the charge would be accepted and this row would pass for the wrong reason.
Deliberately `value_is_invalid` rather than `value_is_mandatory` — see the comment on Plan's interval validation. Pinning it stops a well-meaning refactor from "fixing" the code.
Paying in advance narrows prorated to `standard` only; graduated is allowed prorated only in arrears. This is the row that distinguishes the two proration tables.
Charge#validate_prorated allows prorated only for a recurring, non-weighted_sum metric. A non-recurring metric is rejected outright, so the plan create fails and no billing happens.
weighted_sum_agg already prorates by time, so prorated is rejected even for a recurring metric.
count_agg, max_agg and latest_agg cannot be recurring. This is the rule that makes several prorated cells unreachable — see the note in legality_spec.rb.
regroup_paid_fees needs BOTH pay_in_advance and invoiceable false; this row satisfies only the first. Needs `premium: true` for the same reason as the invoiceable row.

Same gate as the invoiceable row. Worth pinning separately because the consequence differs: a dropped regroup_paid_fees means paid fees are never regrouped onto an advance_charges invoice, which is a billing-output difference rather than a flag difference.
Same contiguity rule as graduated, but a distinct error code — worth pinning both.

TWO INVOICES, AND THE COUPON IS SPENT ON THE FIRST. An invoiceable pay-in-advance charge raises its own invoice the moment the event lands (Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceChargeService), and that service calls Credits::AppliedCouponsService itself at create_pay_in_advance_charge_service.rb:28 — the same reducer calculate_fees_service.rb:54 runs, on an invoice that exists a month before the period invoice. Event invoice: 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ of fees; the `once` coupon's remaining 4_000¢ is below the 10_000¢ base (applied_coupons/amount_service.rb:37) so all 4_000¢ is taken and the applied coupon is terminated (applied_coupon_service.rb:81-82) → 6_000¢ due. Period invoice: the 2_000¢ subscription fee only — the charge is not billed twice — and coupons_amount_cents 0, because there is nothing left to spend. Cash: 6_000 + 2_000 = 8_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the in-advance path did NOT run the coupon stage — exactly how it treats progressive billing, which it omits — the event invoice would be 10_000¢ and the coupon would first meet the 2_000¢ period invoice, where base_amount_cents is 2_000 and amount_service.rb:37 caps the credit at the base. The customer would pay 10_000 + 0 = 10_000¢, 2_000¢ more, and 2_000¢ of coupon would be stranded on a still-active applied_coupon. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 and 2_000 under both orders, which is why coupons_amount_cents and sub_total_excluding_taxes are asserted on BOTH invoices: asserting the period invoice alone would read 2_000¢ due with no coupon and look like a coupon that never applied.

A credit note is spent by whichever invoice reaches the credit-note stage FIRST, and a pay-in-advance charge gets there mid-period. create_pay_in_advance_charge_service.rb:41 calls Credits::CreditNoteService on the event invoice, the same reducer calculate_fees_service.rb:61 runs, and Credits::CreditNoteService#credit_notes takes every finalized, available note of the customer regardless of which invoice it came from. March period invoice: the 10_000¢ subscription fee alone — a pay-in-advance charge is excluded from the period invoice — and no events yet, so 10_000¢ with one fee. A 6_000¢ credit note is cut against it; with no tax anywhere the note's credit_amount_cents equals the 6_000¢ of fee it names. 10 April, 80 units arrive → an event invoice of 8_000¢, which consumes the whole note: compute_credit_amount (credit_note_service.rb:88-94) takes min(6_000, 8_000) = 6_000 → 2_000¢ due and the note is `consumed` with a 0¢ balance. `refresh_amounts` only does `total_amount_cents -= credit_amount_cents`, so sub_total_excluding_taxes stays the full 8_000¢. April period invoice: 10_000¢ with nothing left to credit. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: if the in-advance path skipped the credit-note stage — as it skips progressive billing — the event invoice would be 8_000¢ and the note would survive to the April period invoice, which would then be 10_000 − 6_000 = 4_000¢. The three invoices would read 10_000 / 8_000 / 4_000 instead of 10_000 / 2_000 / 10_000. Total cash is 12_000¢ under both orders — money is conserved — so WHICH invoice the note lands on is the whole observable, and asserting the last invoice alone would show 10_000¢ due and read as a credit note that was never applied at all.

The wallet is drained by the event invoice, a month before the period invoice exists. create_pay_in_advance_charge_service.rb:42 calls Credits::AppliedPrepaidCreditsService on the invoice it just raised — the same last stage calculate_fees_service.rb:62 runs — and the wallet is limited to `charge` fees, so the allocator's buckets (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:70-91, keyed on [fee_type, billable_metric_id]) offer it exactly one bucket to pay into. Event invoice: 80 units × 1.00 = 8_000¢; the charge bucket's cap is 8_000¢ and the wallet holds 50 credits at rate 1.00 = 5_000¢, so `[remaining, wallet_balance, remaining_invoice].min` (:53) is 5_000¢ → 3_000¢ due, wallet 0. Period invoice: the 2_000¢ subscription fee, and `wallets` is scoped `with_positive_balance` (:124-129), so an empty wallet is not even considered → prepaid_credit_amount_cents 0, 2_000¢ due. Cash 5_000¢ against 10_000¢ of billing. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the in-advance path omitted the prepaid stage the way it omits progressive billing, the event invoice would be 8_000¢ and the wallet would still hold 5_000¢ when the period invoice arrived — where the `charge` fee-type limit means it could not be spent either, the only fee being a subscription fee. The customer would pay 8_000 + 2_000 = 10_000¢ cash with 5_000¢ of credits permanently stranded, against 5_000¢ actually paid. prepaid_credit_amount_cents and the wallet balance are asserted because fees_amount_cents is 8_000 and 2_000 under both orders.

THE ONE PAIR THAT NEVER MEETS, and the reason is a missing call rather than an ordering. Invoices::CreatePayInAdvanceChargeService runs coupons (:28), tax (:34), credit notes (:41) and prepaid credit (:42) — every reducer calculate_fees_service.rb:53-62 runs EXCEPT Credits::ProgressiveBillingService. There is no progressive-billing stage in that file at all. The threshold invoice is cut from the arrears charge only: Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService's `charges` scope (progressive_billing_service.rb:107-113) is `.where(invoiceable: true) .where(pay_in_advance: false)`, so `b15_apb_adv` contributes no fee to it — 100 units of `b15_apb_arr` cross the 5_000¢ threshold and it bills 10_000¢, one fee. The 10 March event then raises its own invoice of 30 × 1.00 = 3_000¢ with progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents 0. It is charged in full even though the customer has already prepaid 10_000¢ of this period. The period invoice carries the 0¢ subscription fee and the arrears charge's 10_000¢. `to_credit_amount` is the threshold invoice's 10_000¢ net of nothing (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63) and the cap is the period invoice's charge fees sharing a charge_id with the threshold invoice's (progressive_billing_service.rb:26-31) = 10_000¢, so 10_000 is not greater than the cap, the whole amount is credited and sub_total falls to 0. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: had the in-advance path called ProgressiveBillingService the way calculate_fees_service.rb:53 does, the event invoice would have found to_credit_amount 10_000¢ against its own 3_000¢ of charge fees, been capped at 3_000¢ by progressive_billing_service.rb:36-42, settled at 0¢ instead of 3_000¢, and CreditNotes::CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice would have cut a 7_000¢ note on the threshold invoice. The observable difference is therefore 3_000¢ on the event invoice (progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents 0 and 3_000¢ due, versus 3_000¢ credited and 0¢ due) plus the existence of a credit note that this row expects not to exist. fees_amount_cents is 3_000 and 10_000 under both orders, so progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents is the field that separates them — and asserting only the period invoice would show a perfectly-credited 0¢ invoice and hide the 3_000¢ the event invoice collected on top of a period that was already paid for.

The in-advance invoice IS taxed, and at the CHARGE's rate rather than the plan's. create_pay_in_advance_charge_service.rb:34 calls the same Invoices::ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService that calculate_fees_service.rb:56 does, so the event invoice is not a tax-free surface. Which rate it uses is decided per FEE, not per invoice: Fees::ApplyTaxesService:68 returns `fee.charge.taxes` before it ever reaches the plan rung at :71, so the pay-in-advance charge fee is taxed at 10% and the subscription fee at the plan's 20%. Event invoice: 10_000¢ × 10% = 1_000¢ → 11_000¢. Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96 pro-rates the invoice rate over the fees carrying each tax and only the 10% tax has a fee here, so the invoice's own rate comes to 10 rather than 20 — not assertable, because invoice_expectation carries no taxes_rate, so the row pins the same fact at fee level instead. Period invoice: 2_000¢ × 20% = 400¢ → 2_400¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the in-advance invoice took the customer/entity rate instead of the rate on the fee it carries — i.e. if tax ran on the invoice sub_total rather than on the fee bases produced before it — 10_000 × 20% = 2_000¢ of tax and a 12_000¢ invoice. The customer would pay 1_000¢ more. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 either way, so taxes_amount_cents is what pins the sequence, and the per-fee taxes_rate is asserted because an invoice-level figure cannot distinguish "10% on this fee" from "a blend that happens to average 10%".

The coupon's base is the sum of every fee produced before it, and the charge fee is one of them. calculate_fees_service.rb:43 creates the charge fee, :49-50 sets sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents to the sum of ALL fees, and only then does :54 run Credits::AppliedCouponsService, whose base_amount_cents (applied_coupon_service.rb:103) is that sub_total. 2_000¢ subscription + 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ → 12_000¢ of fees. The `once` coupon's remaining 8_000¢ is below the 12_000¢ base, so amount_service.rb:37-39 grants the full 8_000¢ → sub_total 4_000¢, total 4_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the charge fee were produced after the coupon stage — the only fee then in the base being the 2_000¢ subscription fee — amount_service.rb:37 would return the base instead of the coupon amount, granting 2_000¢ and leaving 12_000 − 2_000 = 10_000¢ due. The customer would pay 6_000¢ more and 6_000¢ of coupon would go unused. fees_amount_cents is 12_000 under both orders, which is exactly why coupons_amount_cents and sub_total_excluding_taxes are the asserted fields. The coupon is a FIXED amount so that the cap is reachable: a percentage coupon would scale with whatever base it was handed and both orders would agree.

A credit note is not applied to the invoice, it is applied UP TO the invoice: credit_note_service .rb:88-94 takes min(note balance, remaining invoice amount), and how much of that remaining amount exists is decided by the producers that ran at :42-46. The charge fee is what makes the difference. March: 2_000¢ subscription + 100 units × 1.00 = 12_000¢. A 9_000¢ note is cut against its charge fee — creditable because the fee is 10_000¢ — and with no tax anywhere it is worth exactly the 9_000¢ of fee it names. May: 2_000¢ subscription + 40 units = 6_000¢ of fees. The note reaches :61 with 9_000¢ of balance against 6_000¢ of remaining invoice, so 6_000¢ is consumed → 0¢ due, and 3_000¢ of the note survives as an `available` balance. `refresh_amounts` never touches sub_total, which stays 6_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the charge fee were produced after the credit-note stage, the remaining invoice amount at :61 would be the 2_000¢ subscription fee alone, only 2_000¢ of note would be consumed, and the customer would owe 4_000¢ with 7_000¢ still on the note. 4_000¢ of cash and 4_000¢ of note balance separate the two orders. fees_amount_cents is 6_000 either way, so credit_notes_amount_cents and the note's own balance_amount_cents are the fields asserted. The balance is read back through `select` rather than from the step, because the step's payload is the note as CREATED and would still say 9_000¢.

prepaid_credit_amount_cents is a single number on the invoice, but it is not computed against a single number: Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService:70-91 buckets the fees produced at :42-46 by [fee_type, billable_metric_id] and lets each wallet pay only into the buckets it is allowed. So which producers exist decides how much of a limited wallet can move at all. Fees: 2_000¢ subscription + 100 units × 1.00 = 12_000¢ → two buckets, ["subscription", nil] worth 2_000¢ and ["charge", b15_chp_sum] worth 10_000¢ (the cap at :77-79 is sub_total_excluding_taxes + taxes − credit notes, all of which is the fee amount here). The wallet holds 120 credits at rate 1.00 = 12_000¢ but is limited to `charge` fees, so applicable_fee? (:108-122) admits one bucket and :53 takes min(10_000, 12_000, 12_000) = 10_000¢ → 2_000¢ due and 2_000¢ of credits left over. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if prepaid credit were subtracted from the invoice total as one figure rather than allocated per fee, the whole 12_000¢ of wallet would go and the invoice would settle at 0 with an empty wallet — the fee-type limitation would be unobservable and 2_000¢ of credits the customer is not entitled to spend on a subscription fee would be spent on one. fees_amount_cents and sub_total are 12_000 under both orders — prepaid credit never moves the base — so prepaid_credit_amount_cents and the leftover wallet balance are what pin it.

The progressive credit is capped at the period invoice's CHARGE fees, and the cap counts every charge the threshold invoice touched — including one it billed at zero. That is what this pair pins, and it is the difference between crediting 7_000¢ and crediting 2_000¢. Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService#create_fees (progressive_billing_service.rb:94-105) iterates every invoiceable arrears charge, so the 5 March threshold invoice carries TWO fees: `b15_cpb_a` at 100 units = 10_000¢ and `b15_cpb_b` at 0 units, whose 0¢ fee is DROPPED by should_persist_fee? because progressive_billing_service.rb:102 passes context: :finalize, not :recurring. fees_count 2 on it is the load-bearing assertion, because Credits::ProgressiveBillingService:26-31 builds its cap from `progressive_billing_invoice.fees.charge.pluck(:charge_id)` — a zero-amount fee still contributes its charge_id. `b15_cpb_a` is latest_agg, so the 20 March event of 20 makes its period fee 2_000¢, and `b15_cpb_b` sums to 5_000¢. Period fees: 0¢ subscription + 2_000 + 5_000 = 7_000¢. to_credit_amount is the threshold invoice's 10_000¢ (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-63, net of nothing here) and the cap is 7_000¢, so :36-42 credits 7_000¢ and hands the 3_000¢ it cannot use to CreditNotes::CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice. sub_total 7_000 − 7_000 = 0, total 0, and with nothing remaining at :61 the note is not consumed — 3_000¢ stays `available`. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: if the cap counted only the charges the threshold invoice actually BILLED — `b15_cpb_a` alone — it would be 2_000¢, the credit would be 2_000¢, the credit note 8_000¢, sub_total 5_000¢, and 5_000¢ of that note would be consumed at :61 leaving 3_000¢. Both worlds end at a 0¢ total and a 3_000¢ note balance, so the total proves nothing: progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents (7_000 vs 2_000) and credit_notes_amount_cents (0 vs 5_000) are the only fields that tell them apart, which is why both are asserted.

Tax is computed FROM the fees, one fee at a time, not from the invoice total — which is what makes a charge fee's own rate matter. calculate_fees_service.rb:43 produces the charge fee; :56 reaches Invoices::ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService → ComputeAmountsFromFees:16-24, which taxes each fee individually through Fees::ApplyTaxesService. That service's ladder returns `fee.charge.taxes` at :68 before it can fall to the plan rung at :71, so the charge fee is taxed at 25% and the subscription fee at the plan's 10%. 2_000 × 10% = 200¢ and 10_000 × 25% = 2_500¢ → 2_700¢ of tax on 12_000¢ of fees, total 14_700¢. The invoice rate is a pro-rata blend, not a rate anyone configured: Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96 gives (2_000/12_000) × 10 + (10_000/12_000) × 25 = 1.66667 + 20.83333 = 22.5 — derived here rather than asserted, because invoice_expectation has no taxes_rate field. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if tax ran on the invoice sub_total rather than on the fees produced before it, one rate would have to win — 12_000 × 10% = 1_200¢ or 12_000 × 25% = 3_000¢, and both are wrong by hundreds of cents. If the charge fee were not in the tax base at all, tax would be 200¢ and the invoice 12_200¢, 2_500¢ less than it is. fees_amount_cents is 12_000 in every one of those worlds. The per-fee taxes_amount_cents are asserted because the invoice blend of 22.5 cannot distinguish "10% here and 25% there" from a uniform 22.5% applied to everything.

THE FLOOR IS SET FIRST, THEN DISCOUNTED — so a coupon under a minimum commitment is worth real money to the customer, and the commitment is not actually a floor on what they pay. 2_000¢ subscription + 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ of real spend against a 10_000¢ commitment. Commitments::Minimum::CalculateTrueUpFeeService:37-41 subtracts the raw fee total from the commitment and adds the 5_000¢ difference as a `commitment` fee at calculate_fees_service.rb:46 — before Credits::AppliedCouponsService at :54. The coupon then takes 50% of the topped-up 10_000¢ = 5_000¢, so the invoice settles at 5_000¢ against a floor the customer committed to at 10_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: had the coupon run first, its base would be the 3_000¢ of real fees, it would grant 1_500¢ (amount_service.rb:26-29), and the floor would then top the invoice back up from 1_500¢ to a true-up of 8_500¢ — fees 11_500¢, coupons 1_500¢, sub_total 10_000¢. The customer would pay the full 10_000¢ commitment, exactly twice what they pay here. A PERCENTAGE coupon is deliberate: it does not commute with the true-up, because the true-up's base is the very thing the percentage is taken of. fees_amount_cents differs between the two orders here (10_000 vs 11_500) but the commitment fee's own 5_000¢ is what says which order ran, so it is asserted at fee level.

Crediting a commitment fee does not lower the floor — it defers cash, and the floor is charged again in full next period. Both periods are identical: 2_000¢ subscription + 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢, commitment 10_000¢ → a 5_000¢ `commitment` fee, 10_000¢ of fees. The March true-up is credited for 4_000¢ (the commitment fee is 5_000¢, so 4_000¢ is creditable) and with no tax the note is worth exactly 4_000¢. May reaches the credit-note stage at calculate_fees_service.rb:61 with 10_000¢ remaining, consumes the whole note → 6_000¢ due, note `consumed` at a 0¢ balance. sub_total stays 10_000¢ because `refresh_amounts` only decrements total_amount_cents. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the credit note were spent BEFORE the floor was computed, the period's fee total going into CalculateTrueUpFeeService would be 10_000 − 4_000 = 6_000¢, the true-up would grow from 5_000¢ to 9_000¢ to reach the floor again, and the invoice would settle at the full 10_000¢ — the note absorbed by the top-up and worth nothing to the customer. 6_000¢ due versus 10_000¢ due. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 in this row and 14_000 in that one, but the field that names the side of the line is credit_notes_amount_cents (4_000 rather than 0) together with the commitment fee still standing at 5_000¢ in a period where 4_000¢ of last month's floor was returned.

A wallet cannot shrink the floor, only pay it — and a wallet limited to `commitment` fees can pay nothing else, which makes the per-fee allocation visible. 2_000¢ subscription + 3_000¢ charge = 5_000¢ of real spend, commitment 10_000¢ → a 5_000¢ `commitment` fee produced at calculate_fees_service.rb:46, long before the wallet is consulted at :62. Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService:70-91 offers three buckets — ["commitment", nil] 5_000¢, ["charge", b15_cmp_sum] 3_000¢, ["subscription", nil] 2_000¢, sorted by size — and applicable_fee? (:108-122) admits only the first, so :53 takes min(5_000, 8_000, 10_000) = 5_000¢. 5_000¢ due, 3_000¢ of the 80 credits unspent. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if prepaid credit were taken off the invoice total as one figure rather than allocated bucket by bucket, all 8_000¢ of wallet would go against the 10_000¢ due, leaving 2_000¢ owed and an empty wallet. 5_000¢ versus 2_000¢ due, 3_000¢ versus 0¢ of balance. And had the wallet's credits counted toward the commitment instead of paying it, the true-up would have been computed against 5_000 + 8_000 = 13_000¢ of "spend", producing no top-up at all and an invoice of 5_000¢ of fees with 5_000¢ of wallet consumed — 0¢ due and 3_000¢ of balance, which is the same balance from a completely different arithmetic. fees_amount_cents (10_000 vs 5_000) and prepaid_credit_amount_cents (5_000 either way) each separate one of those worlds but not the other, so both are asserted alongside the wallet.

THE FLOOR COUNTS PROGRESSIVELY-BILLED USAGE, AND THE CREDIT DOES NOT COUNT THE FLOOR. Two facts, each in the other's blind spot. 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ crosses the 5_000¢ threshold on 5 March, so a progressive_billing invoice bills 10_000¢ — one charge fee, no subscription fee, because Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService#create_fees only walks plan.charges. At 1 April the floor is computed first (calculate_fees_service.rb:46). InArrears:: CalculateTrueUpFeeService#charge_fees selects by subscription and by the fee's own charges_from/to_datetime with NO invoice scoping (calculate_true_up_fee_service.rb:22-38), so it sees BOTH the threshold invoice's 10_000¢ fee and the period invoice's 10_000¢ fee: 20_000¢ of spend against a 25_000¢ commitment → a 5_000¢ commitment fee. Period fees 0 + 10_000 + 5_000 = 15_000¢. Then the credit: to_credit_amount is 10_000¢ and the cap (progressive_billing_service.rb:26-31) is the period invoice's charge fees sharing the threshold invoice's charge_id = 10_000¢ — the `commitment` fee is not a charge fee and does not enlarge it. 10_000 is not greater than 10_000, so no credit note is cut, 10_000¢ is credited, sub_total 15_000 − 10_000 = 5_000¢ and the invoice settles at 5_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the floor were computed from the period invoice's fees alone — the natural reading, and what an invoice-scoped query would give — spend would be 10_000¢, the true-up 15_000¢, fees 25_000¢ and the invoice 15_000¢ after the same 10_000¢ credit. The customer pays 5_000¢ rather than 15_000¢, a 10_000¢ difference decided entirely by whether a threshold invoice counts as spend toward the commitment. fees_amount_cents differs there (15_000 vs 25_000) but the commitment fee's own 5_000¢ is the field that names it, so the fee split is asserted. credit_notes_amount_cents 0 is asserted because a cap that DID count the commitment fee would be 15_000¢ — still above to_credit_amount, so still no note — while a cap that counted nothing would cut one; 0 pins the middle reading.

The true-up is taxed, because it is a fee like any other by the time tax runs — created at calculate_fees_service.rb:46, taxed at :56. So VAT is charged on 5_000¢ that exists only to satisfy a floor. 2_000¢ subscription + 3_000¢ charge = 5_000¢ of real spend, commitment 10_000¢ → a 5_000¢ `commitment` fee. Each fee then finds its own rung in Fees::ApplyTaxesService#applicable_taxes: the charge fee stops at :68 on its own 25%; the commitment fee tries :70 (`fee.invoiceable.taxes` — the Commitment carries none) and falls to the plan's 10% at :71; the subscription fee takes the same plan rung. 200 + 750 + 500 = 1_450¢ of tax on 10_000¢ of fees → 11_450¢. The invoice's own rate would be the pro-rata blend of Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96 — (7_000/10_000) × 10 + (3_000/10_000) × 25 = 7 + 7.5 = 14.5 — derived here rather than asserted, because invoice_expectation has no taxes_rate field. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the floor were applied after tax — to the tax-inclusive total — the real fees would be 5_000¢ carrying 950¢ of tax = 5_950¢, the top-up would be 4_050¢ and the invoice would land on 10_000¢ flat with 950¢ of tax inside it. The customer pays 11_450¢ instead of 10_000¢, and every cent of the 1_450¢ difference is tax on a top-up. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 under both orders. taxes_amount_cents and the commitment fee's own 500¢ are what separate them, and the per-fee figures are asserted because a 14.5% blend cannot show that the true-up was charged at 10% rather than at the charge's 25%.

Two reducers on opposite sides of tax, so they never compete for the same figure: the coupon lowers sub_total (calculate_fees_service.rb:54) and the credit note only lowers the total (:62). The order therefore decides how much of the credit note is SPENT, not what the invoice costs. May bills 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢. The coupon takes 2_000¢ first, leaving 1_000¢ for the credit note to absorb — so 1_000¢ of the credit note is consumed and 3_800¢ of it survives. Had the credit note gone first it would have absorbed the whole 3_000¢ and the coupon would have had nothing to reduce, spending 2_000¢ more of the customer's credit than necessary. Both orders end at a 0¢ total, so credit_notes_amount_cents (1_000 vs 3_000) is the field that separates them. The coupon is `recurring` over 3 periods on purpose: a `once` coupon is consumed by the April invoice — the one that exists only to source the credit note — and the pair would never meet. That consumption is itself asserted by b15/coupon/progressive_billing. The credit note is 4_800¢, not the 6_000¢ of fee it names, because a credited fee returns its share of the coupon too: 6_000/10_000 of 2_000¢ = 1_200¢ comes off.

A fixed-charge fee is inside the coupon's base, and it is the third producer stage rather than the second: calculate_fees_service.rb:44 creates it, :49-50 sums every fee into sub_total_excluding_taxes, and :54 hands that sum to Credits::AppliedCouponsService as base_amount_cents (applied_coupon_service.rb:103). 4 units at 25.00 = 100.00 → 10_000¢ of fixed charge plus the 2_000¢ subscription fee = 12_000¢. The `once` coupon's 8_000¢ is under that base so amount_service.rb:37-39 grants all of it → sub_total 4_000¢, total 4_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the fixed-charge fee were produced after the coupon stage, the base would be the 2_000¢ subscription fee, amount_service.rb:37 would return the base and the coupon would grant 2_000¢ — 12_000 − 2_000 = 10_000¢ due, 6_000¢ more, with 6_000¢ of coupon unusable. fees_amount_cents is 12_000 under both orders, so coupons_amount_cents and sub_total are the asserted fields, and the coupon is a FIXED amount precisely so that the cap can bind — a percentage would scale with whatever base it was given and the two orders would agree.

The per-CHARGE spending floor — Fees::CreateTrueUpService, not the plan-level commitment — is computed inside the charge stage at calculate_fees_service.rb:43, from the charge model's raw result. Fees::ChargeService#init_true_up_fee (charge_service.rb:390-403) sums the charge's own fees into used_amount_cents and create_true_up_service.rb:23,30 tops that up to the prorated minimum. All of it happens before any reducer. 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ against a 10_000¢ minimum over the full 31-day March (prorated_min_amount_cents = 10_000/31 × 31 = 10_000), so a second `charge` fee of 7_000¢ is added and the invoice carries three fees: the 0¢ subscription fee, the 3_000¢ usage fee and the 7_000¢ true-up. The 50% coupon then halves the topped-up 10_000¢ → sub_total 5_000¢, total 5_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: had the coupon applied before the floor, used_amount_cents would be 3_000 − 1_500 = 1_500¢ and the true-up would grow to 8_500¢, giving fees of 10_000¢ net of a 1_500¢ coupon — the invoice would settle at 10_000¢, twice what it settles at here, and the discount would have been swallowed by the top-up. The two charge fees share fee_type, item_code and period, which are exactly the runner's fee identity keys, so they cannot be told apart by `fees:` — fees_count 3 plus coupons_amount_cents and sub_total_excluding_taxes are what this row can assert, and they are enough: 5_000¢ of coupon on a 10_000¢ base is only possible if the true-up was in that base.

Two reductions that look interchangeable and are not: the coupon lands BEFORE tax, the wallet AFTER. Tax present is what makes them distinguishable — without it they would commute and the row would prove only that both were recorded. 10_000¢ of fees; coupon 4_000¢ → taxable base 6_000¢; tax 20% = 1_200¢, so 7_200¢ due; 30 credits at rate 1.00 = 3_000¢ of cover → 4_200¢ owed. Swap their stages — wallet before tax, coupon after — and the base becomes 10_000 − 3_000 = 7_000, tax 1_400, total 8_400 − 4_000 = 4_400¢. A 200¢ difference, entirely from which reduction the tax authority sees.

Both reduce, but they never meet on one invoice: progressive billing runs first (calculate_fees_service.rb:53) and coupons second (:54), so the mid-period threshold invoice is finalized BEFORE the period invoice exists and a `frequency: once` coupon is consumed there. Interim invoice: 10_000¢ usage − 3_000¢ coupon = 7_000¢ paid. Period invoice: fees 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ usage = 15_000¢, coupons 0 (already spent), and the credit is NOT the 10_000¢ already billed but `to_credit_amount = fees_amount_cents − coupons_amount_cents` (progressive_billed_amount.rb) = 10_000 − 3_000 = 7_000¢, i.e. the cash actually received → 8_000¢ due. The alternative orders are both observable here. Had the coupon applied to the period invoice instead, it would read coupons 3_000 / credit 10_000 / total 2_000. Had the credit ignored the coupon (crediting the full 10_000¢ billed), the period invoice would be 5_000¢. Consequence the row pins: 7_000 + 8_000 = 15_000¢ collected, the full undiscounted amount, so a one-time coupon under progressive billing nets the customer NOTHING — the discount is granted on the interim invoice and taken back by the period invoice. Asserting only the period invoice would miss it entirely, which is why both sides are named.

The subscription fee is the FIRST producer (calculate_fees_service.rb:42) and it is in the coupon's base — a coupon larger than the usage on the invoice reaches into the plan's own fee. 10_000¢ subscription + 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ → 13_000¢ of fees. The `once` coupon's remaining 12_000¢ is below that base, so amount_service.rb:37-39 grants all 12_000¢ → sub_total 1_000¢, and the applied coupon is terminated because the credit reached its remaining amount (applied_coupon_service.rb:81-82). THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the coupon's base were the usage alone — the subscription fee produced after the coupon stage — amount_service.rb:37 would cap the credit at 3_000¢ and the invoice would be 13_000 − 3_000 = 10_000¢. The customer would pay 9_000¢ more and 9_000¢ of coupon would be stranded on a still-active applied_coupon rather than terminated. fees_amount_cents is 13_000 under both orders. coupons_amount_cents (12_000 vs 3_000) and sub_total_excluding_taxes (1_000 vs 10_000) are the fields that separate them, and the coupon is a fixed amount so the cap can bind at all.

THE ORDER IS THE BEHAVIOUR. 100 units × 1.00 = 100.00 → 10_000¢ of fees, a 40.00 fixed coupon, and 20% VAT. Lago applies the coupon BEFORE tax (Credits::AppliedCouponsService runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:54, ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService at :56), so the taxable base is 10_000 − 4_000 = 6_000¢ and the tax is 20% of that = 1_200¢. Total 7_200¢. Taxing first would give 10_000 + 2_000 tax = 12_000, then the coupon → 8_000¢ — the customer pays 800¢ more for the same invoice. The row is built so the two orders differ: with a percentage coupon they would coincide, which is why this one is a FIXED amount. fees_amount_cents stays 10_000 either way, so asserting the total alone would not distinguish them — sub_total_excluding_taxes and taxes_amount_cents are what pin the sequence.

A fixed charge is creditable, and it is what gives the next invoice enough remaining amount for the note to be spent — credit_note_service.rb:88-94 takes min(note balance, remaining invoice amount), and the remaining amount is whatever the producers at :42-46 put there. Each period: a 0¢ subscription fee plus 4 units at 25.00 = 10_000¢ of fixed charge. The March fixed-charge fee is credited for 6_000¢ and, with no tax anywhere, the note is worth exactly the 6_000¢ of fee it names. May arrives at the credit-note stage (:61) with 10_000¢ remaining, consumes the whole 6_000¢ → the invoice is 4_000¢ and the note is `consumed` at a 0¢ balance. sub_total stays 10_000¢: the credit is applied after tax and `refresh_amounts` only decrements total_amount_cents. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the fixed-charge fee were produced after the credit-note stage the remaining amount at :61 would be the 0¢ subscription fee, compute_credit_amount would return 0 and nothing would be consumed — the invoice would ask for the full 10_000¢ and the note would still hold 6_000¢. 4_000¢ versus 10_000¢ due, and a `consumed` note versus an untouched one. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 under both orders, so credit_notes_amount_cents and the note's balance_amount_cents are the asserted fields — and the balance is read through `select` because the step's own payload is the note as created and would still read 6_000¢.

The per-charge floor is set inside the charge stage (charge_service.rb:390-403 → create_true_up_service.rb:23,30, at calculate_fees_service.rb:43) and a credit note is spent at :61, eighteen lines and four stages later. So a note survives the floor rather than being absorbed by it. Both periods are identical: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ against a 10_000¢ minimum prorated over the full 31 days = 10_000¢, so a 7_000¢ true-up joins the 3_000¢ usage fee and the 0¢ subscription fee — 10_000¢ of fees, three of them. The credit note is a deliberately small 2_000¢ because both charge fees answer to `fee_type: charge` and the runner resolves the item to whichever it finds first; 2_000¢ is creditable against either. May consumes the whole note against 10_000¢ remaining → 8_000¢ due, note `consumed`, and sub_total stays 10_000¢ because the credit only decrements total_amount_cents. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: had the note been spent before the floor was computed, used_amount_cents would have been 3_000 − 2_000 = 1_000¢, the true-up would have grown to 9_000¢ to reach the same 10_000¢ floor, and the invoice would have settled at 10_000¢ with the note gone. 8_000¢ versus 10_000¢ due, and the 2_000¢ difference is the whole value of the note. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 in both worlds — that is the point — so credit_notes_amount_cents and the note's balance are the asserted fields. The two charge fees are indistinguishable under the runner's identity keys, so fees_count is as far as the fee-level assertion can go.

The last two stages of the pipeline, and the only pair that competes for the SAME money: both reduce total_amount_cents through the same `refresh_amounts`, credit notes first (calculate_fees_service.rb:62) and the wallet second (:63). The May invoice bills 80 units × 1.00 = 8_000¢. The credit note goes first and takes 6_000¢, leaving 2_000¢ for the wallet, so 2_000¢ of the 5_000¢ of credits is spent and 3_000¢ stays on the wallet. Reversed, the wallet would be drained first — 5_000¢ of prepaid credit, only 3_000¢ of credit note, a 0¢ wallet and 3_000¢ of credit note still owed to the customer. Three fields separate the two orders, which is why all three are asserted: credit_notes_amount_cents (6_000 vs 3_000), prepaid_credit_amount_cents (2_000 vs 5_000) and the wallet balance (3_000 vs 0). The total is 0 either way and would prove nothing. The wallet is limited to `b15_cnp_late` so the April invoice, which exists only to be the source of the credit note, cannot spend it — otherwise there would be no credits left to compete.

Progressive billing is the one reducer that can CREATE a credit note rather than spend one, and this is the only row where it does. `latest_agg` lets billed usage fall: the threshold invoice is cut at 100 units (10_000¢), then a later event of 20 makes the period charge 2_000¢. ProgressiveBillingService caps the credit at the charges actually on the new invoice (progressive_billing_service.rb) — 10_000¢ to credit against 2_000¢ of charges — and issues the 8_000¢ difference as a credit note on the threshold invoice instead (CreditNotes::CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice). So the period invoice credits 2_000¢, not 10_000¢, and settles at 0. Without that cap the period invoice would carry a 10_000¢ credit against 2_000¢ of fees — an 8_000¢ negative balance Lago has no way to pay out — and the customer would silently keep it. The 8_000¢ credit note is asserted directly, because that is where the money went: net of it the customer is out 2_000¢, which is what the period actually cost. It is the only credit note in the row and nothing in the timeline creates one, so `select` is what makes it reachable at all — every other credit-note row asserts one the row itself asked for.

The barest form of the producer/reducer question: one producer, one reducer, and nothing else on the invoice. The subscription fee is created at calculate_fees_service.rb:42 and the credit note is spent at :61. Each period is a single 10_000¢ subscription fee. 6_000¢ of the March fee is credited; with no tax the note is worth exactly that. May reaches :61 with 10_000¢ remaining, so compute_credit_amount (credit_note_service.rb:88-94) returns the whole 6_000¢ → 4_000¢ due, note `consumed`. sub_total stays at 10_000¢, which is the fact that makes this reducer different from a coupon: `refresh_amounts` decrements total_amount_cents only, so a credit note never moves the taxable base. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the subscription fee were produced after the credit-note stage, the remaining invoice amount at :61 would be 0, compute_credit_amount would return 0, and the invoice would ask for the full 10_000¢ with the note untouched at 6_000¢. 4_000¢ versus 10_000¢ due. fees_amount_cents is 10_000 under both orders. credit_notes_amount_cents and the note's balance_amount_cents are what separate them; sub_total is asserted at 10_000¢ as the control against the coupon case, where the same 6_000¢ reduction WOULD have moved it to 4_000¢.

A credit note is spent AFTER tax: `create_credit_note_credit` runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:62, past ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService at :56, and `refresh_amounts` only does `total_amount_cents -= credit_amount_cents` — it never touches the sub_total. The April invoice bills 50 units × 1.00 = 5_000¢, so the tax base stays the full 5_000¢ and tax is 1_000¢ → 6_000¢ due, less the 4_800¢ credit note = 1_200¢. The credit note itself is 4_000¢ of fee plus its 800¢ of tax, because crediting a taxed fee returns the tax too (March invoice: 10_000¢ + 2_000¢ = 12_000¢). Had the credit applied before tax the base would be 5_000 − 4_800 = 200¢, tax 40¢ and the total 240¢ — the customer would pay 960¢ less and the tax authority would be short by the same. sub_total_excluding_taxes and taxes_amount are both asserted because they are the two fields the orders disagree on; the total differs too, but these say which side moved. Contrast b15/coupon/tax, where the reducer runs BEFORE tax and does move the base.

`fixed_charge` is a fee type a wallet can be limited to, and the limit is enforced per FEE, not against the invoice total. Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService:70-91 keys its buckets on [fee_type, billable_metric_id] — for a fixed-charge fee `fee.charge` is nil, so the key is ["fixed_charge", nil] — and :108-122 admits a bucket only when the wallet's allowed_fee_types include it. Fees: 2_000¢ subscription + 4 units at 25.00 = 10_000¢ of fixed charge → 12_000¢. Two buckets, 2_000¢ and 10_000¢. The wallet holds 120 credits at rate 1.00 = 12_000¢, enough for both, but is limited to `fixed_charge`, so :53 takes min(10_000, 12_000, 12_000) = 10_000¢ → 2_000¢ due and 2_000¢ of credits stranded. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if prepaid credit were taken off the invoice total as a single figure — which is exactly how prepaid_credit_amount_cents reads on the invoice — the whole 12_000¢ would go, the invoice would settle at 0 and the wallet would be empty. The limitation would be invisible and 2_000¢ of credits would have paid a subscription fee they are not allowed to pay. fees_amount_cents and sub_total are 12_000 either way: prepaid credit runs after tax (calculate_fees_service.rb:62) and never moves the base. prepaid_credit_amount_cents and the residual wallet balance are the fields that separate the two.

A fixed charge is invisible to progressive billing on both sides of the transaction, and that is the pair. On the threshold invoice: Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService#create_fees (progressive_billing_service.rb:94-105) walks `subscription.plan.charges` only, so no fixed-charge fee is ever cut mid-period. 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ crosses the 5_000¢ threshold and the invoice is one charge fee of 10_000¢ — fees_count 1 is the assertion that says so. On the period invoice: the credit is capped at charge fees, and Credits::ProgressiveBillingService:26-31 scopes that sum with `.fees.charge`, so the 10_000¢ fixed-charge fee does not enlarge it. `latest_agg` makes the period's usage fee 2_000¢, fees are 0 + 2_000 + 10_000 = 12_000¢, to_credit_amount is 10_000¢ and the cap is 2_000¢. :36-42 credits 2_000¢ and hands the other 8_000¢ to CreditNotes::CreateFromProgressiveBillingInvoice, which cuts an 8_000¢ note on the threshold invoice. sub_total 12_000 − 2_000 = 10_000¢, and at :61 the note is consumed in full → 2_000¢ due. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: if the cap counted the fixed-charge fee too, it would be 12_000¢, the full 10_000¢ would be credited, no credit note would exist, sub_total would be 2_000¢ and the invoice 2_000¢. The total is 2_000¢ in both worlds — money is conserved — so progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents (2_000 vs 10_000) and credit_notes_amount_cents (8_000 vs 0) are the only fields that distinguish them, and both are asserted. The consequence worth naming: 8_000¢ of what the customer already paid comes back as a credit note rather than as a credit on the invoice, and if the period invoice had been smaller than 8_000¢ the remainder would have sat on their account instead of being netted off.

A fixed charge has its own rung on the tax ladder, one below a metered charge's: Fees::ApplyTaxesService:69 returns `fee.fixed_charge.taxes` — note that :67's add_on rung does not fire, because the fee's type is `fixed_charge` and not `add_on`, so the tax on the underlying add-on is irrelevant. The fixed-charge fee is produced at calculate_fees_service.rb:44 and taxed at :56. 2_000¢ subscription at the plan's 10% = 200¢; 4 units at 25.00 = 10_000¢ of fixed charge at its own 25% = 2_500¢. 2_700¢ of tax on 12_000¢ → 14_700¢. The invoice's own rate would be (2_000/12_000) × 10 + (10_000/12_000) × 25 = 22.5 (Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96), derived here rather than asserted, because invoice_expectation has no taxes_rate field. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if tax were applied to the invoice sub_total rather than to the fees produced before it, a single rate would have to win — 12_000 × 10% = 1_200¢ or 12_000 × 25% = 3_000¢. And if the fixed-charge fee were outside the tax base altogether, tax would be 200¢ and the invoice 12_200¢, 2_500¢ short. fees_amount_cents is 12_000 in all of those. The per-fee taxes_amount_cents are asserted because the 22.5% blend is indistinguishable from a uniform 22.5% rate at invoice level.

A per-charge true-up is a DUPLICATE of the charge fee — create_true_up_service.rb:36 is `fee.dup` — so it keeps the charge, and therefore the billable metric, of the fee it tops up. A wallet limited to that metric can spend against it. 2_000¢ subscription + 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ against a 10_000¢ minimum prorated over the whole 31-day March = 10_000¢, so a 7_000¢ true-up joins them: 12_000¢ of fees, three of them. Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService:82 keys each bucket on [fee.fee_type, fee.charge&.billable_metric_id], and both charge fees produce the same key — so the ["charge", b15_mtp_sum] bucket is worth 3_000 + 7_000 = 10_000¢, not 3_000¢. The metric-limited wallet matches that bucket at :117 and :53 takes min(10_000, 9_000, 12_000) = 9_000¢ → 3_000¢ due and an empty wallet. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the true-up were not bucketed with its parent — a separate fee type, or a fee without the charge association — the metric-limited wallet would see a 3_000¢ bucket, spend 3_000¢, and leave 9_000¢ due with 6_000¢ of credits it could never use. 3_000¢ versus 9_000¢ due, and a wallet at 0 versus one at 6_000¢. fees_amount_cents and sub_total are 12_000 either way — prepaid credit runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:62, after tax, and never moves the base — so prepaid_credit_amount_cents and the wallet balance are the fields asserted. The two charge fees share the runner's fee identity keys, so fees_count 3 is as far as `fees:` can go.

The mirror of b15/fixed_charge/progressive_billing: a true-up fee IS a charge fee, so it ENLARGES the credit cap that a fixed charge could not touch. Same mechanism, opposite answer, and that contrast is the reason both rows exist. The threshold invoice bills 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢, one fee and no true-up: used_amount_cents 10_000 is already above the prorated minimum (create_true_up_service.rb:23), whatever boundary the mid-period invoice is cut on. The period invoice: `latest_agg` drops the usage fee to 20 × 1.00 = 2_000¢, and prorated_min_amount_cents over the full 31-day March is 6_000/31 × 31 = 6_000¢, so a 4_000¢ true-up is added. Both are `charge` fees on the same charge, so Credits::ProgressiveBillingService:26-31 — `invoice.fees.charge.where(charge_id: ...)` — caps the credit at 2_000 + 4_000 = 6_000¢, not 2_000¢. to_credit_amount is 10_000¢, above that cap, so :36-42 credits 6_000¢ and issues the remaining 4_000¢ as a credit note on the threshold invoice. sub_total 6_000 − 6_000 = 0, total 0, and with nothing remaining at :61 the note is not consumed — it stays `available` at 4_000¢. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: if the true-up were outside the cap the cap would be 2_000¢, the credit 2_000¢, the credit note 8_000¢, sub_total 4_000¢, and 4_000¢ of that note would be consumed at :61 — ending on the same 0¢ total and the same 4_000¢ of residual note balance. Only progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents (6_000 vs 2_000) and credit_notes_amount_cents (0 vs 4_000) tell the two apart, which is why both are asserted on the period invoice and the note is asserted as untouched.

A per-charge floor is taxed at the CHARGE's rate, because the true-up fee is a duplicate of the charge fee (create_true_up_service.rb:36) and therefore stops at the same rung — Fees::ApplyTaxesService:68, `fee.charge.taxes`. Both are produced inside the charge stage at calculate_fees_service.rb:43 and taxed at :56. 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ against a 10_000¢ minimum prorated over the whole 31-day March = 10_000¢, so the true-up is 7_000¢ and the invoice carries three fees: 2_000¢ subscription at the plan's 5%, 3_000¢ usage at 25% and 7_000¢ of true-up at 25%. 100 + 750 + 1_750 = 2_600¢ of tax on 12_000¢ of fees → 14_600¢. (The invoice's own blended rate would be (10_000/12_000) × 25 + (2_000/12_000) × 5 = 21.66667 by Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96, but invoice_expectation carries no taxes_rate field, so it cannot be asserted.) THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if the floor were applied after tax, to the tax-inclusive total, real spend would be 5_000¢ carrying 850¢ of tax = 5_850¢, the top-up would be 4_150¢ and the invoice would land on 10_000¢ flat with 850¢ of tax inside it. 14_600¢ versus 10_000¢ — the customer pays 4_600¢ more, of which 1_750¢ is VAT on a top-up that only exists to reach a minimum. fees_amount_cents is 12_000 either way, so taxes_amount_cents is the field that pins the sequence: 2_600¢ is only reachable if 10_000¢ of the 12_000¢ sat at 25%, i.e. if the true-up inherited the charge's tax. The two charge fees share the runner's fee identity keys and cannot be told apart by `fees:`, so fees_count 3 is as far as the fee-level assertion goes.

The asymmetry that makes b15/coupon/progressive_billing a finding rather than a curiosity. `to_credit_amount` (progressive_billed_amount.rb) subtracts coupons, progressive credits and credit notes from the threshold invoice's fees — but NOT prepaid credit. So the wallet's contribution stays credited: the threshold invoice bills 10_000¢, the wallet covers 5_000¢ of it and the customer pays 5_000¢ cash; the period invoice then credits the full 10_000¢ of fees and settles at 0. Total cash 5_000¢ against 10_000¢ of usage with 5_000¢ of credits — correct. Had prepaid credit been subtracted the way coupons are, the credit would be 5_000¢, the period invoice would ask for another 5_000¢, and the customer would pay 10_000¢ cash with the wallet drained on top. That is exactly what happens to a coupon, and this row is the control proving the two stages are treated differently rather than the coupon case being a one-off. The wallet ends at 0: it was spent on the threshold invoice and the period invoice, being already at 0 due, never reaches the prepaid stage.

The inverse of b15/charge/prepaid_credit, and the pair that shows the wallet limit is read against fees rather than against the invoice: a wallet restricted to `subscription` fees can pay the plan and not the usage. 10_000¢ subscription + 50 units × 1.00 = 5_000¢ → 15_000¢ of fees and two buckets in Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService:70-91, ["subscription", nil] worth 10_000¢ and ["charge", b15_psf_sum] worth 5_000¢. The wallet holds 120 credits at rate 1.00 = 12_000¢ — more than the subscription fee — but applicable_fee? (:108-122) admits only the subscription bucket, so :53 takes min(10_000, 12_000, 15_000) = 10_000¢. 5_000¢ due, 2_000¢ of credits left. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if prepaid credit were subtracted from the invoice total as one figure, all 12_000¢ would go and the invoice would be 3_000¢ with an empty wallet — 2_000¢ of credits earmarked for subscription fees would have paid for metered usage. fees_amount_cents and sub_total are 15_000 either way, because prepaid credit is the last stage (calculate_fees_service.rb:62) and moves only total_amount_cents. prepaid_credit_amount_cents (10_000 vs 12_000) and the wallet balance (2_000 vs 0) are the fields that separate the orders.

Prepaid credit applies AFTER tax, so it never moves the tax base. Credits::AppliedPrepaidCreditsService touches only invoice.prepaid_credit_amount_cents; it does not decrement sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents. 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ of fees, taxed at 20% on the FULL 10_000 = 2_000¢, giving 12_000¢ due. 50 granted credits at rate 1.00 = 5_000¢ of cover leaves 7_000¢ owed. Applying the credit first would tax 10_000 − 5_000 = 5_000 → 1_000¢ of tax and a 6_000¢ total, so the customer would pay 1_000¢ less and the tax authority would be short. The row asserts sub_total_excluding_taxes = 10_000 precisely because that is the field the two orders disagree on; the total alone would too, but the sub_total says WHY. Pair this with b15/progressive_billing/tax, which is the same shape with a credit that DOES move the base.

A subscription fee is on neither side of the progressive-billing transaction — not billed by the threshold invoice, not creditable by the period invoice — and this row asserts both halves. The threshold invoice: Invoices::ProgressiveBillingService#create_fees walks plan.charges only, so the 20_000¢ subscription fee is absent and the invoice is a single 10_000¢ charge fee. fees_count 1 is that assertion. The period invoice: `latest_agg` drops the usage fee to 2_000¢, so fees are 20_000 + 2_000 = 22_000¢. to_credit_amount is the threshold invoice's 10_000¢, but the cap at Credits::ProgressiveBillingService:26-31 is `.fees.charge` — 2_000¢ — so only 2_000¢ can be credited and the other 8_000¢ leaves as a credit note on the threshold invoice. sub_total 22_000 − 2_000 = 20_000¢, and at :61 that note is consumed in full → 12_000¢ due. THE OTHER ORDER, with its numbers: if the cap had counted the subscription fee, it would be 22_000¢, the whole 10_000¢ would be credited on the invoice, no credit note would exist and sub_total would be 12_000¢ — the same 12_000¢ due. That coincidence is the reason this row asserts progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents (2_000 vs 10_000) and credit_notes_amount_cents (8_000 vs 0): the total cannot see the difference, and neither can fees_amount_cents at 22_000. Why it matters anyway: a credit note is only netted off if the period invoice is big enough to absorb it. Here 20_000¢ of subscription fee absorbs all 8_000¢; on a smaller invoice the customer would be left holding an available balance instead of a reduced bill.

The mirror of b15/prepaid_credit/tax: this credit DOES move the tax base. Credits::ProgressiveBillingService:56 does `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents -= credit.amount_cents`, and it runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:53 — before ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService at :56. The period's fees are 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ usage = 15_000¢. 100 units of usage crossed the 5_000¢ threshold, so a progressive_billing invoice already collected the accrued 10_000¢ and the final invoice credits it back: sub_total = 15_000 − 10_000 = 5_000¢, taxed at 20% = 1_000¢, total 6_000¢. Crediting after tax would tax the whole 15_000 → 3_000¢, giving 18_000 − 10_000 = 8_000¢ — 2_000¢ more. Two credits, one before tax and one after, with opposite effects on the base: that difference is invisible in either row alone.

The subscription fee is the first producer (calculate_fees_service.rb:42) and it is taxed at the PLAN's rate, not at the charge's and not at any invoice-wide rate. Fees::ApplyTaxesService reaches the plan rung at :71 for a subscription fee — there is no subscription-level rung above it — while the charge fee stops earlier at :68 on its own tax. 10_000¢ at 10% = 1_000¢ and 50 units × 1.00 = 5_000¢ at 25% = 1_250¢ → 2_250¢ of tax on 15_000¢ of fees, total 17_250¢. The invoice's own rate would be the pro-rata blend of Invoices::ApplyTaxesService:87-96 — (10_000/15_000) × 10 + (5_000/15_000) × 25 = 6.66667 + 8.33333 = 15 — a figure no configuration contains; invoice_expectation has no taxes_rate field, so the row pins the two real rates at fee level instead, which is the stronger assertion anyway. THE OTHER ORDER, with its number: if tax were computed on the invoice sub_total instead of on the fees, one rate would apply to everything — 15_000 × 10% = 1_500¢ or 15_000 × 25% = 3_750¢, out by 750¢ and 1_500¢ respectively. If the subscription fee were not in the tax base at all, tax would be 1_250¢ and the invoice 16_250¢. A uniform 15% on 15_000¢ would also give 2_250¢, which is exactly why taxes_amount_cents alone is not enough here and the per-fee taxes_rate values of 10 and 25 are asserted: they are what say the invoice was taxed fee by fee rather than at a rate that happens to average out.

This is the one charge model with a dedicated prorated implementation (ChargeModels::Factory:40-45 → ProratedGraduatedService), and it uses the two numbers for two different jobs: the FULL per-event units decide which tier an event lands in, the PRORATED per-event units are what that tier prices (prorated_graduated_service.rb:11-94, and the comment at :30-33 says exactly this). The two arrays come from ProratedAggregations::SumService#per_event_aggregation (sum_service.rb:116-137): full = [31, 62] from the base aggregator, prorated = `prorated_events_values` = [31 × 21/31, 62 × 10/31] = [21, 20] (postgres_store.rb:96-100), both ordered by timestamp. Walking the loop: event 1 fills tier 1 exactly (full_sum 31 = to_value 31), so the overflow at :84 is 31 - 31 = 0 and its 21 prorated units are priced at tier 1: 21 × 1.00 = 21.00. `range` then advances to tier 2 because full_sum equals tier 1's to_value and another event follows (:135), and event 2's 20 prorated units are priced at tier 2 by the trailing line :91: 20 × 2.00 = 40.00. Both flat amounts are 0, so result_with_flat_amount (:112-123) adds nothing. Total 61.00 → 6_100¢, reported against `units: 93` (charge_service.rb:302-307). The tier boundary is set at 31 on purpose: it falls exactly on an event boundary, so no event is split across tiers and the overflow arithmetic at :84-85 — which rescales a partially-overflowing event's prorated units by prorated/full — contributes 0 rather than a repeating fraction. Three wrong implementations give three different numbers, which is why this row asserts 6_100¢ and not just "less than the un-prorated amount": graduating the FULL 93 units gives 31 × 1.00 + 62 × 2.00 = 155.00 → 15_500¢; graduating the prorated TOTAL of 41 units gives 31 × 1.00 + 10 × 2.00 = 51.00 → 5_100¢; pricing all 41 prorated units at the top tier reached gives 82.00 → 8_200¢. Only tier-by-full / price-by-prorated gives 61.00.

Same machinery as b16/graduated/sum_agg/false, fed by the unique-count breakdown instead: ProratedAggregations::UniqueCountService#per_event_aggregation (unique_count_service.rb:104-124) returns full = [1, 1, 1] — one per relevant `add`, -1 for a relevant `remove` — and prorated = the per-seat day fractions from prorated_unique_count_breakdown, each ceiled to 5 decimals: seat_1 21/31 → 0.67742, seat_2 and seat_3 10/31 → 0.32259, ordered by timestamp then property. ProratedGraduatedService then tiers by the FULL count and prices by the PRORATED one (prorated_graduated_service.rb:11-94). Tier 1 holds one seat, so seat_1's 0.67742 is priced at 31.00 → 21.00002; seat_2 and seat_3 fall in tier 2, and the trailing line :91 prices their 0.32259 + 0.32259 = 0.64518 at 62.00 → 40.00116. Total 61.00118, rounded to the currency's two decimals (charge_service.rb:296-300) → 61.00 → 6_100¢, against `units: 3`.
