The tier boundary at 1 seat is what makes the row informative: the first seat is priced at the cheap tier even though it is the one present LONGEST, because the tier follows arrival order and not duration. Tiering the prorated total (41/31 ≈ 1.32259) instead would put 1 seat in tier 1 and 0.32259 in tier 2 → 31.00 + 20.00 = 51.00 → 5_100¢. Ignoring proration → 1 × 31.00 + 2 × 62.00 = 155.00 → 15_500¢. Neither is 6_100¢.

ProratedAggregations::SumService#compute_event_aggregation (sum_service.rb:164-167) is the persisted prorated sum plus the current one, and the current one is SQL: `SUM(value * ((DATE(to_datetime) - DATE(events.timestamp) + 1) / charges_duration))` (postgres_store.rb:301-315, ratio built by duration_ratio_sql:532-537). March is 31 days, so the 11th weighs (31 - 11 + 1)/31 = 21/31 and the 22nd weighs 10/31: 31 × 21/31 + 62 × 10/31 = 21 + 20 = 41 prorated units. Nothing is persisted from an earlier period, so persisted_prorated_result contributes 0. There is no ProratedStandardService — ChargeModels::Factory:38-39 returns the plain StandardService, whose compute_amount is `units × amount` (standard_service.rb:7-9) where `units` is the aggregation, i.e. the PRORATED 41 (base_service.rb:34). 41 × 1.00 = 41.00 → 4_100¢. The fee's `units` field is the OTHER number: for a prorated charge Fees::ChargeService:302-307 reports `full_units_number`, the un-prorated aggregation (sum_service.rb:25) = 31 + 62 = 93. So 93 units are reported and 41 unit-months are billed, and that mismatch is what the row pins — asserting the amount alone could not tell 41 prorated units from a discount on 93. An implementation that ignored `prorated` would bill 93 × 1.00 = 9_300¢; one that prorated by days ELAPSED instead of days remaining would use 11/31 and 22/31 → 31 × 11/31 + 62 × 22/31 = 11 + 44 = 55 → 5_500¢. Neither is 4_100¢.

An invoiceable pay-in-advance charge bills on each event (Events::PayInAdvanceService:30-32), and a prorated one bills only the part of the period the units will be present for. Per event the amount is a CUMULATIVE DELTA, `amount_from_aggregation - amount_excluding_event` (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:20-24), and the event's own contribution is prorated by `date_diff_with_timezone(event.timestamp, to_datetime) / period_duration` (prorated_aggregations/base_service.rb:16-24). date_diff ceils, so the 11th gives 21 days and the 22nd gives 10, of 31 — the same day counts the arrears SQL produces. 11 March: cumulative prorated = 31 × 21/31 = 21, less nothing → 21.00 → 2_100¢. 22 March: cumulative prorated = 21 + 62 × 10/31 = 41, less the 21 already billed → 20.00 → 2_000¢. The two March fees sum to 4_100¢, exactly what b16/standard/sum_agg/false bills for the same period in arrears — the same 41 prorated unit-months, collected event by event instead of once at the end. Each fee reports its own event's raw value as `units` (31, then 62), because for a prorated charge compute_units returns `full_units_number` (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:118-119), which prorated_aggregations/base_service.rb:13 sets to the UN-prorated per-event aggregation. The third invoice is the 1 April renewal. A pay-in-advance charge on a RECURRING metric is not excluded from the billing invoice (calculate_fees_service.rb:131-132 excludes only pay_in_advance + non-recurring), and on the billing date proration is deliberately skipped — `bill_full_amount?` is true when there is no event (sum_service.rb:143-145) — so the 93 persisted units are billed for a whole period: 93 × 1.00 = 9_300¢. Note the fee is LABELLED with the upcoming period even though it aggregated the previous one's boundaries (Fee#date_boundaries, fee.rb:318-327). If proration were applied on the billing date too this would be 4_100¢; if the per-event fees were not prorated they would be 3_100¢ and 6_200¢ instead of 2_100¢ and 2_000¢.

Prorated unique_count weights each distinct property by the days it was present, from its `add` to the next event on the same property or to the end of the period — UniqueCountQuery's period_ratio_sql (unique_count_query.rb:302-329) is `(DATE(LEAD(timestamp, default to_datetime) + 1 day) - DATE(timestamp)) / charges_duration`. No seat is ever removed, so each LEAD falls back to 31 March and every seat runs to the end of the month: seat_1 from the 11th → (1 Apr - 11 Mar) = 21 days, seat_2 and seat_3 from the 22nd → 10 days each. Aggregation = (21 + 10 + 10)/31 = 41/31, ceiled to 5 decimals by unique_count_service.rb:22 → 1.32259. StandardService prices the aggregation (there is no prorated standard service — charge_models/factory.rb:38-39): 1.32259 × 31.00 = 41.00029, rounded to the currency's two decimals by Fees::ChargeService:296-300 → 41.00 → 4_100¢. The ceil is why the raw product is not exactly 41; the currency rounding is what makes the expected integer safe. The fee reports `units: 3` — the un-prorated count (unique_count_service.rb:23 sets full_units_number, charge_service.rb:302-307 prefers it for a prorated charge). Three seats reported, 41/31 of a seat-month billed. Un-prorated this would be 3 × 31.00 = 9_300¢. Counting only seats present at period end would also give 9_300¢. Prorating by days elapsed rather than days remaining would give (11 + 22 + 22)/31 × 31.00 = 55.00 → 5_500¢.

The seats case: each seat is charged, when it appears, for the rest of the period only. Per event the fee is the cumulative delta (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:20-24) over the prorated aggregation, and the event's own share is `1 × date_diff(event.timestamp, to_datetime) / 31`, ceiled to 5 decimals (prorated_aggregations/base_service.rb:16-24). seat_1 on the 11th: cumulative = 21/31 → 0.67742; delta = 0.67742 × 31.00 = 21.00002 → rounded to 21.00 → 2_100¢. seat_2 on the 22nd: cumulative = (21 + 10)/31 = 1.0; already billed = (1.0 - 0.32259) × 31.00 = 20.99971; delta = 10.00029 → 1_000¢. seat_3, same day: cumulative = 41/31 → 1.32259 → 41.00029; already billed = 1.0 × 31.00 = 31.00; delta = 10.00029 → 1_000¢. A seat added on the 22nd of a 31-day month costs 10/31 of 31.00, i.e. 10.00 — which is why the per-unit price here is 31.00 rather than a round number. The three March fees sum to 4_100¢, the same total b16/standard/unique_count_agg/false reaches in arrears for the same three seats. Each fee reports `units: 1`: compute_units returns full_units_number for a prorated charge (apply_pay_in_advance_charge_model_service.rb:118-119), which is the event's own un-prorated contribution of one seat. The fourth invoice is the 1 April renewal: pay-in-advance charges on a recurring metric are still billed there (calculate_fees_service.rb:131-132) and proration is skipped on the billing date when there is no event (unique_count_service.rb:20), so all 3 seats are billed for a whole period: 3 × 31.00 = 9_300¢. If the per-event fees ignored proration each would be 3_100¢; if they were per-event rather than cumulative deltas, seat_2 and seat_3 would not both be 1_000¢.

There is no ProratedVolumeService: ChargeModels::Factory:52-53 always returns VolumeService, which handles proration in one line — `number_of_units` is `full_units_number` when the charge is prorated (volume_service.rb:62-64) and is used to pick the tier and nothing else, while `per_unit_total_amount` multiplies the PRORATED `units` by that tier's rate (volume_service.rb:52-54). So the tier is chosen by the 93 un-prorated units — 93 > 50, so tier 2 at 2.00 — and the 41 prorated units (31 × 21/31 + 62 × 10/31 = 21 + 20, postgres_store.rb:301-315) are all priced there: 41 × 2.00 = 82.00, plus tier 2's flat amount of 0 → 8_200¢. `units` on the fee is again the un-prorated 93 (charge_service.rb:302-307). The 50-unit boundary is deliberately between the prorated total (41) and the full total (93), so the two candidate readings disagree: choosing the tier from the PRORATED units would land in tier 1 and give 41 × 1.00 = 41.00 → 4_100¢. Ignoring proration altogether gives 93 × 2.00 = 186.00 → 18_600¢. Volume, unlike graduated, prices every unit at the single tier reached, so a graduated reading of the same ranges would give 50 × 1.00 + 43 × 2.00 = 136.00 on full units. Only "tier from full units, quantity prorated" gives 8_200¢.

Same VolumeService reading as b16/volume/sum_agg/false — tier from `number_of_units` = full_units_number, quantity from the prorated `units` (volume_service.rb:52-64) — plus the half of compute_amount the other volume row leaves at zero: the tier's FLAT amount is added whole, un-prorated (`compute_amount` = per_unit_total_amount + flat_unit_amount, volume_service.rb:11-13 and :44-46). 3 un-prorated seats (unique_count_service.rb:23) select tier 2, from_value 3. The prorated aggregation is (21 + 10 + 10)/31 = 41/31, ceiled to 1.32259 (unique_count_query.rb:302-329, unique_count_service.rb:22), priced at 62.00 → 82.00058, plus the flat 10.00 → 92.00058, rounded to two decimals (charge_service.rb:296-300) → 92.00 → 9_200¢. That the flat fee is NOT prorated is the specific thing this row records: a subscriber who reached tier 2 for the last 10 days of the month still pays its full entry fee. Prorating the flat amount as well would give 82.00 + 10.00 × 41/93 ≈ 86.41 → 8_641¢. Choosing the tier from the prorated units instead would use `number_of_units.ceil` = 2 → tier 1 → 1.32259 × 31.00 = 41.00029 → 4_100¢. Ignoring proration gives 3 × 62.00 + 10.00 = 196.00 → 19_600¢. Neither is 9_200¢.

The three reducers that all take from the customer's own money — a discount, a credit they are owed, and credits they hold — with no tax between them, so the only question is how much of each is consumed and in what order. April invoice: 100 units of `early` = 10_000¢ less the 2_000¢ recurring coupon = 8_000¢. The wallet is limited to `late` and cannot touch it. Crediting 6_000¢ of the charge returns its share of the coupon (6_000/10_000 × 2_000 = 1_200¢) → a 4_800¢ balance. May invoice: 80 units of `late` = 8_000¢, coupon 2_000¢ again → 6_000¢ base. The credit note goes first and takes 4_800¢, leaving 1_200¢. The wallet is then capped per fee at `sub_total_excluding_taxes + taxes - precise_credit_notes` = 6_000 - 4_800 = 1_200¢, so despite holding 5_000¢ it contributes exactly the remainder and keeps 3_800¢. Each earlier stage shrinks what the next one is allowed to spend, and the wallet balance is the only field that records it: every ordering of these three ends at a 0¢ invoice, and they differ only in how much of the customer's credit was burned to get there.

coupon + credit_note + prepaid_credit quoted and then billed, asserted with identical numbers on both sides. April bills 100 units = 10_000¢ less the 2_000¢ coupon = 8_000¢, all of it covered by the wallet. Crediting 6_000¢ of the fee returns its coupon share (1_200¢) → 4_800¢ of balance. The draft of coupon + credit_note + prepaid_credit, rebuilt by refresh. Coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit are all gated on `not_in_finalizing_process?` (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-379), so a draft carries none of them and shows a total the customer will not be billed. Four of the five reducers, and the only clean four-stack available: progressive billing is the fifth and cannot join without dragging in the tax defect recorded by b17/pb-coupon-tax/invoice. Everything here is derivable in one pass because each stage is on a known side of tax. April: 100 units of `early` = 10_000¢, coupon 2_000¢ BEFORE tax → 8_000¢ base, 20% = 1_600¢ → 9_600¢. Crediting 6_000¢ of the fee returns its coupon share (1_200¢) and the tax on what remains: (6_000 − 1_200) × 1.2 = 5_760¢. May: 80 units of `late` = 8_000¢, coupon 2_000¢ → 6_000¢ base, 1_200¢ tax → 7_200¢ due. The credit note is spent AFTER tax and covers 5_760¢ of it, leaving 1_440¢; the wallet, also after tax and limited to `late`, is capped at 6_000 + 1_200 − 5_760 = 1_440¢ and contributes exactly that, keeping 3_560¢. Every stage lands on a different quantity — the coupon on the base, the tax on what the coupon left, the credit note on the taxed total, the wallet on what the credit note left — so the eight asserted numbers are eight independent statements rather than one restated four times.

Every stage of the pipeline on one invoice, and each one asserted separately so a divergence names the stage that produced it rather than just a wrong total. Threshold invoice (5 March): 100 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ of charge, the recurring coupon takes 2_000¢ before tax → 8_000¢ base, 20% = 1_600¢, total 9_600¢. A credit note is then raised on it for 5_000¢ of fee, which returns its share of the coupon (5_000/10_000 × 2_000 = 1_000¢) and its tax: (5_000 − 1_000) × 1.2 = 4_800¢ of spendable balance. Period invoice (1 April), stage by stage: fees 5_000¢ subscription + 10_000¢ charge = 15_000¢; progressive billing credits what was actually collected, not what was billed — `to_credit_amount = fees − coupons − pb_credits − credit_notes` = 10_000 − 2_000 − 4_800 = 3_200¢, under the 10_000¢ charge cap; the coupon takes another 2_000¢ (it is `recurring` over 3 periods, so unlike a `once` coupon it survives the threshold invoice — see b15/coupon/progressive_billing); base 15_000 − 3_200 − 2_000 = 9_800¢, tax 1_960¢; the credit note is spent after tax, all 4_800¢ of it → 5_831¢ left; the wallet is spent last and is limited to `subscription` fees, and a limited wallet is capped per fee at `sub_total_excluding_taxes + taxes - precise_credit_notes` (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_service.rb:74-77). The credit note had already absorbed 2_253¢ of the subscription fee, so only 2_733¢ of the wallet's 3_000¢ is usable → 3_098¢ due and 267¢ left on the wallet. The charge fee is skipped outright by that service because its base is 0 — a consequence of the tax defect below, not a separate rule. CHARACTERIZATION — the tax figure is wrong and this row records what Lago does, not what it should do. Derivation says 20% of the 9_800¢ base = 1_960¢; Lago charges 831¢, under-collecting 1_129¢ of VAT. Cause, from `Credits::ProgressiveBillingService#apply_credit_to_fees`: `fee.precise_coupons_amount_cents += progressive_fee.amount_cents`, clamped to the fee amount. It adds the amount the threshold invoice BILLED (10_000¢), not the amount actually credited (3_200¢), so the charge fee's taxable base clamps to 0 and the fee is taxed at 0 — visible in the fee assertions above. The invoice-level `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` is meanwhile reduced by only 3_200¢, so the invoice's own base (9_800¢) and the sum of its fees' bases no longer agree, and tax follows the fees. The two coincide whenever `to_credit_amount` equals the billed amount, which is every case B5 and B15 cover. They diverge exactly when something already reduced the threshold invoice — a coupon or a credit note — which is why it took a three-deep stack to surface. Correct behaviour would distribute the CAPPED credit across the fees. What the stack tests that the pairs cannot: the credit note reduces the progressive-billing credit (3_200¢ rather than 8_000¢) while ALSO being spent in full on the same invoice — counted once on each side of tax, for two different purposes. That is the interaction that exposed the tax defect.

progressive_billing + coupon + tax + credit_note + prepaid_credit predicted before the period closes — the deepest stack in the block, quoted rather than billed. All invoice arithmetic is derived in b17/full-stack/invoice. PREVIEW DIVERGES FROM THE INVOICE HERE, AND THIS ROW RECORDS BOTH SIDES. Preview credits progressive billing at invoice level but never at fee level, so every fee is still taxed on its undiscounted share and the wallet's per-fee ceiling is computed from bases the credit never reached. The invoice makes the opposite error: `apply_credit_to_fees` writes the amount BILLED rather than the amount CREDITED into the charge fee and clamps its taxable base to zero. One missing distribution, two different wrong answers, and a quote the customer cannot rely on. Fixing `apply_credit_to_fees` to spread the capped credit settles both, and this row should then agree with its /invoice sibling.

Four reducers with no tax between them, so every stage acts on the same running figure and the only question is how much each is allowed to take. The subscription fee therefore absorbs the credit note alone and is left 2_272.73¢ of room. The wallet spends 2_273¢ of its 3_000¢ and keeps 727¢; 2_727¢ remains due. Note what the wallet cannot reach: 5_000¢ is owed and it holds enough to cover 3_000¢ of it, but the limitation plus two earlier reducers cap it at 2_273¢. A wallet that emptied here would mean the limitation had been ignored.

Two threshold invoices with the edit landing between them, so the question is not just whether the mutation applies but which of the two already-issued demands it can still reach. 60 units on 5 March cross the 5_000¢ threshold and are billed at once; 70 more on 15 March take cumulative usage to 13_000¢, past the 12_000¢ threshold, and the second demand credits what the first collected. The period invoice on 1 April then credits what the SECOND collected — `to_credit_amount` reads the most recent threshold invoice, net of its own coupons and credit notes but not of credits granted against it, which is why it is 13_000¢ and not 7_000¢. Repricing to 3.00 between the two demands re-rates the cumulative usage rather than only the new part: the second demand bills 130 units x 3.00 = 39_000¢, credits the 6_000¢ the first collected at the old price, and the period invoice credits the full 39_000¢ back. Nothing is owed at the end, but the customer has paid 6_000 + 33_000 = 39_000¢ — the whole period at the new price, including the 60 units metered while the old price was in force. Two threshold invoices with the edit landing between them, so the question is not just whether the mutation applies but which of the two already-issued demands it can still reach. 60 units on 5 March cross the 5_000¢ threshold and are billed at once; 70 more on 15 March take cumulative usage to 13_000¢, past the 12_000¢ threshold, and the second demand credits what the first collected. The row that resolves the draft-refresh asymmetry rather than just recording it. Charges::UpdateService never flags drafts, so b18/charge_amount/on-draft/regenerated shows the repricing failing to reach the invoice through the refresh job — but finalization recomputes unconditionally, so the same edit lands here: 100 units at 3.00 plus the 5_000¢ subscription fee = 35_000¢. The customer is therefore billed at the NEW price even though every intermediate view showed the old one. The missing flag delays the correction; it does not lose it.

April is quoted at the new 3.00 per unit (35_000¢) while the March draft remains at the old price it was cut with. CHARACTERIZATION — repricing a charge does not reach a draft that is already open, and this row records that rather than endorsing it. Same shape as b18/tax_rate/on-draft/regenerated: a draft held by a 5-day grace period, the configuration corrected, the refresh clock run. Changing the TAX rate rebuilds the draft. Changing the CHARGE price does not: the draft still reads 10_000¢ at the old 1.00 per unit, though a refresh would produce 30_000¢. Cause: `Invoice.ready_to_be_refreshed` is a flag, and only some writers set it. Plans::UpdateService (update_service.rb:82), Taxes::UpdateService (:30), Taxes::DestroyService, BillableMetrics::DestroyService and Customers::ApplyTaxesService all flag the customer's drafts. The asymmetry is the finding: the same repricing reaches the draft through `PUT /plans/:code` (Plans::UpdateService, which flags) and does not through `PUT /plans/:code/charges/:code`. Two endpoints for one intent, two outcomes, and the grace period silently stops being a correction window for the one people reach for.

March keeps its 2_000¢ discount, which is unsurprising, and April is quoted the same 2_000¢, which is the actual content: the edit reaches neither. Extending the grace period from 5 days to 10 leaves the draft open and unchanged at 15_000¢: the setting moves the issuing date, never the amounts. The direction matters, and not symmetrically. SHORTENING the grace period does not merely change a date — Customers::UpdateInvoiceIssuingDateSettingsService walks the customer's draft invoices and enqueues Invoices::FinalizeJob for each one (update_invoice_issuing_date_settings_service.rb: 24-32), so the drafts are issued there and then rather than waiting for Clock::FinalizeInvoicesJob. That is why this cell is reached by extending: a row that shortened the period would find a finalized invoice and could not observe a draft at all.

Shortening the grace period is what closes a draft, so this row proves the setting is acted upon rather than merely stored. The 1 April invoice sits in `draft` under a 5-day grace period; the period is then set to 0 and the finalize-refresh clock run, and the invoice becomes `finalized` with its amounts unchanged at 10_000¢. Rows write `invoice_grace_period` flat and the runner nests it under `billing_configuration`, which the API requires in both directions. Sent at the top level it is dropped by strong params with an HTTP 200, and the failure mode is the nastiest kind: the customer gets NO grace period, the invoice is finalized immediately, and a row asserting `finalized` passes while never having tested anything. That is exactly how the first draft of this row passed — b18/charge_amount/on-draft/regenerated, which needs a real draft, is what caught it. `premium: true` for the same reason: the field is discarded without a licence.

Extending the grace period and refreshing changes nothing: the invoice is rebuilt, stays open, and stays at 15_000¢. A refresh cannot close an invoice and the grace period cannot alter its amounts, so this cell is the intersection of two independent no-ops — worth pinning precisely because it is the kind of combination that would be assumed rather than checked.

Here the flag and the finalization agree — Plans::UpdateService marks the draft and finalization would have rebuilt it anyway — which is what makes the charge_amount sibling above worth having as the case where they disagree.
April is quoted at the new 9_000¢ plan price. The plan carries no charges deliberately: `PUT /plans/:code` replaces the plan wholesale and would delete them.

The positive half of the draft-refresh asymmetry, and the direct comparison that makes b18/charge_amount/on-draft/regenerated a finding rather than a design choice. A 5_000¢ monthly plan bills 5_000¢ into a draft held by a 5-day grace period. The plan price is raised to 9_000¢ through `PUT /plans/:code`, and because Plans::UpdateService flags the plan's draft invoices `ready_to_be_refreshed` (update_service.rb:82) the refresh job rebuilds the draft at 9_000¢. The identical intent expressed through `PUT /plans/:code/charges/:code` does not reach the draft at all, because Charges::UpdateService sets no such flag. Same grace period, same refresh, two endpoints, two answers. The plan carries no charges on purpose: `PUT /plans/:code` replaces the plan wholesale, so a charge-bearing plan would have its charges deleted by this call and the row would be measuring that instead.

A rate cut after the invoice is issued must not reach it. March was taxed at 20% — 15_000¢ of fees, 3_000¢ of tax, 18_000¢ — and stays there even after the rate drops to 10% and a refresh is attempted: Invoices::RefreshDraftService operates on drafts only. Taxes::UpdateService does flag draft invoices for refresh, so this row is the proof that the flag cannot reach a finalized one. A failure here is retroactive re-taxation of money already invoiced.

The same edit seen from the next period: the quote for April uses the NEW 10% rate, 1_500¢ on 15_000¢ of fees. So one rate change produces two correct answers at once — March keeps 3_000¢ because it was already issued, April is quoted 1_500¢ because it has not been. The pairing is the point: neither number alone shows that the boundary is drawn at issuance.

A rate cut from 20% to 10% lands before anything is billed, so there is nothing yet for it to disagree with — every surface must show the new rate. 5_000¢ subscription + 100 units = 15000¢ of fees, taxed at 10% = 1_500¢ → 16_500¢. Tax is the one thing a draft computes exactly as a finalized invoice does: it is applied by ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService before the finalizing gate that withholds coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit, which is why this family reads the same on all four surfaces while the coupon and wallet families below do not.

A tax rate is read when the invoice is built, not when the usage happened. The rate is cut from 20% to 10% on 20 March, after all the usage was ingested but before the period closes, and the 1 April invoice taxes the full 10_000¢ at the NEW rate: 1_000¢, total 11_000¢. Had the rate been read per event, or snapshotted at subscription time, this would be 2_000¢ and 12_000¢. fees_amount_cents is asserted with it: all 10_000¢ of usage is on the invoice, so 1_000¢ of tax can only be 10% of the whole base and not 20% of some part of it.

A preview is a quote, so it is the surface a customer sees BEFORE the invoice exists, and a rate change between quote and invoice is the obvious way for the two to disagree. The rate is cut from 20% to 10% on 20 March, after all the usage and before the period closes. The preview on 25 March and the invoice on 1 April must both read the new rate: 10_000¢ of usage, 1_000¢ of tax, 11_000¢ total. Asserted on both sides with identical numbers, so a preview that kept the old 20% shows up as 2_000¢ against 1_000¢ rather than as a plausible-looking quote. Pairs with b18/tax_rate/before-first-invoice/final, which asserts the invoice alone: that row says the rate is read at build time, this one says the quote is built the same way.

Tax is the one thing a draft computes exactly as a finalized invoice does: it is applied by ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService before the finalizing gate that withholds coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit, which is why this family reads the same on all four surfaces while the coupon and wallet families below do not.

A rate cut landing between two threshold invoices, which is the only stage where the same period carries two different tax rates. The first demand is cut on 5 March at 20%: 60 units = 6_000¢ plus 1_200¢ of tax = 7_200¢. The rate drops to 10% on 10 March. The second demand on 15 March bills the cumulative 13_000¢, credits the 6_000¢ the first collected, and taxes the 7_000¢ that remains at the NEW rate = 700¢ → 7_700¢. Tax is read when each invoice is built, so a single period is legitimately taxed at two rates, each correct for the moment its demand was issued. Observed as an open draft, and it reads exactly as the issued invoice does: 13_000¢ billed, 13_000¢ credited, 0¢ of tax. This is the one family where a draft and a finalized invoice agree completely, because the only reducers in play are progressive billing and tax — both computed ahead of the finalizing gate that withholds coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit. Every other mutation in this block has a draft that differs from its final.

A rate cut landing between two threshold invoices, which is the only stage where the same period carries two different tax rates. The first demand is cut on 5 March at 20%: 60 units = 6_000¢ plus 1_200¢ of tax = 7_200¢. The rate drops to 10% on 10 March. The second demand on 15 March bills the cumulative 13_000¢, credits the 6_000¢ the first collected, and taxes the 7_000¢ that remains at the NEW rate = 700¢ → 7_700¢. Tax is read when each invoice is built, so a single period is legitimately taxed at two rates, each correct for the moment its demand was issued. The period invoice then credits the 13_000¢ the second demand collected, leaving a 0¢ base and 0¢ of tax — nothing further is owed and nothing further is taxed. All three invoices are asserted because the story is the sequence: 1_200¢ at the old rate, 700¢ at the new one, and nothing left to tax. Note the fee-level clamp does no harm here. `apply_credit_to_fees` writes the second demand's 13_000¢ into the period invoice's charge fee, zeroing its taxable base — and the invoice's own base is 0 too, so the two agree. The clamp only misprices when a coupon or credit note has made `to_credit_amount` smaller than the amount billed, which is b17/pb-coupon-tax/invoice.

CHARACTERIZATION — the quote disagrees with the invoice, and the disagreement is the whole value of the cell: preview says 1_300¢ is owed where the invoice says 0¢. Preview credits progressive billing at invoice level, so its base is correctly 0. But it never applies the credit at FEE level, so each fee is still taxed on its full 13_000¢ at 10% = 1_300¢ — tax on money the customer has already paid, against a base of zero. The invoice reaches 0 through the opposite error: `apply_credit_to_fees` clamps the charge fee's taxable amount to zero by writing the amount billed into it. Here that lands on the right answer by luck, because the base is zero anyway. Fixing the fee-level distribution settles both, and this row and its /final sibling should then agree.

A rate cut landing between two threshold invoices, which is the only stage where the same period carries two different tax rates. The first demand is cut on 5 March at 20%: 60 units = 6_000¢ plus 1_200¢ of tax = 7_200¢. The rate drops to 10% on 10 March. The second demand on 15 March bills the cumulative 13_000¢, credits the 6_000¢ the first collected, and taxes the 7_000¢ that remains at the NEW rate = 700¢ → 7_700¢. Tax is read when each invoice is built, so a single period is legitimately taxed at two rates, each correct for the moment its demand was issued. Observed after `PUT /invoices/:id/refresh`. The draft is rebuilt from current configuration — the 10% rate, the same two threshold invoices — and lands on the same 0¢. A refresh recomputing the progressive credit from scratch is the risk here: were it to credit the 6_000¢ of the FIRST demand instead of the 13_000¢ of the second, the invoice would show 7_000¢ due on a period already paid in full.

An open draft is not recomputed when the world changes — only when something refreshes it. The draft is cut on 1 April at the then-current 20%: 15_000¢ of fees, 3_000¢ of tax, 18_000¢. The rate drops to 10% the next day and the draft still reads 3_000¢, because nothing has asked it to rebuild. Taxes::UpdateService flags it `ready_to_be_refreshed`, but a flag is an intention rather than an act: b18/tax_rate/on-draft/regenerated runs the refresh job and gets 1_500¢. The pair is what separates 'stale' from 'wrong'. A customer reading this draft between the two moments sees a number that is real but superseded.

Finalizing an open draft rebuilds it, so the rate cut DOES reach it: 1_500¢ of tax on 15_000¢ of fees, 16_500¢ issued, where the draft had read 3_000¢ and 18_000¢. Invoices::RefreshDraftAndFinalizeService calls RefreshDraftService with `context: :finalize` unconditionally — it does not consult `ready_to_be_refreshed`. Finalization is therefore the moment a draft stops being stale, whatever did or did not flag it.

A quote taken while a stale draft sits open reads the CURRENT rate, not the draft's. April is previewed at 10% — 1_500¢ on 15_000¢ — while the March draft still shows 3_000¢ at the old 20%. Two views of the same customer, minutes apart, disagreeing correctly: one is a period already computed, the other a period not yet computed.

The regenerate path, end to end: a draft is not a snapshot but a recomputation, which is the whole reason a grace period exists. Under a 5-day grace period the 1 April invoice stays `draft`, taxed at 20% → 2_000¢, total 12_000¢. The rate is then cut to 10%. Taxes::UpdateService flags the customer's draft invoices `ready_to_be_refreshed`, Clock::RefreshDraftInvoicesJob picks them up, and the draft is rebuilt at the new rate: 1_000¢ of tax, 11_000¢ total. Fees are asserted unchanged at 10_000¢ so the row distinguishes "re-taxed" from "re-billed". Without the flag the refresh job would never see the invoice — see b18/charge_amount/on-draft/regenerated, where exactly that happens.

March spent the 3_000¢ the wallet held at the time and is not revisited when 50 more credits arrive: 15_000¢ of fees less 3_000¢ = 12_000¢. Prepaid credit is consumed at finalization, and consumption is a transaction against the wallet rather than a figure recomputed from it. A failure here would mean topping up a wallet retroactively altered invoices already paid.

April is quoted against the wallet as it now stands. March emptied the original 30 credits, the top-up added 50, so 5_000¢ of cover remains and 10_000¢ is due. Together the two rows show the wallet has a history rather than a balance: the invoice records what was spent, the quote reads what is left.

The draft spends NOTHING from the wallet — 15_000¢ due where the customer will be billed 7_000¢. `should_create_applied_prepaid_credit?` is gated on finalization (calculate_fees_service.rb:375), which is what stops a draft from burning credits that a later refresh would have to return.

A wallet topped up mid-period pays with everything it holds at billing time, not with what it held when the subscription started: 30 granted credits plus 50 more = 8_000¢ against 15_000¢ of fees, leaving 7_000¢. Granted credits are spendable immediately. Purchased ones are not until the top-up invoice is settled, which is the distinction B6 covers and the reason this row grants rather than sells.

The quote reflects the top-up too: 8_000¢ of cover, 7_000¢ due. Preview allocates prepaid credit through the same AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService the invoice uses, reading the wallet's balance at quote time.
Refreshing changes nothing: a refreshed draft is still a draft, so the wallet stays untouched at 15_000¢ due. The credits are spent only when the invoice finalizes.

Two threshold invoices with the edit landing between them, so the question is not just whether the mutation applies but which of the two already-issued demands it can still reach. 60 units on 5 March cross the 5_000¢ threshold and are billed at once; 70 more on 15 March take cumulative usage to 13_000¢, past the 12_000¢ threshold, and the second demand credits what the first collected. The period invoice on 1 April then credits what the SECOND collected — `to_credit_amount` reads the most recent threshold invoice, net of its own coupons and credit notes but not of credits granted against it, which is why it is 13_000¢ and not 7_000¢. The wallet pays each demand as it arrives and the top-up joins in for the second: 6_000¢ spent on the first, leaving 14_000¢; 50 more credits arrive; the second demand's 7_000¢ net is covered, leaving 12_000¢; the period invoice's remaining 5_000¢ subscription fee is covered too, leaving 7_000¢. Three invoices drawn from one balance in sequence, and the balance is the only field that records the order. The draft sibling of this row shows 5_000¢ still due and 12_000¢ still on the wallet, because a draft spends nothing. Observed as an open draft, so coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit are all withheld (`not_in_finalizing_process?`, calculate_fees_service.rb:364-379) while the progressive credit, which runs ahead of that gate, is present. The draft therefore shows the credit but not the discount.

Three invoices drawn from one balance in sequence, and the balance is the only field that records the order. The draft sibling of this row shows 5_000¢ still due and 12_000¢ still on the wallet, because a draft spends nothing. Observed as the issued period invoice, which is where the arithmetic above is settled.

The draft sibling of this row shows 5_000¢ still due and 12_000¢ still on the wallet, because a draft spends nothing. Observed as a quote taken before the period closes. Preview reimplements the pipeline in Invoices::PreviewService, so it credits progressive billing at invoice level — added in this session — and applies the reducers a draft withholds.

The period invoice on 1 April then credits what the SECOND collected — `to_credit_amount` reads the most recent threshold invoice, net of its own coupons and credit notes but not of credits granted against it, which is why it is 13_000¢ and not 7_000¢. The draft sibling of this row shows 5_000¢ still due and 12_000¢ still on the wallet, because a draft spends nothing. Observed after `PUT /invoices/:id/refresh`, which rebuilds the draft from current configuration. It must land on the same figures it was created with rather than drifting, and it is still a draft afterwards, so the withheld reducers stay withheld.

The wallet is topped up while the draft is open and the draft does not move — not because the top-up was missed, but because a draft never spends prepaid credit in the first place (`should_create_applied_prepaid_credit?` is gated on finalization). That gating is what makes the top-up safe: had the draft already consumed the original 30 credits, they would have to be returned when it was refreshed. Instead nothing is spent until the invoice is issued, at which point the wallet holds 8_000¢ — see b18/wallet_balance/before-first-invoice/final.

The wallet is spent for the first time at finalization, and it spends the topped-up balance: the original 30 credits were never touched by the draft, 50 more arrived while it was open, so 8_000¢ of cover meets 15_000¢ of fees and 7_000¢ is due. This is the payoff of the gate that keeps drafts from consuming credit. Had the draft spent 3_000¢ on 1 April, the top-up would have had to be reconciled against an invoice that already claimed part of it.

The quote sees the whole topped-up wallet — 8_000¢ against 15_000¢, so 7_000¢ due — because the open March draft has not spent any of it. Had drafts consumed credit, this quote and the March draft would each be claiming the same 3_000¢, and the customer would be shown cover that does not exist twice over.

A refreshed draft still spends nothing from the wallet, even though it now holds 8_000¢. Prepaid credit is allocated at finalization only, so the refresh recomputes fees and tax and leaves the wallet untouched at 15_000¢ due. The wallet's balance is not asserted here on purpose: the claim is that the INVOICE did not draw on it, and prepaid_credit_amount_cents 0 states exactly that.

Two add-on fees on one invoice: do both take effect, and do their amounts add? They do, and the mechanism is a loop over the payload rather than a lookup keyed by add-on. `Fees::OneOffService#call` iterates `fees.each` and builds one `Fee.new(..., fee_type: :add_on, invoiceable: add_on)` per ENTRY (one_off_service.rb:19-68), with nothing de-duplicating by add-on and no upsert; `Invoices::CreateOneOffService` then sums them wholesale — `invoice.fees_amount_cents = invoice.fees.sum(:amount_cents)` and `sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents = fees_amount_cents` (create_one_off_service.rb:51-52). Each fee's `amount_cents` is `(unit_amount_cents * units).round` (:37) where `unit_amount_cents` comes from the payload, and ScenariosHelper#create_one_off_invoice sends each add-on's own `amount_cents` — 5_000¢ x 1 unit, twice, so 10_000¢ of fees. Neither add-on carries taxes of its own and the call sends no `tax_codes`, so `Fees::ApplyTaxesService#applicable_taxes` falls past the explicit-codes rung and past `return fee.add_on.taxes if fee.add_on? && fee.add_on.taxes.any?` (apply_taxes_service.rb:64-66) to the billing-entity default at :81-82, which is where `applied_to_organization: true` put the single 20% VAT. 20% of 5_000¢ is 1_000¢ per fee, 2_000¢ in total, 12_000¢ due. The failure this row is sized to catch is a one-fee-per-add-on-type collapse — a `find_or_initialize_by` or an upsert keyed on `invoiceable`, which reads as a reasonable thing to write and would produce `fees_count` 1, 5_000¢ of fees, 1_000¢ of tax and 6_000¢ due on an invoice that still looks internally consistent. Asserting `fees_count` AND both fees by `item_code` is what separates "two fees" from "one fee that happens to total right", which the invoice totals alone cannot. b19/add_on/unequal/invoice is the companion: there the two add-ons carry DIFFERENT add-on-level taxes, which proves the ladder is walked per fee rather than once per invoice.

Two add-on fees that must be taxed DIFFERENTLY on the same invoice, which is the add-on feature's version of "two instances that differ in a way the order exposes": the tax ladder is not walked once per invoice, it is walked once per fee. `Fees::ApplyTaxesService` is constructed with `fee:` and resolves `applicable_taxes` from that fee alone; the add-on rung is `return fee.add_on.taxes if fee.add_on? && fee.add_on.taxes.any?` (apply_taxes_service.rb:64-66), reached because `Fees::OneOffService` sends no `tax_codes` and so the explicit-codes rung above it does not fire. `Invoices::ComputeTaxesAndTotalsService` calls it per fee, and the invoice's `taxes_amount_cents` is the SUM of what each fee resolved, never a single rate applied to the sub-total. 8_000¢ at its own 20% = 1_600¢; 2_000¢ at its own 5% = 100¢; 1_700¢ of tax on 10_000¢ of fees, 11_700¢ due. Both taxes are created `applied_to_organization: false` and the customer carries none, so the billing-entity fallback at :81-82 cannot smuggle either of them onto the other fee. Four counterfactuals, all separated by these amounts. First-fee-wins (the ladder resolved once and reused): 20% on 10_000¢ = 2_000¢, 12_000¢. Last-fee-wins: 5% → 500¢, 10_500¢. Both taxes on both fees (a resolution that unions rather than selects, i.e. the additive answer): 25% on 10_000¢ = 2_500¢, 12_500¢, and each fee's `taxes_rate` would read 25.0. A blended average rate applied to the sub-total: 12.5% → 1_250¢. The amounts are deliberately 8_000/2_000 rather than two equal ones, because with equal amounts first-wins, last-wins and blended all land on 1_250¢ and the row would prove nothing. Asserting each fee's own `taxes_rate` as well as its `taxes_amount_cents` is what pins the per-fee resolution itself rather than an invoice total that several wrong implementations share. b19/add_on/equal/invoice is the control: with no add-on-level taxes anywhere, both fees fall to the same billing-entity default and the rates really are identical.

TWO charges on ONE billable metric, priced identically: the same 100 units are aggregated twice and billed twice. 5_000¢ plan + 10_000¢ + 10_000¢ = 25_000¢. That this is even expressible is the first half of the row. `Charge#validate_code_unique` (charge.rb:182-188) makes a charge's CODE unique within a plan, not its billable metric, and `Plans::CreateService#charge_params_with_code` (:143-148) fills the code in from `Charges::GenerateCodeService`, which auto-suffixes on collision — the second charge is created as `b19_w1_chei_sum_2`. `Plans::ChargeablesValidationService` only checks that the metrics exist. Nothing anywhere de-duplicates by metric. The second half is that both are then billed. `CalculateFeesService#create_charges_fees` iterates `subscription.plan.charges.where(invoiceable: true)` and calls `Fees::ChargeService` per charge (calculate_fees_service.rb:117-147), each with its own aggregation and its own `ChargeCacheMiddleware` key — so the units are not shared or netted, they are re-aggregated. Two fees of 100 units at 1.00. A wrong implementation that de-duplicated by billable metric, or that let the second charge's cache entry collide with the first's, reads 15_000¢ — the loud difference this row is sized for. The two charge-fee expectations are deliberately IDENTICAL: `Fee#item_code` is the billable metric's code for a charge fee (fee.rb:117-118), so the two fees share every one of `GoldenRunner::FEE_MATCH_KEYS` and could not be told apart if their amounts differed (F67). Equal amounts make the match unambiguous, which is another reason this arrangement is the one that gets a per-fee assertion.

Two identically priced charges on one metric, forecast: 5_000¢ plan + 100 units × 1.00, twice = 25_000¢ of fees (the arithmetic derived and finalized in b19/charge/equal/invoice). Tax is 20% on the two CHARGE fees only — 2_000¢ + 2_000¢ = 4_000¢ — because it is attached to the charges rather than to the plan or the organization, so the subscription fee falls through `applicable_taxes` to a billing entity with no default tax and is untaxed. 29_000¢ forecast. `fees_count: 3` is load-bearing: it distinguishes two charge fees from one at twice the price, which the totals cannot. Per-fee amounts are unassertable because both charge fees carry the metric's code as `item_code` (fee.rb:117-118, F67). THE SHAPE OF THIS ROW IS DICTATED BY TWO DEFECTS, both verified in the container against the real service, and both invisible to every existing preview row because b17's whole preview column has exactly ONE charge per plan. F72: with two or more charges and no charge-level tax, `POST /invoices/preview` raises NoMethodError. The preview's charge fees come back with a nil `subscription` once `add_charge_fees` returns more than one fee, so `Fees::ApplyTaxesService`'s `plan` falls back to `fee.subscription&.plan` = nil and `plan.taxes.any?` (apply_taxes_service.rb:71) blows up. The `tax_codes` on the charges are therefore not decoration — they make the chain return one line earlier, at `fee.charge.taxes` (:68), before `plan` is read at all. F73: the same two-charge path leaves the caller on a different database connection — `add_charge_fees` wraps each charge in `ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.with_connection` inside `Parallel.flat_map` (preview_service.rb:203-229), and after the second block every query in the example reads an empty database (ApiKey, Organization and Plan all count 0). Three consequences, all measured. NOTHING can follow `preview_invoice` here: no `perform_billing` and no `expect.invoice`, because the invoice read is an HTTP call needing the organization's API key — so the preview is asserted alone and its agreement with the real invoice is carried by b19/charge/equal/invoice, which bills the same fees over the same period. The invoice-level tax reads 0 even though both charge fees carry 2_000¢ each, which is why `taxes_amount_cents: 0` is asserted and why this row is CHARACTERIZATION: 29_000¢ is the correct forecast and 25_000¢ is what Lago returns. And a SECOND multi-charge preview in the same RSpec process comes out wrong (a 35_000¢ plan previewed 25_000¢), which is why b19/charge/unequal/preview does not exist — that cell is blocked on F73, not on a derivation. Unrelated later examples are unaffected; verified both ways in the container.

Two identical charges on one metric, rebuilt. Producers are not gated on finalization — only coupons, credit notes and prepaid credit are (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-379) — so the draft carries the full 25_000¢ that b19/charge/equal/invoice finalizes: 5_000¢ plan + 100 units × 1.00, twice. A refresh is a destroy-and-rebuild, and that is precisely why duplicate charges are worth asserting on this surface. `Invoices::RefreshDraftService` drops the draft's fees and re-runs `CalculateFeesService`, so the second charge has to be re-discovered from `subscription.plan.charges` and re-aggregated with its own cache key. Two failure modes are excluded by the numbers below: a rebuild that emitted one charge fee (15_000¢, `fees_count` 2) and a rebuild that ADDED to the existing fees instead of replacing them (45_000¢, `fees_count` 5) — the second being a real hazard, because the two charge fees are indistinguishable by content and a duplicate would not look out of place. `fees_count: 3` is what turns that into an assertion. The two charge-fee expectations are identical, which is what makes them matchable at all given that both fees carry the metric's code as `item_code` (fee.rb:117-118, F67). The three withheld reducers are asserted as 0 so a draft that quietly allocated one cannot pass.

Two charges on ONE metric with DIFFERENT models, so the same 100 units are priced twice by two different formulas and the invoice carries both answers. Standard leg: 100 × 1.00 = 10_000¢. Package leg: `paid_units = 100 − free_units(0)`, `package_count = 100.fdiv(30).ceil = 4`, and `4 × per_package_unit_amount(50) = 200.00` → 20_000¢ (package_service.rb:7-13, :60-70; the same "amount is per PACKAGE, rounded up" convention b03/package/sum_agg pins). Plus the 5_000¢ plan: 35_000¢. The point of mixing the models is that the two legs cannot be confused for one another, and neither can be confused for a doubled copy of the other: 10_000 + 20_000 is distinguishable from two standard legs (20_000), two package legs (40_000), and a single surviving charge of either kind (15_000 or 25_000). Each aggregation is run independently — `CalculateFeesService#create_charges_fees` calls `Fees::ChargeService` per charge with its own `Subscriptions::ChargeCacheMiddleware` key (calculate_fees_service.rb:133-146) — so a cache keyed on the metric rather than the charge would show up here as the same amount twice. NO per-fee assertion, deliberately. `Fee#item_code` is the billable metric's code for both fees (fee.rb:117-118) and the two share `fee_type`, `item_type`, `from_date` and `to_date` as well, so every key in `GoldenRunner::FEE_MATCH_KEYS` collides and `assert_golden_fees` would match the 10_000¢ expectation against whichever fee `has_many :fees` returned first — a coin flip, not an assertion (F67). `fees_count` plus the invoice total is what is honestly assertable here; the equal sibling above can assert the split only because its two fees are interchangeable.

The same metric priced by two models, rebuilt: 5_000¢ plan + 10_000¢ standard + 20_000¢ package (ceil(100/30) = 4 × 50.00) = 35_000¢, the arithmetic derived in b19/charge/unequal/invoice and unaffected by the surface because producers run before the finalizing gate (calculate_fees_service.rb:42-47 vs :364-379). What the regeneration adds is that the rebuild has to re-resolve WHICH charge is which. The two charges differ only in `charge_model` and `properties` and share a billable metric, so a rebuild that re-read the plan's charges in a different order, or that carried one charge's properties onto the other, would still produce two fees over the same 100 units — and 35_000¢ is the only total that comes out of pricing them once each with their own model. Both-standard is 25_000¢, both-package 45_000¢, and either charge lost is 15_000¢ or 25_000¢. `fees_count: 3` guards the shape (subscription + two charge fees) and the three finalizing-gated reducers are asserted as 0 so the draft cannot pass by having allocated something it should be withholding. Per-fee amounts stay unassertable: both charge fees carry the metric's code as `item_code` and collide on every `FEE_MATCH_KEYS` field (F67).

Two coupons worth 16_000¢ against a 10_000¢ invoice. The interesting part is not that the discount is capped at 10_000¢ — it is that the second coupon is never looked at, and therefore survives. March: the 12_000¢ coupon is older so it goes first and takes the whole 10_000¢. The loop then stops — `break unless invoice.sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents&.positive?` (applied_coupons_service.rb:28) — so the 4_000¢ coupon is not evaluated, not partially consumed, and not terminated. The large one is not terminated either: it gave 10_000¢ of its 12_000¢ and keeps 2_000¢. April proves both of those claims at once. The large coupon returns with exactly its 2_000¢ remainder and is terminated on using it; the small coupon then contributes its untouched 4_000¢ — 6_000¢ of discount and 4_000¢ due. Had the second coupon been consumed to its cap in March, April would carry no discount at all and read 10_000¢. Had it been partially consumed, April would be somewhere between. The two invoices together are what pin it; neither alone can.

PINS F03. 16_000¢ of `once` coupons against a 10_000¢ invoice, previewed in the period AFTER the cap bit — which is the only place the surviving remainder is visible. March (invoice 0): the 12_000¢ coupon is older so it goes first and, because `AppliedCoupons::AmountService` returns the whole base when `remaining_amount > base` (amount_service.rb:34-38), takes all 10_000¢. The loop then stops on `break unless sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents&.positive?` (applied_coupons_service.rb:28), so the 4_000¢ coupon is never evaluated. Neither is terminated: `should_terminate_applied_coupon?` needs `credit_amount >= remaining_amount` (applied_coupon_service.rb:78-85) and 10_000 < 12_000. That is F03 — a "one-time" coupon larger than the invoice keeps discounting later periods — and April is where it is collected: the large coupon returns with exactly its 2_000¢ remainder (terminated on using it), the small coupon contributes its untouched 4_000¢, so 6_000¢ of discount and 4_000¢ due. The preview taken on 20 April must reach the same 6_000¢ from the same two applied_coupons: `PreviewContextService` reads `customer.applied_coupons.active`, which still contains both, and `Coupons::PreviewService` calls the same `AmountService`, so remaining_amount 2_000 (< the 10_000¢ base) yields 2_000 and then 4_000 against the 8_000¢ that is left. Had March consumed the second coupon to the cap, both surfaces would read 10_000¢ due in April; had the remainder been forfeited on termination, they would read 6_000¢ due. Neither the invoice nor the preview alone separates those; the pair of periods does.

The capped pair, with the surviving remainder held on a draft instead of being spent. March, finalized out of its grace period: the older 12_000¢ coupon takes the whole 10_000¢ and the loop breaks before the 4_000¢ coupon is looked at (applied_coupons_service.rb:28), so the large one keeps 2_000¢ and the small one is untouched — 6_000¢ of live coupon going into April. That is the whole point of asserting the draft here: it reads 10_000¢ due while 6_000¢ of allocatable coupon exists, because `should_create_coupon_credit?` refuses to run outside the finalizing process (calculate_fees_service.rb:368-373). The refresh rebuilds it and must land on the same 10_000¢. The counterfactuals are all visible in that one number. Had the draft applied the coupons it would read 4_000¢ — and would have consumed a `once` coupon that a later refresh could not give back, which is precisely what the gate is for. Had March consumed both coupons to the cap there would be nothing left to withhold and the distinction would be invisible; the finalized invoice above is what rules that out, by showing the discount stopping at 10_000¢ of 16_000¢. b19/coupon/capped/preview is the same configuration on the surface that DOES apply the remainder, and reads 6_000¢ of discount in April — the two rows bracket the gate.

The base case the other two arrangements are measured against: two coupons small enough that neither constrains the other simply add. 15_000¢ of fees less 2_000¢ less 2_000¢ = 11_000¢. The second invoice is what makes this more than arithmetic. Both coupons gave their full amount, so both satisfy `credit_amount >= remaining_amount` and both are terminated — April carries no discount and bills the bare 5_000¢ subscription fee. That is the distinction from b19/coupon/capped/invoice, where the same `once` frequency leaves one coupon alive with a remainder and the other untouched entirely. `once` does not mean "one invoice"; it means "until exhausted", and only asserting a second period tells the two apart.

The `equal` question — do both instances take effect at all — asked of the surface that reimplements the pipeline. 5_000¢ plan + 100 units × 1.00 = 15_000¢ of fees, and two 2_000¢ coupons neither of which constrains the other. Preview walks the same sort as the real invoice (`Invoices::PreviewContextService:98-103` uses the identical `limited_billable_metrics DESC, limited_plans DESC, created_at ASC` order as `Credits::AppliedCouponsService#applied_coupons`, applied_coupons_service.rb:50-53) and the same per-coupon arithmetic (`Coupons::PreviewService` calls the very same `AppliedCoupons::AmountService`). Neither coupon is limited, so each takes its base from the running `sub_total`: 15_000 → credit 2_000 → 13_000 → credit 2_000 → 11_000. The invoice then recomputes `sub_total = fees − coupons` = 15_000 − 4_000 = 11_000 (preview_service.rb:305-308), which is what makes the two surfaces comparable at all. A wrong implementation that applies one applied_coupon and silently ignores the second — the plausible failure here, because `Coupons::PreviewService` iterates and `next`s in four places — reads 2_000¢ of discount and 13_000¢ due on ONE of the two surfaces, which is exactly the divergence this row exists to catch. The three events (50/30/20) are deliberately not one event: one event cannot tell sum_agg from max_agg or latest_agg, and this row would then also pass with the charge misconfigured.

Two identically configured coupons, one period finalized and the next rebuilt as a draft, so the row asserts the multiplicity AND what a regeneration makes of it. March, finalized by hand out of its grace period: 5_000¢ plan + 100 units = 15_000¢, each coupon takes its 2_000¢ from the running sub_total → 11_000¢ due. Both are `recurring` over 3 periods, so `decrement_frequency_duration_remaining` leaves each with 2 and NEITHER is terminated (applied_coupon_service.rb:49-53, :86-88) — this is the deliberate difference from b19/coupon/equal/invoice, where the same pair is `once` and both die on the first invoice. April therefore has two live coupons worth 4_000¢, and the draft shows none of them: 5_000¢ of fees and 5_000¢ due. `should_create_coupon_credit?` begins `return false if not_in_finalizing_process?` (calculate_fees_service.rb:368-373), so a draft is fee producers and tax alone — which is what stops a grace-period draft from consuming a coupon that a refresh would have to give back. `PUT /invoices/:id/refresh` rebuilds the draft from scratch and must land on the same 5_000¢, not on the 1_000¢ the customer will eventually be billed. Two wrong implementations are excluded at once: one that applied a single coupon in March (12_000¢ instead of 11_000¢) and one whose refresh allocated the April coupons (1_000¢ instead of 5_000¢, and two coupons burned a month early).

Two coupons of the SAME size, 5_000¢ each, and the invoice discounts 7_000¢ rather than 10_000¢ — because the order they are applied in decides how much of the limited one can be used at all. `Credits::AppliedCouponsService#applied_coupons` sorts metric-limited first, then plan-limited, then oldest first (applied_coupons_service.rb:50-53). So the metric-limited coupon goes first even though it was declared second, and it may only reduce the fee for its metric: 20 units × 1.00 = 2_000¢. It contributes 2_000¢ of its 5_000¢ and, because 2_000 < 5_000, is NOT terminated — `should_terminate_applied_coupon?` requires `credit_amount >= remaining_amount` (applied_coupon_service.rb:78-85). The unlimited coupon then takes 5_000¢ of the remaining 8_000¢, leaving 3_000¢ due. Reverse the order and the invoice is different: the unlimited coupon would take 5_000¢ of the 10_000¢ first, spreading pro rata so only 1_000¢ of the 2_000¢ charge fee survives for the limited coupon to reduce — 6_000¢ of discount and 4_000¢ due. The plan fee is deliberately four times the charge fee so that the limitation binds; with two unlimited coupons the totals commute and the row would prove nothing.

CHARACTERIZATION — the preview and the invoice it forecasts disagree, and the row records what Lago does rather than what it should do. Same configuration as b19/coupon/unequal/invoice: 8_000¢ plan + 20 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢ of fees, one unlimited 5_000¢ coupon and one 5_000¢ coupon limited to the metric. THE INVOICE (derived in b19/coupon/unequal/invoice): the metric-limited coupon sorts first (applied_coupons_service.rb:50-53), may only reduce its own metric's fee, so it contributes 2_000¢ of its 5_000¢ and is not terminated; the unlimited coupon then takes 5_000¢ of the remaining 8_000¢ → 7_000¢ of discount, 3_000¢ due. THE PREVIEW: `Coupons::PreviewService#fees` returns `Fee.none` for any coupon with `limited_billable_metrics?`, and the loop then `next`s on `fees.none?` (coupons/preview_service.rb:22-27, :78-86) — so the metric-limited coupon is not merely mis-based, it is skipped entirely. Only the unlimited coupon runs, taking 5_000¢ of the 10_000¢ sub_total → 5_000¢ of discount, 5_000¢ due. The preview overstates the invoice by 2_000¢, i.e. by the whole contribution of the limited instance. The `Fee.none` carries `# TODO: update later when charges will be added to the preview`, which is stale: `PreviewService#add_charge_fees` (preview_service.rb:173-230) builds charge fees, and this row's preview contains the 2_000¢ charge fee the coupon was supposed to reduce. Correct behaviour would be 7_000¢ / 3_000¢ on both surfaces; a fix must move BOTH the fee scope and the base (`base_amount_cents` uses gross `fees.sum(&:amount_cents)` here where applied_coupon_service.rb:96-105 nets out `precise_coupons_amount_cents`).

The metric-limited-first sort, finalized once and then regenerated on an identical period. March, finalized out of grace: 8_000¢ plan + 20 units × 1.00 = 10_000¢. The metric-limited coupon sorts ahead of the unlimited one (`limited_billable_metrics DESC`, applied_coupons_service.rb:50-53) even though it was declared second, and its base is only the fee for its own metric — 2_000¢ (applied_coupon_service.rb:96-105) — so it contributes 2_000¢ of its 5_000¢. The unlimited coupon then takes 5_000¢ of the remaining 8_000¢: 7_000¢ of discount, 3_000¢ due. Reverse the order and the invoice reads 6_000¢ / 4_000¢, because the unlimited coupon would have spread pro rata and left only 1_000¢ of the charge fee for the limited one to reduce. April is deliberately given the same 20 units, so the period is arithmetically identical and the ONLY difference is the surface. Both coupons are `recurring` and still live with 2 periods each, yet the draft shows 10_000¢ of fees, zero coupon and 10_000¢ due — the finalizing gate at calculate_fees_service.rb:368-373 — and the refresh must reproduce that rather than drifting to the 3_000¢ the finalized twin carries. Asserting only the draft would leave the sort unasserted; asserting only the finalized invoice would leave the gate unasserted. The two selectors are what make the cell mean something.

14_000¢ of credit notes against a 5_000¢ invoice, so the interesting fact is not that the credit is capped — it is that the SECOND note is never looked at, and therefore survives whole. March: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units = 20_000¢, and two notes are raised off its charge fee — 8_000¢ on 2 April, 6_000¢ on 3 April (14_000¢ of a 15_000¢ fee, so both are creditable). April (invoice 1): `remaining_invoice_amount` = 5_000¢. The older note's 8_000¢ balance exceeds it, so `compute_credit_amount` returns 5_000¢, the balance drops to 3_000¢, and `break if remaining_invoice_amount.zero?` (credit_note_service.rb:66) ends the loop — the 6_000¢ note is not evaluated, not partially consumed, not flipped to consumed. May (invoice 2) proves both halves of that at once: the first note returns with exactly its 3_000¢ remainder and is exhausted, and only then does the second contribute — 2_000¢ of its 6_000¢, leaving 4_000¢ available. Both invoices settle at 0, so neither of them alone says anything; the second note's final balance is the assertion. Newest-first would leave it at 0 (6_000¢ spent in April, then 1_000¢ from the other note in May); sharing the 5_000¢ pro rata by balance would leave 3_857¢. 4_000¢ is oldest-first with a hard break, and only that.

The capped pair forecast: the older note alone exceeds the invoice, so the second must be left entirely alone — on the preview as well as on the invoice. March: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units = 20_000¢, credited 8_000¢ (2 April) and 6_000¢ (3 April) off the charge fee. April carries 20 units so the preview has usage to price, giving 5_000 + 2_000 = 7_000¢. Both surfaces: `remaining_invoice_amount` = 7_000¢, the 8_000¢ note is capped to it by `compute_credit_amount` (credit_note_service.rb:80-86), and `break if remaining_invoice_amount.zero?` (:66) ends the walk before the 6_000¢ note is even read. 7_000¢ of credit, nothing due. The invoice writes that back — first note down to 1_000¢, second untouched at 6_000¢ and still `available` — while the preview writes nothing (`context: :preview` skips `update_remaining_credit`, credit_note_service.rb:57-62), which is what makes the balance assertion below a statement about the INVOICE having consumed in that order and about the preview not having consumed at all. Had either surface shared the 7_000¢ across both notes, the second would read 3_000¢; had the preview persisted its consumption, it would read 6_000¢ but the invoice would then find only 1_000¢ of the first note and bill 1_000¢ instead of 0.

The capped pair on a draft: 14_000¢ of notes, a 7_000¢ period, and nothing consumed. March, finalized out of grace: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units = 20_000¢, credited 8_000¢ (3 April) and 6_000¢ (4 April) off its charge fee. April carries 20 units → 5_000 + 2_000 = 7_000¢. The draft withholds the credit entirely (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-366) and the refresh reproduces it: 7_000¢ of fees, 7_000¢ due. The assertion that carries the weight is on the OLDER note — `select: {index: 0}` — at its full 8_000¢. Had the draft allocated, that note would be the one capped to the period and would read 1_000¢, while the newer note stayed at 6_000¢ either way; asserting the newer one would therefore prove nothing here, which is the difference from the unequal sibling above. Finalized, this period reads 0¢ due with the older note down to 1_000¢ (b19/credit_note/capped/preview forecasts exactly that). The draft is 7_000¢ higher and both notes are intact — the gate holding a `once`-like resource unspent while the invoice is still editable.

Two credit notes of the SAME size on one invoice: do both get drawn on, or does the second silently go unspent? March bills the bare 10_000¢ plan and carries no credit note of its own — the notes are raised AGAINST it, and `Credits::CreditNoteService#credit_notes` excludes `where.not(invoice_id: invoice.id)` (credit_note_service.rb:70-78), so a note can never reduce the invoice it was issued from. Both notes credit 3_500¢ of the 10_000¢ subscription fee, which fits: the second is validated against `creditable_amount_cents`, already reduced to 6_500¢ by the first. April (invoice 1) is where both are consumed. `apply_credits` starts from `remaining_invoice_amount = invoice.total_amount_cents` = 10_000¢ and walks the notes oldest first: 3_500 then 3_500, neither capped, 7_000¢ of credit and 3_000¢ due. Because both notes are fully drawn, `update_remaining_credit` zeroes each balance and flips each to `consumed` (credit_note_service.rb:88-96) — which is why the newest note is asserted at balance 0 rather than the invoice alone. One-applied is the failure this row exists to exclude, and it is loud: 6_500¢ due instead of 3_000¢, with a note still sitting at 3_500¢ available. The notes are also each smaller than the invoice, so no cap is involved and the arrangement really is `equal` — the capped variant is b19/credit_note/capped/invoice.

Two equal notes, forecast before they are spent. The arithmetic is the one derived in b19/credit_note/equal/invoice — 10_000¢ of fees, two 3_500¢ notes raised against March, 7_000¢ of credit and 3_000¢ due in April. What the row adds is that the preview reaches it through the SAME service and must therefore agree exactly: `Invoices::Preview::CreditsService#persisted_credits` calls `Credits::CreditNoteService` with `context: :preview` (credits_service.rb:22-26), so the ordering, the `compute_credit_amount` cap and the `break` on a fully covered invoice are shared code rather than a reimplementation. What `context: :preview` skips is the writes — no `Credit` row, no `update_remaining_credit`, and no `apply_credit_to_fees` — so a preview is repeatable and the two notes are still `available` at 20 April even though the preview has "spent" them. That skipped `apply_credit_to_fees` is why this cell is worth asserting on its own rather than assumed from the invoice: it is the one place the two paths differ, and it is invisible until a fee-level consumer (a limited wallet, whose ceiling is `sub_total + taxes - precise_credit_notes`) is present. This row deliberately has none, so the two surfaces must match to the cent, and any difference is a defect rather than a known gap. A preview that applied only one note would read 6_500¢ due against the invoice's 3_000¢.

Two equal notes, and a draft that must not touch either of them. March is finalized by hand out of its 5-day grace period at the bare 10_000¢ plan; the two 3_500¢ notes are then raised against it. April's invoice is generated as a DRAFT and rebuilt by `PUT /invoices/:id/refresh`, and it reads 10_000¢ of fees with 0¢ of credit note — `should_create_credit_note_credit?` is `!not_in_finalizing_process?` (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-366), so a draft carries no credit note at all. Asserting that 0 rather than omitting it is the point: an omitted field would let a draft that HAD consumed the notes pass. The other half of the assertion is the notes themselves. Both are still `available` with their full 3_500¢ after the refresh, because nothing was allocated and so nothing had to be given back. A draft that allocated them would show 3_000¢ due, a consumed note at balance 0, and a refresh would then have to un-consume it — which is exactly the state the gate exists to prevent. Finalized, the same period reads 3_000¢ (derived in b19/credit_note/equal/invoice), so the draft is 7_000¢ higher than what the customer will owe. That is expected behaviour, not a defect, and this row is what stops it from being "fixed" by accident.

Two notes of DIFFERENT sizes drawn on the same invoice, sized so the invoice runs out inside the second one — which is the only arrangement in which the consumption order of credit notes is observable at all. March: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units × 1.00 = 20_000¢. Two notes are raised against it: 4_000¢ off the subscription fee (2 April) and 11_000¢ off the charge fee (3 April). April has no usage, so invoice 1 is the bare 5_000¢ plan. `apply_credits` walks `order(created_at: :asc)` (credit_note_service.rb:70-78) with `remaining_invoice_amount` = 5_000¢. The OLDER note is consumed whole (4_000¢, remaining 1_000¢) and the newer one is then capped by `compute_credit_amount` at that 1_000¢ (credit_note_service.rb:80-86), leaving it 10_000¢ of its 11_000¢ and still `available`. 5_000¢ of credit, nothing due. The invoice cannot tell the two orders apart — either way 5_000¢ of credit clears a 5_000¢ invoice — so the ONLY load-bearing assertion is the surviving balance. Newest-first would have spent 5_000¢ of the big note (balance 6_000¢) and left the 4_000¢ note untouched; pro-rata sharing would leave 7_333¢. 10_000¢ is oldest-first, and nothing else.

Two notes of different sizes, forecast in a period that can absorb the first whole and only part of the second — so the preview has to reproduce not just the total but the split. March: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units = 20_000¢. Notes of 4_000¢ (subscription fee, 2 April) and 11_000¢ (charge fee, 3 April). April carries 30 units of its own, deliberately: a preview over a charge with NO usage in the period dies on nil associations, so the period is given usage and invoice 1 is 5_000 + 3_000 = 8_000¢. Preview and invoice both walk oldest-first: 4_000¢ from the older note, then the newer note capped at the remaining 4_000¢ → 8_000¢ of credit, nothing due. Only the invoice writes it back, so the big note ends at 11_000 − 4_000 = 7_000¢ and stays `available`. Newest-first would give the big note the whole 8_000¢ (balance 3_000¢) and leave the small one untouched — the same 8_000¢ of credit and the same zero due on BOTH surfaces. The forecast total is therefore not the assertion; the surviving balance is, and it is only readable after the real invoice has run.

The unequal pair on a regenerated draft, where the assertion is that the ORDER never got a chance to run. March, finalized out of grace: 5_000¢ plan + 150 units = 20_000¢. Notes of 4_000¢ and 11_000¢ are raised against it. April carries 30 units, so the period is 5_000 + 3_000 = 8_000¢ — the identical period b19/credit_note/unequal/preview forecasts at 0¢ due. The draft reads 8_000¢ with zero credit note (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-366), and the refresh must reproduce that. The newer note is still at its full 11_000¢: had the draft allocated in the documented oldest-first order it would sit at 7_000¢ (the older note absorbing 4_000¢ and this one the remaining 4_000¢), and had it allocated newest-first it would sit at 3_000¢. 11_000¢ says neither happened. That is a stronger statement than the draft total alone. `credit_notes_amount_cents: 0` says the invoice did not SHOW a credit; the untouched balance says no credit note was consumed and silently lost, which is the failure mode a refresh cycle would make permanent.

Two identically configured fixed charges on one plan: 4 units at 100.00 each, twice. 40_000¢ + 40_000¢ = 80_000¢, with the plan at 0¢ so the fixed charges ARE the invoice and the subscription fee is a 0¢ period marker (the convention B13 uses). A fixed charge prices an ADD-ON, and each needs its own add-on here — `FixedCharge`'s code is defaulted from the add-on's code by `Plans::CreateService#fixed_charge_params_with_code` (:150-157), so two charges over one add-on would be a code collision rather than a duplicate. Two add-ons at the same price with the same units is the honest reading of `equal` for this feature, and it is also what makes the two fees separable: `Fee#item_code` is `fixed_charge_add_on.code` for a fixed-charge fee (fee.rb:121), so unlike the two charge fees in b19/charge/equal/invoice these two are distinguishable by content and the per-fee split really can be asserted. `CalculateFeesService#create_fixed_charge_fees` runs as its own producer at :44, independent of `create_charges_fees`, and iterates the plan's fixed charges — so the failure this excludes is one fixed charge being billed and the other silently dropped: 40_000¢ and `fees_count` 2. The add-ons' own `amount_cents` (10_000¢) is deliberately NOT the price: the fixed charge's `properties.amount` is, which is why the fees read 40_000¢ rather than 10_000¢ and why this row would be unchanged if the add-ons were priced differently.

Two equal fixed charges, forecast: 4 × 100.00 twice = 80_000¢, the arithmetic derived in b19/fixed_charge/equal/invoice. The preview builds fixed-charge fees in its own loop, `add_fixed_charge_fees` (preview_service.rb:232-257), which iterates `subscription.fixed_charges` and calls `Fees::FixedChargeService` with `context: :invoice_preview`. The preview is deliberately taken on 20 MARCH, inside the first period: `should_create_fixed_charge_fee?` refuses an arrears fixed charge when `is_starting_subscription?` is true, and that predicate is `invoice_subscriptions.count == 1 && the last one is subscription_starting?` (preview_service.rb:319-330, :447-452). Before the first invoice exists the count is 0, so both fees are built; in the SECOND period the count is exactly 1 and both would be suppressed — a preview of 0¢ against an invoice of 80_000¢, which is a trap and not this cell's subject. `fees_amount_cents` rather than a `fees:` list, on purpose: whether the preview emits the plan's 0¢ subscription fee alongside the two fixed-charge fees is not something this cell should pin (a 0¢ fee changes `fees_count` without changing a cent), and 80_000¢ is the same number either way. One fixed charge lost gives 40_000¢; both charges built from the same add-on's units gives 80_000¢ but is excluded by the invoice sibling's per-fee assertion.

Two equal fixed charges on a draft that is rebuilt: 4 × 100.00 twice = 80_000¢, unchanged from the finalized b19/fixed_charge/equal/invoice because fixed charges are producers and only the three reducers are gated on finalization (calculate_fees_service.rb:44 vs :364-379). This is the surface where BIL-537 lived — a fixed-charge units change that thirty-six B13 rows could not see because none of them held an invoice open long enough to refresh it — so a duplicate fixed charge on a refreshed draft is worth pinning per fee rather than in aggregate. `Invoices::RefreshDraftService` destroys the fees and re-runs the producers, so both fixed charges must be re-found on the plan and each must re-read its OWN units from its own `FixedChargeEvent`. `fees_count: 3` plus the two per-fee lines exclude a rebuild that emitted one fee (40_000¢), one that duplicated a single charge (80_000¢ but with the same `item_code` twice, which the per-fee expectations reject because they name different add-ons), and one that appended to the existing fees rather than replacing them (160_000¢). The three withheld reducers are asserted as 0, per the rule that any row asserting a draft must say so explicitly rather than omit them.

Two fixed charges that differ on BOTH axes a fixed charge has — 4 units at 100.00 = 40_000¢ and 2 units at 300.00 = 60_000¢ — so neither the units nor the unit price of one can be substituted for the other's without changing the answer. 100_000¢ in total, on a 0¢ plan. The numbers are chosen so that every plausible cross-wiring is a different total: swapping the units between the charges gives 20_000 + 120_000 = 140_000¢; applying one charge's price to both gives 80_000¢ or 180_000¢; billing either charge alone gives 40_000¢ or 60_000¢. That matters because a fixed charge's units live on a `FixedChargeEvent` emitted at creation rather than in the charge row that prices them (`FixedCharges::EmitEventsService`), so units and price are read from two different places and a duplicate is the case where they can be paired up wrongly. Per-fee assertion is available here — `Fee#item_code` is the add-on's code for a fixed-charge fee (fee.rb:121) and the two add-ons differ — so the split is asserted rather than just the total, which is what makes the cross-wiring counterfactuals above detectable at all rather than only the "one charge lost" one. Both charges are arrears and not prorated, and the subscription runs a whole calendar month, so no proration coefficient enters and the row is not calendar-sensitive.

Two fixed charges differing in units AND price, forecast: 4 × 100.00 = 40_000¢ plus 2 × 300.00 = 60_000¢ = 100_000¢ (derived in b19/fixed_charge/unequal/invoice). 100_000¢ is not reachable by any pairing mistake the preview's separate loop could make — swapped units give 140_000¢, one charge's price applied to both gives 80_000¢ or 180_000¢, either charge alone gives 40_000¢ or 60_000¢ — so the total alone carries the assertion even though the per-fee split is not asserted on this surface. As in the equal sibling, the preview is taken inside the FIRST period on purpose: `should_create_fixed_charge_fee?` suppresses an arrears fixed charge while `is_starting_subscription?` holds, which is true only once one invoice_subscription exists (preview_service.rb:319-330, :447-452), so a preview taken in April would quote 0¢ against a 100_000¢ invoice. Both fixed charges reach `Fees::FixedChargeService` with `context: :invoice_preview` and each reads its own units from its own `FixedChargeEvent`, which is the pairing this row exists to check. `fees_amount_cents` rather than `fees_count`: whether the 0¢ subscription fee of a 0¢ plan appears in a preview payload is not this cell's subject, and it moves the count without moving a cent.
