Progressive billing is the one reducer that is NOT gated on finalization: Credits:: ProgressiveBillingService runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:53, above the three `not_in_finalizing_process?` guards at :364-379. So the draft both books the 3_000¢ credit and calls apply_credit_to_fees (progressive_billing_service.rb:68-84), which pushes the credit into the charge fee's precise_coupons_amount_cents. fee.sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents is `amount_cents - precise_coupons_amount_cents` (fee.rb:238-240) = 0, so the fee's own tax is 0 and the invoice's is 0 too. A draft that showed the credit at invoice level but not at fee level would read taxes 600¢ and a 600¢ total — tax charged twice on usage already taxed on the threshold invoice. That is exactly what b21/b5/preview finds on the OTHER surface, which is why this row asserts taxes_amount_cents explicitly rather than only the total: 0 and 0 look identical in a total that is zero either way. The threshold invoice is asserted too, and asserted as `finalized`: Invoices:: ProgressiveBillingService ends in Invoices::FinalizeService.call! (:47) without ever consulting grace_period?, so a threshold invoice is never a draft — the grace period only reaches the period invoice, and a row that assumed otherwise would be selecting the wrong invoice.

PINS F84, AND THE TWO SURFACES DISAGREE. The same period is quoted on 20 March and then issued on 1 April, and the issued invoice is asserted in the same row so the gap is a fact rather than a claim: 0¢ due, 600¢ quoted. Both surfaces agree on the credit. Invoices::PreviewService#apply_progressive_billing_credits (preview_service.rb:330-359) deliberately reuses the read-only Subscriptions:: ProgressiveBilledAmount, so it finds the same 3_000¢ and :302 subtracts it from sub_total_excluding_taxes — 3_000 − 0 − 3_000 = 0 on both surfaces. They disagree on the tax, and the reason is one missing line. The real pipeline calls apply_credit_to_fees, so the charge fee carries precise_coupons_amount_cents 3_000 and Fees::ApplyTaxesService taxes `fee.sub_total_excluding_taxes_amount_cents` = 0 (apply_taxes_service.rb:38, fee.rb:238-240). The preview's copy of the arithmetic bumps only the invoice-level counter and never touches a fee, so :309 taxes the GROSS 3_000¢ at 20% = 600¢, and :312-317 then reads sub_total_including 0 + 600 and a total of 600¢. So the preview quotes 600¢ of VAT on a taxable base it has itself computed as zero — tax on usage the customer already paid tax on, on the threshold invoice this row also asserts. It is the exact shape of F70 reached from the other side: there the invoice lost the per-fee reduction because a churn broke the charge_id join, here the preview never attempts one. A zero-tax scenario cannot see this at all, which is why this row carries VAT while b05/fixed/single/credited-on-final does not: with rate 0 both surfaces read 0 and agree.

The same period as b21/b5/draft, rebuilt from scratch, and the interesting number is that the credit is booked ONCE and not twice. Invoices::RefreshDraftService#reset_invoice_values destroys the fees AND `invoice.credits.progressive_billing_invoice_kind` (refresh_draft_service.rb:123) before zeroing progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents (:132). Credits::ProgressiveBillingService then runs again on the rebuilt fees and re-derives the same 3_000¢ from Subscriptions:: ProgressiveBilledAmount, whose to_credit_amount is the threshold invoice's fees_amount_cents net of coupons, its own progressive credits and its credit notes (progressive_billed_amount.rb:60-64) — a figure that does not move when a different invoice is refreshed. Had the reset missed the Credit rows, the second pass would ADD another 3_000¢ and the invoice would read progressive_billing_credit 6_000¢ against 3_000¢ of fees; had it missed apply_credit_to_fees, the per-fee reduction would be lost and the 600¢ of tax would reappear. The row asserts progressive_billing_credit_amount_cents, sub_total and taxes together because the total is 0 under all three readings and cannot separate them. `refresh_invoice` names its target with `select: {invoice_type: subscription}` rather than defaulting to the newest: the newest invoice here is the period invoice by creation order, but the threshold invoice is finalized and PUT /invoices/:id/refresh on it would be a no-op (refresh_draft_service.rb:32 `return result unless invoice.draft?`) — a silent pass.

b06/granted/none/partial-cover held open. That row's finalized invoice reads fees 3_000¢, prepaid_credit 1_000¢, total 2_000¢, and the wallet ends empty. The draft reads 3_000¢ due and the wallet still full. should_create_applied_prepaid_credit? begins `return false if not_in_finalizing_process?` (calculate_fees_service.rb:375-379), so Credits::AppliedPrepaidCreditsService never runs and no WalletTransaction is written. Both halves are asserted because either alone is ambiguous. prepaid_credit_amount_cents 0 with an empty wallet would mean the credits were spent and the invoice failed to record it — money gone with nothing to show for it. A full wallet with a 2_000¢ total would mean the reverse. 0 and 1_000 together are the only reading in which nothing has happened yet. And nothing happening yet is right: the gate is what makes a grace period reversible. Were a draft to burn 1_000¢ of prepaid credit, a refresh would have to give it back, and Invoices:: RefreshDraftService has no code that does — it recredits nothing (compare Invoices::VoidService, which recredits coupons and wallet transactions explicitly, :37-49). The draft overstating by 1_000¢ is the price of never having to un-spend a wallet.

The two surfaces AGREE, and the row is built so that agreement is not free. Both read fees 3_000¢, prepaid_credit 1_000¢, total 2_000¢ — the preview on 20 March and the invoice b06/granted/none/partial-cover already pins on 1 April. PreviewService reaches it through its own #create_applied_prepaid_credits (preview_service.rb:369-378), which calls the SAME Credits::AllocatePrepaidCreditsByWalletsService the real pipeline calls; that service only computes a hash of wallet → amount and writes nothing (allocate_prepaid_credits_by_wallets_ service.rb:29-67), which is why it can be reused on an unpersisted invoice. The proof that the preview did not spend the credits is the INVOICE, not the wallet. The wallet ends at 0 because the 1 April invoice spent it; had the 20 March preview spent it first, the invoice would have found an empty wallet, reported prepaid_credit 0 and billed the full 3_000¢ — and the wallet would read 0 in that world too. So `invoice.prepaid_credit_amount_cents: 1000` is the assertion and `wallet.balance_cents: 0` is the control that the credits were consumed exactly once, by the surface entitled to consume them. This is the reducer that the draft withholds and the preview reports, on one scenario, in two rows — which is the whole point of separating the surfaces rather than adding an axis.

The b21/b6/draft period rebuilt. Same numbers, and the wallet is the assertion. PUT /invoices/:id/refresh calls Invoices::RefreshDraftService with the default `context: :refresh`, so CalculateFeesService still answers true to not_in_finalizing_process? and the prepaid-credit gate is still shut — a refresh is a recomputation, not a partial finalization. The wallet at 1_000¢ after TWO passes over the same period is what a row that only refreshed once could not say. Had the gate depended on how many times the invoice was computed rather than on the context, the second pass would have spent the credits on an invoice that is still a draft, and the eventual finalization would spend them again — the double-spend shape the B20 lead found in credit notes, in the wallet. Compare b21/b6/preview, where the same 1_000¢ IS reported: the difference between the two rows is not the wallet, it is whether the surface intends to collect.

b08/manual-full/credit/plain, followed by a second period held open. March is finalized by hand out of its grace period and credited in full, exactly as that row does: 30 units × 1.00 = 3_000¢ of fees, a 3_000¢ spendable note. April then accrues 20 units = 2_000¢ and, finalized, would spend 2_000¢ of the note — Credits::CreditNoteService#apply_credits takes min(balance, remaining invoice amount) (credit_note_service.rb:40-46) — leaving credit_notes_amount_cents 2_000, a total of 0 and a balance of 1_000. As a draft it reads 2_000¢ due and the note untouched at 3_000¢. should_create_credit_note_credit? is `!not_in_finalizing_process?` (calculate_fees_service.rb:364-366), the bluntest of the three guards. The note is asserted with `select: {index: -1}` rather than bare, because a bare credit_note expectation compares the payload captured when the note was CREATED — on 3 April, before April's invoice existed — and would report balance 3_000¢ whether or not the draft had spent it. The whole row would pass while asserting nothing. This is the pair the B20 lead turned on, in the direction where the gate helps: there the credit was diverted into a note that a finalized invoice spent on the spot, so the total came out right and only the draft showed the double-bill. Here the withholding is what it is designed to be — the customer sees 2_000¢ due, will be billed 0, and the note is still theirs.

The two surfaces AGREE, and the credit note is the reducer for which agreement was least obvious — it is the one the B20 lead caught the draft withholding. March is finalized at 3_000¢ and credited in full; April accrues 20 units = 2_000¢ and both surfaces settle it at 0 with credit_notes_amount_cents 2_000 — the preview on 20 April and the finalized invoice on 1 May, asserted side by side. The preview reaches it through Invoices::Preview::CreditsService#persisted_credits, which calls the very same Credits::CreditNoteService with `context: :preview`. That context skips every write — no Credit row, no apply_credit_to_fees, no update_remaining_credit (credit_note_service.rb:47-63) — but the invoice-level counter is bumped regardless, at :67, so the breakdown is reported as fully as on a real invoice. Two routes worth naming as excluded: a preview reporting the right total with a 0¢ breakdown (the total is computed at :317 from a credit_notes_amount_cents that is still zero, and only :320-321 subtracts the credits, so the field could easily have been left behind), and a preview that ignored inbound notes altogether and quoted 2_000¢ due. The note's balance is asserted at 1_000¢ with `select: {index: -1}` — the 3_000¢ note less the 2_000¢ the FINALIZED invoice spent, and NOT less a further 2_000¢ for the preview. A bare credit_note expectation would compare the payload captured on 2 April, before either surface had seen the note, and would report 3_000¢ whatever happened afterwards. So the balance at 1_000¢ and the invoice's own credit_notes_amount_cents at 2_000¢ are together the proof that the note was read twice and spent once. Compare b21/b8/draft, where the same note is neither: 2_000¢ due, 3_000¢ still on the books.

The b21/b8/draft scenario with April rebuilt, and the number that matters is the note's balance after a refresh: still 3_000¢, not 1_000¢. Invoices::RefreshDraftService#reset_invoice_values nulls the fee_id of the items belonging to credit notes RAISED FROM this invoice (:120) and re-points them afterwards through CreditNotes::RefreshDraftService. The note here was raised from MARCH's invoice, so it is not in `invoice.credit_notes` at all and none of that machinery touches it — it is an inbound balance, reachable only through Credits::CreditNoteService, which the refresh does not reach because context is `:refresh` and the guard at :364 holds. Two failure modes are excluded. If a refresh had counted as finalizing, the draft would read credit_notes 2_000 / total 0 and the note would sit at 1_000¢ — spent against an invoice nobody has issued, and spent AGAIN at finalization if the recredit path were missed. If the refresh had instead confused the inbound note with an outbound one, its items would have been re-pointed at April's fees and the March credit would be attached to the wrong period. `select: {index: 1}` on the refresh is load-bearing: index 0 is March, which is finalized, and refresh_draft_service.rb:32 returns early on anything that is not a draft — so a defaulted selector that drifted to March would make this row pass having refreshed nothing.

b09/create-mid-period/arrears/none held open, and it must be identical: 16–31 March is 16 days at 3_100¢ / 31 = 100¢ per day = 1_600¢, on the window 16–31 rather than 1–31. Proration is entirely producer-side. Fees::SubscriptionService runs at calculate_fees_service.rb:44, above the finalizing gate, and the window comes from DatesService#from_datetime clamping the computed 1 March to started_at (dates_service.rb:73-75) — nothing in either path consults the invoice's status. So this cell is an AGREEMENT, and the reason to pin it is that the whole B9 block had only ever measured proration on the finalized path: with sixteen of twenty blocks in that position, "the first invoice is prorated" and "the first invoice is prorated whenever we look at it" were the same statement, and only one of them had a test. from_date and to_date are asserted, not just the amount, for the same reason the borrowed row asserts them: a draft charging the right 1_600¢ for the wrong 1–31 March window would otherwise pass, and that window is what the customer reads.

"What will my first invoice be?" asked on 20 March, four days into a subscription that started on the 16th, and then compared with the invoice itself. Both must say 1_600¢ for 16–31 March. The preview does NOT price the period it is asked in. PreviewService#billing_time is `end_of_periods.first + 1.day` (preview_service.rb:145) where end_of_period comes from a current_usage DatesService at Time.current, so a preview taken on 20 March resolves 31 March + 1 = 1 April and then computes boundaries AT that instant — which is why it forecasts the same period perform_billing raises on 1 April rather than the period after it. This is the projection context (`fetch_context` returns :default for a live subscription, :81-85; Preview::SubscriptionsService #context returns :projection because subscriptions.external_ids is present), and it is what a row meaning "predict my next invoice" has to be in: with no external_ids the request would silently become a PROPOSAL, which skips charge fees entirely and would answer this question with 0. A preview that fell into the following period would read 3_100¢ on 1–30 April, and one that priced the current period without the started_at clamp would read 3_100¢ on 1–31 March. Both are plausible readings of "next invoice" and both are wrong; the fee window is what tells them apart, so it is asserted on the preview as well as on the invoice.

The same partial period rebuilt on 2 April — a day AFTER the period it prices ended, which is the reason this cell is not a duplicate of b21/b9/draft. A refresh does not remember the boundaries; it recomputes them. Invoices::RefreshDraftService#reset_invoice_values destroys the invoice_subscriptions outright (:122) and CreateInvoiceSubscriptionService is called again with `refresh: true` at a timestamp taken from the destroyed row — `invoice_subscriptions.first&.timestamp` (refresh_draft_service.rb:96-104), i.e. 1 April, NOT the 2 April wall clock. That indirection is the whole assertion: if the refresh had used Time.current, DatesService would resolve the period containing 2 April and bill 1–30 April, and the customer would be charged 3_100¢ for a month they have not had while the 16 prorated days vanished. 1_600¢ on 16–31 March therefore excludes three implementations at once: the correct one, the wall-clock one (3_100¢ on 1–30 April), and one that recomputed the period correctly but lost the started_at clamp (3_100¢ on 1–31 March). Only the fee window separates the last two, which is why fees_count and both dates are asserted rather than the total alone. This is BIL-537's shape without its bug: there a refresh deleted a fee it should have kept, here it rebuilds one it must reproduce exactly.

THE CUMULATIVENESS ROW for count_agg, and the pairing is the whole assertion: after both periods are billed, current usage is 0 and lifetime usage is 700¢. Those two numbers in the same row are what distinguishes this surface from B7's current-usage slice, where the same timing legitimately reports 0. 700¢ is derived, not observed: CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `invoice.fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over EVERY finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the lineage — 3 March events → 300¢ plus 4 April events → 400¢. A per-period implementation would report 400¢ (only the invoice just produced); one that reset on billing would report 0¢; one that double-counted the period being billed would report 1_100¢. Both invoices are asserted so the addends are checkable independently of the sum. current_usage_amount_cents is 0 because the May period is empty and CalculateService recomputes the current component on every run (calculate_service.rb:28), and 0 is asserted rather than omitted: a stale current component left at April's 400¢ would make lifetime usage 1_100¢ and double-bill anything measured against it. perform_billing runs a usage update of its own (ScenariosHelper#perform_billing:431-437), and the May 1 invoice re-flags the row (Invoices::SubscriptionService#flag_lifetime_usage_for_refresh:203-205 → FlagRefreshFromInvoiceService:18-25), so this read is of a freshly recalculated row, not a stale one.

Two periods, read in the middle of the second. March carries 3 events, April 4, and count_agg prices event CARDINALITY: 3 units → 300¢ and 4 units → 400¢ at 1.00 per unit. The event property `amount` is deliberately populated with 10/30/20 (/40) even though count_agg has no field_name — an implementation that summed the field would report 60 in March and 100 in April, a max 30/40, a latest 20/40, so every neighbouring aggregation gives a different number here. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is NOT the current period: LifetimeUsages::CalculateService# calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the subscription lineage, so it is 300¢ — March, carried forward across the boundary. current_usage_amount_cents is the live per-period figure (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56, Invoices::CustomerUsageService with apply_taxes: false), so it is April's 400¢. The row asserts April's 400¢ TWICE — once through GET /customers/:id/current_usage and once as lifetime usage's current component — which is what pins them to the same source; a lifetime figure that quietly kept its own accumulator would diverge here. The 700¢ total the two columns sum to (lifetime_usage.rb:23-25) is the whole point of the surface: current usage alone can never report it. The read is armed, not stale: the April events create a UsageMonitoring::SubscriptionActivity (Events::PostProcessService#track_subscription_activity → TrackSubscriptionActivityService:25), and perform_usage_update's ProcessAllSubscriptionActivities pass recalculates the current component on every run (process_subscription_activity_service.rb:30-31). Clock::RefreshLifetime UsagesJob alone would NOT have refreshed it — it only picks rows with recalculate_invoiced_usage true (refresh_lifetime_usages_job.rb:14-19), and that flag was already consumed by the April 1 billing run.

The instant is chosen so an off-by-one moves the number in BOTH directions. The fourth April event is timestamped 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z — the last representable second of the calendar month — and the read happens at that same instant. Invoices::CustomerUsageService#boundaries (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180) asks Subscriptions::DatesService with current_usage: true, so charges_to_datetime is the period end: the boundary event is INSIDE April and the count is 4 → 400¢. Drop the last second (an exclusive upper comparison) and the count is 3 → 300¢. Roll the period one second early and the current period is May, empty, → 0¢. Only at this instant do those three implementations disagree. invoiced_usage_amount_cents stays 300¢ — March's charge fee, summed over the subscription's invoices by CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) — which is the cumulativeness claim: the boundary read does not fold April into the invoiced column, and it does not lose March either. `amount` values 10/30/20/40 are carried on the events so a regression to sum (100), max (40) or latest (40) is a different number from 400¢ by coincidence only in cents, and differs in `units` (4 vs 100/40/40).

March 10/30/20 on the 5th, 10th and 20th → latest 20 units → 2_000¢; April 25/5/15 on the same days → latest 15 units → 1_500¢ (LatestService, latest_service.rb:16-18, over the store's `last` ordered `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC`, postgres_store.rb:235). Both invoices are pinned so the addends are checkable, and invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 3_500¢ — CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` across every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the lineage. 3_500¢ is the number that shows what lifetime usage actually accumulates. Re-running latest_agg over the subscription's entire history would return 15 units → 1_500¢ and be indistinguishable from April alone; a per-period column would give 1_500¢; reset-on-billing 0¢; counting the just-billed period twice 5_000¢. Current usage is 0 in the empty May period, and the pair — 0 on the current-usage surface, 3_500¢ on lifetime — is the assertion. A current component left stale at April's 1_500¢ would put the total at 5_000¢, which is exactly the double-count a usage threshold measured against lifetime usage would act on.

latest_agg prices the last event of the PERIOD by timestamp — LatestService#compute_aggregation (latest_service.rb:16-18) delegates to the store's `last`, which orders `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC` (postgres_store.rb:235). March's events are 10, 30, 20 on the 5th, 10th and 20th, so the answer is the LAST one, 20 units → 2_000¢, and neither the largest (30 → 3_000¢) nor the sum (60 → 6_000¢). April's are 25, 5, 15 on the 5th, 10th and 20th → 15 units → 1_500¢, again distinct from max (25 → 2_500¢) and sum (45 → 4_500¢), and the two periods differ so a swap between the columns shows. Read mid-April: invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 2_000¢ — March's charge fee, still there — because CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums charge fee CENTS over the subscription's invoices; it does not re-run latest_agg over the whole life, which would return April's 15 units and lose March entirely. current_usage_amount_cents is April's 1_500¢ (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56), asserted a second time through GET /customers/:id/current_usage so both surfaces are pinned to one source. The 3_500¢ they sum to (lifetime_usage.rb:23-25) is what a usage threshold reads and what current usage can never report.

latest_agg is the aggregation for which the boundary event is always load-bearing: it IS the answer. April's last event carries 15 units and is timestamped 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, the last representable second of the period, and the read is at that same instant. LatestService (latest_service.rb:16-18) takes the store's `last`, ordered `timestamp DESC, created_at DESC` (postgres_store.rb:235), within boundaries taken from Subscriptions::DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180) → 15 units → 1_500¢. Lose the last second to an exclusive upper comparison and the latest becomes the 5 → 500¢; roll the period one second early and April is not the current period → 0¢. All three timestamps are distinct, so `last` has no tie to break arbitrarily. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 2_000¢: March's latest, 20 units, priced at 1.00 and carried past the boundary by CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52), which sums charge fee cents on the subscription's invoices. A lifetime figure that re-ran latest_agg over the whole subscription would answer 15 units for everything and March would vanish.

5_500¢ is the number that proves lifetime usage accumulates PRICED FEES rather than re-aggregating events. March max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units → 3_000¢; April max(5, 15, 25) = 25 units → 2_500¢; and CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over both invoices → 5_500¢. A lifetime figure computed by taking the maximum over the subscription's whole event history would report 30 units → 3_000¢ and be indistinguishable from March alone; a per-period column would report 2_500¢; a reset-on-billing column 0¢. Each invoice is asserted separately so the two addends are checkable. Current usage is 0 in the fresh, empty May period, and asserting it in the same row is what makes the pair meaningful: the current-usage surface says 0 while lifetime says 5_500¢, and that difference is the only reason this surface exists. A current component left stale at April's 2_500¢ would make the total 8_000¢.

max_agg is where lifetime usage's real definition shows: units do NOT accumulate but MONEY does. March max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units → 3_000¢ (sum would give 60, latest 20 — the largest value sits in the middle of the three so a regression to either neighbour changes the answer). April max(5, 15, 25) = 25 units → 2_500¢. Nothing anywhere adds 30 and 25 into a 55-unit maximum: CalculateService# calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) accumulates `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` — CENTS off already-priced fees — so invoiced_usage is 3_000¢ and, once April is billed too, becomes 5_500¢. That is the derivation a reader most needs: a lifetime figure built by re-aggregating raw events over the subscription's whole life would report max(10,30,20,5,15,25) = 30 units → 3_000¢ for the two periods together, and would be indistinguishable from March alone. current_usage_amount_cents is April's 2_500¢ (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56), asserted a second time through the current-usage endpoint so the two surfaces are pinned to one source.

The boundary event is deliberately the largest one: April's 25-unit event lands at 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, the last representable second of the period, and the read is at that same instant. max(5, 15, 25) = 25 units → 2_500¢. Drop the last second and the maximum falls to 15 → 1_500¢; roll the period one second early and April is not the current period at all → 0¢. Invoices::CustomerUsageService#boundaries (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180) takes charges_to_datetime from Subscriptions::DatesService with current_usage: true, which is what makes 2_500¢ the correct answer. Choosing the maximum as the boundary event is what gives the off-by-one somewhere to show: had it been the 5, excluding it would have left the answer unchanged and the row would have guarded nothing. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is March's 3_000¢ — max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units priced at 1.00 — and it is still there at the boundary because CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums charge fee CENTS over the subscription's invoices and is indifferent to which period is being read.

The sharpest cell of the slice, asserted as a pair: current usage RESETS at the boundary and lifetime usage MUST NOT. March 60 units → 6_000¢ and April 45 units → 4_500¢ are each pinned on their own invoice, and lifetime usage's invoiced column is their sum, 10_500¢ — CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` across every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the lineage, so the addends and the total are independently checkable in this one row. The wrong answers are all nameable: 4_500¢ if the column were per-period, 0¢ if billing reset it, 15_000¢ if the period being billed were counted both as invoiced and as current. current usage is 0 in the fresh May period — asserted, not skipped, because a stale current component would leave lifetime at 15_000¢ and silently inflate anything measured against it. The row reads a freshly recalculated state: the May 1 invoice sets recalculate_invoiced_usage (Invoices::SubscriptionService:203-205 → FlagRefreshFromInvoiceService:18-25) and perform_billing's own usage update (ScenariosHelper:431-437) consumes it.

March 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 units → 6_000¢; April 25 + 5 + 15 = 45 units → 4_500¢, at 1.00 per unit. Both periods use three events whose sum, max and latest all differ (March: 60/30/20; April: 45/25/15), so nothing here collapses onto a neighbouring aggregation, and the two periods carry different totals so a swap between the columns is visible. Read halfway through the second period: invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 6_000¢ — March's charge fee, still there after the boundary, because CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums charge fees over the subscription's invoices rather than over the current period. current_usage_amount_cents is April's 4_500¢ (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56). The same 4_500¢ is asserted a second time through GET /customers/:id/current_usage, which is what proves the two surfaces read one source; the 10_500¢ they sum to (lifetime_usage.rb:23-25) is what a usage threshold would be measured against and what current usage cannot express. A lifetime column that had reset at the April 1 boundary would report invoiced 0¢.

The third April event carries 15 units and is timestamped 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, the last representable second of the period, and the read happens at that same instant. April's sum is 25 + 5 + 15 = 45 units → 4_500¢. An exclusive upper boundary that dropped the last second would report 30 units → 3_000¢; a period roll one second early would put the read in an empty May and report 0¢. Invoices::CustomerUsageService#boundaries (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180) takes charges_to_datetime from Subscriptions::DatesService with current_usage: true, so the correct answer is 4_500¢ and the two wrong ones are 1_500¢ and 4_500¢ apart respectively — an off-by-one invisible at any other instant. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 6_000¢ throughout: March's 60 units, held across the boundary by CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52), which sums charge fees on the subscription's invoices and has no notion of the period being read. The row therefore pins both halves at the one instant where the split is most fragile.

March mar_a/mar_b/mar_b → 2 distinct → 200¢; April apr_a/apr_b/apr_b/apr_c → 3 distinct → 300¢ (UniqueCountQuery#operation_value_sql, unique_count_query.rb:276-287, scores each repeated add as 0, so count_agg's 3 and 4 are visibly different numbers). Both invoices are pinned, and invoiced_usage_amount_cents is their sum, 500¢ — CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` across every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the lineage. Per-period would give 300¢, reset-on-billing 0¢, double-counting the billed period 800¢. The 500¢ is a sum of PRICED FEES, not a distinct count over the subscription's whole life — a distinction this row can only hint at, since the two ref namespaces were kept disjoint so both readings coincide; the max_agg after-billing row is where they separate. Current usage is 0 in the empty May period, asserted so that the pair — 0 on the current-usage surface, 500¢ on lifetime — is what the row records, and so a stale current component left at 300¢ shows up as 800¢.

March ingests refs mar_a, mar_b, mar_b — three events, two distinct properties. Postgres UniqueCountQuery#operation_value_sql (unique_count_query.rb:276-287) scores a repeated `add` for a property already added as 0, so the aggregation is 2 units → 200¢, where count_agg on the same events would give 3 → 300¢. April ingests apr_a, apr_b, apr_b, apr_c — four events, three distinct → 3 units → 300¢ against count_agg's 4 → 400¢. Every period therefore contains the duplicate that separates unique_count from count. Distinctness is scoped to the period, not to the subscription's life: the metric is non-recurring, so UniqueCountService sets event_store.use_from_boundary = true (unique_count_service.rb:11) and each period aggregates only its own events. Lifetime usage nonetheless carries March forward — invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 200¢ because CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums charge fee cents across the subscription's invoices — while current_usage_amount_cents is April's 300¢ (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56). Note what the sum of 500¢ is NOT: a distinct count over both periods, which would also be 5 here only because the ref namespaces were kept disjoint on purpose.

The boundary event carries a ref nobody has sent before — apr_c at 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, the last representable second of the period — so it is the third distinct value and moves the answer if it is lost. April is apr_a, apr_b, apr_b, apr_c: four events, three distinct (UniqueCountQuery#operation_value_sql, unique_count_query.rb:276-287, scores the repeated apr_b as 0) → 3 units → 300¢. An exclusive upper boundary that dropped the last second would report 2 → 200¢; a period roll one second early would read an empty May → 0¢. A duplicate ref at the boundary would have hidden both. March is mar_a, mar_b, mar_b → 2 distinct → 200¢, and that is what invoiced_usage_amount_cents still reports at the boundary: CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums charge fee cents on the subscription's invoices, so the March figure survives the roll while current_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56) tracks April's open period.

Two exact weighted periods, then the cumulative claim. WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql (weighted_sum_query.rb:102-118) weights each running total by the seconds until the next event over charges_duration, with the upper edge at to_datetime.ceil (postgres_store.rb:358). MARCH — 31 days: events on the 10th (+10), 13th (+30), 25th (+20) held 3, 12 and 7 days → (10x3 + 40x12 + 60x7)/31 = 930/31 = 30.0 units → 3_000¢. APRIL — 30 days: events on the 3rd, 6th, 9th held 3, 3 and 22 days → (10x3 + 40x3 + 60x22)/30 = 1470/30 = 49.0 units → 4_900¢. The metric is non-recurring, so April starts from initial_value 0 (WeightedSumService#initial_value, weighted_sum_service.rb:91-95) rather than inheriting March's 60 — a recurring metric would carry the running total forward and April would price the whole period at 60 units, 6_000¢. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is 7_900¢ = 3_000 + 4_900, both addends pinned on their own invoice: CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52) sums `fees.charge.sum(:amount_cents)` over every finalized-or-draft subscription invoice of the lineage. Per-period would report 4_900¢, reset-on-billing 0¢, double-counting 12_800¢. Current usage is 0 in the empty May period and is asserted alongside, because that pair — 0 on the current-usage surface, 7_900¢ on lifetime — is the entire distinction the surface exists to make.

Postgres WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql (weighted_sum_query.rb:102-118) sums, per event, the running total up to that event multiplied by the seconds until the next event, divided by charges_duration in seconds; the upper edge is to_datetime.ceil, i.e. the next period's midnight (postgres_store.rb:358). Every timestamp is chosen so both periods come out exact. MARCH — 31 days = 2_678_400s. Events on the 10th (+10), 13th (+30), 25th (+20) give running totals 10, 40, 60 held for 3, 12 and 7 days: (10x3 + 40x12 + 60x7) / 31 = 930/31 = 30.0 units → 3_000¢. APRIL — 30 days = 2_592_000s. Events on the 3rd, 6th, 9th give 10, 40, 60 held for 3, 3 and 22 days: (10x3 + 40x3 + 60x22) / 30 = 1470/30 = 49.0 units → 4_900¢. Both are integers by construction, so a wrong month length is not hidden by rounding — hence calendar_sensitive. The three events per period carry 10/30/20, so plain sum would report 60 units (6_000¢), max 30 (3_000¢), latest 20 (2_000¢): none of them is 4_900¢, and none is 3_000¢ in April. The mid-period read at April 25 is nonetheless 4_900¢ and not a pro-rated fraction of it, because current usage weights to the END of the period (customer_usage_service.rb:162-180, DatesService with current_usage: true) rather than to "now" — an implementation that weighted to the read instant would report (10x3 + 40x3 + 60x16)/30 = 39.0 units → 3_900¢. invoiced_usage_amount_cents is March's 3_000¢, carried across the boundary by CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52); current_usage_amount_cents is April's 4_900¢ (calculate_service.rb:28 → :54-56), asserted twice so the current-usage endpoint and lifetime usage's current column are pinned to one source.

Read at 2024-04-30T23:59:59Z, the last representable second of April. For weighted_sum the boundary bites on PERIOD SELECTION rather than on event inclusion: an event landing at the boundary would be held for ~0 seconds and contribute nothing (WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql, weighted_sum_query.rb:102-118, returns 0 for a zero-length interval), so the sharp question is which period the read belongs to. At 23:59:59 April is still current and the answer is 4_900¢; one second later the current period is May, empty, and the answer is 0¢. A period roll implemented one second early therefore produces a 4_900¢ error visible only here. APRIL — 30 days = 2_592_000s, events on the 3rd (+10), 6th (+30), 9th (+20) → running totals 10, 40, 60 held for 3, 3 and 22 days to the upper edge to_datetime.ceil = 2024-05-01T00:00:00 (postgres_store.rb:358): (10x3 + 40x3 + 60x22)/30 = 1470/30 = 49.0 units → 4_900¢. Note this is unchanged from the mid-period read: the weighted sum projects to the end of the period, so moving the read from April 25 to the last second changes nothing — which is exactly why an implementation that weighted to "now" instead would be caught, reporting 60x22 → the full 49.0 only here and 39.0 (3_900¢) at April 25. MARCH — 31 days: (10x3 + 40x12 + 60x7)/31 = 930/31 = 30.0 units → 3_000¢, and that is invoiced_usage_amount_cents at the boundary, carried forward by CalculateService#calculate_invoiced_usage_amount_cents (calculate_service.rb:41-52). Both figures are integers by construction, so a wrong month length cannot be absorbed by rounding.

What the invariant MEANS once an invoice exists: usage is per-period, so the read taken after March was billed must describe April alone, and it must equal the invoice April then produces. March's 3 events -> 3 units -> 300¢ on invoice[index=0]; April's 2 events -> 2 units (CountService:9) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 200¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted BOTH as the usage read on 25 April — after the March invoice exists — and as the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. Both April figures are 200 and not 500: current usage takes charges_from_datetime from the CURRENT period (customer_usage_service.rb:162) and the metric is non-recurring, so March's units do not carry. If either surface reported 500 the customer would be charged twice for March on one side of the product and not the other — asserting the two together is what makes a one-sided leak visible.

The final usage read and the final invoice. 3 events -> 3 units (CountService:9) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 300¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted as the last usage read the customer can obtain and again as the termination invoice. The read is taken at 10:00 and the DELETE at 12:00 on purpose: GET current_usage resolves the subscription through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216), so once terminated the endpoint answers no_active_subscription and there is no usage surface left to compare — the last obtainable read IS the one that must match. The two windows are not identical (usage still ends at the period end, the invoice ends at terminated_at, dates_service.rb:117), but count_agg depends only on WHICH events fall inside, and every event is before 20 March, so the two must agree exactly. The plan is 0¢, so invoice.fees_amount_cents carries only the charge and equals the usage figure directly.

ONE derivation, asserted on BOTH surfaces. count_agg counts events, not their values (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::CountService:9 — event_store.count), so the three events give 3 units, priced by ChargeModels::StandardService:8 as 3 x 1.00 = 3.00 EUR, rounded to cents at Fees::ChargeService:295 -> 300¢. The SAME three events would give 60 under sum_agg, 30 under max_agg and 20 under latest_agg, so the number is aggregation-specific rather than an artefact of the fixture. 300¢ is then asserted twice: as current usage read on 10 March (Invoices::CustomerUsageService#compute_charge_fees:120, context :current_usage) and as the charge fee on the invoice April's billing run produces (Invoices::CalculateFeesService:136, no usage context). These are two different call paths into Fees::ChargeService and nothing else in the suite compares them. No event is ingested after the snapshot, so the two figures MUST be equal — a divergence means one of the two paths mis-aggregates or mis-prices the same events, and the failure names which side moved. The plan is 0¢ so that invoice.fees_amount_cents carries only the charge and the equality is not destroyed by a legitimate subscription fee.

The canonical form of the invariant for count_agg: the usage read in the LAST hour of the period is the number the customer sees just before being billed, and it must be the number they are billed. 3 events -> 3 units (CountService:9) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 300¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted as current usage on 31 March 23:00 and again as the charge fee on the invoice produced at 01:00 on 1 April. Both reads span the identical window: current usage takes charges_to_datetime from Subscriptions::DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162,179) which for a calendar month is end_of_month (monthly_service.rb:25) — the very boundary the invoice uses. A divergence here is the defect this block exists for: usage and invoice disagreeing over the same closed period with the same events.

March's last event is 20 -> 2_000¢ on invoice[index=0]. April's last event is 7, so 7 units (LatestService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 700¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted both as the usage read on 25 April — taken after the March invoice exists — and as the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. latest_agg is the aggregation where "after billing" is least obvious: the last event of the PERIOD is not the last event of the subscription's life, and LatestService relies on the event store's from-boundary (latest_service.rb:16, use_from_boundary defaulting to true) to tell them apart. The row pins the period reading — 700, not 2_000 — on both surfaces, so a path that reached back past the period boundary fails whichever side did it.

The last event before termination carries 20, so 20 units (LatestService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 2_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295) — the final usage read at 10:00 on 20 March and the invoice the DELETE raises at 12:00, both asserted against that derivation. The read must precede the DELETE: current_usage resolves the subscription through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216). Truncating the window to terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117) cannot change which event is last here, because all three are on 4-6 March and inside both windows — so the numbers must agree, and if they do not, the closing invoice is reading a different "latest" than the surface the customer watched.

latest_agg takes the value of the last event by timestamp (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::LatestService:16 — event_store.last), so 10 on 4 March, 30 on the 5th and 20 on the 6th give 20 units x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 2_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). The three events are ingested on three separate days precisely so that "last" is unambiguous — same-instant events would leave the answer to a tie-break and the row would be asserting the tie-break rather than the aggregation. 2_000 is not reachable by another aggregator on this fixture (sum 6_000, max 3_000, count 300), and it is asserted twice: as the usage read on 10 March (customer_usage_service.rb:120) and as the charge fee on the April invoice (calculate_fees_service.rb:136).

The canonical invariant for latest_agg: the last event of the period carries 20, so 20 units (LatestService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 2_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), read in the last hour of March and asserted again on the invoice raised two hours later. Both surfaces bound the period the same way — charges_from/to_datetime for current usage come from DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162,179), which on a calendar month is the month itself (monthly_service.rb:25) — so "last event in the period" must resolve to the same event on both sides. A divergence would mean one path is reading a different last event, which on a gauge metric is the difference between the customer's displayed level and the level they are billed for.

March's peak is 30 -> 3_000¢ on invoice[index=0]. April's peak is max(5, 25, 15) = 25 units (MaxService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 2_500¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), and 2_500 is the single number asserted both as the usage read on 25 April — after March's invoice exists — and as the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. April's peak is deliberately LOWER than March's: if either surface let the closed period's events into the window the answer would be 3_000¢, and because max_agg does not accumulate, a leak of that kind is invisible unless the leaked peak is the larger one. That is why the assertion is on both surfaces at once — a period-scoping bug on the usage path alone would otherwise never be seen.

max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units (MaxService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 3_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295): the final usage read at 10:00 on 20 March and the invoice the DELETE raises at 12:00, asserted against the one derivation. The read has to come first — after termination current_usage resolves nothing, because it looks the subscription up through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216). The invoice's window stops at terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117) while the usage window still ran to the end of March; max_agg only cares which events are inside, and all three are on 5 March, so both must return 30. A divergence would mean the closing bill and the last visible usage disagree about a period neither can revisit.

max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::MaxService:16 — event_store.max) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 3_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted as the usage read on 10 March and as the charge fee on the April invoice — one number, two code paths (customer_usage_service.rb:120 vs calculate_fees_service.rb:136). The peak arrives in the MIDDLE of the three events so that a regression to either neighbour changes the answer: 6_000¢ would be a sum, 2_000¢ the latest value, 300¢ a count. No event is ingested after the snapshot, so equality is the assertion rather than an accident of timing.

The canonical invariant for max_agg. max(10, 30, 20) = 30 units (MaxService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 3_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), read as current usage in the last hour of March and asserted again as the charge fee on the invoice raised two hours later. Both surfaces span the same window — current usage takes charges_to_datetime from DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162,179), which for a calendar month is end_of_month (monthly_service.rb:25), the boundary the invoice also uses — so any difference is a difference in the two computations, not in what they were asked. max_agg has zero prior invoice coverage in spec/scenarios (README's census), which is exactly why the peak is asserted on both sides here.

March sums 10 + 30 + 20 = 60 -> 6_000¢ on invoice[index=0]. April sums 5 + 15 + 25 = 45 units (SumService:22) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 4_500¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), and 4_500 is the single number asserted on both surfaces: the usage read on 25 April, taken AFTER the March invoice exists, and the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. The two candidate wrong answers are named by construction: 10_500¢ if either surface carried March's units into April (the metric is non-recurring and the usage window starts at the current period's charges_from_datetime, customer_usage_service.rb:162), and 6_000¢ if the usage read were still describing the closed March period. Only asserting both surfaces against 4_500 catches a leak that exists on one side only.

10 + 30 + 20 = 60 units (SumService:22) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 6_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted as the final usage read at 10:00 on 20 March and as the termination invoice raised by the DELETE two hours later. The read must precede the DELETE: current_usage resolves the subscription through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216), so after termination the surface no longer exists. The invoice window is truncated to terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117) while the usage window still runs to the end of March, but sum_agg is insensitive to the window's END as long as no event falls between the two — every event is on 5 March — so the two figures must agree exactly. A mismatch is a real defect: the last number the customer saw is the one the closing bill must charge.

10 + 30 + 20 = 60 units (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::SumService:22 — event_store.sum) x 1.00 (ChargeModels::StandardService:8) = 6_000¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). ONE derivation asserted on both surfaces: current usage read on 10 March (Invoices::CustomerUsageService#compute_charge_fees:120) and the charge fee on the invoice April's run produces (Invoices::CalculateFeesService:136). The read is deliberately MID-period with no event after it, which is what makes equality assertable at all — with a later event the two figures would differ legitimately and the row would prove nothing. Distinct event values keep the aggregations apart: the same events give 3 under count_agg, 30 under max_agg, 20 under latest_agg. A divergence means the usage path and the invoice path disagree about the same three events.

March's three distinct ids (m1, m2, m3 across four events) -> 300¢ on invoice[index=0]. April's three events carry two distinct ids (a1, a2, a1) -> 2 units (UniqueCountService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 200¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), asserted BOTH as the usage read on 25 April, after the March invoice exists, and as the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. The April ids are disjoint from March's so a period-scoping failure is unambiguous: 500¢ if the closed period's distinct values were still in the window on either surface. The metric is non-recurring, so use_from_boundary is true (unique_count_service.rb:11) and each period counts only its own values.

Three distinct unique_id values across four events -> 3 units (UniqueCountService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 300¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295): the final usage read at 10:00 on 20 March and the termination invoice raised at 12:00, both asserted against that one derivation. The read precedes the DELETE because current_usage resolves through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216) and a terminated subscription is no longer there. The invoice's window ends at terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117) rather than at the end of March, which does not change the distinct count: every event is on 5 March, inside both windows.

Four events carrying three distinct unique_id values -> 3 units (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::UniqueCountService:16 — event_store.unique_count, which sums one adjusted value per property, Events::Stores::Postgres::UniqueCountQuery#query) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 300¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). The repeated "u2" is what separates this from count_agg: 400¢ would mean the repeat was counted, so the number cannot be produced by the wrong aggregator. 300¢ is asserted as the usage read on 10 March (customer_usage_service.rb:120) and as the charge fee on the April invoice (calculate_fees_service.rb:136); nothing is ingested after the snapshot, so the two must be equal.

The canonical invariant for unique_count_agg: 4 events, 3 distinct unique_id values -> 3 units (UniqueCountService:16) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 300¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295), read in the last hour of March and asserted again on the invoice raised at 01:00 on 1 April. The distinct count is where the two surfaces are most free to drift, because UniqueCountService sets use_from_boundary from the metric's recurring flag (unique_count_service.rb:11) — the metric here is non-recurring, so both surfaces must scope to the same period and return 3, not 400¢ (the raw event count) and not a cumulative figure.

March (31-day period, denominator 31 days, monthly_service.rb:35): running total 0 for 5 days = 0; 31 for the 10 days to the 16th = 31x10/31 = 10; 124 for the 5 days to the 21st = 124x5/31 = 20; 186 for the 11 days to 1 April = 186x11/31 = 66. Total 96 units -> 9_600¢ on invoice[index=0]. The values 31/93/62 are chosen so every March segment divides exactly by 31. April (30-day period): 0 for 4 days; 10 for the 6 days to the 11th = 2; 40 for the 6 days to the 17th = 8; 60 for the 14 days to 1 May = 28. Total 38 units (WeightedSumService:16, WeightedSumQuery:115) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 3_800¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295) — the single number asserted as the usage read on 25 April, after the March invoice exists, and as the charge fee on invoice[index=1]. The reset is the point: the metric is non-recurring, so WeightedSumService#initial_value returns 0 rather than March's closing level of 186 (weighted_sum_service.rb:89-92). If either surface carried it, April would read 186x(period)/30 + 38, roughly 224 units, and asserting both surfaces is what makes a one-sided carry-over visible. calendar_sensitive: the 31- and 30-day denominators are the arithmetic.

The only construction in which a weighted-sum usage read and a TERMINATION invoice can be equal at all, which is why the fixture looks the way it does. The two surfaces disagree about the window's end — usage still runs to end_of_month (customer_usage_service.rb:162, monthly_service.rb:25) while a terminated period ends at terminated_at (dates_service.rb:117) — and a weighted sum is an integral over that window, so any non-zero running total at the read instant would make the two figures legitimately different. Here the third event, -40, returns the running total to 0 on 19 April, so every segment after it contributes 0 whether the window closes on 25 April or on 1 May. What is left is exact and identical on both paths: 0 for 3 days; 10 for the 6 days to the 10th = 10x6/30 = 2; 40 for the 9 days to the 19th = 40x9/30 = 12; 0 thereafter. Total 14 units (WeightedSumService:16, WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql:115, denominator 30 days from monthly_service.rb:35 — computed from the period start, so termination does not shorten it) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 1_400¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). The read is at 11:00 and the DELETE at 12:00 because current_usage resolves through Customer#active_subscriptions (customer.rb:216) and answers nothing once the subscription is terminated. Trade-off stated plainly: with a zero tail this row cannot detect a wrong DENOMINATOR, only a wrong integral or a wrong window — the non-terminated rows above carry the denominator. calendar_sensitive: April's 30 days are the arithmetic.

weighted_sum_agg is a time-weighted integral of the running total over the period: sum(cumulative_value x seconds_to_next_event) / period_seconds (BillableMetrics::Aggregations::WeightedSumService:16 -> Events::Stores::Postgres::WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql:115, denominator charges_duration.days). April 2024 is a 30-day period. Running total 0 from 1-7 Apr contributes 0; 10 for the 3 days to the 10th gives 10x3/30 = 1; 40 for the 6 days to the 16th gives 40x6/30 = 8; 60 for the 15 days to 1 May gives 60x15/30 = 30. Total 39 units x 1.00 (ChargeModels::StandardService:8) = 3_900¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). Every segment divides exactly, so 39 is an exact decimal and not a rounding artefact. THIS is the row where a usage/invoice divergence is most plausible and most invisible: the usage read on 20 April already projects to the END of the period, because current usage takes charges_to_datetime from DatesService with current_usage: true (customer_usage_service.rb:162,179) and for a calendar month that is end_of_month (monthly_service.rb:25) — not "now". So the mid-period read and the invoice must return the same 39. If usage instead weighted to the read instant it would report 10x3/30 + 40x6/30 + 60x(4 days 10h)/30 ~= 17.7 units (1_770¢) against the invoice's 3_900¢, and calendar_sensitive is set because the 30-day denominator IS the arithmetic.

The canonical invariant for the one aggregation that is a function of TIME as well as of values. April 2024, 30-day period: running total 0 for the 6 days to the 7th contributes 0; 10 for the 6 days to the 13th gives 10x6/30 = 2; 40 for the 9 days to the 22nd gives 40x9/30 = 12; 60 for the 9 days to 1 May gives 60x9/30 = 18. Total 32 units (WeightedSumService:16, WeightedSumQuery#period_ratio_sql:115) x 1.00 (StandardService:8) = 3_200¢ (Fees::ChargeService:295). Each segment divides exactly by 30, so 32 is exact. Read at 23:00 on 30 April and asserted again on the invoice raised at 01:00 on 1 May: both use the same window (charges_to_datetime = end_of_month on both paths, customer_usage_service.rb:162 and monthly_service.rb:25) and the same 30-day denominator (monthly_service.rb:35), so any difference is a difference in the integral itself. calendar_sensitive: the 30-day period is the arithmetic.
